<meta>This is the title page for 'Philosophia Moysaica' (Mosaic Philosophy). The transcription indicates significant ink bleed-through from the following page, which is common in 17th-century manuscripts and early printed books.</meta>

# MOSAIC
# PHILOSOPHY.

<note>The term "Mosaic Philosophy" (original: *Philosophia Moysaica*) refers to a 17th-century philosophical and scientific tradition that sought to derive all knowledge of the natural world and the cosmos from the books of Moses in the Bible. Its most famous proponent was the English physician and mystic Robert Fludd, who argued that divine revelation was a more reliable source of truth than ancient Greek philosophy.</note>

<summary>The title page for Robert Fludd's work on Mosaic Philosophy, representing a bridge between biblical theology and natural science in the early modern period.</summary>

<keywords>Mosaic Philosophy, Robert Fludd, biblical science, 17th-century philosophy, Pentateuch</keywords>

<meta>continuity: This page provides a detailed explanation of the symbolic frontispiece or "hieroglyphical figure" mentioned on the title page of Robert Fludd's 'Philosophia Moysaica'. It establishes Fludd's core cosmological argument: that the universe arises from the tension between divine light and primordial darkness.</meta>

# Description of the Hieroglyphic Figure or the Opposite Emblem.

<margin>
Psalm 139:12.
Psalm 81.

Isaiah 45:6-7.
1 Timothy 3.
Psalm 18:11.
</margin>
**A.** Denotes God insofar as he is called the "dark Aleph" rather than the "bright Aleph" by the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Cabalists are practitioners of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) who interpret the Hebrew alphabet as containing the secrets of creation.</note>. That is to say, in his dark, hidden, and concealed property, as well as in his bright, manifest, and open property. Whence the Psalmist says: *As is his darkness, so is his light.* <note>original: "Sicut tenebræ ejus ita lux ejus"</note> And so he is called the Sun giving grace and glory; and he himself *places darkness round about his pavilion.* Finally, if he wills, he reveals his bright nature, or offers his grace to the world; if he does not will it, darkness is created, according to that saying of the Prophet: *I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil,* and so forth.

**B.** *Darkness was upon the face of the abyss.* (Genesis 1). And <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic Corpus, a collection of Egyptian-Greek wisdom texts.</note> says: *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss, but water and a thin Spirit were within the abyss,* etc. And David: *He made darkness his secret place.*

<margin>
1 John 1.

Wisdom 7.

1 John 1.

Isaiah 44:24.
</margin>
**C.** Here, God (who is light in whom there is no darkness at all) reveals himself out of the darkness; and this emanation is called by the wise man <note>referring to Solomon in the Wisdom of Solomon</note> the *brightness of eternal light and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty God,* which is more precious in splendor than the sun itself and is found to be superior to every arrangement of the stars. In this state, it is taken for the divine essence or act by itself—that is, without any mixture with worldly matter—and is called by the Cabalists the *Aleph* changed from dark to bright. Regarding this, the Apostle says: *The darkness has now passed, and the true light illustrating all things now shines.* In this bright Word was the life of all things. This made all things; he alone stretched out the heavens and established the earth, and none with him.

<margin>
1 Timothy 3.

Wisdom 11:18.
Job 12:22.
Genesis 1.
2 Peter 3.
Isaiah 44:24.
Psalm 74:16.
Psalm 19:4.
</margin>
**D. E.** Where, out of the darkness (or divine power) and the light (or divine act), a single world is forged after the image of the divine <term>Monad</term> <note>The Monad refers to the number one, signifying unity, the source of all things, and the Divine Mind.</note>. For out of the immense abyss of darkness (**B.**) the waters emerged according to that saying of Hermes: *An infinite shadow was in the abyss, but the water and his Spirit were within the abyss, and a holy splendor flourished,* etc. From this water, the existence of the world arose, as if derived from an incomprehensible source. (**C.**) That essence was derived which gives form to the watery existence of the world. Whence the text says: *The hand of the Almighty created the world out of unformed matter.* And elsewhere: *He reveals the foundations out of darkness and brings the shadow of death into light.* And Moses: *The Spirit of God moved over the waters.* Finally, the Apostle: *The heavens were of old, and the earth out of water and through water by the assistance of the word.* For this Jehovah stretched out the heavens and established the earth; the effect of his private and dark property is Night, but of his bright and positive property, Day. He himself fashioned the dawn and the sun, and *in it he placed his tabernacle.*

<margin>
Psalm 104:19.
Job 34:13.
Deuteronomy 23.
Wisdom 6:13.
Isaiah 45:6-7.
</margin>
**F.** Finally, denoting the daytime hemisphere of the world, and **G.** the nocturnal, these demonstrate those two contrary effects which the one God produces in this symbolic world under two names. For according to the mystical theology of Orpheus, Hesiod, Euripides, and Aeschylus (who used fables to wrap the mysteries they learned from divine persons), the Sun in the divine <term>Archetype</term> <note>The Archetype is the original "blueprint" or ideal pattern in the mind of God from which the physical world is modeled.</note> is splendor, ornament, and beauty, encompassing the rhythmic harmony of life. He is said to have piety and benevolence in his right hand, and severity and punishment in his left. Hence, they called this created or worldly sun (in which that Archetype placed its tabernacle) **Apollo** in one respect, whom they imagine to have grace, life, and health in his right hand, but to carry a bow and arrow in his left. But by another reasoning, they called him **Bacchus** and **Dionysus**. Under the name of Apollo, they assigned to him a diurnal (daytime) property, whose nature it is to forge all things out of seven parts and preserve them, thereby indicating him as the author of life, generation, multiplication, and health. Through the name of Dionysus, they intend his harmful nature, in which he destroys, tears apart, and scatters the creatures forged by Apollo in the daytime from seven parts; thus arguing that he is the cause of death, corruption, and decrease. For this reason, the Athenians called him by the name of *Apollo Alexicacon* <note>original Greek: "Alexicacon," meaning the averter of evil</note>, and the ancients used *Apellin* instead of Apollo as a disperser of evils, and Homer called him *Vlion* <note>original: "Vlion," likely from the Greek "Oulios," meaning health-giving or destructive</note>, that is, the author of health. And David says: when God gives, the creatures gather life; when he takes back their breath, they expire; when he sends forth his Spirit, they are recreated. And Job: *God applies his breath to man, which if he should take back, all flesh would expire.* *I will kill,* says the Lord, *and I will make to live.* And Solomon: *God has the power of life and death, who leads down to the gates of death and brings back again.* Finally, the Lord God says: *and there is no other, forming light, creating darkness, making good and creating evil. I the Lord do all these things.*

# MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY
## [Philosophia Moysaica]

->In which<-
->The Wisdom and science of creation and creatures, truly Sacred and Christian (inasmuch as its basis or Foundation is that unique Cornerstone Jesus Christ), is accurately and clearly explained.<-

->B Y   T H E   A U T H O R,<-
## ROBERT FLUDD, also known as DE FLVCTIBVS,
->Esquire and Doctor of Medicine of Oxford.<-

> *Christ is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, for in him were all things created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones, or Dominions, or Principalities, or powers: All things were created through him and in him: he is before all, and in him all things consist. Colossians 1: 15. 16.* <note>Fludd quotes the Vulgate Latin version of the Bible here to emphasize Christ as the central organizing principle of the cosmos.</note>

**A.** Denotes God insofar as he is called the "dark Aleph" <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, often used in mysticism to represent the oneness of God.</note> rather than the "bright Aleph" by the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Cabalists are practitioners of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) who interpret the Hebrew alphabet as containing the secrets of creation.</note>. That is to say, in his dark, hidden, and concealed property, as well as in his bright, manifest, and open property. Whence the Psalmist says: *As is his darkness, so is his light.* <note>original: "Sicut tenebræ ejus ita lux ejus"</note> And so he is called the Sun giving grace and glory; and he himself *places darkness round about his pavilion.* Finally, if he wills, he reveals his bright nature, or offers his grace to the world; if he does not will it, darkness is created, according to that saying of the Prophet: *I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil,* and so forth.

**B.** *Darkness was upon the face of the abyss.* <note>original: "Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi"</note> (Genesis 1). And <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic Corpus, a collection of Egyptian-Greek wisdom texts that heavily influenced Fludd.</note> says: *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss, but water and a thin Spirit were within the abyss,* etc. And David: *He made darkness his secret place.*

<margin>
1 John 1.

Wisdom 7.

1 John 1.

Isaiah 44:24.
</margin>
**C.** Here, God (who is light in whom there is no darkness at all) reveals himself out of the darkness; and this emanation is called by the wise man <note>referring to Solomon in the Wisdom of Solomon, a book of the biblical Apocrypha</note> the breath of the power of God, and a most pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty; and also the brightness of the eternal light, the unspotted mirror of the majesty of God, and the image of his goodness. He is also that Word of Life, which we have seen and heard, and our hands have handled. He is the first-born of all creatures, by whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made.

# ON MOSAIC
## PHILOSOPHY.
-> Section One. <-
-> In which <-
### The true and sincere basis or unique Cornerstone of Mosaic Philosophy—which is the radical reason and mystery of the Existence and Essence of all creatures—is taught; meanwhile, from the opposite side, those spurious and imaginary Foundations of Heathen Philosophy are uncovered, overturned, and reduced to nothing.
-> BY THE AUTHOR, <-
-> ROBERT FLUDD, also known as DE FLUCTIBUS, <-
-> *Esquire, and Doctor of Medicine of Oxford.* <-

<margin>Prov. 2. 6.</margin> God gives wisdom, and from his mouth comes prudence and knowledge. Proverbs 2:6.

<margin>1 Cor. 3. 19, 20.</margin> The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God; God knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain. 1 Corinthians 3:19, 20.

<margin>1 Cor. 2, 12, 13.</margin> We have received not the spirit of this world, but the spirit which is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God, which we also speak, not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the doctrine of the Spirit; comparing spiritual things with spiritual: but the natural man does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand. 1 Corinthians 2:12, 13.

<margin>Coloss. 2, 8, 9.</margin> In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; walk in him, rooted and built up in him, confirmed in faith: See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit; according to the tradition of men and according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ, for in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily. Colossians 2:8, 9.

<margin>1 Cor. 3:10 onwards</margin> According to the grace of God which is given to me, like a wise <term>Architect|Architectus</term> <note>Fludd uses the term 'Architectus' to mirror the Divine Architect of the universe; he sees the philosopher's role as mirroring God’s creative structure.</note> I have laid the foundation, but another builds upon it; let each one see how he builds upon it: For no one can lay another foundation except that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, each one’s work shall be manifest: For the Day of the Lord shall declare it, because it shall be revealed in fire, and the fire shall prove what sort each one’s work is; if anyone’s work remains which he built upon it, he shall receive a reward; if anyone’s work burns, he shall suffer loss.

Israel has forsaken the oracle of God, which is the fountain of wisdom, to seek out art, science, and understanding among foreign nations and among the <term>Heathens|Ethnici</term>, who did not know true wisdom, as did the Hagarenes and those who were in Teman. Baruch 3. <margin>Baruch 3.</margin> <note>The "Hagarenes" and "Temanites" were biblical peoples associated with worldly, human wisdom rather than divine revelation.</note>

<margin>Hebr. 1. 3. Psal. 118. 22.</margin> Here exists the brightness of the Glory of God and the character of his substance, who carries all things by the word of his power. This is the <term>Cornerstone|Lapis angularis</term>, which the builders rejected, which is the head of the corner of every Creator. <note>Fludd identifies Christ not just as a religious figure, but as the literal structural "cornerstone" of the physical universe.</note>

<margin>Job 38. 4.</margin> This is from Jehovah, and it is wonderful in our eyes: Upon this foundation the earth is situated and its measure. Colossians 1:13.

<margin>John 1.</margin> Finally, in this wisdom God made all things, and all things are and consist in it, and upon it, and without it all things are nothing.

<meta>This page transitions from the formal title and scriptural justifications to Fludd's personal introduction (the Proemium). He establishes his credentials as a physician and his methodology: using the Bible as the primary source for understanding the physical world, a system he calls "Mosaic Philosophy."</meta>

# PREFACE.

It is my intention—and I trust it shall seem neither hostile nor injurious to anyone—that I, as a Professor of Medicine, should follow the example of my *Theo-Philosophical* <note>A term combining "Theology" and "Philosophy," suggesting that true wisdom must integrate divine and natural knowledge.</note> and *Medical* Patron, namely the Sainted Luke. In doing so, I shall use the testimony of the Sacred Scriptures alongside the most effective principles of that eternal Wisdom—*since it is that unique foundation or Cornerstone upon which every creature is based*—to uphold a true and *essential Mosaic philosophy*. <note>The idea that Moses received not just the Law on Mount Sinai, but also a secret, perfect understanding of the natural world and the physics of the universe.</note> If it were the function of *Jacob’s ladder* <note>Referencing Genesis 28:12; a bridge between the earthly and the divine.</note> that by its mediation both Souls and Angels might ascend from earth to heaven, and likewise descend from heaven to earth, and this by steps corresponding to both Elementary and heavenly nature; or (*as the mystical Poet says*) if the *Chain of Nature* <note>The "Golden Chain of Homer," a classical concept where all parts of the universe are linked to the throne of God (Jupiter).</note> has its highest link fixed to the foot of *Jupiter’s* throne in Heaven, just as its lowest link is bound to the earth; then how is it possible for us earthly creatures—or rather, divine images inhabiting huts of clay—to ascend from the confused chaos of the creature (which is its exterior) toward the splendid Essence of the Creator hidden in its center, to seek out and investigate the mysteries of true wisdom, unless we first look into its earthly circumference or dwelling-place with *Lynx-like* eyes? <note>original: "Linceis." Referring to the legendary sharp sight of the lynx; also a nod to the "Lincean" approach of careful observation.</note> And then afterward, by descending deeper step by step, we may gradually reach the central seat of the divinity, or the truly *Cornerstone*, upon which every creature is founded and established. For He is the Word without whom nothing exists—that is, the incorruptible Spirit of God who is in every thing, that supreme Divinity who gives life to all things, and causes all things to be and to exist. He is, finally, the form of forms, who is the *Being of Beings*, and *All in All*. If, therefore, God made all creatures in and through His eternal Word, and gave them life, and has preserved each of them in its own species even to this day, who (I ask) among the Philosophers, however skilled, can explain the mysteries of the Creator within the Creature, or can discern with a mental judgment the Creator in the creature, without the documents of the sacred writings and

<column-break/>

the guidance of the Holy Spirit? Shall we imitate the Hagarenes <note>Descendants of Hagar, often used to represent those outside the divine covenant.</note> and those who were in *Teman*, <note>A region mentioned in the Bible (Baruch 3:22-23) famous for its "wise men" who nonetheless failed to find true understanding.</note> and leave behind the fountain of all Wisdom to seek true Wisdom where it cannot be found? And yet, nonetheless, let it be far from anyone to interpret my intention or mind in this work in a sinister way, or to rashly think that I strive either to violate or to attack the laws and statutes of sacred Theology established and ordained by the ancient Fathers of the Church. Rather, I wish it to be known that, just as a single and identical text in Sacred Scripture is accustomed to claim for itself a double sense—namely, the internal or Spiritual, and the external or literal—and yet both of these are true, even though they seem in some respect to be separated and to differ from one another; no differently than under the name and person of one and the same man we understand a twin nature, namely a Spiritual Soul and a material body; so also, besides that mystical interpretation which the text of the Scriptures contains, the text itself can outwardly express and outline such created realities as belong primarily to the true subject of the most *Essential Philosophy*. Furthermore, it must be diligently considered that the subject and the method of treating and proceeding in both professions—namely, Theology and true Philosophy—differ from each other in a certain way. For the former, namely Theology, indicates the sincere and naked nature of the divine Essence *directly*—that is, by a demonstration *a priori* <term>from cause to effect</term>—not unlike how, to prove the existence of a Circle, we begin our inquiry from the formal Center, or the middle point, and so gradually descend to the circumference through the steps of the radius. This Philosophy, however, proceeds in its inquiry by a contrary action and method, for it ascends from the creature, or the circumference of the created instrument—which is like an external demonstration *a posteriori* <term>from effect to cause</term>—toward its central essence, so that by this industry we may investigate that radical internal Spirit which acts and works within it.

<meta>The catchword "Nonne" at the bottom of the Latin page suggests the next page begins with a question, likely "Is it not..."</meta>

<summary>In this preface, Fludd argues that true natural philosophy must be based on Scripture and the Holy Spirit, using the "Cornerstone" of divine wisdom to bridge the gap between the material world and the Creator. He distinguishes his "Mosaic Philosophy" from traditional theology by its method: while theology starts with God and moves toward creation, his philosophy starts with the physical world and ascends toward the divine spirit within.</summary>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>The previous page established the title and scriptural basis for the "Mosaic Philosophy," framing it as the only true knowledge compared to pagan philosophies. This page begins the Preface, where Robert Fludd justifies his role as a physician-philosopher by likening himself to St. Luke and explains his methodology of finding God through the study of nature.</meta>

# PREFACE.

<meta>catchword: Is not</meta>

It is my intention—which I trust would seem neither hostile nor injurious to anyone—that I, a Professor of Medicine, in imitation of my Theo-Philosophical and Medical Patron, namely the divine Luke <note>St. Luke the Evangelist, traditionally considered a physician.</note>, should use the testimony of the Sacred Scriptures alongside the most effective foundations of that eternal Wisdom to support the true and essential philosophy of Moses. For this Wisdom is the unique foundation or Cornerstone <note>original: "Lapis Angularis"</note> upon which every creature is founded. If Jacob’s ladder was a means by which both Souls and Angels might ascend from earth to heaven, and likewise descend from heaven to earth—and this by steps corresponding to both Elementary and celestial nature—or (as the mystic Poet <note>A reference to Homer’s "Golden Chain" (Iliad 8.19), often interpreted by alchemists and Hermeticists as the "Chain of Nature" connecting all things to God.</note> says) if the Chain of Nature has its upper ring fastened to the foot of Jupiter’s throne in Heaven, while its lowest ring is bound to the earth, how then is it possible for us earthly creatures (or rather, divine images inhabiting tabernacles of clay <note>original: "tabernacula lutea"; a reference to the mortal human body.</note>) to ascend from the confused chaos of the creature, as if from its exterior, toward the splendid Essence of the Creator hiding in its center, to seek and investigate the mysteries of true wisdom, unless we first look into the earth’s own circumference or dwelling-place with the eyes of a lynx <note>original: "oculis Linceis"; meaning exceptionally sharp or penetrating vision.</note>? And then afterward, by descending deeper step by step, we may gradually reach the central seat of divinity or the truly Cornerstone, upon which every creature is founded and established. For this is indeed the Word without which nothing exists; that is, the incorruptible Spirit of God which is in every thing, or that supreme Divinity which gives life to all things, and causes all things to be and to exist. It is, finally, that form of forms, which is the Being of Beings <note>original: "Entium Ens"</note>, and All in All. If, therefore, God made all creatures in and through his eternal Word, gave them life, and has preserved each of them in its own kind even unto this day, who (I ask), however skilled a Philosopher they may be, can explain the mysteries of the Creator within the Creature, or discern the Creator in the creature with mental judgment, without the documents of the sacred scriptures and

<column-break/>

the guidance of the Holy Spirit? Shall we, by imitating the Hagarenes <note>original: "Agarenos"; descendants of Hagar, often used to represent those who rely on worldly rather than divine wisdom.</note> and those who were in Teman <note>A region in Edom famous in the Bible for its "wise men," yet their wisdom was considered worldly.</note>, abandon the fountain of all Wisdom to seek true Wisdom where it is not to be found? Nevertheless, let it be far from anyone to interpret my intention or mind in this work incorrectly, or to rashly think that I strive to either violate or attack the laws and statutes of sacred Theology established and ordained by the ancient Fathers of the Church. Rather, I wish it to be known that, just as one and the same text in Sacred Scripture is accustomed to claim a double sense—namely an internal or Spiritual one, and an external or literal one, and yet each of these is true, even though they seem in some respect to be separated and different from one another (no differently than we understand two natures, namely a Spiritual Soul and a material body, under the name and person of one and the same man)—so also, besides that mystical interpretation which the text of the Scriptures contains, it can outwardly express and outline those created realities which primarily belong to the true subject of the most Essential Philosophy. Furthermore, it must be diligently considered that the subject and Method of treatment and procedure in both professions—namely Theology and true Philosophy—differ from each other in a certain way. For Theology indicates the sincere and naked nature of the divine Essence directly, that is, by a demonstration *a priori* <note>Reasoning from cause to effect; starting from the source (God) and moving to the result (creation).</note>, much like how, to prove the existence of a Circle, we begin the inquiry from the formal Center or middle point, and so descend gradually to the circumference through the steps of the radius. This Philosophy, however, proceeds in its inquiry by the opposite action and method; for it ascends from the creature, or the circumference of the created instrument (as if by a demonstration *a posteriori* <note>Reasoning from effect to cause; starting from the observed world and moving back to the divine source.</note>), toward its central essence, so that by this industry we may investigate the radical Spirit of that interior, which acts and works within it.

<summary>Robert Fludd introduces his "Mosaic Philosophy," arguing that true science must be based on divine wisdom and scripture. # PREAMBLE.

<margin>Wisdom 13:1</margin> Are we not admonished by the Wise Man <note>A reference to the author of the Book of Wisdom in the Apocrypha.</note> to learn about the craftsmanship that is unknown and hidden from us through his works, if we do not wish to be considered foolish? That is to say, should we not grasp the divine and eternal Cause through its created and temporal effects? Or as that sacred Philosopher, Saint Paul, has it: so that we may see and understand the invisible things of God, <margin>Romans 1:20</margin> even his eternal power and divinity, through those things which have been made: namely, in his creatures and through his creatures. This is exactly how the internal and central monad <note>original: "monas"; a term from Pythagorean philosophy meaning "unity" or the fundamental "one" from which all numbers and things arise.</note> or point of a circle is found: by beginning an investigation from the circumference and descending through the parts of the radii toward the center. In this very way, the true Philosopher immerses himself in the study of creation, proceeding from its outer circumference, as it were, all the way into the center, in which his <term>Cornerstone</term> <note>original: "lapis angularis"; Fludd uses this biblical term to represent the divine spark or Christ as the foundation of the physical world.</note> lies hidden. Since this is so, and since the Holy Scripture is full of demonstrations for both of these professions or sciences, I trust that it will seem out of place to no one if I use the axioms and testimonies of the Bible—the highest truth—to establish the foundations of this sacred Philosophy. Moreover, the sacred text, throughout almost its entire thread, delineates the subject of both Philosophy and <term>Theosophy</term> <note>Divine wisdom; distinct from regular philosophy as it focuses specifically on the nature of God and the divine realm.</note>, because it copiously describes the acts and operations of the aeviternal or Angelic world, as well as the temporal world (both celestial and elemental), and the eternal world of the divinity. It is clearly evident that the eternal world (which has neither beginning nor end), being filled solely with the divine Majesty, exists as that primary and most solid foundation upon which **Theology** is situated and placed. On the other hand, the temporal or "lower" world—which has both a beginning and an end, and is visibly distinguished by its creatures into the heavens and the earth—is the unique subject or basis of true **Philosophy**. As for the Angelic or <term>aeviternal</term> <note>original: "ævialis"; a scholastic term for beings like angels who have a beginning in time but will never have an end.</note> world, which has a beginning but no end, and is ordained by God as the seat and receptacle for Angelic spirits and blessed Souls, it holds its site and position between the two aforementioned extreme worlds (namely the eternal 

<column-break/>

and the temporal). Indeed, it possesses such an immediate connection and relation with both extremes that it receives its light and life—or its formal essence—immediately from eternity. Afterward, it pours a portion of that light downward and communicates it to the temporal world or "lower dwelling," so that the world and its creatures might be created and brought to life from it. From this it follows that just as the **form** of the temporal world is the Angelic or aeviternal, so the **soul and life** of the aeviternal world is the divine or eternal. By this, it is made manifest that the nature or property of angels should not be excluded from the subject of Theology (since they participate in the divine light or the splendid and shining presence of the divinity); nor can they be removed from the substance of Philosophy, insofar as the Angelic light becomes the soul and life of temporal nature. Consequently, it is necessary for one experienced in true philosophy to acknowledge that his science—the very foundations of his Philosophy—radically proceeds from the eternal God through His aeviternal or Angelic Spirits into His temporal creatures (by which I mean the stars, the winds, the Elements, meteors, and perfectly mixed bodies). Therefore, to the extent that the Philosophical subject is animated by angelic influences, we must believe that by mental intuition we may penetrate into that eternal light which gives life to both temporal and aeviternal spirits or creatures—beyond which nothing can be discerned or even imagined by the mind.

This is, therefore, that tripartite measure of **Jacob’s Ladder**, which he saw in his dream while his head rested upon a stone in place of a pillow. Upon the length, breadth, and depth of that stone, the images or characters of the three aforementioned worlds were delineated or depicted; and for this reason, that Stone was called the "House" or "Tabernacle of God." From this it is certain that, just as that stone had its own exterior and interior, so the Patriarch <note>Jacob</note> in this divine dream saw the angels ascending from the earth (which is the footstool of God’s feet) as if from the external and corporeal, through the aeviternal or Angelic world, toward the eternal world as if toward the center and the most internal part, in which is

# THE FIRST SECTION,
## BOOK ONE.
### ON THE EXPERIMENTAL OR DEMONSTRATIVE INSTRUMENT.
#### THE ARGUMENT OF THIS BOOK.

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:22</margin>
This first book, which serves as a sort of preamble and preparation for the four following books, declares that because the minds of worldly men today are raised and elevated to the highest peak of infidelity, they are like the Jews who refuse to believe without signs and demonstrations: "The Jews seek signs," (says Paul) "and the Greeks seek wisdom," etc. <note>original: "Iudæi signa petunt... & Græci sapientiam"; referencing 1 Corinthians 1:22, where Paul discusses the difficulty of preaching the Gospel to those who demand physical proof or intellectual logic.</note> The author of this treatise believed that the chief means of victory in this Herculean conflict—which must be fought between two most powerful enemies and rivals, Truth and Falsehood (that is, the wisdom of God and the wisdom of the world)—would be to find some common and well-known experiment or practical instrument. This instrument could serve our heavenly Athlete, namely Truth, in the place of a mace or Herculean club to tame and drive out that deformed and horrendous monster, Infidelity, which so stubbornly sets itself up to uphold the laws and privileges of its own master, the prince of error and darkness. For those who refuse to be directed and led to the center of truth by a real, practical, and visible demonstration are rightly to be judged more irregular and more straying from the polished and square rules of reason than beasts or brute animals; for even beasts are governed by experience (which for that reason is called the "mother of fools" <note>An allusion to the proverb *Experientia est magistra stultorum* (Experience is the teacher of fools), meaning even those without wit learn through physical consequences.</note>), and they usually choose what they have proved to be good, while they avoid with great effort what they have found to be bad for them. For this reason and to this effect, the author has chosen a certain spiritual machine, called the **Mirror of the Calendar** <note>original: "speculi Calendarij"; this refers to a thermoscope or "weather glass." Fludd viewed this device not just as a thermometer, but as a "mirror" that revealed the hidden movements of the world-soul and the divine breath reacting to heat and cold.</note>, which he himself calls his experimental or demonstrative instrument. Through its visible and practical experiments, he is able to sketch out the falsity of worldly wisdom and philosophy and defend the Truth—which, taking its origin from the Father of Lights, is life, truth, and the true Cornerstone, in which and through which every creature exists and is preserved in its being.

<header>THE FIRST SECTION, BOOK I.</header>

Those devoted to the truth will be more faithfully established in these matters, provided that holy authority agrees with the rest. Even though two such testimonies seem sufficient to confirm truth to the wise, the disbelief of this world—and especially of common men—seems to boil with such a fervor of obstinacy; indeed, such cunning and subtlety have crept into the spirits of some rather learned men, who are led more by practical sense than by spiritual speculation, that unless they see and touch with their hands like Saint Thomas <note>original: "Divo Thoma"; a reference to the Apostle Thomas who required physical proof of Christ's wounds (John 20:24-29).</note>, or at least see some evident sign, they are sometimes unwilling to give faith to a thing, however true it may be. For this reason, since I am entering the philosophical arena alone against those pagan philosophers who, relying on worldly wisdom, have fashioned a human philosophy, I find it necessary to arm myself first with Herculean weapons.

# CHAPTER II.

->*That the instrument commonly called* the Mirror of the Calendar, *is falsely claimed by certain men of our century for themselves,*<-
->*who falsely boast that it is*<-
->*their own invention.*<-

Man is so exceedingly greedy for glory and desirous of fame and reputation that it matters little to him how or by what means he acquires it—whether directly or indirectly. This was the sole reason why the pagan philosophers surreptitiously ascribed to themselves those principles of philosophy which by the highest right belonged to the wise and divine philosopher Moses. They veiled and, as it were, gilded their theft with new names or titles, so that in this way they might show off those things as having been established by their own inventions (as will be said more extensively below). In a clearly similar way, this experimental instrument or mirror of ours has many spurious or counterfeit inventors, who, because they changed the shape of the model slightly, boast that its invention was first thought out by them. As far as I am concerned, I think it fair and honest to give to each what is his own.

<column-break/>

For as the Apostle fought against beasts at Ephesus in the likeness of men <note>original: "contra bestias Ephesi"; referencing 1 Corinthians 15:32, where Paul describes his struggle against human opponents using the metaphor of wild animals.</note>, so I set out to contend against those Athenian, Protean-shaped <note>original: "Protei formes"; Proteus was a Greek sea-god known for changing shape, here used to describe the slippery logic of his opponents.</note> philosophers of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, whose philosophy dominated the universities and which the author seeks to challenge with his own chemical-spiritual theories.</note>. Therefore, I have proposed in the first place to forge solid weapons from reasons found in the more secret treasury of Nature, and to temper them with the authority and power of the Holy Scriptures. Finally, I will produce an ocular experience or demonstration, by means of which—in place of a Herculean mace or club—I may more easily tame and subjugate that irrational monster, Incredulity, for there is no enemy more destructive or fierce to the human race. To better lead this to the desired end, I bring to light here an experimental instrument, commonly known to the world, by which the eyes of the unfaithful may be directed into the way of truth, and turned away from the sayings of spurious and sophisticated philosophy toward the goal of truth.

For it will be no disgrace to me to ascribe the principles of this my philosophy to my teacher Moses, since he received them formed and designated even by the divine finger. Nor can I rightfully claim or take credit for the primary construction of this instrument, although I have used it in the history of my <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>original: "Macrocosmi"; The author refers to his earlier works on the "History of the Macrocosm" (the universe), where he used this device to show how air reacts to light and heat.</note> and elsewhere to demonstrate the truth of my philosophical argument (albeit in a different form). I acknowledge that I found it graphically specified and geometrically drawn in an old manuscript of at least five hundred years of antiquity. First, therefore, I will explain to you the form under which I found it in the aforementioned ancient monument; then I will describe here its figure and position as it is commonly known and used among us.

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the "Mirror of the Calendar" or thermoscope. The author, Robert Fludd, is explaining the physical mechanics of the device—how heat expands air and cold contracts it—to provide an empirical, visible foundation for his philosophical arguments about the nature of the universe.</meta>

Fol. 2.

### ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

**Apparatus 1 & 2**
<note>The image shows two early thermometers. On the left, a curved tube connects a globe to a jug. On the right, a vertical tube stands in a jug. Both use the expansion of air to move water, indicating temperature changes.</note>

From which it can be seen that these two [instruments] differ from one another only in their shape, and not in their nature: For the solar rays, acting with their heat upon the hollow globe at the head, marked **A**, cause the air trapped inside—having been expanded <term>rarefied; made thinner and taking up more space through heat</term> by their action—to descend through the pipe **A-B** into the jar of water and exit through the surface of the water in the form of bubbles. However, when the sun sets and the cold of night approaches, that trapped air—which on the previous day had been expanded by the presence of the Sun and its hot action—is again cooled, contracted, and thickened <term>condensed; made more dense and taking up less space through cold</term>. But because there is not enough air in the lead sphere <note>original: "sphæra plumbea"; while the globe is often glass, Fludd occasionally refers to lead components or early metal versions of this weather glass</note> and the pipe to bring about such a thickening in the proper proportion (since part of it, as was mentioned, had been exhaled the day before), a volume of water is sucked up from the jar **C** into the lead pipe equal to the amount of air that was exhaled during expansion, so that a vacuum might be avoided. Again, when the Sun rises the next day, the air trapped in the glass globe and pipe will expand once more, and then, by dilating itself, it will push the water that had risen into the pipe

<column-break/>

back into its former place. And so this alteration of thickening and expansion will always behave in the same way, more or less, according to whether the Sun is closer or further from us, or according to the coldness or heat of the wind blowing in the element.
&nbsp;&nbsp;The same thing will also happen to the air trapped in the second "mirror" <note>original: "speculo"; referring to the "Mirror of the Calendar," a name for this type of weather glass</note>. For the globe or ball at the top of the glass is full of air, and in every respect corresponds exactly to the leaden ball; thus the straight pipe, which rises out of the water and is joined to the head, is exactly comparable to the curved pipe of the first instrument. Indeed, if the leaden ball were raised up and the curved pipe were made straight so that it rose from the water jar perpendicularly into the leaden sphere, there would be no difference between the form or shape of the first and second machine or instrument; so that anyone can see that the condition and use of both are the same in effect.

SECTION I, BOOK I.

### CHAPTER III.

->*In which the construction of this organ or instrument, which the common people call a calendar mirror <note>original: "speculum calendarium"; a device for observing changes in the air</note>, is described, along with the preparation of the glass and the fitting of its opening or "nose" into a small vessel full of water; here also, the opinions of those who think that water is sucked up and raised into the neck of the glass or flask by heat are deservedly refuted.*<-

It must be observed first of all that this experimental instrument of ours is composed of three parts. Two of these belong to the nature of the machine itself—namely, the **Flask** <term>matratium; a long-necked glass vessel used by early scientists and alchemists</term> or glass, and the lower vessel full of water into which the "nose" or opening of the glass must enter. The third part is more auxiliary, being designed so that it supports the glass in its vertical position.

As for the flask or glass, it must have a sufficiently spacious head, either round or oblong, with a long and narrow neck. The opening or mouth of this neck must be proportional to the rest of the neck and must be prepared and fitted in two ways. First,

<column-break/>

And now, with the tube of the flask or glass thus divided into parts, you ought to prepare and arrange the glass in this manner, so that it is made magnetic and attractive by cold, and expansive or dilating by heat: I would have you, therefore, take the opening of the flask in your hands and extend the head—whether it be round or oval—over a fire until it becomes very hot. For the heat of the fire will rarefy the air enclosed in the glass, and cause a good portion of that same rarefied air to fly out from the opening of the glass; and it will remain in that state as long as the glass stays at that degree of heat. At that moment, if you suddenly place the "nose" of the tube into the water of the instrument’s vessel, you will perceive that as the flask cools, the water will gradually rise upward into the neck of the glass. It should also be observed that the hotter the glass was made, the higher the water will rise into the neck of the glass as cold approaches. The reason for this is that the more the air is rarefied in the glass by the power of heat, the smaller the proportion of air will be, and consequently, the greater or lesser the proportion of water in the neck of the glass

### CHAPTER V.

->*In which it is clearly proven, notwithstanding any objection that might be made to the contrary, that this experimental instrument has a relationship not only to the Great World, but also that the spirit enclosed in this instrument is ruled and governed by the Great World-Machine.*<-

---

But before I proceed with a further comparison between the spirit <note>In Fludd’s physics, "spirit" refers to the subtle, invisible air or "pneuma" that fills the glass.</note> contained in this small model <note>original: "typo"</note> or machine of ours and the properties of the active and passive forces therein compared to those of the Great World <note>The Macrocosm or universe</note>, it is necessary that I first respond to a certain doubt or objection that might be raised. Unless this is removed and resolved, such a relationship or comparison might seem ignorant, inept, or entirely impossible to those who do not know. I know, therefore, that not a few will object that no suitable comparison can be made between this small artificial machine of ours and that natural fabric or instrument of the world. Since the spirit in our glass is closed in everywhere, or strictly enclosed in its vessel, and therefore the air is forced to move according to the form or figure of the glass; yet the matter is far different with that spirit which occupies the vast cavity of the world, in which the air or spirit is observed to move freely hither and thither by any impulse, just as we are taught by the daily observation of the winds from every quarter of the world.

To this I respond: the principle of motion and relationship is the same from a thick or dense nature to a thinner one, and likewise from a thinner or rarer nature to a thick and dense one, in a small subject as in a larger one—provided that similar respects are maintained, and that in an equal weight and proportional measure of heat and cold. Indeed, I boldly affirm that the whole world is as completely filled with spirit or air as is this experimental vessel of ours. For if it were not so, it would follow as a consequence that a vacuum would be admitted into the nature of things—which any philosopher would believe to be absurd <note>Following Aristotle, Fludd argues that "nature abhors a vacuum"; therefore, the glass and the world are both "full," making them comparable.</note>.

Therefore, I boldly conclude that the spirit contained in the cavity of this instrument (considering its size) is

<column-break/>

proportioned in quantity, measure, and weight to that of the Great World. For experience testifies that in every part of the year, heat and cold have proportional dominion, both in the spirit of the glass and in the mundane air, and they are accustomed to produce the same effects in both, as much in the rarefaction <term>Rarefaction: the process by which air becomes thinner and expands when heated.</term> as in the condensation <term>Condensation: the process by which air becomes denser and contracts when cooled.</term> of the air, as was declared in the preceding pages. For the more heat abounds in the mundane air, the more the water is depressed in the neck of the instrument, and consequently the air enclosed in said neck is dilated and rarefied. Conversely, the more the inclemency of cold flourishes in the external air, the more the water is elevated into the tube of the instrument.

By these things, it is evident that the aforementioned doubt or scruple is entirely removed. In this respect, therefore, I would have every learned and self-consistent reader understand that, when he looks upon the nature or condition of this instrument, he may indeed observe the action in the rarefaction and condensation of a certain Minor World <note>The Microcosm; the idea that a small system mirrors the large universe.</note>, which in every way seems to agree and correspond with the Major World. This instrument has its own northern as well as southern hemisphere—distinguished from each other by the line passing through mark 1, just as the hemispheres in the Major World are distinguished by the equinoctial line <note>The celestial equator.</note>. It also seems to have two tropics with its own poles; only we consider the southern pole or hemisphere to be hot with respect to us, because the breath <note>original: "spiraculo"</note> proceeding from it is from the Sun, which is positioned southerly in relation to us. # THE SECOND BOOK of the FIRST SECTION of MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

### The Argument of this Book.

<margin>1 Corinthians 3:19</margin>
In this book, it is first proven that the philosophy of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum," referring to non-Christian, particularly Greek, thinkers like Aristotle</note> is counterfeit and false—both because it is founded upon worldly wisdom which, as the Apostle witnesses, is mere foolishness in the eyes of God, and insofar as it contradicts the truth. Consequently, it does not descend from the Father of Light who is in heaven, but from the prince of darkness, who has his seat in the region of obscurity and ignorance. Therefore, this wisdom, or <margin>James 3:15</margin> **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sophia"</note>, is called by the Apostle "earthly, sensual, and devilish." Hence, we are warned by that eminent Divine Philosopher, Saint Paul, that we should by no means be deceived by a philosophy of this vain sort, which is found in the traditions of men and according to the Elements of this world, and does not have the <margin>Colossians 2:8</margin> **Cornerstone**, Jesus Christ, for its secure foundation.

# CHAPTER I.

### The Etymology, Definition, and Division of Philosophy.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' featuring a landscape with a seated figure (possibly a scholar or saint) in a natural environment with architectural structures in the distance.</image-desc>

Before I immerse myself in the deepest abyss of the most essential Philosophy, the foundation of which is true **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sophia"</note> or divine wisdom—which is a matter so difficult to execute that nothing except the swift and nimbly-winged soul of man is able to lead it to a happy conclusion—I have judged it worthwhile and not at all inconsistent with reason that we first consider the etymology of the word **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sophia"</note>. We hunt so greedily for its naked nature, and desire it with a Tantalic thirst <note>A reference to the Greek myth of Tantalus, who was cursed with eternal hunger and thirst for things just out of his reach; Fludd uses it to describe the human drive for knowledge</note>, so that afterward, by a better method and a surer understanding, we may arrive at its essence or definition. Finally, we may descend with firmer confidence into the divisions and distinctions of the subject, so that by such a progression we may more directly depict the truth and better distinguish it from falsehood and error. Since, therefore, the business of this our treatise is the study of Philosophy, it must first be known that the word is generally accepted to mean "wisdom"; however, in a more proper and peculiar sense or significance, they interpret it as the Love, or friend—and as others call it, the study—of wisdom. For the word **Philosophy** is composed of **Philos**, which is "friend," and **Sophia**, which is "wisdom"—as if it were the "love or study of wisdom." It is clear, then, that it is so named by the Greeks insofar as it contains within itself the love of wisdom, or because men, in treating wisdom, are incited and enticed toward its love. In ancient times, this science was called **Sophia**, or simply "wisdom," but that distinguished philosopher Pythagoras later added the word **Philos**, as one who preferred to be regarded as a "Philosopher"—that is, a lover or student of wisdom—rather than to impudently arrogate the title of a "Wise Man" to himself.

<column-break/>

From the sense of this etymology, it will not be difficult to elicit its nature and definition: namely, that it is the love or study of wisdom, an ardent and burning application of the soul to seek and apprehend it, insofar as the word implies what the sincere love of wisdom is. It evidently appears from these things, therefore, that the complete subject of philosophy is wisdom, the perfect knowledge of which is the highest good of mortal life, and that lovable goal toward which the wise men of every age have, above all, aimed. Truly, just as from the beginning of things there was a distinction and opposite difference in matters—namely between light and darkness, good and evil, justice and injustice, and (to conclude all in one word) between the real and true things of God and the deceptive, vain, and imaginary things of the Devil and worldly men, for whom he is the Leader or rather the deceiver—so also there is an extreme distinction between true wisdom, which is from God, and that false and fantastical wisdom, the effect of human invention and tradition, whose father is the Devil. Indeed, it is he who impressed it upon the concepts, fantasies, and chimeras of the Pagan men, so that he might deceive even the elect (if it were possible) with his subtle and crafty fallacies. Hence, since the origin of the world, such great discord has been sown between essential philosophy and that which is false or counterfeit; hence arises such great contempt for philosophers and philosophy by worldly people. Do we not have all this sufficiently confirmed by the Sacred Page? "We have behaved in this world," says the Apostle, "not in fleshly wisdom, but in the grace of God." And again: "The wisdom of the flesh is Death, because the wisdom of the flesh is an enemy to God; the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace." And elsewhere more clearly: "My preaching is not in the persuasive <margin>2 Corinthians 1:12</margin> <margin>Romans 8:6</margin>

First, that the fullness of all intelligence and knowledge consists in the revelation and knowledge of the mystery of God and of his Son, Christ Jesus. Since (as the Apostle says) the Treasure of wisdom and knowledge consists in Christ alone: <margin>Colossians 2:3</margin> hence Christ spoke these words: *Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added to you.* Consequently, it is mere folly to seek true knowledge, understanding, and wisdom from those who do not possess it. 

Second, that honey-tongued orators, deceitful and fallacious sophists, and the vain philosophers of this world are to be avoided at all costs and in no way believed; for their doctrine and words are superficial and scarcely probable, insofar as they have nothing else for the foundation of their structure but an empty and imaginary figment. 

Third, that there is a certain Philosophy, and consequently a wisdom, which draws its beginning from the invention or tradition of men and according to the elements of this world and not according to Christ; therefore, it is to be avoided and repelled by true Christians with every effort, or at least not observed with such sincerity as if it had been sent from heaven to earth by some divinity. 

Fourth, that sincere philosophy—and consequently true wisdom—is that which is according to the nature of Christ, in whom all the treasures of perfect knowledge, cognition, and wisdom are located. This doctrine is built not according to the teaching or traditions of men, nor according to the elements of the world—which is earthly, animal, demonic, and contradictory to the truth—but according to that which descends from God, the Father of Lights, as we are taught by the <margin>James 3:15</margin> Apostle James. 

Therefore, upon the bases of this human or worldly wisdom was erected (as we have said) that wisdom of the Greeks, which is today the chief pillar of Christian philosophy. This is explained clearly enough from his speeches delivered to the Athenian philosophers. But before we proceed further in this discourse of ours, it will be worth the effort to first open to the world the account of the rise or origin both of human or worldly wisdom and of the animal man (of which the scriptures speak in many places), as well as of that divine wisdom and the spiritual man. It must be known, therefore, that supreme wisdom is the very taste of the soul, intelligence is its vision, the mind its eye, reason its gaze, and reasoning itself is the inquiry into the object, so that where intelligence does not receive this primary taste or flavor from supreme wisdom, it is often accustomed to be mistaken and deceived in its judgment; nor is it enough to have the mind as an eye, by whose act vision occurs—for it is occupied in the intuition of both inferior and superior things—but it is necessary that judgment proceed directly from wisdom. Intelligence, therefore, is that faculty or power of the soul by which man perceives, knows, and discerns all intelligible things: And we must understand that vision of this kind happens in three ways: namely, either by the assistance of the external senses—and then it is occupied, by the mediation of the <term>Phantasy (Phantasia): In Renaissance psychology, this was the faculty that processed sensory data into mental images or "phantasms."</term> phantasy, with sensible bodies, which are sometimes (indeed, usually) accustomed to direct and assist the intellect and reason of the natural man; or by the spirit of the phantasy alone, and then it is occupied with the imaginary likenesses of both bodies and spiritual things: and in both of these, it will be seen that the intellect is easily corrupted, and can be seduced by means of the phantasy, through which the knowledge of corporal and intelligible things is conducted and offered to reason, and finally to the intellect: For it is impossible but that the phantasy (since it is an interior sensitive faculty, which receives a deep impression in itself of va-

<column-break/>

rious sensible things, whether present or absent, and strives to produce and extract similar forms in thought from various forms of real sensible things, and since it cannot transcend beyond the knowledge of natural, sensitive things and corporeal substances), it is (I say) impossible that it should not represent to the soul or intelligence such sensible notions as its special objects assign to it: Hence it happens that the mind or intelligence is deceived in perceiving things rightly and justly, and in knowing and discerning sensible and intelligible things; and this is especially so the more the phantasy strives to extract and draw out an imaginary concept of some intelligible thing from certain sensible things: For in such an action, the intelligence or mind (seduced in this manner by the phantasy itself) can very easily be deceived in discerning and perceiving such a thing, insofar as that intelligible thing is spiritual and supernatural, and consequently exceeds the circle of the capacity of human reason. For example, when mention is made to a natural or animal man of the "God of Hosts," then immediately an image is painted in his phantastic spirit of some sensible and corporeal Potentate, or an eminent Emperor fortified by his princes. Furthermore, if he wishes to contemplate the Holy Spirit, he will project the impression of a dove or cloven tongues of fire and other things of this sort. ...be perceived, etc. But if a <unclear>vision</unclear> <note>original: "ico"</note> comes immediately from the senses into the **phantastic spirit**, then even such an object deceives the intellectual vision. For example: a straight stick placed in water will appear curved to the sight, and in such a manner it will be depicted in the phantastic spirit. Trees, cities, and mountains will seem to move to those who are sailing; a post or a column will appear to the imagination as a man during the night. Similarly, the sound of a cannon to the hearing, and the flash of the ignited powder itself, will be held by the imagination to be thunder and lightning; just as the wailing of a cat is taken for the cry of a child, and so forth. Furthermore, the phantasy represents false images to itself both in sleep and in waking hours, as can be seen in those seized by delirium, frenzy, or mania. Indeed, it sometimes even fakes things that never were, are, not ever will be. It is from this that so many errors have crept into the world, by which the senses and intellect of the **animal man** <term>animal man (homo animalis): A term used by St. Paul to describe a person who relies only on natural reason and physical senses, lacking spiritual illumination.</term>, led by mere likenesses of truth in place of real truth itself and leaning upon mere probability, is said to be seduced into an opposing path. He seems to understand nothing except the bodies offered by the phantastic sense, or those created by the merely imaginary spirit of phantasy itself. From this arose that worldly or human wisdom and, consequently, that vain philosophy of the Heathen, which proceeded from the tradition of men and according to the elements of this world, and not according to Jesus Christ, the true wisdom specified by the Apostle. From this kind of deceptive vision of the intelligence, the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle, so named because he famously walked while teaching.</term>, with their leader, imagine and dream of the eternity of the elements of earth, water, etc., of the heavens, of the stars, and of the world itself. They have fashioned the dominion of Fortune in the world; they say God acts by necessity regarding generation and corruption; they speak of a **Vacuum** which they can imagine within the substance of the world; they believe the celestial spheres are carried by the swift and violent motion of the "first moveable"; they think that **Meteors** <term>Meteors: In the 17th century, this term referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</term> are made from smoke and vapors raised from the earth and waters, and are crowded together in turn by **antiperistasis** <term>antiperistasis: An Aristotelian concept where a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more intense when compressed by cold.</term>, and they think these are sublimated into the heights by the attractive force of the sun, stars, and so forth. They imagine earthquakes are caused by winds enclosed in the bowels of the earth; they maintain that springs are generated from vapors condensed in the veins of the earth; and that clouds are procreated from those same vapors raised into the heights and thickened by means of Antiperistasis. And they gather this from the senses and imprint it upon the spirit of phantasy because they observe in **distillations** that vapors ascending from a pot or a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: A gourd-shaped chemical vessel used in a distillation apparatus.</term> into the top of an **alembic** grow into drops and coagulate. Furthermore, they assert that winds are made from exhalations ascending from the earth and from their repercussions from others descending, because they observe the smoke of liquids or ignited coals being pushed sideways in its ascent by a wind descending in the air. They even think that thunders are made by the murmuring of fire in water, be-

<column-break/>

-cause they notice that red-hot iron itself, when thrown into water, makes such murmurs and noises, and so on. Wherefore it is evident that that mind or intelligence of the animal man uses two kinds of visions in the phantasy—namely, those from the bodily perceptions of the senses and those from spiritual images impressed upon it. This mind is entirely addicted to looking at exterior and superficial things, while neglecting those that are interior and central—that is, the superior, divine, and true things. From which it follows that his reasoning is frequently deceived regarding the objects he investigates, so that for the most part he accepts what is scarcely probable as truth. This is because the notions he seeks from the impressions of sensory things in the phantasy are uncertain, insofar as the images of the present, past, and future delineated in his spirit in an imaginary way are for the largest part fabricated and imaginary—appearing, of course, as they are not in the reality of the thing. Such, therefore, is the condition of the natural or animal man; such, I say, is the root and foundation of human or worldly wisdom, for his mind does not understand or look with spiritual eyes, nor is it instructed by the "taste of wisdom," whose role it is to look back upon those things which have neither bodies nor the forms of bodies. Such things are God, the Mind, the Word, Wisdom, <margin>James 3:15</margin> Justice, Truth, and the essential good affections of the soul. It is concerning this kind of wisdom that the Apostle intends when he says: *That the wisdom which is from below is earthly, sensual [animal], and devilish.* <note>original: "sapientia, quæ est de infra sit terrena, animalis & Diabolica"</note> <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> From this it is clear that the animal man cannot (according to the opinion of Saint Paul) perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; nor is it possible for them to be understood by him in any way, as they are to be discerned spiritually. But the spiritual discerning of things is not a natural work, but a supernatural work of faith, insofar as it arises not from sensory notions, but from supernatural knowledge infused spiritually into the illuminated soul. 

But on the other hand, in the third species of the vision of the soul's intelligence—in which it has directed its regard toward the highest wisdom (which is its taste and nourishing mother) by the sharpness of the mind, neglecting inferior things—therein is situated the infallible notion of all things. In this state, the soul can neither be deceived, deluded, nor seduced. And through that vision, which looks upon things that are neither corporeal nor have the forms of bodies (which we listed above), the mind or intelligence can arrive at a true recognition of the soul. This is by no means possible through the former senses and imaginations, insofar as these rather deceive the mind and make things seem to be what they truly are not. Therefore, by a withdrawal from the senses and the images of bodies, the internal or spiritual man is accustomed to reach the knowledge of himself, of God, of His wisdom, and of the angels; by withdrawing (I say) from the senses, and leading his mind away from the multitude...

...true wisdom, namely that which descends from on high from the Father of Lights <note>original: "Patre Luminum"; a reference to James 1:17.</note>, which is born from the intelligence or the soul. That is to say, by rejecting physical bodies and their images <note>In this context, "images" or "simulacra" refer to the deceptive appearances of the material world.</note>, it turns the sharp focus of its light toward those things which are neither bodies nor the likenesses of bodies, but are the naked and infallible ideas of truth. For whose Spirit is unique to Christ, his spirit will have been made one in Him, and as a result, it will not be difficult for him to know all things without the risk of doubt.

Nor should this seem strange to you, Reader, since all things in the **macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm: The "great world" or the entire universe.</term> are retained according to due proportion in the **microcosm** <term>Microcosm: The "little world," referring to man as a miniature reflection of the universe.</term>. Indeed, that uncreated Divinity—which fills the world and all things in the world, and occupies the whole man centrally and through irradiation from the center—is not divided from itself. Wherefore it is certain that those things concerning God, the Word, Eternal Wisdom, Justice, Virtue, and others in the microcosm

<column-break/>

are understood everywhere in the scriptures, they are also to be understood in the microcosm itself. For just as earth, water, air, fire, ether, and the empyrean spirit <note>The "empyrean" was considered the highest, most refined part of heaven, composed of pure light or fire.</note>, as well as intellect, reason, mind, wisdom, the Word, and God are contained within the macrocosm, so also are all these things proportionally contained in the microcosm. They are no more divided from those in the macrocosm than solar rays are divided from the sun. Truly, as it is in human nature sometimes to look toward the lower things of the world—which is the duty of the **animal** or **natural man** <note>The "animal man" refers to someone living only by their physical senses and biological soul, lacking spiritual enlightenment.</note>—and sometimes to turn the focus of one's contemplation toward higher things—which is the affection of the **spiritual man**—so man is rendered more prone either toward human wisdom (and consequently toward inventing and fashioning worldly philosophy, which is false, being foolishness and vanity before God) or toward preaching and establishing that divine wisdom in both worlds, which is just and acceptable before God. These things having been considered with diligence, so that every doubt may be removed from the scholars of this world in the investigation of this philosophy of ours, we shall proceed in this manner.

To proceed methodically in this business of ours, it remains now that we first investigate with diligence the origin, source, and spring of the essence of Wisdom and philosophy from the testimonies of Holy Scripture. Afterward, we may express the definition and nature most suitable to it with greater ease. Then, let us show that it is the real foundation not only of true philosophy and the sciences depending on it, but also of all hidden mysteries or secrets; indeed, it is the revealer and detector of all things, both past and future. As for the origin of this most holy wisdom, I will prove by the testimony and consensus of the sacred page that its source is God Himself, who is the Father of Light. From this it is clear that it is entirely opposed to worldly wisdom, which is indeed earthly and animal. Hence the Apostle says: *God is the giver and inventor of wisdom.* And elsewhere: *Wisdom and strength belong to the Lord.* And Job: *Wisdom is in the ancient, and prudence in much time.* <margin>Job 12:12. Proverbs 2:6.</margin> And the wise man: *The Lord gives wisdom; from his mouth comes prudence and knowledge.* And elsewhere: *God possessed wisdom in the beginning of his ways, before...*

...stands, so that the creature acts by itself—that is, by a certain free choice or its own will—which is absolutely divided and plainly distinguished from the immediate act of Divinity. To these inconsistent views, according to our established rules or canons regarding the Divinity, I respond that the divine essence is indivisible. Therefore, it is evident that God does not usually impart any essential act—such as the soul, life, and the functions depending on them—to any creature in a way that could be discontinued or separated from His own nature, according to that axiom: *what God gave, He never let go.* <note>Original: "quod dedit Deus, nunquam dimisit." This is a central legal and theological maxim suggesting that God's gifts are sustained by His ongoing presence.</note> And for this reason, Christ, who is the eternal spirit of wisdom, is said to fill all things. 

Indeed (the worldly-wise man of this age will reply), he who attempts to distract men from the simple truth with vain distinctions says: "this presence of the divinity is in every thing <term>virtually</term> <note>Meaning by way of power or effect, like the heat of a distant fire.</note> and not <term>essentially</term> <note>Meaning by way of His actual substance or being.</note> or substantially." To whom I say: I would like to know (considering such academic distinctions as nothing) why St. Paul commands Timothy: "If anyone," he says, "teaches another doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the doctrine of the fear of God, he is one who puffs himself up; and while he knows nothing, he is sick with disputes and the questioning of words, from which come envy, strife, slander, and evil suspicions; and the friction of men of corrupt minds, who are destitute of the truth and think that godliness is a way of gain. But you, keep yourself far from them." 

I would (I say) gladly like to know whether the power of God is not His essence, or whether one can be distinguished or separated from the other? If he should answer that the divine power is not the essence, but an <term>accident</term> <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that a thing might or might not have without changing its fundamental nature (like the color of a shirt). The author argues God has no accidents; He is entirely His own nature.</note>, it is certainly to be believed that such an answer is erroneous. For it is manifest and known even to the Jews and the Gentiles that God is free from every accident, since He is the "most essential essence" of all things, existing in and through Himself, subject to no accident. Furthermore, where His essential act is present, there also is His power; and where His power is, there likewise is His essence. If this were not so, the Word of God or the divine act—whose role is to give life to all things and to make every creature agile and movable—would seem to be nothing but a mere accident; indeed, an accident divided from the divine essence. How absurd this would be is proven by the immortality of the root itself. 
<margin>Psalm 33:6</margin>
For David says in the aforementioned text: *By the breath of his mouth is all their power*—namely, of the heavens, etc. I believe no one is so lacking in mind as to consider that power an accident. It follows, therefore, that the divine power is the same as the divine essence, and consequently is never divided in God Himself or from God—that is, from the divine spirit.
<margin>Wisdom 7:25, 26</margin>
But why say more? Since we have this expressly confirmed by the scriptures: "The Spirit," says

<column-break/>

Solomon, "is a vapor of the power of God, and a pure flow from the glory of the Almighty, and a splendor from the eternal light," etc. What? Shall we call this power or splendor proceeding from the eternal light an accident, when it is the Holy Spirit of wisdom, as the wise man confesses? Hence also St. Paul, in the place cited before: "In him 
<margin>Colossians 1:16. John 1.</margin>
all things were founded in the heavens and on the earth, both visible and invisible; all things were created in him and through him, and all things consist in him," etc. By which it is clear that outside of that Spirit, there is nothing. And John says: "In the Word was life," etc. Consequently, it is clear that the creature is continued and annexed to the divinity by the bond of this divine nature—that is, by one and the same Spirit of Life which is within it. Without this bond, union, or relationship to one another, it is impossible for a creature to exist for even a moment of time. 

Hence the Royal Psalmist says: "All creatures 
<margin>Psalm 104:24 etc.</margin>
look to you, that you may give them food in its time. When you give it to them, they gather it; when you open your hand, they are satisfied with good. When you hide your face, they are troubled; when you take away their spirit, they expire; when you send forth your spirit, they are recreated with good," etc. By this we may see that it is the immediate act of this Wisdom which makes the creature live and exist, and that it is Wisdom which works all things. For the scriptures testify that God gives life to all things; and that "in him we live, move, and have our being"—and not only we, but also all flesh in general, as we gather from this very text. And also from this testimony of Job: "If God, applying his soul to man, should 
<margin>Job 34:14</margin>
withdraw his spirit or breath to himself, all flesh would fail and expire together, and man would return to ashes," etc. 

Behold, therefore, the Cornerstone upon which all flesh is built, and without which it is reduced to nothing. Furthermore, the Prophet says: "God gives breath to the people who are upon the earth, and spirit to those who walk upon it," etc. How (I ask you) is it possible that this spirit of life should be present in and with all things, and therefore essentially in every thing, and yet cease and rest from its immediate action, when it is in itself the swiftest of all things, and most agile and movable, as we are taught by Solomon? 
<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>

And finally, I shall declare how all secret acts, mystical revelations, and miracles are perfected by it, confirming that passage of scripture where it is said: "The other sciences are the handmaidens of this one." Therefore, regarding all these things, we shall speak in order in the following sections.
