# ON THE MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

## C 2
<meta>catchword: or</meta>

If some say that these words of Solomon should be understood in a sense other than those sciences which are included under natural philosophy, I warn them to turn their minds toward the teachings of the wise man for their better guidance. He sets out quite clearly to remove any doubt: <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 7:2, 7</margin> "It was given to me," he says, "by the **spirit of wisdom** that I might know the **constitution of the world** and the **power of the Elements**, and the **Beginning, middle, and end of times**, the changes of the **solstices**, and the varieties of the seasons or tempests, the circuits of the year, and the **positions of the stars**, and the **natures of living things** and the tempers or rages of beasts, and the force of the winds or spirits, and the thoughts of men, and the **differences of plants** and the **powers of roots**: I have even known whatever things are hidden and manifest; for **wisdom, the artisan of all things**, taught me," etc. From these things we gather that by the revelation of this divine spirit, this most wise king arrived at the knowledge of all things and sciences. For since wisdom is the **central root**, or the **Cornerstone** of all things, how is it possible for us to reach knowledge of the center when we are ignorant of the secrets of the circumference? This is especially true since the circumference, or the external part of a thing, is nothing other than that which is ordered and disposed by the center. For this reason, this divine spirit is not undeservedly called by the most profound Philosopher **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational texts of alchemy and philosophy were attributed.</note> the **center of every thing**, whose circumference is nowhere, but which nevertheless encompasses all circumferences within itself. From the aforementioned discourse of Solomon, therefore, we can learn first that wisdom revealed to him those hidden mysteries concerning the fabric of the world, just as she did for **Moses**. Second, that she taught him the nature and power of the **Elements** with their hidden actions and miraculous generation, as well as the properties of **meteors** <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> which are fashioned from elementary matter. Third, that she provided him with the reason and method of the rising and production of winds, the astronomical division of the year, the site or position of the stars in the heaven, and their astrological natures. Fourth, that she opened the principal mysteries of the **art of healing**: for he confesses that he learned from his mistress, Wisdom, the natures of all creatures, the conditions of beasts, the differences of plants, and the powers of roots. Fifth, he relates that by the mediation of this spirit he was made a participant in all things hidden or concealed, and consequently in the **Mysteries of the Angels**—and indeed even the secrets of God himself.

<margin>THEOLOGY. On the eternal world.</margin>
As for what pertains to **Theology**, it is well known that the word is derived from *Theos* <note>Greek for "God"</note> and *Logos* <note>Greek for "Word" or "Discourse"</note>, as if to say "a discourse about God." This high science is also founded upon these divine bases, whence the wise man says: "The spirit of wisdom will transfer itself into Holy souls <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 7:27</margin> and the friends of God, and she establishes prophets." For

<column-break/>

God loves no one except him who lives with wisdom. Again, elsewhere: "God sends forth Wisdom from the holy heavens, he sends her from the throne of his glory to man, so that she may be present and labor with him, that he may know <margin>Ecclesiasticus 24:45</margin> what is pleasing to Him: for she knows all things." For this reason also Wisdom says: "I will illuminate all who hope in the Lord." And elsewhere: "I am the **book of life**, <margin>Ecclesiasticus 24:32</margin> the testament of the most high and the recognition of truth." And Solomon says: "The desire for Wisdom leads to a perpetual kingdom." And again: "Wisdom is the teacher of the discipline of God and the chooser of his works." And elsewhere: <margin>Wisdom 6:21. And this was also the spirit which delivered the discourses in the Old Testament as if they were oracles of divinity through the mouths of the Patriarchs and Prophets. Therefore, it is necessary that we look back to those things as the literal fountains of Theology, since under their <term>typical or graphic instructions</term> <note>original: "typicis seu graphicis." This refers to the idea that the literal stories of the Bible act as symbols or "types" for deeper, hidden spiritual truths.</note> the hidden spirit of this secret sense lies concealed; which, by the mediation of the precepts of **mystical Theology**, can be extracted and unshelled.

Colossians 1:16. Colossians 2:9. Ephesians 1:20.</margin> "In him," (says St. Paul in the place cited before) "all things were created in the heavens, whether **Dominations**, or **Thrones**, or **Principalities**, or **Powers**." <note>These are specific ranks or "choirs" within the traditional hierarchy of angels.</note> And elsewhere: "In Christ dwelt all the fullness of divinity bodily, who is the head of all Principality and power." Nor indeed is it a wonder if it is in his will to uncover all in all, since it is known by the wise that **He is all in all**.

### BOOK II OF THE FIRST SECTION.

...to animals and minerals, he has imparted their virtues, both hidden and apparent. That supreme spirit, I say, who is **all in all** and works all things in all, can consequently teach and instruct through external revelation what occurs within the interior of a creature, and by what power he operates in each individual thing. 

And although the Pagan Philosophers and Physicians have discovered the hidden properties of plants through effects perceived by practice alone and through sensory observation—as if by a "demonstration from the effect" <note>original: "demonstratione à posteriore," a logical term for reasoning from consequences back to causes</note>—for example, that the **Linden** tree, **Oak Mistletoe**, and **Peonies** cure **Epilepsy**; or that the herb **Rupturewort** regards the rupture called a **Hernia** (from which it received its name); just as **Coltsfoot** (insofar as it is used to cure a cough, or *tussis*); and that **Eyebright** contributes to the clearing of dimness in the eyes; and among animals, that the **Toad** stops blood; that the feet of a **Donkey** or a **Frog** are effective against the "falling sickness" <note>An old term for epilepsy</note>; and that **scorpions** cure the sting of Scorpions, and so on. 

Nevertheless, because these thinkers lack the central foundations of **sympathy** and **antipathy**—which consist in the "Will" and "Un-will" <note>The author uses "voluntate & Noluntate" to describe the spiritual attraction and repulsion underlying nature</note> of one and the same spirit—they can provide no other reason for these wonderful and abstruse things, except that they are "hidden properties." In the end, they can infer nothing further about the matter except that "they are such because they are such." Thus, from these learned Doctors of this world, we receive nothing as a conclusion except the **Unknown explained by the even more Unknown**.

<margin>MUSIC.</margin>
That the action and virtue of this spirit is also engaged in every species of **Music**—namely, in that common and artificial kind as well as in the more essential and mystical kind, whether it be of the **macrocosm** <note>the great world or universe</note> or the **microcosm** <note>the "little world," meaning the human being</note>—is a fact that may be drawn out not only by common observation but by a more internal inspection. 

As for **worldly harmony**, and the manner in which every sublunary **Element** and every superlunary sphere is disposed by a certain essential species of sympathetic concord, the entire series of the Scriptures seems to confirm it: namely, that it is perfected by the mediation of the act of the Divine Spirit itself. Above all others, **Solomon** testifies to the marvelous effect of that Spirit in worldly harmony in these words: <margin>Wisdom 19:17</margin> *For the elements, while they change among themselves, are like the stops on an organ changing the quality of the sound, yet all things keep their own tone.* 

But the **Apostle** <note>Paul</note> expresses all of this with even greater excellence and efficacy, saying: <margin>Colossians 1:19</margin> *In Christ all things in heaven and on earth were established, and all things visible and invisible were created through him and in him; he is before all, and all things consist in him. In him it pleased all the fullness of the Divinity to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things in himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven,* etc. Behold here the perfect and **Universal** <note>original: "Catholicum," used here in its literal sense of "universal" or "all-encompassing"</note> fountain of Love, Sympathy, and Harmony! It is he who not only takes away the discordant sins of the world, but also cleanses heaven and 

<column-break/>

earth from discord, harmonizing them and adorning them with his peaceful power of harmonic peace or symphonic love. 

Hence it is that this spirit is said by the wise and mystical philosopher to be the **bond** or **ligament** of the **Elements**, by means of which the discord of the world and the elements of the microcosm (or man) are bound together and reduced into a fitting harmony and quiet union. Therefore, in imitation of that worldly consonance, the concert of external Music is formed—both vocal and instrumental—which stands in relation to that true and sincere Symphony of the Spirit as a shadow to the object that casts it, or as an image to the real person whom it represents.

Now we come to **Arithmetic** and **Geometry**, which the wise man seems to include in his discourse: *You have ordered (or tempered) all things by measure, number, and weight.* By **measure**, he understands the progress of a thing in length, width, and depth, pertaining to Arithmetic and the **Cossic** art <note>An early term for algebra, derived from the Italian "cosa," meaning "the thing" or the unknown variable</note>. This is the measure which that almighty spirit makes in its emanation: from a **point** into a **line**; and from a line (or root) into a **square**; and finally from a square to a **cube**—as if moving from the point or starting term to the surface, and from the surface to the body or final term. 

By **numbers**, he understands those Arithmetical dimensions in arithmetical progression by which that spirit has gone out from **unity** into **multitude**. For example, from **1 to 10**, as if from the eternal center of all things into the "aevial" or **Angelic** state <note>"Aevial" refers to *aevum*, the mode of existence between time and eternity, typical of angels</note>, which progression was the first and simplest degree of composition or mixture. Then from **10 to 100**, which multiplicative progress denotes the composition of the **temporal world**. And finally from **100** (a hundred) to **1000**. This progression proves the composition of creatures from the elements, or from various alterations of the **Universal Element**. 

Thus, every Christian can see from these things how God is **all in all** and yet outside of all things, and (as it says in the text) in heaven, in the sea, in the abyss, and in the lower regions. For this reason, the **Pythagoreans** included all things in these three Arithmetical principles: **1, 2, and 3**. They attributed **1** to God in his abstruse existence; **2** they referred to the matter of all things; and **3** to the universal form of the world. Under these three, therefore, all things are comprised. I shall make more abundant mention of these (God willing) in the second section, where I will discuss the essentials of Sympathy and Antipathy. 

The **Patient Man** <note>Job</note> speaks thus in the person of **Jehovah**: <margin>Job 38:4</margin> *Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding. On what were its bases fastened, or who laid its **Cornerstone**?* By these words he proves that this spirit, who is the Cornerstone...

## Fol. 12.

...singular <note>The text begins with "gularis," a continuation of "Singularis" (singular) from the previous page.</note> or the Basis of all things (for without it nothing was made or can exist, as St. John testifies). It is not only that the earth has its site, dimension, and geometric position; but also the Celestial Sun, the Moon, and the Stars, and all things in heaven as well as on earth, acquired their weights, proportions, magnitudes, and locations in this world through it. Indeed, even the air itself is shaped into multiform meteorological characters or images according to various measures and proportions: For the sacred text says: *God by wisdom fits the weight to the air, and weighs the waters by measure, and establishes the laws for the rain and a path for the lightning of the thunder,* etc. <note>original: "Deus sapientiâ aptat pondus aëri..." refers to Job 28:25.</note>

<margin>RHETORIC.</margin> It follows that we should explain its virtue and power in the science of Rhetoric and the art of Oratory. We shall prove in a few words that Wisdom itself is the most exact mistress in teaching those arts, and also the most essential mover in the souls or spirits of men. By its action, men who are plainly mute and barbaric are rendered eloquent and effectively persuasive; and what is more, it is that essential spirit within the voice and words of orators by which the minds of listeners are enticed and drawn to pay attention and give faith to their speeches. For Moses, having a conversation with that divine spirit, said: *I am not,* he says, *an eloquent man, nor have I ever been, not even since you have spoken to your servant, but I am slow of mouth and tongue.* <margin>Exodus 4:10.</margin> Then Jehovah said to him: *Who set the mouth of man, or who can make one either deaf or mute? Is it not I, who am Jehovah? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and I will teach you what you ought to speak,* etc. By this we are taught: that eloquence and the proper arrangement of words, sentences, and speeches—both in the rhetorical theory and in the orator—are from God, whose power alone it is to give or take away fluency according to his pleasure. Wherefore the Evangelist says, *they shall all be <margin>John 6:45; Isaiah 54:13.</margin> taught by God.* And the Prophets: *all your children shall be taught by Jehovah.* But Christ expresses all this in even more explicit words: <margin>John 14:26.</margin> *The Holy Spirit,* he says, *whom the Father will send, he will teach you all things, and will suggest to you all things, whatever I have said to you.* Now, that this spirit is that eternal Wisdom, which effects and awakens this Rhetorical and Oratorical function in men, the scriptures teach elsewhere: <margin>Wisdom 10:21.</margin> *She opened,* says the Wise Man, *the mouth of the mute and made the tongues of infants eloquent.* And the son of Sirach: <margin>Ecclesiastes 39:7.</margin> *He will pour forth the words of his wisdom like showers, and in his prayer he will confess to the Lord,* etc. I could bring forward many other examples from the sacred page in this place to confirm this assertion of mine: namely, to prove that Rhetorical eloquence is from this good spirit of wisdom; but for the sake of brevity I will now omit them, so that I may pass on to the mechanical arts. I will prove that the inventions of all these had their origin from the instinct and guidance of this good spirit,

<column-break/>

although they have been defiled and stained in the present day, partly by the antiquity of time and partly by the envy and ignorance of men.

<margin>MECHANICAL ARTS.</margin> Regarding the mechanical arts, it should be known that their invention and origin (as we have said) were from the inspiration of this spirit. For example: the Art of Tailoring or garment-making proceeded from the instruction of this spirit. Hence Jehovah said to Moses: <margin>Exodus 28.</margin> *You shall speak to all who are wise of heart, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, that they may make Aaron's garments, in which he, being sanctified, may minister.* Furthermore, the <margin>Exodus 31.</margin> work of the Goldsmith, the craft of the Jeweler, the Carpenter, and the Wood-carver took their beginning from that very same fountain. Wherefore Jehovah said to Moses: *Behold, I have called Bezalel and I have filled him with the spirit of God, with Wisdom and understanding and knowledge in every work, both for devising whatever can be crafted from gold, silver, and bronze, marble and gems and various woods; and I have given him Oholiab as a companion, and in the heart of every learned man I have placed wisdom, that they may make all things that I have commanded you,* etc. From these things it is evident that the true knowledge of any mechanical art is in the spirit of God, in whose power alone it is to teach men all things. But all this is expressed more plainly elsewhere: for Moses says to the children of Israel: <margin>Exodus 35:30.</margin> *Behold, the Lord has called Bezalel, and filled him with the spirit of God, with wisdom and intelligence and knowledge and all doctrine for devising and doing work in gold and silver and bronze and iron, and in carving stones and in carpentry.* Whatever can be skillfully devised, he has put in his heart: he also instructed both him and Oholiab with wisdom, that they may do the work of the joiner, the weaver, and the embroiderer in hyacinth <note>A term often used for blue fabric in biblical translations</note>, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen, and that they may weave all things, etc. Moreover, we read that Noah was instructed by this spirit in the construction of the Ark: for the text says: <margin>Wisdom 10:4.</margin> *Wisdom healed the earth, governing the just man through a contemptible piece of wood.* Through its mediation, the art of Music was revealed to Tubal: for the text says: *Tubal was the Father of those who sing with the kithara and the organ.* And Tubal-Cain was the first inventor of works in iron and bronze. And from Adah, Jubal <note>The author likely means Jabal, as Jubal is cited for music above; the text attributes pastoral arts to the lineage of Adah.</note> was the Father and author of the art of tents and the pastoral life. We conclude, therefore, that there is no true mechanical art which does not have its origin from that omnipotent spirit, whose role alone it is to teach all things.

<margin>ETHICS.</margin> Furthermore, it must be observed from the entire thread of the holy sacred scriptures that true Moral philosophy is rooted in this wisdom. For it was the voice of this essential spirit which taught the Christian world through the mouth and tongue of Christ, so that it might follow good and avoid evil. Also from the mouth of the wise man: *Wisdom preserves the paths of justice, guarding the ways of the saints.* <margin>Proverbs 2:7.</margin> *Through her you will understand justice and judgment, equity and every good path; if counsel enters your heart, prudence will guard you...*

By her revelation, the prophets prophesied concerning future things. Christ and the Apostles, and also Elijah and Elisha, cured the desperately ill and restored the dead to life; they cast out demons from human bodies, transmuted water into wine, fed five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes, and multiplied flour and oil; they uncovered the secret speeches and intentions of enemies; through this spirit they were miraculously carried from place to place. Through it, Christ restrained the winds and walked upon the waters, rose from the dead, entered through a closed door, was transfigured on the mountain, and a horrible earthquake occurred; and the Sun, contrary to the common laws of nature, was deprived of its light.

<margin>1 Corinthians 2:10, Romans 15:18, Daniel 2:22</margin>

And the Prophet Daniel says these things: He reveals the deep and hidden things, and knows what is established in darkness, and light is with him. Since this is so, it is clearly evident that there is no true and genuine art or science—whether it be manifest, or abstruse and mystical—which is not derived from the doctrine of this true wisdom, insofar as without it nothing real or essential can be either known or acquired in art.

### CHAPTER V:
### *Concerning false wisdom, spurious philosophy, and the adulterous philosopher, along with their characteristics.*

<margin>James 3:17</margin> Now truly, since I have clearly enough explained the nature or essence of true wisdom—and consequently of pure philosophy and the pure Philosopher—it will be fitting that I describe the false and adulterated wisdom of this world, along with the Philosophy based upon it. I shall likewise describe the signs and characteristics not only of this wisdom and impure Philosophy, but also of the Philosopher who is nourished and educated by it as if he were a bastard <note>original: "spurius," referring to a philosophy that lacks a legitimate "father" in Divine Truth.</note>. The Apostle says that true wisdom, which arises from the Father of Light, is pure, peaceful, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits; not judging, without envy or hypocrisy. But on the other hand, he asserts that the wisdom which is from below, and not from the Father of Light, is earthly, animalistic, demonic, and contradictory to the truth. Consequently, it is litigious, immodest, not open to reason, devoid of good fruit, and full of envy, strife, and disputation. Therefore, just as the basis or foundation of the former philosophy is Jesus Christ—insofar as he is true wisdom—so indeed the foundation of the latter is the tradition and invention of worldly men, animated by the deceptive suggestions of the Devil, so that by this path he might create strife, disputes, and opposition in this world. Hence that divine Philosopher [St. Paul] said, in placing a difference between these two opposites: In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, etc. <margin>Colossians 2:7, 8</margin> By this series of words, St. Paul seems to assert that all wisdom and knowledge—and consequently true Philosophy and all sincere sciences derived from and included within it—are contained and to be sought and found in Christ, who is that eternal wisdom and the true Cornerstone <note>original: "lapis Angularis," a reference to Christ as the essential structural support of all knowledge.</note>, who fills, informs, and gives life to all things. Such wisdom is not to be sought by any human industry in the vain science and wisdom of the world and the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum," specifically referring to the non-Christian Greek and Roman philosophical traditions.</note>, which is indeed deceptive and barely adorned with the appearance of probability, insofar as it rests on the obscure and erroneous precepts of worldly men and not on the spiritual ordinances of Christ. And for this reason, while the Apostle condemns Philosophy in general terms, he recognizes upon closer inspection that the love of true wisdom, and therefore its Lover [the Philosopher], is to be regarded and revered with the highest honor by the wise. Therefore, it is certain that by "Philosophy" he means the study of worldly wisdom. For in that place he confesses that Christ is true Wisdom, insofar as in him dwells all the fullness of the Divinity bodily. Therefore it follows that he highly praises the lover or friend of such Wisdom, and by consequence [he praises] Philosophy,

<column-break/>

which is built upon such a basis—upon such a Cornerstone, I say—he could not possibly disapprove. From this it is evident that he intends a twofold Philosophy in that Text, and that the warning he gave to the Colossians to avoid philosophy and vain deceit indicated only that of the Athenians, which is born from the tradition of men and according to the elements of the world. But he seemed to approve of that which was established upon Christ. Therefore the Text says ("and not according to Christ," etc.) and in the same place, he shows the reason why such Philosophy is primarily to be embraced: "Because," he says, "in him dwells all the fullness of the Divinity bodily." And consequently, he says, that wisdom descending from the Father of Light is that upon which every creature is founded. It follows, therefore, that he who is a *God-lover* <note>original: "Theophilos," from the Greek θεόφιλος.</note>, or a friend of Christ, is a true Philosopher, since Christ himself is that true wisdom, which is truly the root and basis of all things. The meaning of this passage from the Apostle, therefore, is that the word "Philosophy," since it was a term according to the invention of the Pagans, was to be rejected with respect to its erroneous rudiments and rules; insofar as it was made and fabricated according to the tradition of unfaithful men, which leads Christians themselves, and much more the Pagans or Gentiles, into errors and away from the true knowledge of God, rather than directing them into the way of truth and the knowledge of divine things. And for this reason, the condition of much varied Idolatry has arisen, which is the cause of the neglect of the true worship of the Creator. Indeed, it even leads to contempt for his name, so much so that men are incited to the veneration and worship of creatures in place of the Creator, through whom they themselves live and exist. Hence it is that we are warned to avoid such philosophy with the greatest effort. Concerning such Philosophers, then, who did not place their knowledge upon the Cornerstone, and those Christians who rely on such Pagan fictions, the same Apostle says: "The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the impiety and injustice of those men who hold the truth of God in injustice: Because what is known of God is manifest to them; for God has revealed it to them." <margin>Romans 1:18</margin> For his invisible things are seen from the creation of the world through those things which have been made; his eternal truth and divinity also, so that they are without excuse, because although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, but in saying they were wise, they became vain in their imaginations. For they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of man, and birds, and four-footed beasts, and serpents, etc. By which St. Paul intimates,

### BOOK II OF THE FIRST SECTION.

Paul shows how great is the iniquity among the wise ones or Philosophers of this world, who hide divine truth—indeed, the incorruptible Divinity that exists within every creature—from worldly men through the false inventions of humanity. It is as if he said that the false Philosophers of this world strive in every way to use their manufactured delusions to hide essential things, so that human darkness might not comprehend that essential life or light, sent down from heaven, which dwells within all creatures and especially within man. This light shines in the darkness, even if it is not granted to those philosophers to discern that divinity within the creatures. Regarding these men, Solomon also says: 
<margin>Wisdom 13:1</margin> All men are vain by nature in whom there is ignorance of God, and who, from those good things that are seen, could not understand Him who is; nor by considering the works did they acknowledge the craftsman, etc. 
<margin>Wisdom 12:1</margin> Moreover, he argues elsewhere that this divine Spirit is in every creature by affirming that *the incorruptible spirit of God is in every thing*, etc. This is also confirmed in many other places, as has been said before. For this reason, every Christian needs to be cautious in reading the philosophy of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum," referring to non-Christian, Greek, or Roman thinkers.</note>, and must ensure he is well-grounded, pondering seriously and repeatedly the opinions of the two aforementioned types of philosophers. But especially let him remember the precepts of the former of them (namely, St. Paul), who, when he found the worldly Athenian Philosophers worshipping an unknown God, preached to them a new philosophy and a wisdom entirely unknown to them—namely, Jesus Christ. This doctrine seemed so foreign to them that they burst out in anger with these words: 
<margin>Acts 17:18</margin> *What does this babbler <note>original: "feminiverbius," a Latin rendering of the Greek 'spermologos,' literally a 'seed-picker' or one who picks up scraps of knowledge.</note> wish to say?* Others said, *He seems to be a proclaimer of new demons*, because he was announcing Jesus and his resurrection. By this it is clear enough that true wisdom neither reached their ears nor ever took root in their hearts. Indeed, I would wish for one to consider that the Apostle was thinking of these spurious Philosophers and their wisdom or Philosophy in the place cited before, where he says: *See that no one deceives you through Philosophy and empty fallacy*, etc. This refers to what was taught at Athens: namely, with vain fallacies, subtleties, contentious quibbling, and Protean <note>Proteus was a sea-god in mythology who could change his shape at will; here it refers to logic that shifts meaning to avoid the truth.</note> distinctions. By these, such a philosopher, like Proteus, can turn his meaning into any significance, whether true or false. From this, it happens that men are filled with doubts by such doctrine, so that by leaving the level path of true doctrine and wisdom, they conduct their inquiries through their own labyrinths and cloudy, uncertain paths. Are we not taught that the spirit, which is the foundation or the unique and simple subject of true philosophy, is consequently to be sought in all simplicity? Is it not said that this spirit is modest, sweet, clear, kind, peaceful, and without jealousy? And

<column-break/>

<margin>James 3:15</margin> yet we Christians would rather embrace a spirit and philosophy deformed by quarrels, fallacies, contentious disputations, and ambiguities. Therefore, true Wisdom, since it is peaceful and relies on no ambiguity, has no need for litigious disputations and quibbling, nor does it require for its investigation infinite distinctions or vain quiddities <note term="quiddity">The "what-ness" or essence of a thing; used here as a critique of overly technical scholastic jargon that obscures meaning.</note> birthed from human invention. Such things lead the student into ignorance by the very reason of their multiplicity, rather than introducing him into the light of naked truth. On the other hand, false wisdom so abounds in distinctions, swarms with so many subtle evasions, and is so subject to sophisticated and contentious disputations; it is composed of such great multiplicity and is in the end so difficult and void of good fruit, that in place of the grain of true and essential truth, we find nothing but husks—words, I say, in place of reality. To put it in a word: it appears to be something, but is not real. It looks like a body, while in truth it is a mere shadow. This the Apostle also confirms: 
<margin>1 Corinthians 2:4; 1 Corinthians 12:12; Galatians 3:5</margin> *My preaching is not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the spirit and of truth.* And elsewhere: *The signs of my apostleship were performed among you in all power, in signs, wonders, and mighty deeds.* And again: *He who gives you the spirit and works powers or miracles in you*, etc. Behold, therefore, how this wisdom of the Christians is accustomed to bring with it power and virtue, which St. James calls *good fruits* in the text cited earlier. Conversely, St. Paul calls the philosophy of the Pagans *empty fallacy*, and consequently bereaved or destitute of good fruits. From this they seem to conclude that there is no fruitful philosophy, nor any philosopher who has truly borne fruit, except that which is occupied with the true and essential wisdom of Jesus Christ. We Christians see these things to be true; and yet, in this fleeting age (in which Satan seems to hold dominion), the aforementioned vain and earthly philosophy—which is darkened by a deceptive confusion—holds such great esteem in this world that Christ, who is the true wisdom, is continually crucified among his philosophical worshippers because of their ignorance. He is buried in the clouds or the dark abyss of that Pagan philosophy, which they seem to adore with such veneration and embrace with remarkable fervor and devotion, following Aristotle, its inventor, as if he were another Jesus Christ, who had descended from the heavens to the earth for the salvation of the people and to open the treasure of true science and wisdom to the human race. But observe, I pray, with what characters and colors the Apostle describes such vain philosophers with their contentions and sophistications: *If anyone*, he says, *teaches otherwise and does not acquiesce to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to that which is according to godliness...*

### ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY. Fol. 14.

<margin>1 Tim. 6:5</margin>
...of the doctrine, he is proud, knowing nothing, but doting about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings, perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth, supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself, etc. I vehemently desire that any Christian Peripatetic <note>original: "Peripateticus," referring to a follower of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note>—who wastes his time according to the laws and customs of Aristotle in vain disputes and quibbling, and considers himself foolish if he does not hope to reach that highest summit of the philosophers through such effort—I desire and warn him, I say, to consider these things patiently (setting aside all partiality and envy). Let him think seriously within himself that there is no such custom in the Church of God—that is, the place where true philosophy is practiced, the tabernacles of true Wisdom, or (if you prefer) the house of sincere philosophy and true wisdom—as the Apostle teaches us. For this wisdom of multiform human invention is so dissonant from that true, unique, and simple wisdom of God, that from it have arisen the infinite religions of this world's philosophy, all disagreeing with that true and unique wisdom which is from God. Hence it is that there are so many different sects of that philosophy: Peripatetic, Stoic, Epicurean, and others, each of which has attempted to establish and sustain its own sect through infinite disputes and litigious quibbling. This was also the cause of such great errors in the Church of God, among Christians as well as Turks <note>In this period, "Turks" was often used as a general term for Muslims.</note> and Jews: for among Christians, it was the origin of many schisms and heresies, all of which it nevertheless seems to value as an inquiry into the true God (who is eternal unity) and His simple wisdom.

<margin>1 Cor. 11:16</margin>
Hence St. Paul says: *If any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God*, etc. But it must be known that the house of holy wisdom is the Church, inasmuch as it is the house of Christ. We conclude, therefore, that there are so many ways of deception in this Christian world by reason of the evasions, distinctions, and Aristotelian sophistries—which, like another Proteus <note>A sea-god in Greek mythology capable of changing his shape to avoid capture; here used to describe slippery logic.</note>, are accustomed to transform the subject of an argument into various and multiform meanings—that they often strive to hide the truth behind a deceptive veil of falsehood. Thus they shape the truth (which is inherently naked and simple) like a **nose of wax** <note>A common Reformation-era metaphor for something easily manipulated or twisted to suit one's purpose.</note>, turning and changing it into various appearances as they please. Here, not only is the truth violated, but the simple man of good will is deluded and seduced into evil instead of good. The Apostle depicts this race of enigmatic philosophers or sophists of this age—who are elevated in their own imaginations like boastful Thrasos <note>A "Thraso" is a stock character of a "braggart soldier" from Roman comedy.</note>—in these living colors: *In the*

<margin>2 Tim. 3:1</margin>
*last days*, he says, *perilous times shall come*, etc.

<column-break/>

*Men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, etc., ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the Truth. Now as Jannes and Jambres* <note>In Jewish and Christian tradition, these are the Egyptian sorcerers who opposed Moses by mimicking his miracles.</note> *withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith. But they shall proceed no further: for their folly shall be manifest unto all men, as theirs also was. But thou hast fully known my doctrine*, etc. Now it is certain that his doctrine was concerned with true philosophy, the foundation of which was Jesus Christ; the true wisdom, I say, and the **Cornerstone**, who sustains the entire fabric of the creature and is *all in all*, and fills all things with His essential power, and finally works *all in all*. This doctrine is contrary to the purpose and basic principles of the Heathens <note>original: "Ethnicorum," referring to non-Christian/Pagan Greek philosophers.</note>, who (as has been said) posit infinite agents in this world, such as Angels, Demons, Stars, Elements, Meteors, Fire, Water, heat and cold, Man, beast, Plants, minerals, and the rest—all of which they want to hold the place of subordinate acting causes. For they think these things operate of themselves and without the assistance of any divinity; and yet it is nonetheless certain, and decreed by the sacred page, that there is no agent except the unique **Universal Agent** <note>original: "agens Catholicum."</note>, indivisible in Essence across the many and almost infinite dwellings or organic vehicles of this world, which works all things in them, in all, and above all. And this doctrine of theirs has intoxicated the philosophers of the Christian world (who firmly adhere to that sect) with such a poison of ignorance and error that they say, making a distinction, that God is present everywhere *virtually* <note>i.e., by His power or "virtue" only.</note> but not *substantially* or *essentially*. As if, truly, the power of God could exist without His essence, or could be separated from His Divinity, which is indivisible! And so they seem to dream that there are accidents in God which can be divided from His essence; or at least they distinguish and say that He Himself works all things *principally* and *mediately*—that is, as the primary cause of things—and (they say) there are infinite *secondary causes*, as we said before, which are accustomed to work of and by themselves. But if this assertion of theirs be true, I wonder how God can be said to *fill all things* and *work all in all*, if He is only the primary or universal efficient cause of the world through His word or spirit which He sent into the world? But does His will excel in heaven as on earth? What need is there for more words? Since the Apostle expressly teaches us: *For though there be that are called gods, whether in*

<margin>1 Cor. 8:5</margin>
*heaven or in earth (as there be gods many, and lords many), but to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him*: but not in all...

...this knowledge is for the faithful. Thus he says: by which speech of the Theosophist <note>A term used here for a philosopher who seeks divine wisdom rather than human logic.</note> any discerning Christian might judge how contrary he is to that imaginary power and immediate action—whether of demons and intelligences, or of stars and their influences, or of the qualities of the elements, or of winds and other meteors, or of other creatures according to the decree of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>—since they imply by his word that all acts, whether mediated or immediate, are from God the Father through the Son, Jesus Christ.

<margin>Wisdom 12:1</margin>
And although creatures of this kind appear in outward demonstration to act and operate through themselves and without any more internal and central agent: nevertheless, this sacred philosopher of ours teaches us through the Rules of his philosophy (whose basis is true wisdom, Jesus Christ) that he can grasp no other truly essential acting cause besides the one from which all things are, and the other through whom all things are: both of which persons he nevertheless recognizes to be but one in essence. For since one agent is nothing but the emanation of the other; and consequently in no way more divided from the essence of the other than a ray of the Sun is from the Sun, it is indeed no wonder if He alone, in a twofold property, works all in all without changing His Essence, and especially since He is essentially in all things (as Solomon says). This is the firmest and truest assertion of pure philosophy: Therefore, whatever the worldly or Aristotelian philosophers say, and seem to persuade us with fallacious subtlety, which is opposed to the axioms of true philosophy; we must by no means believe them.

<margin>Galatians 1:8</margin>

There are some who trouble you, and want to pervert the Gospel of Christ: but though we, or an Angel from heaven, preach any other Gospel unto you than that which we have preached, let him be accursed, etc.

Therefore, since the doctrine and wisdom of Aristotle is for the most part opposed to the positions and rudiments of true wisdom and pure philosophy, it is not fitting for any pious Christian to give faith to it, insofar as (according to the opinion of St. James) it contradicts the truth and is contrary to the doctrine of the Holy Bibles. Therefore, such spurious doctrine or wisdom is said by him to be *earthly, sensual, and devilish*. And hence it is that St. Paul writes these things to his disciple Timothy.
> O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane novelties of words, and oppositions of science falsely so called: which some professing have erred <note>original: "exciderunt," meaning to fall away or wander from.</note>

<column-break/>

concerning the faith. Grace be with thee. By which he seems to forewarn his disciples that they should by no means be captured or deceived by the allurements of the worldly philosophy of the sophists, which is indeed contradictory to the truth, and is not peaceful, but full of wordy disturbances and vain disputes; he expressly intimates that such Philosophy ought to be held as a "science" falsely and not in the truth of the thing, no less than other spurious sciences which depend therefrom. Furthermore, he also seems to suggest to his disciples that such Christians who profess it with excessive devotion and fervor are—through the cunning and fallacious sweetness of that philosophy—led into notable errors regarding the faith, which clings firmly to the anchor of that eternal wisdom.

<margin>Colossians 2:8</margin>
Furthermore, in the same sense, he gives to his Colossian disciples the caution I cited before:
> Beware (he says) lest any man spoil you through Philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the elements <note>or "rudiments"</note> of this world, and not after Christ Jesus, etc.

By which he commands us Christians to leave the false Philosophy of Athens, and to embrace that true one which is according to Christ. And for this reason he says, in the same Text:
> Walk in Christ, rooted and built up in him, etc.

By which he argues that Christ is the only Cornerstone and basis of true Philosophy: Inasmuch as all creatures—indeed, the whole world itself—have Him as the foundation for their existence and essence (which are the subject of Philosophy). And consequently it is clear that the foundation of Ethnic <note>Pagan or non-Christian</note> Philosophy is sandy or fabulous and therefore of no value, vigor, or esteem. Hence elsewhere St. Paul says: *Other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.* But now, the same Apostle proves how this is opposed to the false foundations of the nations.
<margin>Ephesians 4:17-18</margin>
> This I say, that you walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart, etc.

As if he were to say: Do not walk according to the vanity of the philosophy or wisdom of the nations and Pagans, because they have their understanding obscured by darkness—that is, they are led by a false and imaginary wisdom—and consequently are alienated from the ways of the true wisdom of Jesus Christ because of their ignorance.

It remains now, in the next place, for us to come to the opening and unfolding of the particular errors and false positions of Aristotelian philosophy, so that I may more clearly and lucidly expose them to the judicious world by comparing their vanity and falsehood with the goodness and perfection of the other.

# ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

### CHAPTER VI.

#### *In which the false and erroneous doctrine of the Ethnic <note>The "Ethnici" refers to the pagan or Gentile philosophers of antiquity, as opposed to sacred or divinely inspired writers.</note> Philosophers—and especially that of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking about while lecturing.</note>—is explained: where it is also proven, for certain reasons, that their doctrine is built upon the foundations of the wisdom of this world, and not upon the wisdom descending from God.*

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:20. 1 Corinthians 3:19.</margin>
I hear even now (as it seems to me) some of the sharper-witted Aristotelians replying and saying: "How can this wordy man prove that the wisdom which is the foundation of Peripatetic philosophy is not 'from above'—that is, from God, who is the Father of Light?"

<margin>1 Corinthians 2:12.</margin>
To examine this objection, it is necessary that we compare those two types of wisdom proposed by the Apostle. First, **St. Paul** says: **God** has made the wisdom of this world foolish. And elsewhere: *The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God: for God knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.* And for this reason, the Apostle says elsewhere: *We have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we might speak of the things given to us by God, not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the doctrine of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.* For the natural <note>original: "Animalis homo." This refers to the "soulish" or unspiritual man who relies only on his physical senses and reason without divine grace.</note> man does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, etc. With these words of the Apostle well-weighed, we must first inquire whether Aristotle was a "natural man" or not. If indeed he is found to be such, what can be expected from him except worldly wisdom and a philosophy that **St. James** calls "soulish, earthly, and demonic," which in itself is nothing but sheer foolishness? For the natural man (to use his words) does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him.

<margin>Colossians 2:8–9.</margin>
The Apostle therefore commands us to beware of this kind of philosophy, since it is founded upon the traditions of men and the elements of this world, and not upon Christ. Indeed, he explains Greek wisdom more directly in this way, distinguishing it from that of the Jews and Christians: *The Greeks seek wisdom; the Jews seek signs; but we preach Christ crucified,* etc. By this he argues that the Greeks seek worldly wisdom, which consists chiefly in speculation or contemplation, just as, on the other hand, the wisdom of the Jews is occupied with practice—namely, in signs and ocular demonstrations—without which they are unwilling to have faith.

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:22.</margin>
And finally, he names a third Wisdom, which is truly the real one: Jesus Christ, in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily.

<margin>Colossians 2:9. 1 Corinthians 3:11.</margin>
And this is that real and sincere wisdom from above, from the Father of Light, which is to be sought with all diligence by Christians; for upon this, every true philosopher ought to place the foundation of his philosophy, according to this saying of the Apostle: *No one can lay any other foundation

<column-break/>

than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.* But if the sophists of this age reply that perhaps Aristotle arrived at a knowledge of Christ in some way, or at least looked upon the wisdom of Moses and the Prophets even if from a distance; to these I answer: just as Aristotle’s age preceded the incarnation of the Word, so it is also made manifest that he understood little or nothing at all of the Mosaic doctrine (which consists in the creation and ordering of the world through the spagyric <note>The "spagyric act" refers to an alchemical-like process of separation and refinement. The author views God’s creation of the world as a process of separating light from darkness and matter from spirit.</note> act of the divine Word), inasmuch as he taught in his writings that the world has existed from eternity.

I confess that Plato, who was his teacher, was more occupied with the subject of true wisdom, as it is right to gather from his writings.

But his disciple Aristotle, puffed up with vain glory, through a certain monstrous deviation from the Stoic or Platonic discipline, and desiring to claim the name of "the Wise One" for himself alone in the world, named a new wisdom—or rather a worldly philosophy—which he afterwards called "Peripatetic" (distinguishing it from others and trumpeting that he was its leader). Thus, inflated with a remarkable Philautia <note>original: "Philautia." A Greek-derived term for "self-love" or excessive vanity.</note>, he defiled the truth with infinite fictions and falsehoods produced from his own imagination or personal concepts.

From this arose the Aristotelian philosophy, from a bad origin; a mixture, I say, of the false and the true, made from a small amount of wisdom and a great deal of foolishness. Whereas, on the other hand, pure and simple wisdom is constituted from truth alone, being ordered by the Spirit of God alone.

<margin>Acts 17.</margin>
Furthermore, if the Peripatetic, Stoic, or Epicurean doctrine had been perfect and according to the instructions of the true wisdom of Jesus Christ, why did the false sages of Athens persecute that true and sacred philosopher, **St. Paul**, with such hatred when he preached the true wisdom of Jesus Christ to them?

From these things it is right to conclude what kind of wisdom it is upon which Aristotle built his philosophy: namely, a wisdom discovered and handed down from himself, and consequently worldly and human, and not that sincere wisdom which is from God.

But so that I may approach the matter itself more closely, as if to the very kernel: I shall compare the two types of wisdom proposed by the Apostle **James** with one another, so that you may understand from this which of them is more worthy and more to be embraced by pious men. **James** says: *Wisdom that contradicts the truth is not from the Father of Light, nor is it peaceful, nor modest, but is earthly, natural, and demonic.* And the Aristotelian wisdom and philosophy is of this kind, since it is litigious and full of disputes—
<margin>James 3:15.</margin>

By contrasting the teachings of St. Paul and St. James with Aristotle's belief in an eternal universe, the author portrays Peripatetic thought as a "demonic" or "earthly" deviation from the true Mosaic and Christian foundation.</summary>

# FIRST SECTION, BOOK II.

...full of computations, fallacies, quibbles, and controversies: all of which properties are opposed to the nature and condition of true wisdom. 
<margin>2 Timothy 2:23.</margin>
Hence it was that Timothy was warned by his teacher Paul to separate himself from the company of those who teach a doctrine differing from true wisdom: asserting that those who do so are puffed up with pride and know nothing, but are obsessed with vain questions and wordy contentions, from which arise strife, etc. But such is the doctrine and philosophy of the **Christian Aristotelians** <note>These are the Scholastic theologians who integrated Aristotle's logic into Christian doctrine, a practice the author rejects as overly intellectualized.</note>, seeing as its custom and habit is to always be engaged in questions, disputes, and quibbles. And this is the reason (as has been said) for such great ambiguity and the multitude of "distinctions" <note>In Scholastic logic, "distinctions" were technical nuances used to resolve contradictions; critics argued they were merely tools to avoid the plain truth.</note> which pave the way both for sustaining falsehoods and defending truths. From this have arisen among men not only sects of Philosophers (as we declared above), but even sects of Religion and opinions, from which come disputes and litigious contentions—not only in the academic schools but even among the different factions of the common people in religion. 

But truly, if their Philosophy or wisdom were built upon **Jesus Christ**, the sole **Cornerstone** (who, as He is all in all, is indeed the single and simple essence), then without doubt both the learned scholars and men of lower or lesser condition would agree in a single unity with Him, who is but one and the same in us all. For in Him and through Him we are made brothers, and even heirs with Him of the eternal kingdom; and again, in Him we live, move, and have our existence <margin>Acts 17.</margin> (as Saint Paul testifies). We ought, without any question or dispute, to know that highest good within ourselves, which the true wise men of every age have sought with such diligence and desired with a Tantalus-like appetite <note>A reference to the Greek myth of Tantalus, suggesting a deep, unquenchable yearning for a truth that seems just out of reach.</note>. 
<margin>Luke 17:21. 1 Corinthians 6:19.</margin>
Does not **Christian Philosophy** teach us that the kingdom of God is within us? And that the operator of all wonders is within us? And that we are the **Temple of God** and the **Holy Spirit**? And that we are members of Christ? Since this is so, why should contentions, disputes, and vain quibbles arise among us regarding the ambiguities of manifold questions and words? Or why should we corrupt and disturb our more mature senses with dull distinctions? We depart from the **Unity** when we follow human inventions and the foolish, diabolical wisdom of this world. # BOOK II OF THE FIRST SECTION.

It is a wonder that some of our Academics, <note>In this context, "Academics" refers to university scholars and students.</note> who have been devoted to Peripatetic philosophy <note>The "Peripatetic" school refers to the followers of Aristotle, whose teachings dominated European universities for centuries.</note> for a span of seven years or even longer, are so corrupted by its false rudiments and understand so little of the essential nature of Divinity in creatures, that when they are promoted (after that time has expired) to a higher office or profession—namely, Theology—they become most hostile to those who recognize the mystery of divinity within created things. And although they notice that the scriptures, in many places, speak of the Word of God or the incorruptible spirit, they nevertheless assert—using Academic distinctions which they take from clearly pagan <note>original: "ethnicis"</note> philosophers and their agile and compliant commentators—that the naked and simple truth is so wrapped in clouds of equivocation that they sink it into an abyss of deeper doubt and ambiguity than it was before. For example, while the entire harmony of the divine Bible is that God is in all things and over all things, and that the holy spirit of discipline is in every thing; some of them immediately respond with a distinction (as was declared above) that He is in all things *virtually*, but not *essentially*. As if, forsooth, His power <term>virtus: the active power or "virtue" of a thing</term> could be distinguished from His essence! Again, where it is said that God works all things in all, they say: "It is true, insofar as He is the principal and primary cause." But, they say, "there are many secondary and subordinate agents which act of themselves and in themselves without the first cause of things, such as Angels, Stars, Elements, Meteors, <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note> and composite creatures, etc." And so, with Aristotelian sophistries of this sort, they attempt to stain the truth of the matter testified by the scriptures—which say in simple and plain speech that God works all things in all. For if God, with, in, and through His essential spirit, fills all things, we must believe that this spirit works all things in all and in every creature which it immediately fills; and this occurs without any assistance from the creature, seeing as the creature has nothing it did not receive from the creator. Moreover, what it has received from God cannot be separated from God. For how is it possible for a created instrument <note>original: "organum"</note> to help its creator by any act of its own, when the creator fills it and acts and works in it alone, doing what He wills and when He wills?

<margin>Isaiah 44:24.</margin>
The prophet says: *I am the Lord, making all things alone, and there is none with me.* Nor should this seem foreign to anyone, since the scriptures themselves testify that He is all in all.

<margin>
1 Corinthians 15:25.
Wisdom 12:1.
Colossians 1:16.
</margin>
And again (as before): *The incorruptible Spirit of God is in every thing.* And the same elsewhere: *In Christ all things were founded; through Christ and in Christ all things were created; all things consist in Him; He is the one holding preeminence in all things,* etc. He does not mean that this presence of God is by accident, but essentially. Since this is so, it follows that this Distinction (along with all others of the same grain) is false, which says that God works mediately, but not

<column-break/>

immediately, and consequently, that a creature could act by itself or immediately without the assistance of the divine act. It is as if someone were to say that the divine essence or power could be divisible, or that the divine nature must therefore be partitionable and separable from the divine root because it exists in different instruments. I can therefore boldly conclude and make it known to everyone: that if Christian scholastics <note>The "Scholastics" were medieval and Renaissance theologians who sought to reconcile Christian doctrine with Greek logic.</note> spent those seven years, which they waste in mastering the discipline of Aristotelian philosophy, in learning the knowledge and doctrine of true and sacred wisdom, they would without doubt not wish to wander so monstrously in the manner of the pagans. Nor would they attack the precepts and laws of true wisdom with so many questions, disputes, contradictions, and quarrels at the end of that time. Instead, they would be rendered more fit or prepared to proceed in the strict and direct way of seeking and acquiring that mystical wisdom which God (as the Apostle witnesses) revealed and ordained to be revealed in its own time to the elect and those best deserving of God. Thus, at the end of that holy inquiry, following the examples of the Apostles and holy men, they might become as powerful in virtue and power as they currently seem to prevail in this world by words alone, without any evident essential effect. For they are deprived of that good fruit which usually accompanies true wisdom by the erroneous doctrine of their seducing master. But lest our Aristotelian Academics believe my words are vain, or publish or argue that this Peripatetic doctrine can bring them greater fruit and utility than any other drawn from the Sacred Text: let me first enumerate those fruits in this place which our sacred philosophy can bestow upon the world. Then, afterward, let those worldly philosophers see if they are able to extract such real and essential utility from the Aristotelian text. If not, I would have them be silent, and grant praise and honor to the more worthy wisdom, and relegate the inferior philosophy to eternal exile from human memory. That is, let them follow the better Philosophy with the greatest diligence, and embrace it with serious Christian veneration. # BOOK II OF SECTION I.

<margin>
Johannes Velcurio’s commentary on Physics, Book 3, Chapter 5.
</margin>
...whether they agree or not. All the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking around the colonnades of the Lyceum.</note> agree on this point: namely, that winds, lightning, thunder, comets, clouds, and other such meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and snow, not just falling stars.</note> are produced by the attractive power of the sun and other stars. They say that by means of this power, vapors and exhalations are "attracted" and raised up from the earth and waters into the higher regions of the air. Hence Velcurio, following the mind and opinion of Aristotle’s physics (of which he was a commentator), says: "Just as vapors are more or less hot, so they are raised higher or lower from the heat of the sun and other stars, just as we see the sun 'drinking' and attracting water," etc. But I shall demonstrate that the matter is far different. I will ensure that anyone endowed with human sense may very easily discern with open eyes that neither the heat nor the power of the sun, nor stars, nor fire, nor any living creature, possesses the faculty of attracting anything to itself, but rather of repelling and dispersing from itself. For example: if it were in the power of fire to attract vapors to itself, then it would not allow the smoke of wood and coal to depart so easily from its embrace. But experience witnesses the opposite: for we are taught that the entire duty of fire is to rarefy <note>To "rarefy" means to make something less dense or thinner.</note> the dense substances of vapors and exhalations, making them subtle by penetrating and dividing their compact parts; it does not attract the vapors and smoke so generated to itself in any way. For we see with our own eyes that fire disperses those things created by its own action and scatters them through the vast spirit of the world. Furthermore, if we place a cloth soaked in water near a fire, we will perceive that the watery substance in it is converted into a smoky vapor by the power of the fire. Yet, so far is that smoke from being attracted by the fire, that we notice it expanding and dissipating everywhere through the space of the room without any evident attraction by the fire. It happens in exactly the same way in the operative nature of the sun: for by its own heat, it thins or rarefies water and any moist, thick, or combustible substance, and by rarefying it, expands it. However, the fact that a moist thing reduced to vapor tends upward does not happen because of some "attractive" faculty in the sun or stars, but by that natural appetite and inclination by which light things are accustomed to be raised on high. Therefore it follows that water thinned into vapor, or any solid or oily thing reduced to smoke or exhalation, ascends to the place destined for it by Nature—not by the compulsion of some external agent, but spontaneously and by itself. It is no different, conversely, than how a thing that is heavy and weighty makes its motion downward by its own inclination. But so that their error may shine even more clearly—the error of those who establish that the movement of vapors and exhalations from the earth and sea into the upper regions is caused by solar attraction—I will refer you

<column-break/>

to the experience of our experimental instrument, the weather-glass <note>original: "vitri calendari" — an early form of thermometer or barometer used to show the expansion and contraction of air.</note>. Through ocular intuition, you will find that all attraction from the circumference to the center (which is properly called attraction) is caused by cold and not by heat. For we see that by the power of cold, the water enclosed in the glass is raised upward into the neck of the vessel, and that this happens through the thickening of the air and its reduction into a narrower space within the glass. But on the other hand, we observe that if the sun, or a fire, or a human hand touches the glass, heating it, then the enclosed air will expand and suddenly fly out from the action of the heat. Indeed, so far is the air from being attracted by heat, that it precipitates and pushes down by several degrees the water that had previously been "attracted" up by the freezing and thickening faculty of the cold. Since this is the case, I wish the Christian Peripatetics would consider and diligently note the unhealthy teaching of their master <note>Aristotle</note>, which they follow so piously and with such affection to this day. Let them reflect on how immensely and crudely he erred in the chief argument of his *Meteorology*. What else is to be expected from him, other than that his entire fabric should collapse upon itself in the eyes of the wise? Briefly, I say that this and many other of his palpable errors are the reason why various saner-minded disciples of his have disagreed with his mind and judgment in many things: namely, in his opinion on the origin of winds, thunder, springs, and other meteors. For Johannes Freigius, a learned man well-versed in the discipline of Aristotle, who gave no small effort to investigating the mysteries of nature according to Peripatetic teaching (as appears from the contents of a large volume published by him called *Physical Questions*), writes these things in that same volume:

<margin>
Freigius, book 25, "On the Cause of the Winds."
</margin>
> "Although," he says, "the entire dispute concerning the winds, as with other meteors, is full of the wonderful works of God, for which no firm and sufficient causes can be brought forth in nature, nevertheless it is profitable to see how far human reason can progress. Sacred Scripture indeed says that God brings the winds out of his treasures, whence we hear their blowing, but we do not know whence they come or whither they go." These are his words.

<margin>
*Margarita Philosophica*, Book 9, Chapter 20.

### CHAPTER VII.

->*In which our almighty God Jehovah seems to call into question the spurious wisdom of this world and the wise men—or philosophers—for their false and erroneous doctrine concerning the causes of the world's existence, its origin, and finally the birth of Meteors.*<- <note>In the 17th century, "Meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note>

---

It was not for nothing that Aristotle was called *Cacodæmon* <note>original: "Cacodæmon," meaning an evil spirit or a "malicious genius"</note> by the Greeks. Indeed, with his subtle inventions and sophistries, he deceived the world—not only in that age but in those that followed—and led it away from the path of truth through the paths of error and ignorance, like a *will-o'-the-wisp* <note>original: "igne fatuo"</note>. For this sophist, through reasonings that are more fallacious than they appear by their mask of probability and truth, pretends that those things are mere accidents and have arisen by chance or "Hap" <note>original: "Casu"</note>, when in truth they are from above and, consequently, are essentially and divinely produced by the Holy Spirit. 

Also, according to his own doctrine, the heavens, the earth, the stars, and the elements were from eternity and not created; and he seems to support this assertion of his with arguments drawn from the quiver of his fictional philosophy and inventions prompted by his own brain, saying: *that from nothing, nothing is made.* <note>The famous Aristotelian axiom "Ex nihilo nihil fit," which contradicts the Christian doctrine of creation out of nothing.</note> Furthermore, he gives a human account of life and motion, and assigns limits to the sea in his own manner; he fancies the causes of all things according to his own imagination, and at his own pleasure assigns the occasion for the generation and corruption of things. 

He makes mention of "First Matter" <term>First Matter: the fundamental, formless substance that Aristotelians believed underlies all physical reality</term> and the natural form of things, yet he remains utterly ignorant of their internal essences. He attempts to teach us—quite irrationally and by conjecture alone—the causes of snow, frost, ice, hail, rain, clouds, mists, lightning, etc., by saying that they are generated in an external manner from vapors and exhalations drawn upward from the earth and water by the heat of the Sun and Stars, attracted into the middle region of the air, and condensed by the accidental cold of that place into the forms they possess. 

He produces many substances from his own invention and weak proofs, by which he shows that he is not at all deceived in such opinions of his; he even suggests that winds occur by hap and "accident" <note>original: "per accidens"</note>, namely by the attraction and elevation of hot and dry exhalations through the power of the aforementioned agents. He says that after those exhalations reach the middle region of the air in their ascent, they are driven downward again by the cold of that place, and then later, in their descent, they encounter other ascending exhalations and are forced to move

<column-break/>

sideways. This man, puffed up by excessive *philautia* <note>original: "philautia," meaning self-love or conceit</note>, also presumes to understand the causes of thunder and lightning, thinking that they likewise occur by accident along with the rest—namely, from the clash of vapors mixed with exhalations—along with infinite other frivolous and hardly believable fictions of this sort. He has veiled all of these with honeyed and subtle words, which are plainly external and superficial probabilities, in place of a real and central view of the truth itself.

But almighty God of heaven and earth, who is the sole author and operator of all these things, forms them all immediately through His eternal power and virtue, and sends them forth from His treasures whenever and wherever He pleases. He, the supreme judge of human actions, seems to mock that inventor of lies and his followers with the very words He used to address Job (rebuking him for his erroneous imaginations): <margin>Job 38:2.</margin> *Who is this that wraps sentences in unskillful words?* <margin>3.</margin> *Gird up your loins like a man:* <margin>4.</margin> *I will question you, and you answer me: where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have wisdom and understanding.* <margin>5.</margin> *Who set its measurements, if you know?* <margin>6.</margin> *Or who stretched the line upon it? Upon what are its bases fastened? Do you not profess, through your Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: Referring to the school of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking about</term> philosophy, to understand the causes of all things, both celestial and terrestrial? For by this power, my servant Joshua made the sun stand still in the heavens; and for the love of Hezekiah, my Spirit made the sun move backward in the sky. Can you perform these things by means of your wisdom? Will you 
<margin>34.</margin> lift up your voice to the clouds, so that a flood of waters might cover you? Will you send forth lightnings, and they shall go, and returning say to you: "Here we are," etc.? If the bases and foundations of your 
<margin>35.</margin> philosophy were essential and substantial, you would be able to perform all these things and far greater. For certain men chosen by me have performed all these things by means of my Spirit. For example: after a long absence of rain, Elijah made clouds appear in the sky, by which the parched earth was watered. And my prophets Moses and Samuel, by that same power, produced horrific thunder and lightning to the terror of their enemies. Elijah called down fire from on high, and Joshua called down stupendous 
<margin>36.</margin> hailstones. Who put wisdom in the inward parts of man, or who gave understanding to the heart? And yet you have dared—relying on the frivolous and vain effects of your own invention, which is founded upon the elements of this world and not upon my Spirit (which is true wisdom)—to ascribe my works (I who am the one and only creator and progenitor of all things) to your own

<column-break/>

creations; or rather, to attribute them to the operations of chimerical accidents <note>original: "Chimæreorum accidentium," referring to the Aristotelian idea that weather is an accidental byproduct of matter rather than a primary divine intent</note>. Shall he who contends with God rest so easily? In these words, the great God 
<margin>Job 39:32</margin> Jehovah seems to have addressed Aristotle and philosophers "of the same flour" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "of the same ilk" or "cut from the same cloth"</note>, who, being far too elated by their own concepts, presume with such audacity and rashness upon their own earthly and animal wisdom that they even dare to contradict and resist the truth that springs from God. I desire, therefore, from the depths of my heart, that these worldly philosophers—turning themselves away from that human wisdom of the Heathens—might humbly convert to the true wisdom and philosophy founded upon Him. For in doing so, they will humble themselves before the sole Creator of heaven and earth, and with a man as patient as he was repentant, they will answer Jehovah, saying:
<margin>Job 39:34; Job 42:2</margin> "Behold, we are contemptible; what shall we answer you? We have laid our hands over our mouths. We know that you can do all things, and no thought is hidden from you; therefore we have spoken foolishly, concerning things that far exceed our knowledge; we rebuke ourselves and perform penance in dust and ashes." By acknowledging now that there is no true wisdom except that which is from You, who are the Father of Light, by whose power You work wonders. Wherefore we confess that the wisdom of this world is mere foolishness, and that such worldly men who devote themselves to it are deceived, insofar as they neglect the divine wisdom, Christ Jesus, in whom is hidden the treasure of knowledge and wisdom, as the Apostle teaches us.

And so, I have expressed to you the duplicity of wisdom with its various effects, and consequently the two-fold nature of natural philosophy; I have taught the reason why all good Christians (contrary to the custom of our current age) ought to embrace the one with supreme reverence, and avoid and flee the other with great prudence. Now, in the following book, I shall propose the Mosaic principles upon which the entire fabric of sacred philosophy is supported.

HEADER: SECTION 1, BOOK III.

### *Mosaic Philosophy, Book Three, in which the true principles of Philosophy are elucidated.*

->Summary of the book.<-

In the present book, the author treats the true and essential principles of divine philosophy in general, and specifically expresses how inconsistent and varying the Pagan philosophers were in their opinions concerning the principles of all things. Here he also proves that the more excellent of the Greek philosophers or Naturalists took the foundations or principles of their philosophy from the true and holy philosopher Moses in a surreptitious <note>original: "surreptitio" — meaning stealthy or stolen</note> manner. This Mosaic philosophy was impressed or outlined by the finger of God, as its fiery characters were, so to speak, engraved and depicted in the dark *hyle* <note>original: "hyla" — from the Greek word for "matter," referring to the primordial substance of the universe</note> through the divine word or eternal wisdom.

He simultaneously shows that although these Athenian philosophers usurped these Mosaic principles to build their own philosophy and claimed them for themselves—imposing new names on them to hide such a monstrous theft from the world—they were nevertheless unable to penetrate to the profound and central understanding of them, nor could they rightly apprehend the mystery of holy wisdom or the Word with mature judgment. Therefore, they erected nothing but an adulterated structure or philosophy upon those poorly understood foundations: namely, a vain and deceitful worldly wisdom which is not carved from the essential rock of truth and power, nor rests upon Christ the only Cornerstone, but proceeds from the tradition of men and is fashioned according to the Elements of this world. It is no different than if we saw a fortress built of straw atop a rock, exposed to the winds on all sides and tossed by every whirlwind and storm.

After this, the author explains the true Mosaic principles, which are Darkness, Waters, and Light. Then he teaches that all fullness and emptiness consist in the presence or absence of the radiant and formal Spirit of God. And finally, he shows how two active properties, namely Cold and Heat, arise immediately from the aforesaid principles—Darkness and Light—just as two passive natures of the world, namely Moist and Dry, appear to claim their origins from those two active ones.
