## CHAPTER I.

### *In which the uncertainty and inconsistency of the Greek and Arabian philosophers regarding their natural principles is explained.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial E featuring foliate scrollwork and floral motifs.</image-desc>

It is a clear argument that the Pagan philosophers were not well-grounded in the principles of their philosophy, but were quite inconsistent and wandering in the primary causes of nature; for among their various sects, different and sometimes contrary accounts of the origins of things arose. For example, Thales of Miletus, who was counted among the seven sages of the Greeks, thought that waters were the beginning of all things. But Anaximenes with his disciples said that infinite air was the first cause or source of all

<column-break/>

things. And for this reason, Anaximander even thought that this universal <note>original: "Catholicum" — used here in its literal sense of "all-encompassing" rather than referring to a church</note> air was God. On the other hand, Zoroaster holds that all things have their origin from fire and light, as do the Pythagoreans themselves, who affirm that fire is universal in all and above all.

And certainly, each of these opinions, if considered rightly and in the proper manner, will be seen to approach the Mosaic truth. For by the power and presence of the Divine fire or light emerging from the depth of the dark abyss, the invisible waters were revealed and manifested, of which the subtler portion was converted into the vast spirit of the air. For this reason, both Thales and...

than ***Anaximenes*** <note>Anaximenes (c. 586–526 BCE) was an Ionian philosopher who proposed that air was the primary substance of all things.</note> seem to agree in some way upon one and the same subject. But truly, if we penetrate a little deeper into this business, we will perceive that these two philosophers insisted only upon a single, namely the material or passive Principle, from which the heavens, the earth, and every other thing has its substance or material existence. On the other hand, ***Zoroaster*** <note>The legendary Persian prophet and sage, often associated in the Renaissance with the philosophy of divine fire.</note> did not choose fire as his primary principle of all things without consideration or reason; for fire proceeded and appeared in act before the Waters or the moist nature were revealed—just as action is observed to precede passion, or a cause its effect. Nevertheless, he seems to have erred in his assertion, because an active principle can in no way be rightly considered except insofar as it has a relation to some passive principle. ***Zeno*** the Stoic seems a little more cautious than the rest, asserting that the substance of fire, converted into water by the mediation of air, was the primary cause of all things. But ***Empedocles*** attempts an even more certain way than ***Zeno***, since he chose the four Elements for his radical principles, of which he made two Active and just as many passive. 

Now, the chief error of these philosophers in their aforementioned opinions regarding the principles of things was that they did not consider that the divine power or the holy Word <note>original: "verbum sacrum"</note> was of greater antiquity than any of those principles they named. For if they had understood this with more mature judgment, they would undoubtedly have confessed—being instructed by reasons brought forth from the eternal unity of things or the essential center—that the divine Light or holy emanation (which the scriptures name with the title of the **Holy Spirit**) was the actual origin or principle of all creatures. Nevertheless, another divine property preceded this in one and the same essence, which is called Divine Power, which precedes its own act or emanation just as a Father precedes a Son in respect to time, order, and existence; it is said, not without justice, to exist before the Son, or the Creator before the creature. And hence the wise man says:

> Wisdom was created before all things.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 1:4</margin> Nevertheless, it is certain that some of the Greek and Egyptian philosophers—namely ***Plato*** and ***Pythagoras*** among the Greeks, and ***Hermes Trismegistus*** <note>A legendary Egyptian figure to whom many mystical and philosophical works were attributed; he was thought to be a contemporary of Moses.</note> among the Egyptians—were so upright and exalted in their minds, partly by observing the doctrine of their predecessors and partly by way of experience (which they acquired in their long travels and wanderings from the wise men of Ethiopia and Egypt, as well as from the Hebrews, Armenians, Arabs, Babylonians, and even the Indians). For we have received from trustworthy authors that ***Plato***, ***Pythagoras***, ***Hippocrates***, and others made journeys through those regions so that they might 

<column-break/>

increase and multiply their science and knowledge. This they would undoubtedly discern, albeit from afar and as if in a cloud: the true light clothed in a moist nature as if in a garment. Among others, it is handed down concerning ***Plato*** (and this same thing can be clearly drawn from some of his writings) that he had notice and a vision of the Word of God, and that he had read the books of **Moses**, and that he was very deeply versed in the mysteries of divinity; for which reason he is called "Divine" by the Christians themselves. 

In a similar way, that distinguished philosopher ***Mercurius Trismegistus*** <note>Another name for Hermes Trismegistus.</note> seems to prove through his Divine writings that he had read through the books of **Moses** and also had no small insight into the hidden secrets of God. This can be gathered from his profound discourses published under the name ***Pimander*** <note>The "Poimandres," the first and most famous book of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, which describes the creation of the world in a way similar to Genesis.</note>, in which he seems to acknowledge the holy Trinity, and also apprehends the logic of the creation of the world and the Elements in the **Mosaic** fashion, which he confesses was made and completed through the Word of God. Therefore, let me be permitted to ascribe a portion of Divinity to these two among all other philosophers. 

In this one thing, however, I cannot commend either ***Trismegistus*** or ***Plato***: namely, that after reading the **Mosaic** books (the subject of which the Divine Spirit dictated to **Moses**), although they professed the doctrine and truth regarding the principles of things which they extracted from them, they nevertheless refused to acknowledge their master in their writings. Instead, they usurped his principles for themselves and their own philosophers, having changed their names. But just as ***Plato*** acted inhumanely and ungratefully toward his master **Moses** in this matter, so too was he treated harshly in the very same way by his own disciple, ***Aristotle***. For ***Aristotle***, perceiving that the three principles of **Moses** had been veiled and hidden by his master ***Plato*** under new titles so they might be held as his own, also imitated his master. Paying him back in the same coin, he altered and obscured the names and titles of the ***Platonic*** principles with a new pretense and finally claimed them for himself, so that he might build upon them a philosophy newly invented by himself. 

By these things, one may see how poorly and insecurely a philosophy birthed from human tradition is established upon good foundations. It is no different than if a house of straw, or made of some other fragile and non-durable thing, were built upon a hard rock; regardless, with respect to the weakness and imperfection of the material from which it is fabricated, it cannot be long-lasting, insofar as its matter is heterogeneous <note>Meaning of a different or incompatible nature.</note> to the solid substance of its base, and consequently poorly joined and subject to every wind or whirlwind. In no other way is the structure of that ***Aristotelian*** philosophy basely arranged, being so spurious and heterogeneous in respect to those essential principles,

Regarding the Second Principle, it is that unique *passive* beginning from which the material existence of all things had its origin, which Moses marked with the name of "the Waters." For this reason, the **Ternary Number** [The Triad/Three] is held by all the wise—philosophers, Theosophers, and Kabbalists alike—as the root of all perfect numbers.

And this is the reason why they do not acknowledge, or at least very little admit, that any true meteorological philosophy can be taught through the records of the Holy Spirit in the sacred page; they believe that only those things which regard the salvation of the human soul can be drawn from there. This is so, even though it is nonetheless evident that there are entire pages, as much in the books of Moses, Job, the Psalms, and the Prophets, as in the New Testament, which primarily invite Christians to the unlocking of the mysteries of true Meteorology and to the knowledge of the immediate actors within them (that we may offer them the highest honor and reverence), as a royal way and without any deceit or disguise.

BOOK III OF THE FIRST SECTION.

so that by this reasoning we may admire the marvelous works of the Creator, as much in the heavens as on the earth, which He has wonderfully produced by the mediation of His Word from the origin of the world to this very day—and especially in this sublunary <note>The "sublunary" world refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, the region "below the moon" which was traditionally thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</note> world—so that

The Mosaic principles are plain and evident to those who wisely contemplate the words of that most excellent philosopher, Moses, expressed in the first chapter of Genesis. For before any mention was made of that <term>spagyric<gloss>A term from alchemy referring to the process of separating and recombining elements to purify them.</gloss></term> separation which was performed by the power of the Word of God—or the Spirit of that divine *Elohim*—in the work of the six days of creation, it is said that darkness was over the face of the abyss, and that the earth was empty and void. From these words it is clear that heaven and earth were not yet reduced into "act" or essential form, but remained as one unformed thing: that is, a rude, singular, and undigested mass. Thus, all things were "folded up" <note>original: "complicitè"</note> and contained within a single dark abyss, which was as of yet "unfolded" into nothing. For example: we see that a great tree, with its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, and fruit, is folded within a nut or seed; yet we find nothing of the sort unfolded there, except in the imagination alone. St. Augustine compares this Mosaic "NOTHING" or unformed thing to a "potential speech," which, while it exists only in the mind of the speaker, seems like nothing to the listener—that is, it exists in potential, but is nothing in actuality. But when that speech is uttered by a living voice, then that which was previously folded in the mind of the speaker is now unfolded and grasped by the listener. Plato compares this state of "Nullity" to a vision in a dream, which, when a man is awakened from sleep, appears as nothing except in the memory. But, because this phrase, "God created all things out of Nothing," has disturbed the minds of many even very learned men, and caused them to hesitate quite a bit in their understanding of its twin senses, I have proposed to offer a few things regarding "Nothing" itself, and to briefly explain my opinion on it in this place.

The Prince of the Peripatetics <note>A traditional title for Aristotle.</note> says: "Out of Nothing, nothing comes." This is indeed a learned sentiment and an infallible axiom for a person endowed with such great erudition, if the sense of the word "Nothing" were always to be understood and interpreted in one and the same way. All things, therefore, in the beginning were implicitly contained within the divine power (as has been demonstrated). With respect to human capacity, this state was "unformed, thin, and empty," insofar as it was contained in one unformed and invisible mass of waters. For this reason, it was called the Mother of the Elements and the seed of all things. We see this in nature: the entire plant or tree is enclosed within a tiny, misshapen seed or kernel, and it can in no way be grasped by human reason or sense until it explicitly appears from the surface of the earth. In the same way, the primordial water was invisible and without form or shape, as if veiled by shapeless darkness. For darkness was over the face of the abyss, which was called the *First Matter* <note>Latin: *Materia prima*</note>. This matter possessed no formal act within itself that human understanding could perceive, and for this reason, it was said to have existed in potential alone. 

A certain profound philosopher, deeply versed in the mystical works of creation, speaks in these words: "The first matter, from which the waters went out, was Nothing." By this, he means the material of the waters was extracted from "Nothing." However, this must not be understood according to common human sense—namely, that God created the waters from an absolute void. Yet those words are correctly brought forth from the Scriptures, because in the beginning, "Nothing" was visible. But if the wise wish to elevate their minds above common understanding to find the origin of the waters through proper contemplation, then they would certainly realize that before the creation of the waters, there was a certain matter within the supreme mystery, or divine power, or the dark and unformed abyss. This abyss was the Catholic <note>Here meaning "universal" or "all-encompassing."</note> or universal Treasury-Chest of God, from which the waters flowed at creation. 

This is confirmed by many passages in the Hebrew Bible. For in <margin>Hebrews 11:3</margin> the Apostle Paul, in the place cited previously, says: "By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were made from things which do not appear." From this, it is clear that things which are visible were originally made from things that are invisible. Thus it is manifest that things which fall under human sense did not originally appear to the senses, and consequently, in our judgment, were regarded as if they were not. Again, in <margin>1 Corinthians 1:28</margin> <note>The text says "1. Cor. 28," but refers to Chapter 1.</note> he says elsewhere: "God chose the things that are not, to destroy the things that are." Hence also that distinguished Cabalist <note>A practitioner of Cabala, a form of Jewish mysticism.</note>, Reuchlin, says with the 

<column-break/>

<margin>Reuchlin, Book 3, *On the Art of the Cabala*</margin> agreement of others: "It is written," he says, "in the book *Bahir*: 'Nothing' is the principle, except for Wisdom." And this is the infinity itself of the three highest numerations <note>A reference to the Sephirot, the ten attributes or emanations in Cabala.</note> of the Cabalistic tree, which you are accustomed to call the three Persons in divine matters. This is the most absolute Essence, which, while it is withdrawn, immanent, and at rest within the abyss of darkness—or (as they say) looking toward "nothing" <note>original glyph: <image-desc>A cabalistic symbol for the void or 'Ayin'.</image-desc></note>, that is, "Nothing" or "No-Being" and "No-End"—remains so because we, punished by such a meager poverty of intellect regarding divine things, judge those things which do not appear no differently than those things which do not exist. 

But when that essence shows itself, so that it becomes "something" and truly subsists, then the *Dark Aleph* is converted into the *Bright Aleph* <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the author uses it to symbolize the transition from hidden potential to revealed light.</note>. For it is written: "As is its darkness, so is its light." These are his words. It is clear, therefore, that although darkness and invisibility appear to our senses to be "Nothing" in comparison to those things we see by means of light, they are nevertheless all real and essential before God. Therefore, that NOTHING—or that unformed vacuum relative to our weakness and capacity—from which the Waters (the material principle of all things) were imaginarily extracted, appears as a material existence to Him in whose divine power it was reserved. For nothing can be in God that is not <margin>Romans 11:36</margin> an essential reality or an existing thing, as "from Him, through Him, and in Him are all things," as we are taught by the sacred Text. 

Therefore, both the dark matrix of things (the unformed womb of the waters) and the watery infant (the humid Nature which gradually gushed forth from the dark Abyss or unformed Chaos by the power of the Word or Spirit of *ELOHIM* <gloss>God (Hebrew)</gloss>) were actually in God before they appeared. That is, they remained in the power of the Almighty and existed in the disposition of His will, just as the blueprint of all things to be built was first in the mind of the Builder. Therefore, it is clear enough that the word "Nothing" was taken to mean "unformed matter," and consequently it was without name and essence, since it is "form" that usually gives a thing its name and its being. # ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

as an invisible thing, which does not seem to exist for the reason that it does not appear to the senses. Now truly, the text of my Master Moses seems clearly to confirm that this general matter was the Waters, which the presence of the spirit of Elohim <note>Hebrew: God</note> informed in a general way and reduced into action by imposing the name *Shamaim* <note>original: *Shamaim*, Hebrew for "Heavens"</note> upon them; and that they were the primordial material principle from which the existence of the world was fashioned, no differently than a house is shaped from a rough and deformed mass of mud. First, he makes mention of the waters over which the Spirit of the Lord was carried, and this immediately after the naming of the dark abyss, and the Earth without form and void; and this occurred especially before any creature was explicitly formed, and before the Spagyric <note>The "Spagyric" art refers to alchemy, specifically the process of separating and recombining elements to reach a purer state</note> separation of the first Day was made. By which it is clearly argued that the waters were the material Principle of all things when they were informed or actuated by the Spirit of Elohim: For they were marked by the proper name of "Waters" before the work of the first Day. Second, it was the same spirit of Elohim who, acting as a sort of midwife, made that deformed womb bring forth its offspring, and imparted to it form, action, and life. Again, from the same Chapter of Moses we learn that the waters were the subject of all those separations which, in the time of creation, were effected by the spagyric or fiery power of the same Spirit or Word of God. Third, the heavens, which were arranged in the upper region of the world, were cast from the purer, clearer, and worthier portion of the Waters; while the lower Elemental region was cast from their grosser, thicker, darker, and viler substance. Furthermore, there was a certain intermediate consistency of them marked with the name of the Firmament, participating in both extremes, whose office it was to divide the subtler or upper portion from the grosser or lower. Then the lowest portion of the Waters

<column-break/>

(which I call, not without justice, the Universal Element <note>original: *Elementum Catholicum*. In this context, "Catholic" means universal or all-encompassing</note>) is distinguished into other spheres or orbs, which the learned world calls by the name of "elements." In truth, these are nothing else than the alteration of the fourfold Universal element or lower waters, produced by the various-formed breath of the Divine Spirit, as will be discussed more broadly below. We see therefore from the preceding how the Spirit of Elohim fashioned the entire fabric of the world from that moist nature or Waters.
<margin>2 Peter 3:5</margin>
This is also clearly proved from these words of the Apostle: "the heavens," he says, "were of old, and the earth consisting out of water and through water by the Word of God" etc. But the world is composed only of heaven and earth; wherefore it follows that the whole world is made, with respect to its matter, from water and through water, but as for its form or essence, it has this from the Word of God or Spirit of Elohim, who (as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential early Christian theologian</note> says) imparted a fiery power or vigor to the waters. Now truly, since the stars are estimated to be nothing but denser portions of their own orbs, and since every creature of the Elemental kingdom is composed of elemental matter, it must necessarily follow that both the stars of the firmament and the creatures of the lower world—whether they be meteorological phenomena, or of a more perfect mixture, such as Animals, Vegetables, and Minerals—have their existence from the waters. Just as they were brought forth into light by means of the word of God, so also they eternally consist, and are sustained and preserved in their essence and existence by the eternal word or Spirit of Elohim, as will be clearly explained to you in the following chapter.
I come now to the description of that Universal principle, whose role it is to give life and being not only to any portion of the waters in general, but also to every creature fashioned from them.

...yet he remains outside all things. For that power, by which all the waters (which constitute the existence of all things) were drawn from their source or "Dark Well"—that is, from the raw chaos or abyss—is, as previously shown, the Universal emission of spiritual rays, or that fiery and formal power <note>The "formal power" refers to the "Forma" or the soul/pattern that gives a physical thing its specific identity.</note> that gives essence to every thing. From this, it is clear that both the external or passive nature of all creatures in this world, and their internal or active nature, draw their origin or beginning from this eternity, which, relative to us, is **NOTHING**. Nevertheless, in respect to itself, it is "everything in all things" (as has been said); for in its eyes, Darkness and Light, visibility and invisibility—and even our potential "Nothing" (the First Matter) and "Something" (actualized reality)—are one and the same in essence, without any distinction or difference. For this reason, this eternal infinity—this "All in All" and "Above All"—is rightly described, first by the Apostle and then by the more Divine Philosopher, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed.</note>, in this manner:

And although, for the constitution of the world, this eternal Divinity shone forth out of the Darkness, and by the revelation of His hidden wisdom or Essential Power, caused all things—both visible and invisible—to exist formally, and thus the "Dark Aleph" <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet; in Cabalistic thought, the "Dark Aleph" represents God in his hidden, unmanifested state (Ein Sof), while the "Light Aleph" represents God as he begins to manifest.</note> of the Cabalists (the unity in the Aleph) was turned into a "Light Aleph"; nevertheless, that same spirit remains in Himself, not departing from the limits of His own uniformity. This is clearly declared in the disposition of the human mind, which is an essential ray of the divine spirit: for the mind is perpetually stable and without alteration in itself. This is true even though its property may sometimes be negative or privative—namely, when it does not wish to give to a petitioner, in which state its act seems to be "nothing" in effect, or it withholds its positive rays—and sometimes affirmative or positive, namely, when it grants a petition to the one asking, or deigns to emit the rays of its goodness. For if God <margin>Ecclesiasticus 1:10. Wisdom 12:1. Wisdom 7:24.</margin> has poured out this Spirit over all His works; if this incorruptible spirit be in every thing; and even if this Spirit be more agile, active, and mobile than any other thing—what, I ask, can hinder it from working immediately and absolutely by itself in all things? Therefore, the aforementioned distinctions, which are birthed from human invention, ought to be of no weight in respect to divine action, and consequently, all subordinate active or efficient causes ought to be banished into exile by the wise. For it is He Alone who works all in all, and consequently, He animates, quickens, and acts for the preservation of all things immediately and through Himself without the help of any of His creatures: as has been demonstrated above. Hence the Prophet: *I am Jehovah, making all <margin>Isaiah 44:24. Ecclesiasticus 24:8.</margin> things alone, and none with me.* And elsewhere: *I, Wisdom, alone have circled the roundness of the heavens*, etc. It is therefore God the Father who acts through His Son or His Wisdom without the support of any creature—be it Angel, or Demon, or Stars, or winds, or Meteors, or composite creatures—according to that which is often, but not uselessly, cited by me: *Though there be many who are called Gods, whether in heaven or on earth, yet to us there is one God the Father, from <margin>1 Corinthians 8:3, 4.</margin> whom are all things and we in Him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through Him.* But there is not knowledge in all, etc.—as if he had said: It is not the creatures who do anything by themselves, but it is God, who through His eternal spirit, Jesus Christ, works immediately in this world by means of the creatures. We conclude, therefore, that this spirit sent forth from God is the unique, essential, and primary (as well as the final) agent in the world. For He is the Alpha and Omega <note>original: "Alpha & Omega"</note>, the active principle, the central act of the world-soul <note>original: "centralis animæ mundanæ actus"</note>, the Cornerstone of all creatures, animating, sustaining, and preserving their structures. Nor do I know any other essential nature in this, my sacred philosophy, except for this Creator alone within the creature—or the most holy worldly Architect in His works—to speak with the Apostle and Solomon. And in this way, we have the formal principle of all created things, described clearly and graphically enough for the reach of my meager talent, according to worldly reason.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the foundational principles of the universe, specifically addressing the concepts of "Fullness" (Plenum) and "the Void" (Vacuum). ### CHAPTER V.

->*Concerning the Full and the Void, what true Fullness and emptiness are, and by what reasoning the Pagan Philosophers erred in their inquiry concerning them.*<-

Now that the natures of the two constituting and composing principles have been explained—the first being the source of the existence of things, and the second the origin of their formal Essence—it is necessary that we understand the properties of the Full and the Void in their next order, and that we do so according to true and Christian Philosophy. But before I immerse myself into the core of the explanation of this matter, it is necessary that I first compare the opinions of the Pagan <note>original: "Ethnicorum" — referring to the non-Christian Greek and Roman philosophers like Aristotle or the Stoics.</note> philosophers on this subject with those of the Christian Theo-philosophers. As you have seen from what preceded, there is one principle regarding the material existence of things, which we called the **Waters**; and another which pertains to their formal essences. Thus, we find two opinions concerning the Full and the Void. The first is that of the Pagans, whose opinion is that all Fullness and Emptiness must be considered in respect to matter or substance, by which the cavity of the world is filled. Hence, they call that a "void" which is not filled by some material existence. For this reason, where there is nothing of the existence of the waters, they conclude there is a void. These thinkers do not allow even a jar or a well to be "empty," even if they are not filled with a perceptible body, insofar as they are filled by air itself, which they acknowledge to be a body. Indeed, they say that air prevents a void in the world and that an eternal fullness fills all things, insofar as its subtle body penetrates everything, and running everywhere through the world, fills all things with its existence. Therefore, however much any place is called empty, it is nevertheless, in the truth of the matter, full of air. To these I respond thus: that a dispute is made in vain concerning those things which neither are, nor were, nor ever shall be. For since the waters were that material principle from which all things had their existence—insofar as by them, through them, and in them the heaven and earth, from which all things consist, <margin>2 Peter 3.</margin> were fabricated, as the Apostle <note>Saint Peter</note> testifies—it is necessary to believe that the heavens and earth will sooner fail, and finally the whole mass of created waters (and consequently the material principle of things) be reduced to nothing, before any such thing as the Pagans dreamed of shall be found in the world. Therefore, I say the question is made frivolous concerning that which neither has been nor ever will be. But, on the other hand, the Sacred Scriptures seem to intend another "Full" and "Void," namely those which pertain to the formal or Essential principle. For where the Spirit or *Ruah-Elohim* <note>Hebrew: "Spirit of God"</note> did not appear before the beginning of things, and did not give form to the waters obscured by darkness, there, as was said,

<column-break/>

"Nothing" was present, and the "earth was empty and void" <note>Latin: *inanis et vacua*</note>. And therefore, in that respect, it was a **Void**, being nothing other than the absence of that spirit which animates and vivifies all things and gives them form by its presence. Hence it was called the **Dark Abyss**, a divine potentiality and consequently void, insofar as it was deprived of all "act" <note>In Aristotelian and Scholastic terms, "act" or "actuality" is the realization of a potential. Here, Fludd means the matter was "empty" because it hadn't been "activated" by God's light yet.</note>. Hence Moses says: *The earth was empty and void*. And John <note>The text here attributes the quote to John, but the marginal note and content refer to Job 26:7.</note>: *God stretched out the North over the empty and void and hung the earth upon nothing* <margin>Job 26:7.</margin>, that is, in the empty and void Abyss, as it was covered in darkness. By His wisdom God made the heaven and the earth, according to that saying of Moses: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth*. Here, by "the beginning," some of the more learned understand that infinite mystery of the Abyss. Whence also Saint John says: *In the beginning was the Word*. <margin>John 1.</margin> For it was from that dark principle (which according to human grasp seemed empty, void, and plainly Nothing, though it was very well known to God) that this bright Spirit went forth for the creation of the world, as is evident in many places of the sacred writings. And **Mercurius Trismegistus** says: *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss, and water besides, and an intellectual spirit was within the Chaos by divine power, etc.* <margin>Pimander 3.</margin> It is clear, therefore, that by the appearance of this spirit from the dark Mystery, the darkness was put to flight, the waters were brought into the light <margin>Job 12:22.</margin>, and all things were created by the essential Light emitted by that spirit, according to that saying of Job: *He reveals the foundations out of the darkness and brings the deathly shadow into the light.* This is as if he had said: from the condition of the void and nothing, He brought back the Waters, which are the material foundations of all things, and converted nothingness and the void into fullness and real existence by the power of the active and bright fullness emitted by the spirit, in which dwells (as the Apostle testifies) *all the fullness of the godhead bodily*. <margin>Colossians 2:9.</margin> Hence the Poet <note>Likely referring to Virgil or Lucan, common sources for this phrase.</note> said, and not foolishly: *All things are full of Jove.* And elsewhere: *Jupiter is whatever you see, wherever you move.* Do not the scriptures also say that God fills all things? And again: That He is everywhere? And again: That He is all in all? Here, therefore, it is argued that **Voidness**, **Emptiness**, **Nothing**, and **Darkness** are one and the same: namely, the absence of the actual and informing presence of divine power. For all fullness or repletion consists in the immediate action and property of the divine power. But God, through His spirit, had not yet shone forth from the darkness for the creation of the world. Therefore it stands that the first and unformed matter of the world was void and destitute of all grace (as far as we are concerned) in its actuating, creating, and informing. Whence the empty or...

...or empty, void, and Dark, or it was said to be in a formless state, as is clear from the previously mentioned words of Moses. The Earth, he says, was void and empty; that is, it had not yet tasted of the supreme fullness of the Spirit that gives form to all things. For darkness was over the face of the abyss: this is surely evident proof that this Spirit had not yet appeared. But after the appearance of the fullness of the Spirit of Elohim <note>original: "Spiritus Elohim" — the Hebrew term for the Spirit of God used in Genesis 1:2.</note>, the earth was no longer void and empty, but by reason of its participation in the fullness and divine goodness, the Text says that God saw that the work of that day was good—that is, full of divine goodness. Indeed, by the virtue of this Spirit, the earth would thereafter sprout green herbs, producing seed, and fruit-bearing trees yielding fruit according to their kind; and it brought forth green herbs, producing seed, etc. And God saw that it was good. From this, one may argue that the earth, which was previously void and empty, was now full by the salvific presence of that life and form of the Spirit—that is, overflowing with divine fire and the incorruptible Spirit of God 
<margin>*Gen. 1:10, 11.*</margin>
<margin>*Wisdom 1, Wisdom 12:1. Ephesians 4:10.*</margin>
according to that saying of Solomon: *The holy spirit of discipline fills the world.* And elsewhere: *The incorruptible spirit of God is in every thing.* And the Apostle says: *Christ fills all things.* By these we can see that all fullness comes from the essential divine act of the presence of the Divine Spirit, whereas, conversely, "emptiness" is said to be present where that formal life granted by the spirit is absent from the waters. This, indeed, cannot happen totally without the absolute destruction of the subject and its reduction to a state of nothingness, being thus deprived of the Spirit's presence. Nevertheless, it happens in part—as when this spirit sometimes withdraws from a creature, namely at the moment of death or the corruption of a specific creature. This is established by the words of the Royal Psalmist: *When God gives to creatures, they receive; when He hides His face, they are troubled; when He takes back His spirit, they expire and return to their dust; when He sends forth His spirit, they are renewed with good,* etc. 
<margin>*Psalm 104:21* <note>The text cites 104:21, but refers to verses 28-30.</note></margin>
By these things it is therefore clear that it is the presence of the Spirit of God which fills man and creatures with the Good of Life, and that His absence is the emptiness of life in the human spirit. But this emptiness is properly called "privation," insofar as it follows a preceding positive act. This is the reason why the void and the empty are so horrible in the nature of things: namely, because the extreme and absolute absence of the eternal emanation, or the removal of the Spirit from the Waters of the world, can least of all be tolerated. For every thing fashioned out of the waters desires to be informed <term>informed: to be given "form" or soul, moving from potential matter to a living thing</term> by the highest appetite of its nature. Therefore, it is abominable in nature to be deprived of all existence. It follows, then, that unless God had filled all things of this world with His spirit of Life, emptiness, vanity, and deformity would reign everywhere throughout the world, and consequently all things would remain in a state of Nothingness. But since God, by the shining presence of 

<column-break/>

His emanating spirit, created, sustained, and preserved all things from Nothing, it is therefore evidently clear that there is nothing in this world that is now absolutely empty and void—even though before the Beginning of the world the dark Abyss and the deformed matter of heaven and earth were such, as Moses and Job maintain. It is manifest, therefore, how vain and impossible the "void" and the "full" are according to the intentions of the Peripatetic <note>original: "Peripateticorum" — followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> Philosophers, compared to those things understood from the Scriptures. For the Mosaic "Void" and "Full" are Potentiality and Act; hence, through the reduction of potentiality (which is like Nothingness) into Act by means of the presence of the Spirit of Elohim, the void and the empty are converted into fullness. It is indeed no wonder if Aristotle never even thought of this kind of emptiness or fullness, since in one place he says: *Nothing is made from nothing.* And in another place he affirms: *Light is an accident of things,* and consequently it did not appear to his senses that an "accident" <term>accident: a non-essential quality (like color) that cannot exist without a substance to hold it</term> could take away emptiness or void, or confer fullness upon it by reason of its essence. But I now attack the Christian Peripatetics with their own weapons, and with a spear drawn from their own quiver, I oppose their assertion thus. It is a common axiom among them: *That the being of an Accident is to be in something.* I, therefore, shall oppose them with this kind of syllogism: If Light is an accident, then its being is to "be in" or to inhere in a subject. But Light can exist without any adhesion to any subject. Therefore, it is not an accident, but rather the purest and most essential substance of all. The Major premise is proven and conceded from the words of Aristotle—namely, that the being of an accident is to be within a subject. The Minor premise is confirmed by the authority of Moses, who says that Light was produced or created on the first day before any other creature; and consequently, it had no pre-existing matter in which it could inhere. Furthermore, it is beyond human grasp that God would create Accidents in time and order before substances or essential creatures. Moreover, God is called the fountain, origin, and Father of Light, as the Scriptures hand down; and His spirit or Word is defined as Light, in which there is no darkness at all. And again, the Spirit of Wisdom is said to be the brightness or splendor and virtue emanating from Almighty God. 
<margin>*James 3:1, John 1:5, Wisdom 7.*</margin>
We conclude, therefore, that the true mystery of fullness and emptiness was entirely unknown to the Peripatetics, who were completely ignorant of the true wisdom which (as the Apostle testifies) descends from the Father of Lights. This appears even more clearly in that they falsely taught that the essential light or holy splendor—which is the basis and Cornerstone of the essential structure of every creature—is a mere quality or superficial accident.

### CHAPTER VI.

### *How two essential active properties, opposite in condition to one another, and then later as many passive natures arose from the two primary principles of things mentioned before; and by what reasoning all changes or alterations in the sublunary world are effected by their powers.*

It is my intention in this place to recount the births and origins primarily of the two active natures or essential virtues which proceed from the two principles of all things previously recited. I will then briefly explain the two passive conditions or properties that arise from the effects of these two active virtues. It must be understood, therefore, that just as the "potential" or "dark" principle is, in its essential property, contrary to the "actual" emanation of the Spirit or the "light" principle; so also each of them has produced into the world an offspring or essential property contrary and repugnant to the other in its condition—namely, Coldness and Heat. I shall deal succinctly in this chapter with the mystical method and reasoning behind the production of these virtues or properties, and in the first place, I will attempt to explain the profound origin of coldness to the best of my meager capacity.

It is clearly evident from what has been related before—and will be said even more clearly in the first book of this second section—that darkness is the immediate effect of the divine will, specifically of the Divinity when it is latent or contracted within itself. Consequently, darkness is the effect of the "privative" property of God, or the Divine Power, which is the Mother of Privation, Death, Vacuity, Emptiness, Deformity, and other such imperfections. For the deformed property of the <term>Nothingness</term> <note>original: "Nihili" — the void or non-being</note> or the Dark Abyss is naturally to rest, to be fixed, and in no way to act or work. The reason for this is that its desire is to have its existence in and around the center, in which there is no motion or action by which it might dilate itself toward the circumference. This is in direct opposition to the bright Spirit of God, or God in His manifest will or nature, who is occupied with actions and movements that tend from the center toward the circumference. For this reason, the Dark principle claims for itself, by a natural inclination, rest, idleness, and fixation. And this property generates or produces the essential virtue of its own condition, namely Coldness. This Coldness is chosen as the <term>Champion</term> <note>original: "Agonista" or "Athleta" — a combatant or athlete</note> to resist the assaults of its opposite, namely heat (from whose company motion and action arise). Thus, unless Coldness is agitated and incited by the agile action of heat, it does not move, but is seen to serve its somnolent mother—namely Darkness and privation—in a peaceful and 

<column-break/>

quiet manner. The offspring of these, as we have said, are fixation and rest, which cling to the center like sleepers and inhabit it; therefore, it is against their will to look toward the periphery unless they are stirred up by violence. And in truth, coldness is an essential act that proceeds from the Divine Power, which it serves chiefly in its action. For the Divine Power, being more concerned with the center, in that property of its own contracts its rays from the circumference into itself. This is according to that saying of <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic writings on magic and philosophy.</note>: *The Monad generates the Monad and reflected the heat back into itself.*

<margin>Pimander, 3.</margin>
It is as if he had said: that <term>Monad</term> <note>The "Monad" refers to the ultimate state of unity or the "One."</note>, as a divine power emitting its emanation (which was another monad of one and the same essence), reflected it back into itself—that is, toward the central point from which it sent out the Monad—so that it might rest there. And in this way, the archetypal world was produced before any creation of the physical world.

<margin>
Reuchlin, Book 3,
On the Art of the Kabbalah.
</margin>
The eminent Kabbalist, Rabbi Bair <note>Likely referring to the *Sefer Ha-Bahir*, an early Kabbalistic text.</note>, seems to support this: "Wisdom," he says, "when it was retracted into the Abyss of darkness, remaining indwelling and idle and looking toward nothing, is called *Ain* <note>Hebrew for "Nothing."</note>; and in this state, it is frequently called the dark *Aleph* <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet.</note>." In this contracted, or rather sequestered and private state of Divine Unity, it seems to work according to its negative property through its agent, Cold, whose sole endeavor is to make the waters rest. And it is proven that this agent within it is not an "accident" (as the vain doctrine of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, who taught that properties like cold were "accidents" rather than essential substances.</note> teaches), insofar as it is certain that no accident can be found in God. For He is the highest, purest, and absolute simplicity and a purely formal essence, existing in and through Himself, and consequently free from accidents. Therefore, since divinity is nothing but one essence, it is powerful enough out of itself—that is, from its simple nature—to produce any essential property whatsoever, not divided from its divinity, according to its pleasure.

<margin>Wisdom 7:22.</margin>
And for this reason, Divine Wisdom is called a Spirit that is "one and many" <note>original: "unicus, multiplex"</note>; one, I say, in respect to its essence, and many in respect to the essential properties that go forth from it. Furthermore, that the essential property or nature of Cold is that formal agent by which God, in secret and power...

# ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY. FOL. 26.

It is demonstrated by feeling and experience that [the Spirit], in its own state, acts to restrain and oppose the hostile assaults of cunning, as well as those of action and motion itself, and to destroy and reduce to nothing those affects which it produced in its open and positive nature through the power of heat. For while the <term>Spirit of Wisdom</term><note>The 'Spirit of Wisdom' in Fludd’s philosophy is the active breath of God that organizes the universe.</note> in its revealed and manifested property has operated through its warm breath from the South or the Eastern region (inasmuch as by its action, it thins dense waters into air, making what was thick, subtle, and what was opaque and dark, <term>Diaphanous</term><note>Diaphanous: Transparent or translucent.</note> and clear—indeed, even invisible), that same Spirit, by putting on its latent nature, through the mediation of its coldness, again deforms, destroys, and transforms it into a contrary appearance. For the Spirit, endowed with such a property and blowing from the <margin>Ezekiel 37:9</margin> North, condenses and thickens the previously thinned air, and brings it back from an invisible state to a state of visibility. And also that opacity, which had been made transparent or Diaphanous by the scattering and thinning of its parts, is now—by the cold and contractive power of the northern property, sent out by the act and operation of the divine breath—brought back again into an opaque and dense body. Thus, that which was agile, mobile, and alive, having been made so by the power of arriving heat, is now made numb, fixed, dead, and quiet through the invasion of cold. That which was light and of no sensible weight is contracted into a heavy and ponderous body or consistency. Just as we see that when the Northern wind blows, the air is converted into snow, hail, frost, rime, etc. Now, indeed, that it is only a spirit of one and the same essence which brings forth both of these effects by a contrary action or spirit, is established from these words of the Prophet: "Come, spirit," he says, "from the four winds and breathe into these slain," etc. By which thread of words he proves that there is only a single spirit (I say single and simple in essence, but multiple in operation, as the wise man says in the place cited before). But indeed, so that those things which we have proposed may be made even clearer, I would like you to listen to the <margin>Psalm 147:15</margin> words of the Prophet: "The word of Jehovah runs swiftly, who sends out snow like wool, scatters frost like ashes, casts down ice like crumbs; who can stand before his cold? Sending out his word, he melts them; as soon as he blows his wind, the waters flow," etc. From which we observe many things worthy of note. The first is that God, in his hidden and latent state, through his essential property of cold, now contracts toward the center those things previously expanded toward the circumference. Secondly, that the property of cold is attributed or ascribed to the Spirit of God in its Northern action, or in its privative or hidden condition. For the words are: "Who can stand before his cold?" Where-

<column-break/>

fore it clearly appears that there is an essential virtue in Divine power. Thirdly, that it must be an act of the <term>Monad</term><note>The Monad: A term from Pythagorean philosophy representing 'The One' or the unified source of all things.</note> or Unity in its dark, abstruse, and privative nature; both because it renders clear, bright, and transparent things obscure and opaque, and because it seems to take away motion, agility, and life from the air, which previously was moved, acted, and lived by the inciting of essential heat; and finally, because it is entirely opposed to the action of heat, which serves the emanating and life-giving divinity. Fourthly, that the effects of cold are destroyed and reduced to nothing by the act of the revealed nature of God—that is, through his sent-forth word. For the text says: "He sends his Word, and melts them," namely the snow, ice, and frost. Fifthly, that these contrary actions are performed by one and the same Spirit in essence, but multiple in condition, to fulfill the commands of Him who sends it. Furthermore, that the cold virtue in the wind is essential, a depriving or congealing, mortifying and contracting act of God, is indicated by these pages of holy scripture: <margin>Job 37:10</margin><note>The original margin notes Job 27:9, but the text quoted refers to Job 37:10.</note> "The strong God produces ice by his breath; by the blowing of God, the frost is frozen." I conclude, therefore, that coldness is an essential act of divine power, or of eternal wisdom wrapped in a veil of darkness, and therefore we know the divine will in such a state or condition through those effects which it produces; namely, in that by its evident act it contracts from the circumference toward the center, and for that reason, this virtue of God is the cause of congelation, thickening, contraction, constriction, fixation or immobility, weight, rest and leisure, darkening, mortification, privation, numbness, and the like.

...producing [light] out of the opaque and dark, etc. Thus, this formal <term>Champion of Light</term><note>original: "Lucis Agonista." Fludd uses the Greek-derived term "Agonista" to personify heat as a combatant or athlete struggling on behalf of light.</note>, namely heat, produced immediately from the act and motion of light, wages a perpetual war against cold, the guardian of darkness. For one cannot hold dominion until the other is gradually extinguished and, as it were, banished into exile. For this reason, just as Light with all its companions or adherents is said to be the act of positioning, the mother of formation, fullness, motion, life, health, and heat; so also heat operates according to the nature and disposition of its tireless and ever-working mother—namely, Light—to subvert and turn to nothing the effects of Darkness and cold. We see this in the natures of the warm winds, namely the Southern and Eastern. For, just as the Northern and Western winds more or less gather, contract, harden, condense, make heavy, fix, and render immobile and opaque not only the air but also other things (both those of a similar nature and those of a different nature), so, conversely, the aforementioned warm winds are accustomed to dissipate, dilate, and rarefy the air, or make it <term>pellucid</term><note>Pellucid: Translucent or clear.</note> and transparent, volatile, and agile or mobile—the very air which the cold winds had previously altered in the manner described. And all of this is fundamentally accomplished by the <term>spagyric</term><note>Spagyric: A term from Paracelsian alchemy referring to the process of separating and then recombining the essential components of a substance to purify it.</note> or separative act of the Spirit or divine Word. This is proved by the words of the Prophet in the aforementioned text: *He sends out,* he says, *His word and melts them; as soon as He makes His wind blow, the waters flow,* etc.<margin>Psalm 147:18.</margin> It is as if he had said that He sent out His Word riding upon the wings of the winds, and that by the active and warm power of that Word, the snow, ice, and frost were dissolved, and reduced from their fixed, opaque, thick, heavy, and mortal disposition into the mobile, clear, thin, and light consistency of water and air. And thus, that which God worked by His word in its secret, contractive, and cold property—for the text says: *The word of Jehovah runs swiftly, who sends out snow like wool,* etc.<margin>Psalm 147:15.</margin>—all of this, I say, He converts through His word (as soon as He has blown His wind opposite in place and nature) into agile, transparent, light, and thin air. From these things, therefore, it is clearly indicated how these two opposing powers, namely Heat and Cold, have their origin from one and the same Spirit in its fundamental essence. In its latent nature, this Spirit acts as the principle of the formless and the dark; hence it is called the **Dark Aleph**<note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In Fludd’s mystical cosmology, it represents the primal unity of God. The "Dark Aleph" is God in His unmanifest, hidden state (Potentia), while the "Light Aleph" is God in His manifest, creative act.</note> or Divine Potential, in which state it seems in a way to rest and remain idle around the center of the Abyss. But on the contrary, in its open disposition, it puts on the nature of the active, informing, and Lucid Principle, whence it is now called the **Light Aleph** and the divine act. And in that state, it appears

<column-break/>

to us to act and to move from the center toward the circumference, and to cast the rays of its perfection everywhere through the waters, and in this way to communicate its life-giving nature to the creatures. And so it is clear that God is the fundamental principle of all things, from which principle two opposites in nature and condition exist, yet He remains nonetheless one and the same: immobile, unalterable, and permanently existing. Two things, therefore, consist in one Principle from the principles, and with the principles two active essential properties arise, from which all things exist. Hence God is rightly called by the Scriptures "The One and the All," and "All in all," and "Without Him there is nothing," and "The center of all, whose circumference is nowhere," and "In all and above all," etc.

From these things, therefore, you have clearly understood that these two powers, namely Coldness and Heat (however much they are opposed in operation or act), have drawn their origin from one and the same Spirit and Essence of the Divinity, along with two sources likewise distinct from each other in condition, from which they emanate; and that the Spirit of God, mediating through these two properties, operates in the world in a twofold way, namely by <term>rarefaction</term><note>Rarefaction: The process of making a substance less dense (e.g., turning water to steam).</note> and <term>condensation</term>. For it is observed in the universal element of the sublunary world that he produces opposite effects at the will of the Creator in the earth, water, and air, or the general Element; as will be declared below in a more expanded style.

It remains now for us to say a few words about the rise and nature of the two **passive properties**, which seem to have their generations and progressions from the active essential properties—namely, from the mutual action and opposition of Coldness and Heat. These, as has been said, have their roots either in the Will and privative existence of the divine nature, or in the Will and positive emanation of the same. Whence it is clear that the existence of these passive natures depends on the active ones. And first, I will explain to you the opinion of my mind regarding the birth or generation of **Moisture**, and afterwards I will speak of the origin of **Dryness**. 

We ought to imagine that if there were no formal Light to inform or bring into act the dark Abyss or empty Chaos, and consequently no heat to act and make a division between light and Darkness, then the formless and opaque Chaos would incline toward dryness, being as it were congealed by the action of the cold still hidden within it, just as we see in ice and frost. For it is certain that cold has dominion or infinite power where Heat is entirely absent. Just as may be seen under the Northern Sun, where all the waters are gathered into a cold and dry mass by reason of the absence of Solar heat; in a plainly contrary way, where the Sun or warm winds [have] their...

...directly emit the breaths of their heat, there cold is banished into exile, all its actions or effects are destroyed and turned into dryness by the nature of the earth, so that they are reduced to a dry, thirsty, and spongy mass. In no other way and by the very same reasoning (for both the Coldness and Heat, as well as the Moisture and Dryness of the world, derived their actions and passions from the aforementioned primary principles) do our essential properties operate in the primary materials. For <term>Chaos</term><note>The primordial state of existence before the creation of the universe, described here as cold and inert.</note> was a certain confused, cold, and dry mass, until the Divine Light appeared out of the darkness and operated upon the mass of frozen waters. Even Light, considered in itself—certainly without respect to its action upon the passive mass—was of a fiery condition, as heat, warmth, and dryness were perceived within it. Wherefore it follows that, just as coldness is in effect nothing but the act of divine power, and its act and dominion is made manifest and notable by the absence of Heat, so also dryness is nothing other than the passive nature appearing with the two aforementioned active virtues [Heat and Cold] while they are in the degrees of their intensity, in which state of active forces Moisture is perpetually absent. For example, in extreme cold, when all things are exceptionally frozen, dryness is present as Moisture is entirely lacking. Conversely, where the heat of the sun and the breaths of the Eastern winds heat the earth beyond measure, there also moisture is least to be found. As for Moisture, however, we say that it is of a somewhat <term>adulterine</term><note>original: "adulterinæ." Here used to mean "mixed" or "hybrid," rather than pure.</note> nature, or rather, that it holds the place of a <term>Hermaphrodite</term><note>An entity combining both active and passive qualities.</note>, insofar as it is born or derived from two active natures, so that it seems to participate in both at its birth. Hence it is that this passive property is of an intermediate condition between those two. Therefore, it serves to receive the impressions of the actions of either extreme. And all this we prove and demonstrate by such ocular observation. The North Wind, by its dominion, converts the existence of air into snow, hail, frost, and ice; that is, it changes it from a warm and moist substance into a cold and dry one. But where the Southern and Eastern winds begin to have dominion, then their breaths gradually penetrate those hard masses or piles, and by pulling them apart, they change them into a moist or wet substance. According to the sense of the words of the previously mentioned text: *When Jehovah emits his word, the snows and ice melt, etc.; as soon as he blows his wind, the waters flow, etc.* <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 147:18.</note> That is, from dry things they become moist. From this it appears that Moisture is nothing other than a mixture of cold and heat in some aerial or aqueous substance, previously solidified by cold, which is fluid in potential; and then, as the extreme coldness gradually decreases due to the presence of heat...

<column-break/>

...dryness recedes, giving place little by little to moisture, so that, unless Coldness is present with Heat, Moisture cannot appear. Thus, unless the Southern blasts look back upon the sighs of the North, they would hardly produce clouds and rain. So the Western blasts, insofar as they participate in and are in the middle between the warm South and the cold North, are accustomed to produce moister temperatures. But the reason for this fluidity is of this sort: we see from the aforementioned things that extreme cold renders air and water immobile and fixed. Consequently, it is an evident sign that some wind begins to predominate over the frozen mass when it begins to be moistened, moved, and resuscitated—indeed, a function which nothing but heat can perform. In an entirely similar way, the uncreated and all-creating Spirit of Light operated in the dark Abyss, while it was carried over its formless face toward the creation of the waters; it caused that dark mass, full of "potential waters" previously frozen by cold due to the absence of heat, to melt gradually. And then they were openly called by <term>Moses</term> by the name of "actual and real waters," and by <term>Hermes</term><note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom many foundational philosophical and alchemical texts were attributed.</note> they were called by the name of "Moist Natures," and they remain in that same state to this very day. For it is certain that both the subtle or aerial waters, and the coarse and thick ones, such as the seas, springs, and rivers, are moist and fluid; yet they are continually changed and altered from one nature into another, the Creator of all things so willing. These indeed occur in the <term>Universal Element of the lower world</term><note>original: "Elemento mundi inferioris Catholico." This refers to the sublunary realm where the physical elements change and decay.</note> as daily mutations and conversions through his angelic ministers moving upon the wings of the winds, whose task it is to bring it about that the waters rotate from one nature into another—that is, they are transformed from one form into another. But we ought to observe that the visible waters and all visible things, whether they be <term>meteors</term><note>In Fludd's time, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, such as rain, snow, or wind.</note> or other things composed of water, were later made and fashioned from invisible waters according to the doctrine of Saint Paul previously cited. And Moses acknowledges that the sea and the earth, which were the first visible things, were formed from the lower waters, as if from the Universal Air; and in the same place, he seems to establish the earth as the dregs or the <term>hypostasis</term><note>original: "hypostasin." A Greek-derived term meaning the underlying substance or the "sediment" that settles out of a mixture.</note> of the whole mass of waters, following the <term>spagyric</term><note>original: "spagyricam." A term for alchemical separation and purification; Fludd views the creation of the world as a divine chemical process.</note> division of the world by the act of the Word and the completion of the worldly fabric itself.

But, so that the mystical secrets of such a creation may become even more clearly known to you, I shall now more expressly confirm with an ocular demonstration everything that we have previously proven by reasons extracted partly from the Sacred Scriptures and partly from the most exact rules of true philosophy; whereby the faith of diligent readers and lovers of true philosophy may be increased with more confident zeal to believe those things which have been said.

BOOK III OF THE FIRST SECTION.

### An ocular demonstration showing to the reader exactly the origins and operations of each of the essential properties mentioned above.

Before we proceed to this ocular [visual] demonstration of ours, which will be performed in and through our experimental instrument, we must first consider that the universal air <note>original: "Catholicus aër"</note>, or the general element of the sublunary region, is a subtler and more spiritual portion of the Waters below the Firmament, of which Moses makes mention. Therefore, it is certain that any particle of this same air corresponds to its whole, and consequently the air enclosed in the glass of this instrument is of the same nature and condition as the universal air of the world. From which it is clear that by reason of their continuity, as the general air of the sublunary world behaves in its disposition, so also its particular air enclosed in the glass (which is a part of the Universal) behaves. Just as the Spirit <term>Ruah-Elohim</term><note>Hebrew for "the Spirit of God." Fludd identifies this biblical spirit with the active, expanding force of the universe.</note>, which moved over the waters, animated, quickened, and informed them by its presence, and expanded them by giving them motion; so indeed by its absence—or the cessation of its agile act and emanation, or by the contraction of its rays of activity into itself—the waters were similarly contracted, condensed, darkened, and made immobile and quiet. As is indicated by the condition of the North Wind, which proceeds from the privative or contractive power of that Spirit. But, as the waters by their existence fill the ample cavity of the world, so also the all-informing spirit is recognized to possess and be within every particle of them:

<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>
as the scriptures testify in the places previously cited. Wherefore, as that spirit works all things in all, although in diverse properties (whence it is called "manifold"), so indeed it sometimes works in these lower waters in its **Privative** property or power, namely in its breath from the North and West, to a greater or lesser degree; and sometimes in its **Positive** nature, namely, when it blows from the South and East. In the first property, it contracts by its coldness from the circumference to the center, as above; in the latter, namely by its warm power, it expands from the center toward the circumference.

Since, therefore, the Waters are the Universal passive [subject], from which—as the common subject of all things—the figure of the world and of all things in it was cut out and graphically sculpted and depicted, as St. Peter teaches us; and since the eternal, all-actuating and informing Spirit of the Lord is the Universal actor and mover (as Moses testifies), it does all things in all things in the waters, and that in and by means of infinite organs, namely Angelic, Stellar, and Windy; it must follow that it alone is the radical agent in general contraction and expansion, which take place both in the universal air outside the glass of the instrument, and in that

<column-break/>

particular air which is inside the glass. Wherefore, just as the Sun, warm winds, fire, and the heat of a natural creature have their expansive property from the emanating and informing power of that Spirit, and are brought from a privative disposition by its power and the cold temper of the air, winds, and waters: so indeed it follows that both the expansion and the contraction of the air enclosed in the glass of the instrument proceed from the immediate act of either the positive or privative property of that spirit. For when this Spirit blows from the North or West, the air is more or less contracted into a narrower space in the glass.

And that this is true, we prove by the fact that the waters, by the dominion of cold in the Universal Element, are drawn higher or raised into the neck of the glass because of the contiguity [physical contact] of the water and the enclosed air.

And again it is established that the air contained in the glass is so much more contracted as the Northern cold has dominion in the external air: which appears in this, since it is gathered into a more narrow or tight place than it was before the rising of the water in the glass.

On the other hand, if warm winds or the fervor of the summer Sun should ignite the external air, then the enclosed air will also expand itself and in its expansion make a larger space for its existence. That the air is thus expanded by heat is evidently demonstrated in this: because the water enclosed in the vessel is gradually driven further downward than it was before.

Again, if someone places their bare hand over the concave, spherical top of the glass, the water suspended in the neck of the <term>matrass</term><note>A matrass is a long-necked glass chemical flask; here it refers to the body of the weather glass.</note> or glass will tend further downward: for the enclosed air will suddenly expand.

Now truly, that the quickening spirit, which assigned that heat of both human and other animal life, is that eternal spirit which, as the Apostle <note>Likely referring to St. Paul.</note> says, "gives life to all things," the scriptures confirm in many places assigned both before and after in this Treatise.

And again, this is that spirit which the Prophet <note>A reference to Ezekiel 37:9, the vision of the dry bones.</note> calls from the four winds, so that it might restore the spirit of life, flesh, and bones to the slain.

By which it is made manifest and demonstrated to the eye that **Cold contracts** from the circumference to the Center, and that it thickens and densifies the enclosed air: which enclosed and thickened air, though it cannot be discerned by the eye, is nevertheless proven by this, since the water appears to the eyes to be raised higher in the glass by the predominance of cold. Whence it is necessary that the bulk of the air be squeezed into a narrower space, and consequently, that the air be rendered more contracted and dense.

On the other hand, that **heat expands** and dissipates the enclosed air in warm times is clear from the placing of a hand over the top of the glass, which the lowering of the water follows.

# ON THE MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

Note (I pray you, who do not wish to be overly biased toward the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle; Fludd is challenging their long-held scientific dogmas here.</note>) their palpable errors, detected through diligent observation of this experimental instrument. The first of these errors is manifested in that axiom of theirs which says: **heat gathers homogeneous things.** <note>Aristotle's theory was that heat brings together things of the same nature (homogeneous) and separates things of different natures (heterogeneous).</note> But you will perceive here, demonstrated to your own eyes, that heat performs the opposite: For we see it dissipate and drive away the air, which is homogeneous in itself, insofar as it is composed of simple parts of the same nature; and consequently, heat does not gather homogeneous things. On the contrary, it is **Cold** that gathers, binds, thickens, and constricts them. For it is visible to the eye that cold contracts—and by contracting, gathers—the dilated air into a narrower space. Furthermore, outside the glass, we see the air gathered into the

<column-break/>

consistency of snow and frost through the freezing power of cold. Therefore, their assertion also appears to be false when they say that **Cold is only accustomed to gather heterogeneous things.** Another of their massive errors is when they say that the Sun, the Stars, or fire—indeed, even all heat—attracts vapors, exhalations, and other such things to itself. But we find by this visual experiment that the matter behaves far differently; for from it we gather that the heat of the Sun, of the winds, of fire, and that natural heat of animals, by dissipating and expelling the air, consequently thrusts away all vapors and smoke from itself rather than alluring them. And this is demonstrated by the fact that the presence of heat drives the water in the neck of the glass downward: from which it is clear that the enclosed air moves along the same path as the water.

->The Argument of this Book.<-

In this book, the author attempts to thoroughly explain the mystery of rarefaction <note term="rarefaction">The process by which a substance becomes less dense or "thinner," like water turning to steam.</note> and condensation <note term="condensation">The process of becoming more dense or "thicker," like vapor turning to water or ice.</note> according to his own natural talent. Here, he first expresses their causes as well as their miraculous effects during the creation of the world in a general sense. Afterward, he recounts more specifically how the fabric of the world was built through these processes: how the celestial spheres and the glowing stars were established within them, and finally, how the Universal Sublunary Element <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to everything below the moon—the Earth and its atmosphere.</note> was divided into four distinct regions and arranged in its proper order.

### CHAPTER I.

### CHAPTER III.

->*What the opinions have been among the learned of this age concerning the position, seat, and tabernacle of that Universal Spirit—which informs, generates, and multiplies all things in this world. Here it is also proved that Jerome's interpretation of that Text of David, "He placed his Tabernacle in the Sun," is according to the true sense of the scriptures; and finally, the reason for the errors in more recent translations is explained here according to the capacity of the Author.*<-
