### BOOK IV OF THE FIRST SECTION.

...they create a symbolic expression or character of fire or Light, as if the <note>original: "ש" (the Hebrew letter Shin)</note> stood in the middle of the word, which argues for the existence of flame. It is as if by the essence of the word we intended the moist nature of the heavens, contracted in the center, and illuminated by a double proportion of light or emanation, made holy by the Cabalistic Sephirah <term>Tiphereth (Beauty)</term>, descending as if with beauty and splendor. By this it is taught that the heavenly watery mass—or that mass contracted into a globe from the purest ethereal substance—is adapted and prepared as a Tabernacle for the Spiritual Sun. This Sun is that purest and most essential Light in which there is no darkness at all. Not that He is "enclosed" within it, as we have said, but (as the scriptures say, that the Holy Spirit of God was in the fleshly Christ so abundantly that he was called the Word made flesh, or that the flesh was made the Word) and yet that Word or Spirit was not absent from any of the creatures, insofar as He fills all things essentially and by His presence. For this Spirit of God is in all things, as the sacred scripture records in various places.

Regarding the third point, in the book titled *The Resolution of the Theologians*, we find by the consensus of all theologians that the light which was expanded everywhere through the cavity of the heavens and the world before the fourth day of creation—and which served in the place of the sun during those first three days—was, on the fourth day, contracted and gathered into the solar body. But that light, which was thus dispersed, was the immediate act or emanation of that Spirit or <note>original: "Ruah Elohim"</note> <term>Spirit of God</term> who moved over the waters; consequently, that light which is in the sun undoubtedly participates abundantly in Divinity, as will be clearly demonstrated in the discussion of the eighth or final Argument.

The fourth point is drawn from celestial or Astronomical dignity. It is evident that the solar dwelling comprehends in itself no small amount of Divinity, since the more perfection something possesses in itself, and the more it excels others in glory and dignity, the more it seems to approach Divinity. For we are taught by <term>Hermes (Trismegistus)</term>—in this not at all disagreeing with the doctrine of Christ—that "the Good and the Perfect belong to God alone." Now, the dignity and perfection of the microcosmic sun is easily discerned in this: that this royal <term>Phoebus (the Sun)</term> is carried in his fiery chariot through the Center or middle of the heavens, shining with golden hair; he holds the pre-eminent scepter and the government of the world like a supreme emperor. Indeed, it is under his jurisdiction and command that the virtues and actions of all other heavenly bodies consist, as <term>Iamblichus</term> and many other learned men assert. And <term>Proclus</term> says that all the power or potency of the stars is gathered into one at the sight of the sun, which

<column-break/>

then afterward are sown upon the earth by means of the fiery breath of the said sun. Does not the wise man also, by reason of the glory of that Heavenly vessel or organ, compare the clarity of the uncreated sun (or divine emanation) with it, because of its beauty and brightness? <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 7:29.</margin> Does not <term>Sirach (Ecclesiasticus)</term> likewise say that the fabric of the sun is full of the glory of the Lord? But more on these things when we discuss the eighth argument.

The fifth point teaches by what means it is proven in an Arithmetic manner that a notable Divinity must reside in the solar Tabernacle—namely, as it is the one and only stellar virtue from which the entire multitude of Heavenly stars derive their formal essence, or their Light and influence. This is no different than how all numbers, whatever they may be, are derived from Arithmetic Unity. For the number two has the form of Unity conceived twice; and Unity conceived thrice produces the number three, and so on into infinity. Or as one candle lights another, and a second and a third, and so on into infinity; so this candle informs the innumerable stars of heaven with its light, and yet preserves its own unity intact and without any loss of dignity, glory, or virtue. Finally, what could impart so many essential virtues, so many graces and ornaments to the Stars, that is not itself rich in Divinity? Or what perfection can it give which it does not have, or has not received from such great Divinity?

To the sixth Argument, which concerns Geometry: Since, therefore, in a Geometric respect the sun is a spherical body, it is necessary that it be endowed with its central point, in which its illuminating power or virtue consists. For the circumference is nothing other than a certain semi-diametrical expansion of the point-like existence and essence from the center to the circumference. And this is the same thing that the Philosophers intend by this axiom of theirs:

->VIRTUE AND TRUTH CONSIST IN THE MIDDLE.<-

Now, if the admirable beauty and splendid virtue in the sun were not sent out from its Center toward the circumference, it would follow that it did not proceed from an internal Principle; and consequently, that it would require some other external illuminator, in the manner of the Moon. But that this is far otherwise is declared by the fact that there is no body in the entire universe to be equaled to this one in clarity and lucid splendor. By this it is plainly argued that this body of splendor and glory has its beginning from a certain Central Divinity or the lucid and apparent virtue of God, which, like a soul in a creature, gives life and activity at the center, moving from the center toward its circumference. Therefore it follows that the Light visible in the corporal sun is from the light of the spiritual sun—namely, from the invisible Spirit of Divinity—which invisible light is continuous in essence with those portions of light, both invisible and visible, which He has imparted to all creatures.

The seventh argument, that the Divine Spirit *has set His Tabernacle in the Sun*, is confirmed by musical observation from the position of the sun in the heavens. For if we wish to reflect with ourselves that God, as He is said to exist by Himself, is considered by the scriptures to have His seat in the heaven of heavens, and yet does not disdain to look upon the heavens: we can indeed compare Him to the unison in Music (if it be permitted to compose sacred things with profane). For if the string of a musical instrument is struck openly, it will sound a unison from the bridge or base of the instrument to its head. By similar reasoning, if we imagine a string extended from the summit of the heavens down to the center or the earth: for this entire space is filled with Divinity. It is no different than when the struck string of an instrument sounds equally from the head to the bridge of the instrument. Again, if we press that string of the instrument directly in the middle or central point of the line, it will produce the most perfect harmony, the octave <term>Diapason (the musical interval of an octave, representing the perfect consonance between the spiritual and material worlds)</term>. For if any half of the string is struck by itself, it will sound an Octave to the whole. By which it is clear that the perfection of the whole consists or is situated in the center of the unison. For any portion of an equally divided string will be equal to the most perfect harmony relative to the whole, so that this middle point will designate the center to the circle, whose diameter will be that entire string. By a similar relation to the Macro-

<column-break/>

-cosmic Monochord <note>The "Monochord" was a single-stringed instrument used by ancient and Renaissance philosophers to demonstrate that the laws of music and the laws of the universe were the same.</note>, it is necessary that the middle point or semidiameter of the string—extended from the highest heaven to the lowest earth—be the seat of the harmony of highest perfection, which corresponds to the unison as one to two, that is, in a double proportion. It follows therefore, and is clear by the effect, that the sun (which is God's Tabernacle) has its position in that central place of the world, which corresponds to the entire semidiameter of the world, or to the string of the mundane monochord, as 1 to 2. This is also confirmed by Astronomers, saying that the sun has its seat in the center of heaven. Now indeed I would wish you to observe how this perfect mystical harmony or concord was formed from the Divine and radical unity or unison, which sounded or uttered the word "LET IT BE" <note>original: "FIAT"</note> and "IT WAS MADE" <note>original: "FACTVM EST"</note>. Unity said "Let it be," and thus the unison produced a Divine emanation, proving the binary number, and that emanation had the same respect to the Truth from whence it went forth as the Octave <term>Diapason</term> or perfection has to the Unison. Truly this most splendid emanation, from which all things were created and formed in true Harmony, doubtless chose a place for its royal aspect toward the creatures in this world that was most perfect—at the point of the octave, which is perpetually in the middle of the unison, and consequently in the center of the Heavens. But it also appears to our eyes that the sun is disposed by the highest Creator in the middle of the seven Planets. And again, it is evident from that Divine glory which shines forth from it, that it is the seat of the most Divine perfection. This, therefore, was the reason that the Platonists imagined the solar orb or sphere to be the seat of the World Soul <term>Anima Mundi</term>. Now indeed, as that royal harmony of the Octave comprehends in itself two other musical harmonies, namely the Fifth <term>Diapente</term> and the Fourth <term>Diatessaron</term> (for from these two the Octave is joined), it is probable that the whole harmony of the heavens and consequently of the entire world is reduced to action in that created organ, whose actor or musical agent is the eternal Spirit, who every minute utters tones of life and salvation to the creatures from that glorious organ, and imparts to them vivifying, multiplying, and preserving virtues. <margin>John 1.</margin> For this is the unique office of Christ or the eternal Word in this world, since in Him (as St. John witnesses) is life.

The eighth argument is proven by physical or natural consideration: For we, and also the other animals, observe—indeed, even the very herbs and vegetables of the earth seem to recognize—that the treasury of vivification and multiplication consists in the sun. ### SECTION I, BOOK IV.

They form the expression or symbolic character of fire or Light, so that from the region of <term>iaque</term> <note>Likely a reference to the Hebrew name 'Yah' or 'Iah', signifying divine existence</note> standing in the middle of the word, it argues for existence. It is as if, through the essence of the word, we intended the moist nature of the heavens, contracted in the center, and illuminated by a double proportion of light or emanation, descending from the Cabalistic numbering of <term>Tiphereth</term> <note>The sixth Sephirah on the Tree of Life, representing Beauty, Balance, and the Sun</note>, as if by beauty and splendor. By this, it is taught that the heavenly watery mass—or that substance contracted in a globular manner from the purest ethereal substance—was adapted and prepared as a Tabernacle for the Spiritual Sun. This Spiritual Sun is that purest and most essential Light in which there is no darkness at all. Not that He is enclosed within it, as we have said, but (as the scriptures say: that the Holy Spirit of God was in the fleshly Christ so abundantly that He was called the Word incarnate, or that the flesh was made the Word) and yet that Word or Spirit was not absent from any of the creatures, insofar as He fills all things essentially and preferentially. For this Spirit of God is in all things, as the sacred scripture records in various places.

Regarding the third point, in the book titled *The Resolution of Theologians*, we find by the consensus of all theologians that the light which was expanded everywhere through the cavity of the heavens and the world before the fourth day of creation, and which served in place of the sun during those three days, was on the fourth day contracted and gathered into the solar body. But this light, which was thus dispersed, was the immediate act or emanation of that Spirit or <term>Spirit of God</term> <note>original: Ruah Elohim</note> who was carried over the waters; and consequently, that light which is in the sun participates without a doubt abundantly in Divinity, as will be clearly demonstrated in the discussion of the eighth or final Argument.

Fourthly, what is gathered from celestial or Astronomical dignity: It is evident that the solar mansion contains no small portion of Divinity within itself, since the more perfection something possesses in itself, and the more it excels others in glory and dignity, the more it seems to approach Divinity. For we are taught by <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage</note> (in this not differing at all from the doctrine of Christ) that the Good and the Perfect belong to God alone. Now indeed, the dignity and perfection of the macrocosmic sun is easily discerned in this: that this royal <term>Phoebus</term> <note>A name for the sun god, Apollo</note> is carried in his fiery chariot through the Center or middle-point of the heavens, shining with golden hair, and holds the supreme sceptre and government of the world like a sovereign emperor. For under his jurisdiction and empire consist the virtues and actions of all other celestial bodies, as <term>Iamblichus</term> and many other learned men assert. And <term>Proclus</term> says that all the power or potency of the stars is gathered into one at the sight of the sun, which

<column-break/>

then afterward, by means of the fiery breath of the said sun, are sown upon the earth. Does not the wise man also, by reason of the glory of that Celestial vessel or organ, compare the clarity of the uncreated sun or divine emanation with it, by reason of its beauty and radiance? Does not <term>Sirach</term> <margin>Wisdom 7:29.</margin> <note>The author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus</note> likewise say that the fabric of the sun is full of the glory of the Lord? But more on these things when we discuss the eighth argument.

The fifth point teaches how it is proven by the way of Arithmetic that a distinguished Divinity must dwell in the solar Tabernacle: namely, that it is the one and only stellar virtue from which the entire multitude of Celestial stars derive their formal essence, or Light and influence. This is no different than how all numbers, whichever they may be, are derived from Arithmetic Unity. For the number two has the form of Unity conceived twice; and Unity conceived thrice produces the number three, and so on into infinity. Or as one candle lights another, and then a second and a third, and so on into infinity: thus this candle informs the innumerable stars of heaven with its light, and yet preserves its own unity intact and without any detriment to its dignity, glory, or virtue. Finally, what could impart so many essential virtues, so many graces and ornaments to the Stars, that is not itself rich in Divinity? Or what perfection can it give which it does not have, or has not received from such great Divinity?

To the sixth Argument, which deals with Geometry: Since, therefore, in a Geometric respect the sun is a spherical body, it is necessary that it be endowed with its central point, in which its illuminating power or virtue consists. For the circumference is nothing else than a certain semi-diametrical expansion of the punctual existence and essence from the center to the circumference. And this is the same thing that the Philosophers intend by this axiom of theirs:

-> VIRTUE AND TRUTH CONSIST IN THE MIDDLE. <-

Now truly, if the admirable beauty and splendid virtue in the sun were not emitted from its Center toward the circumference, it would follow that it did not proceed from an internal Principle; and consequently, that it required some other external illuminator in the manner of the Moon. But that this is far otherwise is declared in this: that there is no body in the entire universe to be equaled to this one in clarity and lucid splendor. By this it is plainly argued that this body has the beginning of its splendor and glory from a certain Central Divinity or the lucid and apparent virtue of God, which, like a soul in the center of a creature, vivifies and actuates it, moving from the center toward its circumference. ...rendering the sight fiery, bright, and colored: He brings it about that, according to the radiance of the infinite central agent, He pours out or emits His emanation to all the boundaries of the vast worldly sphere. And again, it is said that He **puts on light as a garment** <note>Psalm 104:2</note>; as if one were to say the bright solar body is, as it were, a garment, or as it is in the Text: *The Tabernacle of Divinity.* Finally, God is called the fountain and Father of light, and consequently, there can be no Light, whether visible or invisible, which does not have its origin from that invisible bright fountain. Does not the Apostle acknowledge that it must be believed through faith that those things which are visible were previously from things invisible? <note>Hebrews 11:3</note> Wherefore it follows that the Light visible in the bodily sun is from the light of the spiritual sun—namely, from the invisible **Spirit of Divinity**. This invisible light is continuous in essence with those portions of both invisible and visible light which He has imparted to all creatures.

*The Seventh Argument, that the Divine Spirit placed His Tabernacle in the Sun*, is confirmed by **Musical observation** from the position of the sun in heaven. For if we wish to consider with ourselves that God, as He is said to exist through Himself, is regarded by the scriptures to have His seat in the heaven of heavens, and yet does not disdain to look back upon the heaven: we can indeed compare Him to a **unison** in Music (if it be permitted to compose sacred things with profane). But it also appears to our eyes that the sun is disposed by the highest Creator in the midst of the seven Planets. Every minute, from that glorious organ of life and health, He utters tones to the creatures and imparts to them vivifying, multiplying, and preserving virtues. ### BOOK IV OF THE FIRST SECTION.

...[things] which in the winter season seemed as if they were <note>original: "quasi mortuæ"</note> dead; they are now observed to begin to rise again, to be brought back to life, and to bloom anew by putting on their green garments. Conversely, as the Sun recedes from this region beyond the equinoctial line <note>The celestial equator; Fludd refers to the change of seasons as the Sun moves south</note>, they shed not only their flowers and seeds, but are clothed, as it were, in a mournful dress because of the Sun's departure or distance from them. But Saint Paul says: *God gives life to all things* <note>1 Timothy 6:13</note>. It follows, therefore, that if the Sun by its presence brings life-giving power to the **Elementary world** <note>The physical realm of Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note>, it is manifest that it acquires this gift from that breath of God, which is the **Spirit of Life**. God pours this Spirit abundantly into that little vessel <note>original: "vasculum," referring to the Sun</note> which is full of His glory, rendering it an instrument fit to generously rain down such life-giving acts upon the lower creatures of the world. 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 1</margin>
Does not the Text say that God has poured this spirit out upon all His works according to His gift? Why then should anyone raise a question or have a scruple concerning the dwelling of this Spirit in the Sun? This, therefore, is the chief subject of this 18th Psalm <note>Psalm 19 in modern Bibles</note>: this is its highest intention, to tell mortals (along with St. Paul in Romans 1 and Solomon in Wisdom 13:1) that the glory and Divinity of God appear to man from and within the celestial creatures. That is to say, from the creature itself—or the solar instrument—the eternal Spirit shines forth and reveals His glory to us through them. 
<margin>Job 26:13</margin>
Job also seems to confirm this: *By His Spirit,* he says, *God has adorned the heavens.* And this is that Spirit which, by the presence of its admirable splendor, has rendered the Sun more eminent in beauty than the other stars. For this reason, it is called by the **Platonists** (who in this have imitated the divine Orpheus) the **Eye of the World**, because in it and through it, as if in a clear and polished mirror, all things are detected and made manifest. And again, the philosopher **Heraclitus** says: "If you take the Sun out of the world, what is our little body if the soul is missing?" No pulsating vein is felt there, no vital state or respiration remains in it. For this cause it is also called the **fountain of blood**, which waters and moistens the other members of the body. Thus it is also clear from the effect that the power of growth and the preservation of things, both lower and higher, arises from the Sun. Insofar as it imparts and breathes life and heat into the lower things by its light, it also assigns formal light to the higher things. And now this Light is a certain simple act which, by means of life-giving heat and innate heat, converts all things into itself, penetrates all things, and leads their virtues through all things, while simultaneously scattering and expelling darkness and obscurities. By these things it is sufficiently clear that if life in general is in the **Word** <note>The Logos</note>, as St. John says; and if this Spirit of life gives life to all, as St. Paul and Judith affirm; and if the Spirit of Wisdom is the splendor of Majesty and more brilliant than the Sun, and a pure Spirit which is 

<column-break/>

more mobile and agile than any other thing, and if it penetrates all things by reason of its purity, as Solomon holds; and finally, if all these properties are found in the solar power: What can consistently dissuade a man from believing that the Hebrew text of David was correctly understood by Jerome in his interpretation: *He placed His Tabernacle in the Sun*? <note>Psalm 19:4. Modern translations usually say "In them [the heavens] hath he set a tabernacle for the sun," but Fludd argues for the reading "He placed His [God's] Tabernacle in the Sun."</note> This was indeed quite necessary for man to understand, since up to this very hour there are not many who are willing to acknowledge that the Spirit of God works **immediately** <note>Directly, without middle agents</note> in and through His solar instrument. For they have been seduced by **Pagan doctrine** <note>original: "doctrinâ Ethnicâ," meaning non-Christian/Aristotelian philosophy</note> and admit many active agents and secondary causes which they believe operate by themselves without any relation to the Divine Spirit. From this it follows that many have worshipped the creatures instead of the Creator; indeed, they have offered superstitious worship to the celestial Sun, taking the creature for the Creator within the creature. The Egyptians, distracted by poor teaching, fell into this error: for they, worshipping the illuminated creature instead of the Illuminator Himself, dedicated a Temple and a City 
<margin>Isaiah 19:18</margin>
in honor of the Sun. And for this reason, the horses and chariots of the Sun, which the ignorant Jews caused to be hung before the gate of the Temple of the true God, were justly cast down and utterly abolished by the pious. This error, which to this day clings to those taught in the **Aristotelian** fashion, is described in its own characters by St. John: 
<margin>John 1</margin>
*The Life,* he says, *was in the Word, and this Word or Light was in the world, and the world was made by Him, and the world knew Him not.* But whoever received Him—that is, acknowledged that all things were made by Him and that He is all in all—they are numbered among the sons of God, etc. But there are few, I say, distracted by Aristotelian <gloss>doctrine</gloss>, who are willing to acknowledge this. Wherefore St. Paul says: *There are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth; yet for us* (as if he had said, for Christians) *there is one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in Him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through Him; but this knowledge is not in everyone,* etc. 
<margin>1 Corinthians 8:3-7</margin>
It is as if he had said there are few who know this, because of the ignorance of worldly wisdom. Therefore John says: *The world was made through Him, but the world knew Him not.* By this speech he teaches us that it is the Spirit of God alone, and not the creature, who works all things. Consequently, we can conclude that the Spirit of God is essentially in His creatures; wherefore it is necessary that we simply trust Him and acknowledge Him in His works. For he who professes himself a Christian and yet does not know these things is a Christian in name only, and is consequently vain and miserable, as Solomon seems to testify in the place cited before: 
<margin>Wisdom 13:1</margin>
*Vain are all men in whom there is no knowledge of God; and from those things which are seen to be good, they could not understand Him who IS, nor...*

### CONCERNING MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY. Folio 32.

...paying attention to His works, they recognized who the craftsman was, etc. It is as if he had said: the Divinity of the Creator Himself ought to be discerned within the creature [the created thing] by a true Christian. Wherefore the Apostle [Paul] also says, as noted above:
<margin>Romans 1:21, 18.</margin>
"The invisible things of God from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead." Wherefore the wrath of God is revealed upon such men who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, etc. It is as if he had said: such learned men of this world, who attempt to divert the ignorant worldly folk from the truth using the unjust teachings of Pagan <note>original: "Ethnicorum"</note> philosophers, shall be strictly punished by God; because pure truth is the power and Divinity of God, which ought to be grasped by men. For that philosophy is not to be embraced which consists of human tradition and is according to the **Elements of the world** <note>The physical components of Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note>, but rather that
<margin>Colossians 2:8.</margin>
which is according to Christ, in whom dwells the fullness of the Godhead bodily. He, therefore, is the foundation of philosophy and its subject, as the Apostle testifies. By these things, therefore, it is argued that Divinity can be discerned in the creature [creation] in and through the sight of the creature. But the Wise Man says:
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 1.</margin>
"God poured out Wisdom upon all His works, according to His gift." This means He imparted a larger portion to one creature and a smaller portion to another. We can, therefore, look upon the **physiognomy** <term>physiognomy: here, the practice of judging the internal spiritual nature of a thing from its outward physical appearance</term> of a creature and through it judge the portion of the gift assigned to it by God. But the 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 42:16.</margin>
Text says: "The work of the Solar creature is full of the glory of the Lord." It follows, therefore, that God assigned the greatest portion of His dignity to the Solar Body among the Heavenly things, just as He chose the body of Christ as His "chosen vessel" or **casket of perfumes** <term>original: "myrothecio," a container for precious ointments or medicines</term> among men, so that in it He might hide His precious Divinity for the salvation of humanity.

<margin>Psalm 18:1.</margin>
We conclude, therefore, that the Royal Bard <note>King David</note> sang rightly: "The heavens declare the glory of God and the firmament proclaims the work of His hands." But if all the creatures of the heavens declare the glory of God, much more so and by excellence does the Solar body, which is full of the Glory of God. Wherefore he continues thus: "In the Sun He has placed His Tabernacle"; that is, He chose it for His royal place in the heaven and for the earth of His dominion. Therefore I say that this Spirit, which uses the Sun as the place of His Tabernacle, distributes from it the gifts of form, life, growth, and multiplication to the creatures. And yet I will not acknowledge with Aristotle that "the Sun and man beget man" <note>A common Scholastic axiom from Aristotle’s Physics, suggesting the Sun is a secondary cause of biological life</note>; but rather, that the powerful Spirit who gives life to all things is the only one in all things who is accustomed to breathe out and grant that force of life and the breath of natural heat—both to man and to other creatures—mercifully and sweetly everywhere, but especially from His Solar palace. He rains down the life for multiplication and the innate heat assigned to them from the fullness of the Solar Tabernacle, by which creatures may afterwards be sustained and preserved in their being. But—

<column-break/>

—this (as it seems to me) is sound and true doctrine: to ascribe every life-giving action—both the immediate and that which, according to the world’s teaching, is "mediated" (if such exists)—to Him alone who alone acts and works, and not to the organic creature [the Sun itself] in and through which the Creator and effector of all things is accustomed to work.

As for the translations of **Pagninus** and **Tremellius** <note>Santes Pagnino and Immanuel Tremellius, influential 16th-century Hebraists whose translations Fludd critiques</note>: namely, "He placed a tent for the Sun in them [the heavens]"; if such were truly the original text, what instruction, salvation, or benefit, I ask, can such an interpretation bring to us men? The first translation <note>The Vulgate: "In sole posuit tabernaculum suum"</note> teaches us that the Spirit of the Lord is in the most lucid creature of heaven; thereby admonishing us that we should ascribe praise and glory for His benefits to Him who made such an instrument for the salvation of creatures, and who works within it—and not to the creature itself, or His Tabernacle—just as the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> did, who were accustomed to worship the rising Sun as God. Therefore, there is the greatest usefulness for us in being taught from this to avoid the idolatry of the ancient Pagans, and then to recognize, through its super-excellence, that Divinity reigns in created things. On the other hand, the second exposition <note>The Protestant translation</note> seems to be a matter of such small importance and so little conducive to the salvation of men, that it does not seem worthy or useful enough to be written by the finger of the Spirit of God among the monuments of salvation. Consequently, what news could this interpretation bring to men: "God placed a Tabernacle for the Sun in the heavens"? For who is ignorant, or from whom could it be hidden, that the sun had its seat in the heaven? Does not any boy of unrefined intellect understand this, directed only by the evidence of his eyes without the warning of a Prophet? In what way, I ask, does that interpretation relate to the preceding text:
<margin>Psalm 18:1.</margin>
"The heavens declare the Glory of God," etc? Why did he mention the Sun immediately after? Does it follow logically that God made a tent for the Sun? Not in the least; rather, it was so that we might understand that the beauty and bright glory of the heavens proceed from that splendid Spirit who made the Sun His Tabernacle, and that from Him, sweet and benevolent influences are abundantly distilled and rained down upon the creatures of the lower world.

Now, in this final place, I will come to the later argument, in which I will show you how that interpretation of **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome, translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> is supported by various opinions of the "Theophilosophers" [divine philosophers]. One says (with whom St. Augustine also seems to agree) that every thing claims for itself as much of God as it is capable of receiving light. But the Sun is brighter and more radiant than all the creatures of this world. Many philosophers therefore agree on this: "In the light," they say, "is the divinity; in the divinity is the light" <note>original: "In lumine numen, in numine lumen"</note>. And **Plato** says: "Do not speak of God without light." Do not the Scriptures confirm all of this? "God," they say, "is clothed with light as with a garment." And He is also called...

It is indeed the assertion of the Apostle Peter that the heavens were of old, and the earth consisting out of the **Waters** and through the **Waters** by the Word of God. But what need is there for holy Authority, when common experience teaches us that condensed air becomes clouds, and clouds become rain-water, and ice—which is of the nature of earth—is made from water by Northern condensation? Furthermore, that the earth was water and that water was air is evident in this: that great trees, by burning into vaporous smoke, are consequently turned into air; finally, air is changed into fire by excessive attenuation <note>Attenuation: making something thin or fine; here meaning the thinning of air until it becomes fire.</note>. By which it is certain that earth and waters were previously extracted from an invisible thing, namely from the Universal air, and consequently it is proved that the Universal air of the world, which Hermes called the moist nature, is the Universal Element of the sublunary world. Indeed, if this were not so, how, I ask, would it be possible for so much water falling from the clouds not to cause the seas to swell and increase wonderfully in quantity every day, while the air on the other hand would steadily decrease? This would happen if there were not a constant replenishment through the transmutation of air into water and water into earth. Although the Divine nature effects this alteration or rotation of nature in a secret and insensible manner, yet daily experience teaches that the matter stands thus: for when wood and coals are resolved and consumed by fire, we find that their entire terrestrial bulk goes off into an almost watery smoke and will be changed into vaporous air. Now, it is a philosophical axiom that "anything may be resolved into its primary matter or principle." Therefore, it is manifest that both the water and the airy smoke, from which the terrestrial composition of wood and coal was made, were previously invisible air. Again, if things were not so, that sulfur, those powders and stones daily descending from heaven (as Scripture testifies) <note>Likely referring to meteors or volcanic ash interpreted through a biblical lens.</note> would increase the mass of the earth more and more every day. ### Visual Demonstration.

We observe that the entire portion of the Instrument—or <term>Calendar glass</term> <note>original: "vitri Calendarij"; an early thermoscope or weather glass used to observe changes in air temperature and pressure.</note>—which extends from the lowest part of its neck to its summit or head, is filled only with invisible air. Yet in that small amount of enclosed air, quite a few various alterations and mutations are found by the power and act of the four winds blowing in the open air. For when the **East Wind** blows with dominion, then that enclosed air dilates and extends itself in the neck of the glass, and it presses the water (which had been raised by the power of the cold) downward, more or less according to the proportion of the heat's dominion. By this, it is clear that the dilating spirit of such a wind causes the open air to incline toward a fiery nature; forasmuch as fire is recognized as nothing other than extremely dilated air—even though in reality it is an exuberant presence of the lucid form, which so dilates it through the heat that perpetually accompanies its motion. But if the **South Wind**

<column-break/>

blows, then the enclosed air also flows out, but not to the degree of fire, but only to the degree of air; and consequently, it will not repel the water (raised into the neck of the glass by cold) downward by so many degrees. However, if the **West Wind** has dominion in the free air, then the air enclosed in the glass will render itself even thicker; and for that reason, it does not greatly thrust down the water exalted in the neck, because coldness has sufficient power in 그 wind, and consequently it condenses the air more than it dilates it. Finally, if the **North Winds** govern in the worldly air, then the enclosed air will be all the more contracted and constrained, and consequently will require less space for its habitation, the colder the act of those winds shall be. <column-break/>

Here we have the progression in the creation of the world described in the Arithmetical manner. **1, 0** denotes that Unity which was before all things; while that Unity remained in itself without any emanation, it reserved its active property in a dark potentiality and, as it were, in nothingness, and therefore it was esteemed as nothing in regard to us—even though in itself it was all things folded together. 

Then the second series, **2, 00**, proves the actual emanation of uncreated light from the unity or divine power, by whose presence a moist nature appeared out of the Dark Abyss—namely **1, 0**—in the form of waters: so that light and water are ordained as the Universal active and passive in the series closest to the unity. 

Then, through the fiery spirit of eternal love and unity, those two natures are joined together to produce the nature of the heavens in a single composition: For there, light is considered by itself and the Waters by themselves, and a perfect mixture from these, namely the ether, like a fiery air; or light and air in the existence of heaven, which is called by some the <term>Fifth Essence</term>, <note>original: "Quinta essentia"; the celestial substance that is distinct from the four earthly elements.</note> and this simple mixture from simples is called by the Platonists the <term>World Soul</term>. <note>original: "Anima mundi"; the vital spirit that Fludd believes animates the entire physical universe.</note> For just as the Universal sublunary Element was formed after the creation of the heavens, so also the heavens are said to animate it, either through the acts of the Sun or by the mediation of the Angelic winds—or, if you prefer, the four Elements in a multiform way. Therefore the series stands thus: **3, 000**, as if light, water or air, and heaven. 

The last step in the progression toward the creation of the world stands thus: **4, 0000**, which implies the fourfold alteration of the Universal Element, effected by the word of God in the four winds of the world on the third day of creation: For that Universal element was nothing other than the general waters of the sublunary region altered in a fourfold way—or, if you prefer, let **4, 0000** stand for the four Elements.

This, therefore, was the state of the world in the creation of the world, and it remains in plainly the same condition even unto this day, and will remain in the future, until it perishes in the final fiery trial and is purified.

From this it happens that, by reason of the darkness, they participate in their passive state in both the privative and the positive principle. By withdrawing his life-giving spirit from the watery existence of the creature, he brings it back under the dominion of the privative principle, from which Death and corruption follow. On the contrary, through the continuation and presence of the incorruptible spirit in the creature, it remains without corruption by the power of that spirit. It is manifest, therefore, that by the presence and benign action of the incorruptible Spirit of God, life is present and continued in the creature; and conversely, by its total absence, death is introduced. But by its partial removal and contraction from the circumference to the center, the creature is troubled and falls ill; for it cannot die as long as any portion of the incorruptible spirit of God remains in it.

<margin>Psalm 16:10</margin>

Otherwise, he would not have appeared transfigured on the mountain with **Moses and Elijah**. Secondly, we must observe that it is the presence of the **vivifying Spirit of God** that effects both generation and resurrection from the dead; and conversely, it is its absence that brings about death and corruption. For the scriptures say in the place cited before, that it was the soul of the boy which returned into his inward parts. And in another place, as before, the Spirit of the daughter returned into her and she rose up. Therefore **Job** rightly noted in the place previously marked: "If God should take back his Spirit or his breath from man, he would expire." And **David** says: "If you take away the Spirit of the creature or man, he expires; 
<margin>Job; Psalm 104:29</margin>
but when you send forth your spirit, they are created anew," or they rise again, or are renewed.

Now, if we compare this principle of **generation and corruption** with that of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, whose "secular" physics Fludd frequently opposes.</note>, we will undoubtedly find as much confusion in the explanation 

<column-break/>

of the one (namely the **Aristotelians**) as we find simple and plain explanation in the other (namely the **Mosaic**). For they define **generation** as a 
<margin>Velcurio, book 2, chapter 13, Physics Commentary</margin>
change of matter from a former **substantial form** <note>The essence that makes a thing what it is; e.g., "human-ness" in a human.</note> into another substantial form. Conversely, they make **corruption** a change or loss of the substantial form which was previously in the matter, but is now no longer in it. And so you see, they name a certain "substantial form." But as to what that form actually is, where it radically originates, how it enters bodies to bring about generation, and by what means it departs from them again to produce corruption—all these things, I say, they are utterly ignorant of. Consequently, by such teaching, we gather nothing except "the unknown explained by the more unknown." 

However, according to the **Mosaic doctrine**, the truth is that it is the **Spirit** or **Word of God** that informs and vivifies all things. By its presence and benevolence, it effects both **Generation** (which Aristotle trumpets in such a confused manner) and **Resurrection** (which he could never detect or discern through his worldly wisdom or the power of his fallacious Philosophy), as well as **corruption, privation, and death** by its absence. Thus, in that change of a creature from one state to another, and from one form to another, we find that just as the creature was made according to its existence out of **Dark, potential, or uniform matter** (namely the waters), which the Divine Spirit or holy splendor informed by imparting vital vigor through its actual light; so also by the absence of that all-forming divine light, all things become dark, dead, and destitute of essential form, until a new light or a new power of life manifests itself. This light alienates the watery subject from the form and figure it had before. 

In this way, the body of the dead or a **corpse** is in a state of deformed chaos, because it has lost the accustomed substantial figure or "act" of a human. It is no different than if God had removed his spirit from the world: all things would return again into nothingness—or from their activity into divine potential or the dark abyss—just as they were before in their "enfolded" nature. But when the "act" of a **new form** breaks out from a dead corpse, causing the entire mass to become verminous <note>full of worms/maggots</note>, then we can say that **the corruption of one is the generation of another**. This is always true when **Elemental matter** is present. It is clear, therefore, that **privation** <note>The state of being deprived of light or life.</note> is the middle ground between Generation and corruption; it is like a vacuum, a certain emptiness, or "Nothingness" and non-entity between two formal states.

# SECTION I, BOOK IV.

...we have expressed the series in the creation of the world; of which the first, 1. ☉, signifies the dark **Abyss** <note>original: "Abyssum"</note> or Divine power, in which state all things were enfolded within God. The second was 2. ☉ ☉, denoting the production of light and waters, namely the Universals, both active and passive. The third, 3. ☉ ☉ ☉, depicts the substance of the **ether** composed of light and water—namely, two simple things and the first compound made from them. The fourth, 4. ☉ ☉ ☉ ☉, explains the **Universal Sublunary Element** <term>Catholicum Elementum: Fludd uses 'Catholic' in its original sense meaning 'Universal' or 'All-encompassing'</term>, or the lower waters, altered in a fourfold manner. These are the simple members of the world, from which all things in the world are afterwards composed. And this member, in that state of its existence, shall endure until the final *Let it Perish* <note>Referring to the end of the material world</note>. Here, therefore, we have the bases of all composite creatures; for they are placed upon the foundation of 4. ☉ ☉ ☉ ☉ in respect to their substance, so that they may acquire their form from the **Spirit** that gives form to all things and is present everywhere.

I shall therefore make my progression from **Generation**, starting from the simple Element, altered fourfold through various degrees, to the completion of a **perfectly mixed body**. For, just as between the starting point and the destination there must be a middle ground which is on the way to perfection but has not yet reached that goal, so indeed that middle ground is not improperly called an **imperfectly mixed body**. Its place is between the simple Element, altered in various forms—or, if you prefer, the four Elements—which are simple, and those things which are absolutely mixed. It is therefore evident that in the way of generation, between the Elements and the perfectly mixed body, we must encounter a body of a **meteorological nature**.

For example: in the generation of a human being, his beginning—which is founded upon the watery Elemental nature and has its place in the fifth series of the generation sequence—is the **sperm** itself. This is because it is a watery or fluid substance only slightly altered. And just as in the "unbroken water" <note>the primordial waters of creation</note> the entire fabric of the world and the seeds of all things are contained implicitly, yet nothing appears externally except water; so in the sperm, although nothing appears explicitly in the first series except sperm, nevertheless the whole man—namely his bones, flesh, blood, nerves, etc.—is implicitly contained within it, and they wish to appear explicitly from it by degrees, namely in the sixth series. For it will be altered from moisture to solidity with a certain distinction of the three principal members: the **Heart, Brain, and Liver**. In the seventh series, it will remain in the form of an **Embryo**. And the eighth series will complete the **Cube** <note>A geometric metaphor for physical stability and perfection</note> to the second root of 2, or the square of 4 (which in the Universal Element is depicted by the impressions of the four winds), reaching the completion of a perfectly mixed body in the human creature.

<column-break/>

By a similar regard, we see in the **Macrocosm** <note>the "Great World" or universe</note> that the simple Element—namely, the **Universal Air**—appears externally flat and simple in its existence, almost like something invisible. Nothing is there explicitly, and yet it contains within itself implicitly: the cloud, rain (or water), fire (or lightning), and heavy stones along with Salt, etc. All of these appear explicitly by the power of the four winds, so that **vapor** holds the first series of generation (namely the fifth order in the **Triangular Scale**); the **cloud** holds the sixth; **lightning with rain** the seventh; and the **Ceraunian stone** <term>Lapis Ceraunius: Ancient name for a 'thunderstone,' believed to be a physical stone created by a lightning strike</term> or thunderstone holds the eighth, proving the exact rotation of the four forms or windy natures into a single mixture.

But truly, when a man’s corpse returns to corruption, then it is necessary that its parts proceed backward in resolution through the same steps by which they proceeded to perfect composition—namely, from the perfect disposition of 8 to 7, from 7 to 6, and from 6 to 5—until it returns into a **mucilage** <note>a thick, jelly-like substance</note> not unlike sperm, and is dispersed into the Elemental Nature from which it first arose. And there it begins to put on a new form, or to make a second generation in another form; for the **Spirit** that works all things is never idle. Likewise, the stone is resolved into water, water into a vaporous cloud, and the cloud into the air from which it was first derived. This air is that simple Element and consequently requires no further resolution.

From these things it is clear that the work of **Generation** proceeds chiefly through degrees of **condensation**, by which means the bond of Elemental composition is strengthened. And it is also made manifest from this that the same **Universal Medicine** <note>The vital spirit acting as a transformative agent</note> proceeds through the way of generation from form to form, and from thing to thing. And the work of **corruption** occurs through the way of **Rarefaction**, namely by resolving. This is explained just as in the method of manufacturing snow, ice, and frost by the Northern winds, and their resolution again into waters and vapors by contrary breaths. # SECTION I, BOOK IV.

The greater part of these philosophers believe that God acts and operates in this world by necessity and not by any voluntary motion, as much in the generation and preservation of things as in their corruption and ruin. If this were indeed the case, it would necessarily follow that such an involuntary act in God proceeded from another Nature more powerful than God—one that was either co-eternal with Him or pre-existing—or at least that He was coerced and driven by some of His own creatures to perform this or that against His own will. I shall briefly explain to you how erroneous all of this is and how far it wanders from the central rules of truth. For in the first place, what (I pray) is more ancient than God Himself, or co-eternal with Him? Is it not His nature to have existed before all things? Is there anything in Geometry that is less in measure, or prior in time or order, than the point? Is there any of all the numbers in Arithmetic older than unity?

From this it necessarily follows that God is free and voluntary in His actions, since He is and always has been from and in Himself; He held His existence from eternity without regard to any preceding or co-eternal principle. Therefore, He was sufficient in and of Himself to operate and perfect all things, by Himself, without the help of another from all eternity. Truly, the reasons for these opinions of the *Pagans* <note>original: "Ethnicorum"; referring to non-Christian classical philosophers.</note> are twofold: First, it must be known that God operates by His own virtue and essence, and not by any acquired power. Secondly, because effects in this world appear to be necessary, they conclude from this that they cannot proceed from any cause that is fortuitously contingent or from the voluntary will of another. As for the first point, they argue (as it seems to me) against themselves; for as He acts in His own essence or personally, it is evident that He is moved by Himself, and consequently not by any external coercion, impulse, or internal necessity. Furthermore, the breadth of unity admits no compulsion or motion against the will, since unity cannot "suffer" <note>In the sense of being acted upon by an outside force.</note>. Moreover, it is not possible for God to be urged to work by means of some extraneous or foreign agent, insofar as He, remaining fixed, constant, and firm from the beginning, works in and through Himself alone as the original source of all things. He does this through Himself, emitting formal rays of life according to His pleasure, and drawing them back or abstracting them into Himself again where and when He wills. Regarding the second point, I say that necessary effects are in no way accustomed to include necessity in the first efficient cause. This is because secondary causes—which *Plato* and others call *Handmaidens and servants* <note>original: "Ancillas & servas"</note>—strive to execute His commands in a necessary order, being driven to that work by Him who is the unity of every multitude, and consequently all in all, so that necessity in

<column-break/>

<margin>Wisdom 16:22.</margin> the created, generated, and corrupted things of this world depends upon the will and free command of Him who created them. We have this confirmed from the fountain of truth: The fire grows mild so that it might not burn, yet He makes fire burn in the midst of waters. <note>A reference to the miracles in the Book of Exodus, where the elements behaved contrary to their nature.</note> From this it is clear that God does not act upon fire or within it out of a forced necessity, but according to His own pleasure. Furthermore, when the three servants of God <note>Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the Book of Daniel.</note> walked untouched and without injury despite the violence of the fire in the furnace, God acted out of His free benevolence against the laws of necessity. Again, He made the sun stand still in the heavens in the time of *Joshua*, and again made its motion go backward during the reign of *Hezekiah* against the course of nature, and consequently not out of necessity nor by coercion. And that total, admirable eclipse of the sun which happened at the time of the Savior's passion occurred beyond the expectation and capacity of the *Astrologers and Naturalists*. For in that instant, the Moon was found neither in the "head" nor in the "tail" of the *Dragon* <term>The lunar nodes: a solar eclipse naturally only occurs when the moon is near these specific points where its orbit crosses the sun's path.</term>, as that great astrologer *Firmicus* <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer.</note> testifies. From this it is evident that the event was not brought about through a natural way or by a necessity to preserve or sustain the nature of the world. All these effects, I say, could in no way have been produced if God acted by necessity in the governance of this world. Thus it is manifest that God operates in this world according to His free will and not by compulsion. But come and listen for a moment (O you vain *Philosophers* who believe God is the actor and ordainer of all things bound by the laws and chains of necessity): what glory or honor, I pray, can man attribute to Him for His wisdom, justice, and mercy, if He were coerced to perform those things He does against His will? Namely, if He were urged by some unknown necessity to either create or generate all things, or to form anything else according to this or that shape, and even to nourish and preserve beings and finally lead them to the goal of corruption? What thanks, I say, or what reverence or adoration would we owe Him, if He does anything in this world by coercion and impulse? And why does *Aristotle* himself advise us (if this were true according to his intention) that we should offer sacrifices to the roots of nature? Or what benefit would it bring us mortals to pour out our daily prayers and supplications before God for this or that future benefit (an office which *Plato*, *Porphyry*, *Iamblichus*, and *Proclus* <note>Significant Neoplatonic philosophers who emphasized the importance of prayer and theurgy.</note> nonetheless teach to be very necessary) if He cannot be propitiated by prayers and appeased in His wrath, as one who (if it is right to believe them) acts by necessity and against His own will? Or why were *Socrates* and *Pythagoras* accustomed (who according to the testimony of the oracle were the [wisest] of their...

### ON THE MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY. Fol. 39.

... (the wiser of them) pray to God daily, if He Himself did all things by compulsion and not according to His own will? Or why did the Prophet proclaim that God alone is to be called upon and entreated, if there were any necessity in God regarding how He works in the creation and preservation of things? Indeed, it is clearly declared from what has been said that God is generally inclined toward mercy through the mediation of human prayers, and that it is within His own free choice <note>original: "libero ipsius arbitrio"</note> to act with either severity or clemency toward this world and its creatures. Consequently, it is evident that He is by no means driven by necessity to produce these or those effects in the world, whether through creation, generation, or destruction.

This was falsely taught, in a plainly atheistic manner, by several Pagan philosophers. Among them, I name one of the disciples of Aristotle—extremely well known to the world and especially to physicians (since he is easily the prince of physicians among the Pagans)—namely, Galen. He speaks quite inconsiderately in these words: *Moses thinks that God can do all things, even if He wished to make an ox or a horse out of ashes. We, however, do not feel this way, but confirm that Nature cannot do certain things, and that God does not even attempt them at all; rather, from the things He can do, He chooses that which is best.*

<margin>On the Use of the Parts, Book 2, chapter 14.</margin>
Indeed, regarding the hair on the eyelids <note>meaning the eyelashes</note>, since He had established that they should always be equal in size and number: we do not claim that because He willed this, they were immediately made so; for we claim He could not have done it, and even if He had willed it a thousand times, they would never have become such if they had been produced from a soft Being, etc. Behold how atheistically this rash man speaks, and how he wishes to restrain the omnipotence of God, to bound His actions with limits, and to impose upon Him the intolerable yoke of Necessity and the mark of impotence.

There are, however, some other philosophers who carry themselves more modestly in this business. For Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> affirms that these actions in God occur neither by necessity nor by way of violence or compulsion, but consist in a middle ground between them; and therefore he concludes that it lies within the will of the agent. In this resolution, he seems not to vary much from the sense of Holy Scripture, which falls upon this sentiment: *That God has chastened us for our iniquities, and He Himself will save us for His mercy’s sake.* By this it is argued that there is a free will in God for both punishing and for

<margin>Tobit 13:5</margin>

<column-break/>

bestowing mercy. But this is expressed even more plainly in these words: *God does according to His will, as much in the powers of heaven as among the inhabitants of the earth.* By these words the prophet argues that every operation in this world is perfected according to the will, and in and through the word, of the Almighty; and therefore not by necessity, as Aristotle, Galen, and many others of the Pagans claim, to the derogation of Divine Virtue and the lessening of His Omnipotence.

However, that there is an undoubted Necessity in organic causes <note>natural instruments like the planets</note> and in the effects that proceed from Divine acts, nothing in the world is plainer, nothing in the nature of things more certain. Hence the Prophet

<margin>Daniel 4. Baruch 3.</margin>
Baruch says: *The Sun, Moon, stars, lightning, wind, and clouds obey God in all things.* That is, they are incited by the Word dwelling within them and are snatched up by necessity to do the divine pleasure. It does not follow, therefore, that He who commands fundamentally can be compelled in any way to act thus or so in His empire or dominion, since He is the one who acts primordially—that is, He exists as the first and unique mover in the world. For He has no other agent either before Him or equal to Him; and consequently, He operates voluntarily and from His own free choice. And hence the Apostle says: *Who resists the will of God?* And the Prophet: *My counsel shall stand and all my will shall be done.* And Job: *Whatever He willed, that He does.* Therefore, it is manifest that He does not operate involuntarily or out of Necessity, but according to His own pleasure.

<margin>Romans 9. Isaiah 46:10.</margin>
We conclude, therefore, that just as that which cannot happen otherwise is "necessary" (it must be so by necessity), so that which is "contingent" can happen and be done otherwise. But truly, the "voluntary" is neither of these extremes. Now, it is proven that the acts of God in this world are voluntary and consequently not at all bound by the chains of necessity because a thing can behave differently than in its established state of nature. For example, when it was the will of God that the Sun—destined for perpetual motion in the sky—should remain fixed for a space of time; and that the Sun (though endowed with no epicycle <note>a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary motion</note>, but ordained to progress eternally on its way) should move backward in its journey; or that it should suffer an Eclipse beyond the reason of nature—I mean the Moon wandering from the Ecliptic line either to the North or to the South, that is, existing in no point of the annual intersections, namely being in neither the Head nor the Tail of the Dragon <note>the lunar nodes; the points where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic. Eclipses can only occur when the moon is near these points.</note>, etc.

# THE MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY, SECTION ONE, BOOK V.

->The Argument of this Book.<-

After the Author had expressed the radical nature of the two essential properties, namely Heat and Cold, and had proven—partly by philosophical reasoning and the testimony of Holy Scripture, and partly by ocular demonstration—that condensation and rarefaction were their evident effects (by means of which the orbs of the heavens and the regions of the lower element were fashioned and arranged in their proper places), he now proceeds in this present book to describe those impressions of **Meteorology**, which are the first steps of composition. He indicates that the method of their creation consists in the acts of the **Divine Spirit** within the common sublunary element <note>The "sublunary element" refers to the region below the moon, which in traditional cosmology is the realm of change, decay, and weather.</note>. Consequently, he sets out to prove that their causes do not arise from merely accidental sources or external principles, as the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> falsely imagine. For this reason, he compares Aristotle's meteorological doctrine with that of the Holy Bible; and finally, by reducing Aristotle's philosophy of atmospheric impressions to the "Lydian Stone" or the test of truth <note>A Lydian Stone (or touchstone) was used to test the purity of gold.</note>, he discovers it to be a false and counterfeit metal—indeed, nothing but the mere dross and scum of metal compared to the golden truth.

## CHAPTER I.

->*In this chapter, you will find a brief repetition of the preceding discourse, and indeed, you also have an exposition of the word "Meteor." Furthermore, it is permitted to derive from this the method which the Author intends in this booklet.*<-

In my preceding discourse, I indicated only the principles, or the primary roots of all things: that is, the dark and potential unity, and that luminous and actual unity. I told you that these two unities are but a single thing in essence, insofar as light was to the eternal unity as darkness is <note>original: "quatenus lux erat æternæ unitati, ut tenebræ"</note>, and vice versa, although to our weak capacity they appear to be properties opposite to one another. Then I said that the Dark Unity, by its luminous power, caused the waters to appear out of Nothing: arguing from this that from that unity, through that unity, and in that unity, all things were, are, and have been. Then I proved that the waters were the passive or material principle of all things, just as, from the opposite side, that illuminating spirit was the actuating or informing beginning of every essence. And I proved that both these principles derived their origin from only a single root or stock, which for this reason is rightly said to be "all in all." After this, I recounted that **Cold** was an essential property adhering to privative rest, and that it was the offspring and most powerful champion <note>term: "Agonista" (champion or contestant)</note> of Darkness; conversely, that **Heat** was the son and magnanimous athlete of the motion and action of the Essential Light, always ready to perform its commands. I also expressed to you how **Moisture** and **Dryness** had their

<column-break/>

origins from the mutual presence or absence of the aforementioned properties of heat and cold. And in the final place, I explained the reason and method of the acts of **condensation** and **rarefaction**, while simultaneously indicating that the common subject upon which they operate was **water**. But the action which I expressed as being radical in such an operation was the **Word** or **Spirit of God**, who acts first in His angelic instruments through the stars (and especially the Sun) and the winds, within the general sublunary element, according to His will—altering it in a fourfold way according to the formal properties of the four winds: and this either by way of condensation or rarefaction into various species, figures, and dispositions. 

Now, in this book, I shall open to you the truest way and path (inasmuch as it will agree entirely with sacred history), showing how the most holy Word or blessed Spirit of God produced all meteorological bodies in the universal element of the air by the power and act of condensation and rarefaction. But before I descend into this discourse of mine, I think it will be worth the effort to declare what the philosophers meant by the word "**Meteor**." Those appearances which are seen in the air are called *Meteora* by the Greeks, not indeed with respect to their essences, but by reason of their height in posi- <note>The catchword "posi-" refers to "positione" (position), continued on the next page.</note>

### ON THE MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

By position: Others more properly name these "impressions," insofar as they are impressed and formed from above in the Universal Element <note>original: *Elemento Catholico*; Fludd uses "Catholic" in the sense of universal or common to all</note> of the air. But with respect to their existence, they are even more properly called **imperfectly mixed bodies**. This is either by reason of their unexpected generation, as they suddenly appear and are procreated; or because their composition does not seem to occur through a change of substance or an alteration of quality; or insofar as they are not as exact as other animate bodies, which are **perfectly mixed**. Finally, they are called "impressions" because they have by no means received a complete form, nor does there appear to be a great alteration of parts in such a mixture, insofar as the members of the element thus altered are confused with one another. However it may appear, such names are assigned to these impressions according to the pleasure and intention of the Philosophers, when in truth they are the **great works of God** <note>original: *magnalia Dei*</note>, or mystical bodies formed and fashioned by the finger of God in the sublunary Element according to the divine will on earth, whether to perform judgment or mercy. As will be declared more widely below: so that in this sense they might, without injury, be called "characters" or "signs," and can be named as symbols of either kindness and mercy, or of vengeance and severity. Therefore, my purpose in my Meteorological History is to direct you into the true way of sincere wisdom, so that with a more certain judgment you might be able <column-break/> to unravel and understand a mystery so great as is the Meteorological science of the Spirit of God, and to lead you out of the muddy mire of the philosophy of the Heathen <note>Fludd frequently refers to Aristotle and the Greeks as "Ethnici" or Heathens to undermine their authority in a Christian context</note>, in which the Christian world has stubbornly remained for so many past centuries, and even to this very day, to its own greatest disgrace. To accomplish this better, I will compare the errors and absurdities of the false Peripatetic Philosophy with the infallible truth of the sacred text throughout the entire thread of this treatise of mine. Thus, any consistent Christian, weighing in the scales or balance of justice those immense contradictions found between the one and the other, might thereafter be able—by a clearer virtue and with the eyes of his understanding more open—to discern the better Doctrine and follow it with sincerity; while avoiding the worse and relegating it to eternal exile from their memory. Let him, I say, devote himself entirely to the truth of the sacred scriptures and flee with greatest effort the deceptive Peripatetic Philosophy, so that (to speak plainly) they may discern with a pure and upright mind that great difference between the wisdom of this world, born of human invention—and consequently, by the testimony of scripture, nothing but mere foolishness—and that wisdom proceeding from God, which is real and essential truth. From these few words, you can clearly perceive my intention, order, and method in this book.

## CHAPTER II.

->*In this chapter, the entire mystery of the winds is unfolded according to the intention of the Divine Spirit; and, on the other hand, the false and deceptive spirit of Aristotle and the Christian Peripatetics regarding this subject is uncovered and explained to the world.*<-

---

To more clearly explain that difference which exists between false wisdom and true, essential Philosophy, I have proposed in the first place to express the opinions of the Peripatetic sect and then afterwards to examine them by the Lydian stone <note>A touchstone used to test the purity of gold</note> of the Divine word or Holy Scripture, so that we may gather from there whether their Doctrine is sound and real or not. Now indeed, since (as has been said) the four **Cardinal winds** with their Angelic Presidents are the organic actors in the Universal Element—or the sublunary waters—as those who change them from nature to nature and from state to state; I consider it worth the effort to begin this history or discourse of mine from the deepest mystery of the General winds: insofar as they are observed to be the principles of all other Meteors of the aerial field or Universal Element. And in the first order, I will explain what the Heathen and Christian Peripatetics, their <column-break/> disciples, think about them. It is the opinion of the Peripatetic philosophers that wind is a hot and dry exhalation, ignited with difficulty, ascending from the earth as far as the middle region of the air, from which it is then immediately struck back downwards by the impulsive force of the cold of that place; then, by striving to tend upward again—partly due to its own lightness and partly by reason of other ascending exhalations which it meets in its downward motion—it is forced to move laterally in the lowest region of the air. This air it fans and agitates, lest it should rot due to a lack of its own motion. This is the entire sense of their opinion concerning the generation of the winds. Therefore, I shall dwell upon this description of the winds by the Peripatetics. First, because the spurious Christian Philosophers, as if they were struck by an unbridled madness, apply their best efforts to support this opinion of Aristotle, as much in their public schools and private dealings as in their more mature writings—

# BOOK 5 OF THE FIRST SECTION.

...defending and sustaining their views with such confidence and audacity among the more modern thinkers, as if these ideas had been divinely announced to the world, or published and edited by a sacred oracle of truth. Secondly, they claim the place in which this imaginary exhalation is said to be generated is the Earth, and the "seat" to which it ascends according to their doctrine is the middle region of the air, which it is not permitted to penetrate because of that region's intemperate cold. Yet the medium in which it moves naturally upward—and by compulsion downward or against nature, and finally laterally (that is, toward the right or left) through the struggle and resistance of other ascending exhalations—is the lowest region of the air. Thirdly, they seem to assert through their description that the agent, motor, or efficient cause of this exhalation (by which it is both exalted upward and driven downward, and finally forced sideways) is a triple attractive heat from the sun and stars which lifts it; the coldness of the middle region of the air which drives it back down toward the Earth; and the clashing of other exhalations constantly ascending from the earth. Meeting the smoke thus driven downward, they say these forces cause it to move laterally; they claim that from this struggle and contention of both ascending and descending exhalations, combined with that lateral motion, there arises that noise in the open air which is called wind. And this is that **windy fiction of the Peripatetics** <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, who taught that wind was a "dry exhalation" from the earth.</note>, which, upon proper examination, will appear to be nothing but a water bubble; indeed, something lighter than wind itself—that is, merely words without substance. Now, the final cause or purpose why their "Nature" established these windy motions in the air is (as is clear from their own description) so that the air might be purified, cleansed, and preserved from rot by such ventilation. But to whoever gives credit to this pagan <note>original: *Ethnicae*</note> definition, especially if they be a lover of true wisdom, I warn them to examine every particular part of it first, the better to discern whether it agrees with the laws of true wisdom and reason or not.

Second, whether that smoky substance alone tends upward and only makes its way to the concave surface of the middle region of the air.
