### ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

...a Christian, and then it would follow that either Saint John was erring and a liar in his teaching (which to affirm would not only be a disgrace for a Christian, but the greatest and most profane impiety), or Aristotle's assertion must be false, as it is entirely contradictory to the truth. Aristotle says that the matter of wind is moved upward from the earth and ascends as far as the middle region of the air, from which it is driven downward by the power of cold. But Saint John says that the wind is not moved by compulsion or violent motion, nor agitated by some accidental and external impulse, but voluntarily and according to its own pleasure or appetite: For **the spirit** (as he says) **blows where it wills** <note>original: "spiritus spirat ubi vult"</note>, etc. This Evangelical Doctrine, which differs so vastly from Aristotle's opinion, is supported by various other testimonies of the Holy Bible: <margin>Psalm 135:7. Jeremiah 51:15.</margin> For the Royal Psalmist [David], along with the Prophet Jeremiah, says: **He brings forth the winds from his treasuries.** But elsewhere the scriptures prove that the earth is not God's treasury-chest: <margin>Deuteronomy 28:12.</margin> For it is written: **Jehovah shall open to you his good treasure, the heavens, to give rain to the land in its season**, etc. He does not say the earth, but the heavens. Thus, there is as much discrepancy between these two views as there is between night and day. Therefore, it is evident that heaven, or the <term>Universal Element of Air</term> <note>original: "Catholicum aëris Elementum"</note>, is the secret ark of God, in which all the **Meteorological Wonders of God** <note>original: "Magnalia aut mirabilia Meteorologica"</note> are stored and reserved. And hence elsewhere: **God opened the doors of heaven, raining down manna**, etc. <margin>Psalm 78:23, 24.</margin> Furthermore, it is a matter too difficult for mortal light—for one who is not illuminated by the spirit of wisdom—to find and uncover this secret treasure of God: <margin>Job 38:22.</margin> For Jehovah addressed Job himself (a man just and God-fearing, and much more so than the vain philosophers of this world who were utterly ignorant of the Divine Word), pointing it out with these words: **Have you entered into the treasures of the snow, or have you seen the treasures of the hail?** etc. Arguing from this point that, unless His Spirit had revealed His treasure to him, it would be impossible for him to know it. <margin>Wisdom 9:15.</margin> For this reason Solomon said: **The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and we hardly guess at the things that are upon earth; but who has searched out the things that are in the heavens, unless You have given wisdom**, etc. Now Solomon indeed confessed that he knew the forces of the elements and the powers of the winds, and consequently their radical origin: <margin>Wisdom 7:21, 17.</margin> For **wisdom**, he says, **the artisan of all things, taught me**. But the spurious doctrine of Aristotle, and his ethnic and worldly wisdom, proves that he never reached the treasure of wisdom which is from God. But let us proceed to the second doubt, which is whether, according to Aristotle's intention, the radical matter of the wind comes from the earth, and whether its first motion is upward from the earth. A man in the mysteries of nature

<column-break/>

far more learned than Aristotle responded to this question thus: **Man knows not the way of the wind**, he says, **it is the work of God himself, by what way He does all these things.** <margin>Ecclesiastes 11:5.</margin> But Aristotle was a man—indeed, a pagan man—and consequently he was able to judge such abstruse matters only indirectly. Therefore, Jehovah, mocking the audacity of such a worldly wise man and rebuking him, as it were, for his arrogance, spoke thus in His own person: <margin>Job 38:24.</margin> **Do you know where your <insert>exhalation</insert> is, in which it is divided, which scatters the wind over the earth?** arguing from this how impossible it was for a worldly man's capacity to conceive or understand such things, unless he be taught by the Holy Spirit of Discipline. For so were Adam, Solomon, and many others taught, as is found in the Book of Wisdom. And yet Aristotle seems to answer God quite impudently, saying: **I understand the way and the origin of the wind: For its origin is upward from the earth to the middle region of the air, from whose cold it is again driven downward; and meeting other exhalations successively rising in the path of its descent, it is compelled to move laterally over the face of the earth.** But I shall show the impossibility of this reasoning through those things which are to be said immediately hereafter.

Regarding the second and third parts of this clause, I say that the medium through which the winds move and are carried is far vaster and wider than that assigned by Aristotle. For the wind does not blow only in the lowest region of the air, but also in the middle and even the highest. If, therefore, the wind blows in the middle region of the air, then indeed the force of Aristotle's definition, or rather description, is taken away. For its efficacy is situated chiefly in this: namely, that such a hot and dry exhalation (which is the material cause of wind) is not permitted to penetrate the middle region of the air, but being increased by the coldness of the place through <term>Antiperistasis</term> <note>The intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more intense when compressed by surrounding cold.</note>, it is easily precipitated or reflected downward. Now, if there is wind in the middle region of the air just as there is in the lowest, then this "cause" of the wind will undoubtedly be abolished. For then that exhalation will not be repelled downward into the lowest region of the air (in which it must encounter other exhalations so that, by their mediation, it may move laterally and be dispersed over the face of the earth, creating wind). For the exhalation that makes wind in the middle region of the air will not be precipitated by the cold, but is always observed moving clouds here and there and provoking thunders in that region. Indeed, it is manifested almost daily to human eyes that the upper clouds—which are white and yellow, and for this reason clearer and more subtle by reason of their fiery brightness—than...

...than those lower clouds, which are coarser and darker, being agitated and driven by winds from one quarter of the world to its opposite. From this it most often happens that great and dark clouds, moving from four opposite sides of the world by the power of the said contrary spirits, rush together at a point in either Horizon. Thus, an immense sea of thick clouds is gathered there, which serves as a tabernacle for the **Great Spirit**, the worker of all wonders. From this, tremendous lightning and thunder follow through the collision of opposing **Angelic natures**, who are the messengers and ministers of the windy nature, carrying out the voice of the Almighty. For the Text says: *He ascended upon a cherub and flew upon the wings or feathers of the wind.* By this, any wise person can very easily discern that the worldly wisdom of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking in the "peripatos" or covered walkway of the Lyceum.</note> and consequently the Peripatetic Philosophy is mere foolishness compared to that which is from God. On the contrary, through the Doctrine of true wisdom, it is evidently clear that they are endowed with a most essential and vivid internal agent, and consequently, according to the aforementioned sentence of Saint John, they move of themselves, when and where they will. It appears clearer than light, therefore, that the wind has

<column-break/>

an act, form, and internal Principle within itself, by whose motion it is moved and carried, wherever or whenever the **first mover** within it shall wish. (For the Text says, as before:)

For example, they say stars attract to themselves by their heat—that is, they lift upward—smoky exhalations from the earth; this smoke or exhalation, seeking the heights, is overwhelmed by the cold of that place, and in its downward motion, it is forced sideways by other ascending exhalations. 

I beseech you, who are just and not biased toward the Peripatetics, to faithfully show me which of those "external accidents" in the procreation of such winds can be considered that internal and essential Principle. Therefore, if there is no such essential will or internal and central agent to be found or even imagined in Aristotle's "windy fiction," then his Spirit—which publishes such an adulterated discipline—will undoubtedly seem as absurd and vain to the intelligent world as the Aristotelian Philosophy he teaches is false and deceptive. ->### ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.<-

He affirms to his **Peripatetic disciples** <note>followers of the Greek philosopher Aristotle</note> that the turbulent and tempestuous wind called **Ecnephias** <note>original: "Ecnephia"; a Greek term for a sudden storm-wind bursting from clouds</note>, as well as the whirlwind itself, are indeed sudden and abrupt winds violently emitted from the clouds. Yet, he is unwilling to admit that hot and dry exhalations can penetrate the middle region of the air because of its intense cold. But, to descend deeper into the abyss of his absurdity: he admits that the cause of **ignited meteors** <term>Meteororum ignitorum</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including comets and lightning.</note>, such as comets and others of this kind, is a hot and dry exhalation that is earthy, thick, fatty, and oily—and therefore fit to be inflamed and set on fire. Now, he himself assigns the highest region of the air as the place and seat for the generation of such meteors, namely comets; and yet he seems to deny passage through the middle region of the air to those exhalations which give birth to the winds, even though they are not subject to inflammation and are thin and light in their substance. Could anyone be so lacking in mind and ignorant of natural effects as not to perceive that **Coldness** would sooner resist and hinder a flammable thing of an actually fiery nature—such as the exhalation that creates comets—than a thing or exhalation that is neither actually flammable nor fiery in itself, namely that smoke which is said to be the origin of the winds? Again, it appears from the description of comets that their material existence is heavier, more terrestrial, thick, and compact than that of the winds, and for this reason, it is less fit for ascending and penetrating. For heavy things, by their own natural inclination, tend downward more than the winds do; since the wind-nature is more light and subtle, and consequently fit to tend upward. Therefore, it would be impossible for the thicker smokes that make comets to ascend and penetrate the "diaphragm" of the middle region—indeed, to exalt themselves into the third or upper region—as much by reason of their flammable heat as by the thickness and weight of their substance, if, on the other hand, the thinner and non-flammable vapors were hindered by the middle region of the air in their passage to the heights. Thus, it is evident how weak, frivolous, and devoid of probability is this assertion of **Aristotle** in the aforementioned description.

But I come to the examination of the third part of his description. Although I have said something of it in the preceding inquiry, it will be appropriate, I think, to speak more fully on it, since it contributes much to the detection of the folly and error of this worldly wisdom. In that part, therefore, he describes three things acting upon the generation of wind, all of which he makes **accidents** <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property that isn't essential to the thing's nature, like a person's hair color.</note>. It is as if someone were to say that the winds are not moved by an internal and essential principle, but rather by external accidents—namely, the heat of the sun and

<column-break/>

the stars, the cold of the middle region of the air, and also the struggle of exhalations meeting one another in their descent and ascent. Through these (he says), the exhalation is moved laterally, and thus the wind is procreated. Therefore, in express words (having made no mention of any internal principle), he concludes that the generation of wind happens not essentially, but contingently and in an external or superficial manner. How golden and shimmering is this lie, not at all unlike the fictions of the ancient poets! An assertion, I say, which at first glance seems beautiful, but in truth is like a shadow or a void, destitute of real substance. # BOOK V OF THE FIRST SECTION.

<margin>See 2 Samuel 22:8; Ezekiel 3:7.</margin>
...that Universal spirit, which the Prophet Ezekiel, by the command of the Lord, called from the winds of the earth so that they might breathe life into the slain. It is through the Divine Spirit of Wisdom, which "assigns weight to the winds," and through the **Cherub** <note>In Fludd’s cosmology, Cherubim are associated with the element of Air, while Seraphim are associated with Fire.</note>, who is an aerial Angel—just as the **Seraph** is a fiery one—upon whom Jehovah, descending from the heavens, ascended and then glided upon the wings of the wind. From this it is argued that the wind is moved and animated by that Angelic Cherub, who is the most essential spirit and the very nature of the air. Therefore, when God sits upon the Cherub, the air, through the animation of said Angel, is made into wind. From this it is clear that the wind’s external form is air, but its internal nature is Angelic. And yet, notwithstanding these truths, that **Ethical Prince of Philosophers** <note>A common title for Aristotle.</note> does not blush to say that the wind is a merely accidental thing, and that it derives its motion and action from external principles rather than from that internal and central agent who is the actor and operator in all things. Consequently, according to him, the wind could not "blow where it wills," nor could it hear and understand the voice of the Lord through the Prophet when it was called from the four winds, unless it were essentially inspired by an Angelic Spirit. He [Aristotle], following the figment of his own imagination, recounts that the existence of the wind arises from the earth—an exhalation extracted from the ground by the power of the Sun and the stars. On the contrary, the Scriptures say that the Spirit which animates the winds is more mobile and more vivid than any other thing; and they say: "God brought them out of His Treasury." For in this, both the Prophet Jeremiah and David agree. But in that part of his definition, the Philosopher [Aristotle] seems to conclude that the lateral motion of the winds is produced by the reason of resistance, which occurs from the contrary clash of exhalations. Truly, this is a hollow and weak argument for so powerful a Philosopher—as if that windy motion, which constantly blows from the North toward the South, could remain so certain, constant, and direct in its action if it were guided by an agent so uncertain and variable as the conflict or contention of two exhalations (namely, one ascending and the other descending). I would ask you (my most acute **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>), what exhalation would rise from the earth, or what conflict would there be between an ascending and descending exhalation in 그 emission of the Spirit which occurred when the Prophet said: "Come, O Spirit, from the four winds"? It seems to me that the followers or disciples of the "Christian Aristotle" are utterly mute in resolving this doubt, deprived of the tongues with which they might respond by reason. But if they were to answer that this wind or Spirit was miraculous and not natural, I reply to them that I recognize no other essentially efficient cause in nature or outside of nature ex-

<column-break/>

<margin>Jeremiah 51:16.</margin>
-cept the one and only [God]. And therefore, in the production of meteors within the common nature of the world, it is said that "God blows from the North"; and that He, by His Spirit, produces snow and ice; and that He thunders from the heavens with His voice; and that when He gives His voice, the waters are multiplied, and He makes lightnings for the rain; and that He melts the thick clouds into rain; and that He sends lightnings from His Throne, and "coals of fire from His mouth"; and that He "makes the thick clouds His pavilion"; and that "He comes from the South in thunder"; and that "the voice of Jehovah makes the Cedars of Lebanon bow," and "causes the hinds to calve prematurely"; and that He Himself is a "consuming fire"; and that "no one can resist the cold of God"—and so it is in infinite other places in both the New and Old Testaments. And so that we may conclude with a single text: "God is the only one who works all things in all, and who gives life to all," etc. But our Peripatetic philosophers seem to respond with their scholarly distinction, saying that there is an infinite nature which is the principal efficient cause, but there are various secondary and subordinate causes which operate by themselves.

To these I say (as in the preceding pages) that Truth is simple in its essence, and consequently it hates a duality of essence and action. Therefore, it is necessary that true Christians imitate Truth itself in the unity and simplicity of their intellect. <meta>catchword: From</meta>

The **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> would persuade us that the act of a creature is so divided from the act of God that they are able to act by themselves, by means of an active virtue assigned to them by God; yet they nonetheless deny that this virtue has any further commerce with God. If their assertion were true, a monstrous absurdity would follow: for it would follow that the Divine essence is divisible, which the axiom of true Theology will never permit, as it concludes:

That the **Holy Trinity** is indivisible; and consequently, that act which the creature receives from God is not divided from the giver. Nor is it necessary for it to be divided, since the distributor of that formal virtue is, in respect to that gift, always present with the creature and in the creature, and is by no means separable from that gift of life. Consequently, He works all things in all things immediately; and for that reason, He is said by the **divine Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermetic philosophy, to whom the quote "God is a circle whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere" is attributed.</note> to be the center of every thing, whose circumference is nowhere. Wherefore it is evident that He is in every thing, not as a part of anything, but insofar as He is the composer of all parts and their director.

Therefore, I wish it would suffice for the Peripatetics that creatures are **organic causes** <note>Meaning they act as tools or instruments (organs), rather than independent agents.</note>, in which the Universal Spirit of God acts according to the variety of His own properties, which are annexed to His will. Wherefore it is evident that He Himself works in them and through them, and that immediately and absolutely. And it was in this sense that the Apostle said: *God works all things in all* <note>original: "Deus operatur omnia in omnibus" (1 Corinthians 12:6)</note>. I do not say the creature works by itself, but God acts in it and through it as if it were His organ. Indeed, the Prophet declares all of this more expressly in these words:

<margin>Isaiah 10:5, 7, 13, 15.</margin>
*Woe to Assyria, the rod of my fury and the staff in his hand is my indignation... But he will not think so, nor will his heart so intend. For he said: "By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom I have understood, and I have removed the boundaries of peoples," etc. Shall the axe boast against him who cuts with it? Or shall the saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn? As if a rod should lift itself against him who lifts it, or a staff exalt itself, which is but wood?* etc. By these words the Prophet seems to imply that, since it was the will of God to move and stir the King of Assyria against the Jews—in which action that King was nothing but a creature or organ, in which the Spirit of God moved to fulfill His will—the King himself produced nothing by himself, but produced all things by Divine virtue toward a fruitful end according to the Lord's will. Yet, the business being finished, that King—who was nothing but a mere organic or instrumental cause—foolishly arrogated to himself the glory, wisdom, and power of that action (which belonged to God alone as the actor within him), and thus

<column-break/>

received a rebuke from God in those words: *Does the axe boast against him who cuts?* etc. As if He had said:

"Shall the instrument boast against him who acts in it, or say: 'I did this,' when it is the internal and real agent by whose motion it is seized and moved, whenever and wherever it pleases the mover?" etc. Jeremiah also says: *The Lord has raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes against Babylon.* By this he argues that the kings of the Medes were not the actors, but the organs through which God acted for vengeance. But let us return to the matter at hand. How deaf—indeed, even how absurd—would that invocation of Solomon have been, if the essence and life of the winds were nothing other than that published by Aristotle.

*Awake,* he says, *O North wind, and come, O South wind, and blow through my garden.* <note>Song of Solomon 4:16. Fludd uses the Latin names Aquilo (North) and Auster (South).</note> Finally, if the winds were produced in the manner of Aristotle: whence does it arise that every wind is clothed with a different essential property? For one is hot and moist; another cold and dry; a third hot and dry; and a fourth cold and humid. It would be impossible for such differences to be found among the winds if all winds were informed and created by a single principle—that is, if they derived their origin from a forced lateral motion <note>Aristotle's theory was that wind is a "dry exhalation" moved laterally by the rotation of the heavens.</note>. Furthermore, if this were true, then the same wind would blow now from the right side, now from the left, and in conclusion, blow inconsistently—which experience testifies to be false. I come now to the investigation of the last part of the Peripatetic description, which concerns the final cause of the production or generation of the winds. Aristotle’s opinion is that nature produced such ventilation for the sake of purging, purifying, and preserving the air. Truly, we are taught by experience that this assertion of his is not true: for we observe, along with **Galen** and **Hippocrates** <note>Famous ancient Greek physicians.</note>, that the Southern winds are contagious and pestilential, insofar as they render the air thick, putrid, and corrupt by their malignant heat and loose, spongy humidity. This is also confirmed by the Holy Text: *Fear not,* says David, *the destruction or pestilence, nor the demon that wastes at midday.*

<margin>Psalm 91 [90]. Habakkuk 3.</margin>
And Habakkuk: *When God came from the South, the pestilence preceded him and the carbuncle* <note>original: "Anthrax"; referring to a burning plague or skin sore.</note> *was at his feet.* Indeed, all winds in general, and even other meteors of the sky, are ordained by the Creator as much for a scourge and punishment as for the preservation and health of creatures, as is declared in many places of the scriptures. Wherefore it follows that Aristotle erred by the width of the whole heaven <note>A Latin idiom meaning "entirely" or "completely."</note> in his judgment concerning the winds.

# BOOK V OF THE FIRST SECTION.

From what has been said, we can therefore conclude that the definition or description given by this **Peripatetic philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note>, whom Christians follow with such great veneration, is entirely erroneous and insufficient. This is because winds are creatures of a more essential and eminent nature, and fuller of divinity, than either Aristotle or any of his followers ever understood. They are not things devoid of internal light and essence, and consequently, they are not merely blown together by accidental external agents by means of a smoky existence

<column-break/>

erupting from the earth. Rather, as **Zechariah** teaches us, they are created and animated by an **Angelic Spirit**. They stand before the Lord of the whole earth and are hidden within the power and Treasury of their Lord, from which He calls them at His pleasure to carry out His commands in heaven, on earth, and in the sea—whether for vengeance and punishment, or to offer mercy and kindness to His creatures, as will be explained more fully below.

### CHAPTER III.

->*The true definition or description of the winds is expressed in this chapter in various forms, according to the sense and intention of Holy Scripture.*<-

---

Now, it seems to me that I hear the faction or sect of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> murmuring against me and replying: "If," they say, "the stated definition of Aristotle is not good, as you seem to promise by your arguments, then provide a better one if you can. Tell us more essentially what a wind truly is, or how you can correctly describe it according to the doctrine of the **Holy Page** <note>The Bible or Sacred Scripture.</note>." To these men I reply that this can be provided in many ways, yet all under one and the same essence. In the first place, we can quite relevantly describe it in this manner:

> Wind is an aerial Spirit of moderate consistency, animated by the inspiration or Spirit of **Jehovah**, whom He brings forth from His Treasuries and sends out to carry out His will, whether by way of a curse or vengeance, or of blessing and mercy.

Every part of this definition is proven from suitable passages of Holy Scripture. First, that the external part of the wind is air of moderate consistency is shown by the fact that the words for "air," "wind," and "spirit" are expressed in many places in the sacred letters by a single Hebrew word: ***Ruach*** <note>Hebrew: רוּחַ. Fludd is noting that the Hebrew language uses one word for all three concepts, implying they share a single essence.</note>. Second, that its internal and central soul or "act" is the divine Spirit, or the inspiration of the Almighty, is very easily indicated from the passages cited previously.

For according to the common course of the world—which He ordained to arrange and regulate the temperament of the parts of the year—where the sun (or that Tabernacle of God) is more remotely distant, there the Divine power, or the **cold and privative Spirit of God**, operates more or less. For example, when the sun is absent from our Hemisphere (namely, when it is beneath the earth), darkness, cold, numbness, and thickness of the air are observed to be present. Furthermore, when the sun is beyond the **Equinoctial line** toward the **Tropic of Capricorn**, coldness, frost, snow, ice, dense clouds, and shortness of days present themselves to us Europeans, and Southern winds become frequent among us. For at that time, the **privative property of God** <note>Fludd uses "privative" to describe the contracting, darkening, and cooling aspect of the Divine Spirit, as opposed to its "positive" expanding heat.</note> strives to reign in the northern world. Wherefore herbs, plants, and trees appear naked and as if destitute of life, because the Spirits and humors are congealed and they seem almost dead. Similarly, the earth is destitute of its usual greenness and, like a sterile and desolate widow, begins to almost

<column-break/>

groan and mourn. But on the other hand, as soon as the **Royal commander of the sun** approaches our hemisphere and begins to penetrate the Northern Hemisphere through the reddish and fiery **gates of Aries** <note>The "gates of Aries" refer to the Spring Equinox, when the sun enters the first sign of the Zodiac.</note> (which usually happens in the springtime), then those half-dead creatures, frozen by the Northern cold, begin to revive. The days begin to increase gradually; the harshness of the cold is daily diminished more and more by the welcome presence of heat; and the Spirits and humors in plants, which were fixed and congealed by the cold, melt and are now rendered mobile and fluid. And now the birds trumpet their joys with sweet songs, and the numb, damp air is gradually refreshed, and with light wings and swift flight, it seeks to visit the Southern region for reasons alleged below. And yet, despite the absence of the most active and lucid Spirit in the Sun, it does not follow that the one and same Spirit—inasmuch as it fills all things—cannot alter its **privative property** whenever and wherever it wishes. For we often see, contrary to the common and usual constitution of the year, that through its mediation, thunder, lightning, and other fiery meteors—and even more active winds, namely the Eastern and Southern—are generated sometimes even in the coldest state of the air. All these things are accomplished by Him who placed His **Tabernacle** in the sun according to His pleasure, whose work it is to operate all things in all, in whatever way, through whatever organs, and also whenever and wherever He pleases. Having, therefore, well-weighed these things first, I shall now descend into the state of my **Demonstration**.

In the first chapter of the first book of this first section, I declared clearly enough to you that the air enclosed in the glass of our **experimental instrument** <term>instrumentum experimentale: Fludd’s thermoscope or weather glass, an early thermometer that used the expansion of air to move a column of water</term> has in every respect a relationship to the air or the **Universal Element** of the lower world. It is also proved there that the moist, airy nature so exactly fills the concavity of the world—where earth and water are not—that no empty space is found within it. This is no different than how we see the air enclosed in the glass of the instrument occupy its entire cavity. Consequently, just as the air enclosed in the glass will be altered by the **dilating** <note>original: "dilatativa"—expanding</note> faculty of the present sun (namely, in the summer time when the external air grows warm), so in exactly the same way, the external air of this Northern Hemisphere will be dilated when the sun greets it with its more particular rays. Indeed, the closer the sun is to us, the greater will be the **rarefaction** <term>rarefactio: the process of air becoming less dense and taking up more space when heated</term> of the general air, and consequently of the particular air enclosed within. 

On the other hand, when the sun, leaving the Northern Hemisphere, crosses the Equinoctial line and looks toward the Southern region, then the common air of the said Hemisphere will grow cold and be **condensed**, and with it, that particular air enclosed in the glass will likewise be contracted and thickened in the same proportion. This is established by the fact that the water in the neck of the glass is observed to have ascended higher by many degrees toward the head of the glass; just as, conversely, the rarefaction of that same air is evident from the depression of that same water in the neck of the glass. These things being well conceived or understood by the truly skillful—namely, that the cause of this kind of dilation or rarefaction in the air is the presence and proximity of this Divine act in the **Solar Tabernacle**, and that the reason for that condensation is the absence or removal of the act of that same Spirit emanating from God—it follows that the presence of Divine power is then wrapped in Darkness. 

For, as we have said, the absence of heat is the presence of cold, which is the **Essential operator** in Divine power; and again, the presence of heat, which is the **champion of the Divine act**, is the absence of cold. From this it is clear that the absence of positive light conceives privative darkness, and the absence of privative darkness brings in the presence of positive light. These things, I say, being rightly considered, we can very easily gather the internal as well as the external reason for the Southern winds, and how the air is animated by the life-giving spirit emitted by the sun. It must be noticed, therefore, that when the sun is present to us, summer 

<column-break/>

is created by its presence; the air grows warm by its most bright rays, and through that warming is rendered thinner and more subtle. By reason of this rarefaction, it requires a larger space or place for its existence. 

**For example:** We place two pounds of **Vitriol** <term>Vitriol: a historical term for sulfate minerals, often used in alchemy to produce acidic "spirits" or vapors</term> into a glass **Retort** <term>Retort: a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</term> that is well-sealed with clay, and we fit its nose or orifice to a large **Receiver**, sealing the joints perfectly with clay so that no expiration of the Spirits occurs through the gaps. Then, by degrees of fire, we extract the Spirits from the mass of Vitriol. But being taught by experience, we prove that the spirits—once enclosed in the small and narrow mass of vitriol—are now dilated by the activity of the fire and sent into the very large receiver. If that receiver is not found large and spacious enough to receive those spirits expired from the tiny body, it happens that the spiritual matter, seeking a still more spacious place for its existence, violently breaks that glass into many fragments with a great crash, and fills the open air with the multitude of its vapors. From this it is made manifest that a condensed thing will occupy only a small space; but after it is dilated, it will require a large container for its existence. 

This is certainly demonstrated most evidently by that experimental instrument; for when the sun is present to the enclosed air, or a hot wind holds dominion, the air itself will immediately be more or less dilated and rarefied according to the vigor of the Solar Spirit and the hot winds blowing at that time. But this air, now dilated, will require a container all the more spacious the more it is dilated. And this is proved thus: namely, because the water in the neck of the vessel, which was raised by the act of cold, is now driven downward by the presence of heat by as many degrees as the air excels in rarity. 

From this it is clear that the only reason why the water is precipitated further and further downward by the presence of heat is because the air, being more or less dilated, prepares a larger place for its own existence.

These things being rightly known, we ought to note that when the sun recently enters a Hemisphere in which Winter had its dominion—and therefore where the coldness of the place condensed the air—**for example**, when the sun, leaving our Hemisphere, migrates into the Southern one to convert its air (formerly wintry) into a summer condition, it begins immediately to act toward the rarefaction of the air of that part of the world. And that air, so rarefied and as if animated by the solar rays, becomes agile and seems to be clothed with light feathers. I conclude, therefore, that when the potential property of the Divine Spirit moves or acts in the air, the air is contracted or drawn toward the pole as if toward a center, and is thus transmuted into snow, frost, hail, and the rest. For according to the change of the excluded air—that is, of the Universal <note>original: *Catholici*</note> element of the lower world—the enclosed air is contracted, and the water is raised up toward the head of the glass as if toward the cold arctic pole. And this denotes that the Universal or external air excluded from the glass, by a plainly similar reasoning...

### CHAPTER V.
### That Aristotle’s Doctrine concerning the generation of clouds and raindrops is found to be in every way contradictory to the principles of true wisdom.

---

<margin>The Aristotelian definition or description of a cloud.</margin> Now we proceed to the examination of the Aristotelian science regarding aquatic meteors <term>meteoris aquaticis: atmospheric phenomena involving water, such as rain, mist, or snow</term>. And, since the causes of mists (insofar as they are thin clouds) are included under the common title of "Clouds," I have decided, in the first place, to dwell upon the general description of a cloud. First, therefore, I will cite Aristotle’s opinion on Clouds; afterward, I will compare it with the sentence of the Holy Scriptures concerning them, so that by means of such a mutual relation, we may discern whether the Peripatetics' <note>The "Peripatetics" were followers of Aristotle, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkways where they studied</note> proposition regarding the essence of a cloud agrees with the truth or not. 

The opinion of Aristotle, which Christian Philosophers follow to this day, is that a Cloud is a certain vapor attracted from the earth and water into the middle region of the air by the power of the Sun and stars, and is a contraction or freezing into the consistency of a cloud by the power of the extreme cold of that place; which then later is carried here and there through the middle region of the air, partly by the heat of the sun and partly by the power of the winds. Behold, this is that beautiful intent of the Peripatetics concerning the generation of the Cloud.

Now indeed, so that we may better understand the truth of this matter, and gather whether Aristotle is a true prophet in such a description of a cloud, or a false and spurious prophet, we must first consider what the Sacred Text teaches us about the genuine generation of the Cloud, and how it agrees with the sense of the aforementioned Aristotelian description. Indeed, so that you may discern this with a better method, we will compare their words against each other, so that anyone even moderately learned may be able to determine the truth of this matter.

In his preceding definition, Aristotle makes the efficient and procreative cause of the cloud the heat or action of the sun and stars. For he seems to assert that by their virtue, attracting or elevating the vapors upward, clouds are made in the middle region of the air; at the same time, he affirms that they are moved here and there in the middle region of the air, partly by solar motion and partly by the winds. Furthermore, he also thinks that the cause of that contraction of vapor into the consistency of a cloud is

<column-break/>

the extremely cold temperature of that middle region. Thus, he seems to assign two external agents for the generation or consistency of the cloud, having contrary conditions: namely, the heat of the sun and the other stars, and the cold of the middle region of the air. But he ascribes no internal acting cause to the cloud, and consequently, he seems to conclude that it is a thing almost dead and inanimate, occurring only by accident. 

For this reason, various doubts present themselves to any sagacious consideration in the aforementioned Aristotelian description, which must be resolved and determined by the deeper and sharper edge of the human mind before it can judge directly concerning it. 

The first of these is whether there is any attractive power in the solar heat and the stars to elevate vapors from the earth and water upward into the middle region of the air for the generation of clouds, or not. 

The second: whether the coldness of the middle air is the efficient cause of the condensation of the sublimated <note>vapor turned into a solid or dense form</note> vapor into a cloud. 

The third: whether Clouds are moved only by external efficient causes (namely, through solar motion and the winds) and whether they are devoid of internal principles by which they are agitated, or rather, if the cloud is animated by some internal agent, contrary to the mind of Aristotle. 

I will answer these three questions in order and briefly. To the first, therefore, we say that the assertion of the Peripatetics is erroneous and false, which says that the Sun, Stars, or fire have any power of attracting within themselves, and consequently, that they attract vapors and exhalations from the earth and water upward into the middle region of the air. For it is proven by experience that they rather push away or repel vapors and exhalations from themselves—that is, they dissipate and expand things rarefied by heat—rather than enticing or attracting them to themselves in any way. Consequently, that which most men imagine is false: namely, that the Sun attracts smoke upward, or that fire entices the vapors of thinned water to itself. But we say that their office is to rarefy...

...to make and refine the waters and to reduce the moister substance of the earth into a vaporous existence; and then we affirm that such substances, having been reduced into the existence of vapors, are able to tend upward by themselves and without the help of another. For, just as heavy things tend downward by an innate appetite, so conversely, that which is light seeks the heights by a natural instinct. Indeed, all of this is clearly demonstrated through the observation of our **Experimental Instrument** <note>This "Experimental Instrument" is Fludd’s version of the thermoscope or weather glass, which he used to demonstrate the expansion and contraction of air in response to heat and cold.</note>. For, if you place your hand upon its globular top, the air enclosed in the glass will suddenly expand, and in its expansion, it will fly out away from the rarefying agent; much less will it draw smoky matter toward itself.

From these things, it is evident that although in the eyes of worldly men, vapors or smoke may seem to seek the heights, and they therefore conclude that their movement upward from the earth must proceed from the attractive power of the sun and stars; nevertheless, this assertion of theirs is proved to be false by ocular experiment. Insofar as we are taught by experience, the nature of light and heat is contrary to attraction, inasmuch as its only function is to rarefy, and by rarefying, to dissipate or scatter; whereas, conversely, attraction or contraction is nothing other than a certain condensation or gathering effected by the property of **Cold**: as is clearly demonstrated by our mirror or **Experimental Instrument**. But now I will prove that the foundations of Aristotle—which claim that clouds are created from vapors raised from the earth to the middle region of the air—are in every way discordant with the truth. It is necessary, therefore, in the first place to consider that the sense of Holy Scripture is plainly contrary to this part of his definition. Specifically, we gather that it must be understood by faith <margin>Hebrews 11:3</margin> <note>original: "Heb. 11. 2." The citation refers to the verse stating that "the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear."</note> that the ages were fitted by the word of God, so that from invisible things, visible things might be made. Therefore, it is certain that neither earth nor water are the visible origins of clouds, but rather the simple substance of the air—or the **Universal Element**—condensed into the consistency of a cloud by the opposing blasts of the winds. And this we also have confirmed from various other places in Holy Scripture: <margin>Job 28:25</margin> For Job says: "God in his wisdom fits the weight for the air, and he weighs the waters by measure; <margin>Job 26:9</margin> he binds them in the thick clouds, he makes statutes for the rain and a way for the lightning of the Thunders." By these words, that patient man <note>Job</note> confirms first that God the Father is the radical author of this meteorological work, and that He is the eternal efficient cause through whose mediation it operates. <margin>1 Cor. 8:6</margin> It is the Spirit of His wisdom. This also agrees with that text of the Apostle: "To us there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." Secondly, it confirms that the air is the subject of both fiery

<column-break/>

and watery meteors. For by the condensation of the air, mist and the consistency of a Cloud are made, which then afterward is converted into rain by an even greater condensation and resolution. But if the air is excessively rarefied, it is changed into the condition of lightning. Indeed, I do not say that the act of lightning itself is air; but rather it is an admirable light, which is clothed in air as if in a garment—the wondrous power of the aforementioned wisdom, which manifests itself in many forms in the air, as has been said elsewhere. Now, truly, the preceding text implies with these words that the air is the material subject of **Aquatic Meteors**: "God by his wisdom fits the weight for the air," that is, he condenses it according to his pleasure into mists and clouds. For the following words argue this same thing: "He weighs (says the text) the waters or clouds in measure," etc. Or he thins them into lightnings, as we gather from the rest of the text; and the Spirit of wisdom is always present, which in that vehicle <note>The "vehicle" here refers to the air or spirit carrying the divine force.</note> converts itself into various species like another **Proteus** <note>In Greek mythology, Proteus was a sea-god capable of changing his shape at will; Fludd uses him as a metaphor for the transformative power of the divine Spirit.</note>. Finally, we elicit from the said text that the invisible air is altered in weight and measure into the visible consistency of clouds, which then afterward melt into rains, and of lightnings, which appear to the eyes through compression. Furthermore, it appears from these things that it is neither Earth nor water, but the air alone from which the substance of a cloud arises. "Jehovah shall open to thee (says Moses) his good <margin>Deut. 28:12</margin> treasure, the heavens, by giving rain to thy land in its time." From these words, we observe first that by "the heavens" he understands the air; for in the air clouds are created, and again: the air is called "heaven" in many places of scripture, such as "the birds of heaven," etc. From this, we conclude that the air itself is the treasury-chest of God, from which He, according to His pleasure, produces and forms clouds, as visible things from an invisible thing. Second, we observe that the air is called His "good treasure," and consequently, it is that from which God not only extracts His meteorological creatures, but also from which some wise men expect their highest good. Moreover, we read elsewhere: "Therefore the treasures were opened, <margin>Ecclesiasticus 43:17</margin> and the clouds and mists flew out like birds." But this is rendered even more evident by this speech: <margin>Job 37:21</margin> "Suddenly the air shall be condensed into clouds, and the passing wind shall drive them away." By this, he expressly argues that the air is the treasury-chest of God, from which clouds are drawn out by condensation, and that the heaven is the sole treasure from which they are extracted: and consequently neither earth nor water, as Aristotle thought. If that were indeed true, I would have you notice what an absurd impossibility would follow: For then, when the sun is accustomed to thin the waters in the summer time, it would render the air especially...

...thick with a multitude of vapors; and then an even greater irregularity would frequently arise to subvert Aristotle’s reasoning concerning the generation of clouds. For if his theory were true, we would expect a greater abundance of clouds and rain in the summer than in the winter, seeing as vapors abound more in that season from the evaporation of pools, torrents, and rivers due to the presence of the Sun. But by its actual effect, this is proved false. And finally, it is not the heat of the Sun nor of the stars, but the eternal Spirit of Jehovah <note>Fludd frequently attributes natural phenomena to the direct or "organic" action of God’s Spirit through spiritual agents like the winds.</note>, who holds dominion over the Angelic winds of the world; in these he moves organically and works all those meteorological alterations in and through the air, as shall be declared below. Whence it was said, as above: *With wisdom he made a weight for the air, and weighed the clouds in a measure* <note>original: "Sapientiâ fecit pondus aëri, & nubes appendit in mensura"</note>, etc. But I come now to the second doubt.

For the resolution of the second question, I say that there is another way that invisible vapor or air is condensed into a cloud than that which was devised by Aristotle. For where he asserts that this act of thickening is caused by the contractive cold of the middle region of the air, it becomes a matter worthy of wonder why this effect does not also happen at other times—namely, when the winds blow from their own quarters or regions of the earth. For when the Southern winds <note>original: "venti Australes"</note> hold dominion, we then observe clouds multiplying and rains falling abundantly. I would like to know, I say, from those **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, named for the covered walkways (peripatoi) where they traditionally taught.</term>, why vapors should ascend so flowingly from the earth and water at that particular time when such winds are accustomed to blow—more so than at any other time when those winds do not have dominion—to create such copious clouds in the air. Or why that coldness of the middle region of the air should coagulate or condense vapors ascending in such a way more than at other times, since the thick, airy heat of the clouds, mixed with the warm rays of the place (which are driven Northward from the equinox), ought rather to moderate and mitigate the cold of the middle region. I know for certain that they are utterly ignorant of what to answer; therefore, I shall not press them further in this matter.

But so that you may better elicit the truth of how air is condensed into clouds, I will briefly explain to you an experiment experienced by myself, by which I was instructed in the mystery of the generation of mists and clouds. On my journey from the City of Venice toward **Augsburg** <note>original: "Augustam Vindelicorum," the Latin name for the German city of Augsburg.</note>, as I made my way one day among the Alpine mountains and crags, while the entire sky of the horizon was quite clear and without any speck of a cloud appearing—and consequently the Sun was casting its free rays everywhere without any misty hindrance—I noticed a mist gradually growing and increasing upon the summit of a mountain that was notably tall and steep above the others. This occurred especially on one side of it, against which the rays of the Sun were nevertheless striking strongly, until finally it was

<column-break/>

reduced into the consistency of a dense cloud, which was eventually resolved into rain. During all this time, the air everywhere else (except for that side of the crag, from its peak almost down to its base) was clear and free of mists and clouds. At first, I was certainly struck by the novelty of the thing, and seriously considering the matter, I finally climbed down from my carriage. Seizing some grass with my fingers, I threw it into the open air so that I might discern the path of the wind. I found that its gusts were directed straight against that side of the towering mountain. From this, I immediately gathered that the steps in the progression from airy vapor into the consistency of a mist, and from mist into a cloud, were caused by the greater or lesser compression of the common and **universal air** <term>Catholic air: From the Greek 'katholikos', meaning 'universal' or 'general'. Fludd refers to the standard atmosphere that surrounds the globe.</term>.

The wind, pursuing the fleeing air, coagulated only that portion of the air by addition and compression little by little, whose flight the height of the resisting crag was impeding. In this way, air added to air was altered from an invisible and thin state into a visible and dense form. Whence first a little cloud, then a cloud according to the shape of the front of the mountain, was generated, which was finally resolved into rain by the heat of the Sun, while all the rest of the air remained clear. By this I perceived with open eyes that clouds were not created in the manner described by Aristotle—namely, from vapor elevated from the earth and water—but by the thickening of thin and invisible air into the consistency of a Mist, and from that into a cloud, differing from a little cloud only by one degree of density.

<margin>Job 37:21</margin>
By this observation, I perceived the confirmation of that assertion of Job, who says: *that suddenly the air shall be condensed into clouds, and the passing wind shall drive them away.* <note>Fludd is paraphrasing Job 37:21, which in the Vulgate relates to the wind clearing the sky, but he interprets it as the wind's role in the lifecycle of clouds.</note> Truly, however, my spirit still hesitated a little, considering that mountains and tall crags are not found in every place to impede the fleeing air; yet we see clouds appear and move even in flat deserts and on the open sea, where there are no mountains or crags. Revolving this seriously and often in my mind, I was finally taught by another experience and became somewhat more deeply rooted in my opinion. For I thought to myself, not without deliberation, that there is no wind blowing with dominion in the heavens that does not have another wind—either opposite or collateral—which does not run against it in the common or universal element. Although it is not discerned because of the dominion of the more powerful wind, which obscures the actions of the lesser wind no differently than the presence of the Sun is accustomed to obscure the light of a lit candle. Now, that two winds blow at one and the same time, I was instructed by this experience: I, having often been carried across the seas, observed that when the predominant wind decreased somewhat in its vigor by turns, and pressed the sails of the ship only weakly, the wind opposite to it...

He extends this to the open sea, suggesting that opposing winds provide the necessary compression to form clouds where mountains are absent.</summary>

Where by the "brothers" of Boreas, he seems to understand the South wind and the other Cardinal winds, which, while Boreas blows with dominion, contend in the air in a surging manner; they bring forth not only clouds but also storms in the open Element. Therefore, I was no longer distracted by further doubt, but I established it as certain that either two or more winds can blow at once, whether in an opposing or transverse manner. By their collision, the invisible intermediate air is compressed and reduced into the substance of a mist or cloud; nevertheless, that cloud is driven and put to flight by that wind which holds the greater dominion in the heaven, according to that saying of Job: 
<margin>Job 37:21.</margin>

But in its motion or flight, being hindered by a former wind that is contrary in both position and nature (though perhaps weaker in strength), it gradually thickens and coagulates through the constant adding and compression of parts. This is as I said in my observation near the mountain: it changes from an airy and invisible substance into the consistency of a mist or cloud. These things having been rightly considered, it clearly stands that the opinion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking in the "peripatos" or covered walkway of the Lyceum.</note> concerning the

Now I come to the resolution of the third and final doubt: whether a cloud is moved only superficially and from the outside—namely, by the action of passing winds and Solar heat (as is the opinion of Aristotle)—or whether it is moved by some internal and central agent, to whose commands not only the winds obey, but also the clouds. These are carried hither and thither partly by an internal moving Spirit and partly by winds animated by that same spirit. I answer that, contrary to that vain assertion of the Peripatetics, the cloud enjoys its own internal agent, which "calls" it—that is, incites it to fulfill its pleasure. This internal principle of the cloud, I say, directs it like its own vehicle, where and how it pleases. For as this agent is universal, so indeed it is not absent from the spirit of the wind, which is also present with the cloud, inasmuch as the cloud is blown together and animated by the spirit of wisdom. For since the said acting spirit is present with and in the spirit of the wind, it works centrally in the air through the mediation of the Angelic spirit of the wind. By its gathering faculty, it contracts the air into the form of a cloud, which it afterwards makes its Tabernacle; and ascending upon the Angelic spirit, and flying upon the wings of the wind, it makes its tabernacle move with the wind according to its will. Hence, the scriptures say: *God covers the heavens with thick clouds, who prepare rain for the earth, who makes the mountains bring forth grass...*

One of these is more central than the other, and consequently prior in dignity; for the more internal an instrument is, the more excellent, noble, and powerful it is, as it approaches more closely to the seat of Divinity, which resides in the center, and in the center acts and works all things. That God is the sole mover in thunders, that He speaks from the whirlwind and the cloud, and that He is, according to His will, a consuming fire, and that He acts centrally in the winds, clouds, snows, and tempests, and that all these things are perfected by the spirit of wisdom, is testified everywhere throughout the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, the **Peripatetics** <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle; Fludd is critiquing their purely physical explanations of nature.</note> concluded quite unwisely that clouds are moved only by the heat of the sun or by the wind, as if by external principles alone. ## CHAPTER VII.

### *How the method of composing clouds may be demonstrated visually from the observation of our experimental instrument, and how the false and true definition of snow may be set before the eyes of onlookers.*

Now indeed it is proper that I demonstrate by visual experience the way in which clouds are generated in the sky by the opposing breath of two winds—namely, from the dominion of the South Wind <note>original: "Auster"</note> and the imperceptible breath of the North Wind <note>original: "Boreas"</note>. I told you before in Chapter 4, Book 4 of this section, that just as the air enclosed in the glass of the experimental instrument <term>the weather glass; an early thermoscope Fludd used to show how heat expands air and cold contracts it</term> expanded in its neck by the mere touch of a warm hand, and by that expansion flew away from the hand of the one touching it into the cold region of the water (which is proven because the water previously raised in the neck of the glass is suddenly cast down), so also the thick winter air in the Southern Hemisphere is expanded by the presence of the warm sun as it passes through the Autumnal Equinox. And because that hemisphere is not sufficient to contain all that expanded spirit, it flees with swift motion away from the solar activity, across the equinoctial line into the Winter or Arctic Hemisphere, so that it may find a more spacious place for its existence. But that volatile and expanded spirit, finding the constant air of that place contracted by the Northern cold due to the sun’s absence, is there suddenly condensed into clouds. And this is the reason why, even where no Northern blast is evidently felt, the Southern winds are accustomed to produce an abundance of clouds and rain. Thus, it is made manifest that the thick air of the Northern Hemisphere, though stirred by Northern blasts, meets the warm, thinned air sent from the opposite hemisphere; it resists it and gradually reduces it into the existence of a cloud. This whole process, I say, is explained by the proper observation of the air enclosed in the glass of the machine, as was indicated before.

Finally, I do not wish to explain the Aristotelian definitions of hoarfrost, hail, ice, and similar meteors <term>meteors; in the 17th century, this referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain and snow</term> in this place, nor to prove them contradictory to the sense of Sacred Scripture, since I have made ample mention of those things in my *Cosmic Meteorology*; and therefore, I refer you to that work. But I will now insist upon the definition of snow alone. Aristotle

<column-break/>

In this definition of his—since I find him no less wandering here than in the preceding ones, and especially regarding the origin of the cloud—I shall place no faith in him. Furthermore, he transgresses the intention and laws of Sacred Scripture by a description of this kind. **Snow** is a meteor which God draws out from His secret Treasury, or the Treasury-Chest of God, in the form of wool, to perform His will on earth, whether for punishment and a scourge, or for benefit and kindness.

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s critique of Aristotelian natural philosophy. While the previous page used his weather glass to explain the formation of clouds and snow, he now shifts his focus underground to challenge Aristotle’s theories on the origin of springs and rivers, contrasting them with his own "Mosaic" or biblically-based physics.</meta>

# ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY. Fol. 50.

Aristotle and the rest of his sect <note>the Peripatetics, or followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy</note> are of the opinion that the belly of the earth is filled with various cavities, passages, and fissures. Through these, they claim it is necessary for vapors to rise upward from the center of the earth to avoid a vacuum. As these vapors move, they cling to the sides of the hollows, fissures, or passages and veins of the earth, where they are resolved into water. By dripping down drop by drop, they create springs, which then later give rise to rivers. In this description of the origin of springs, they conclude that their "matter" is nothing other than vapor rising from the bowels of the earth, which is then condensed into water during its passage by the cold and heat of that place. This happens in much the same way as they believe clouds, rain, snow, and hail arise—first from condensed vapor, and then later liquefied.

But if we look into any definition of that school of thought with sharper eyes and examine it a little more accurately, we will perceive that for the birth of springs, they require not only a double "matter," but also a twin "acting form." For they imagine that the "remote matter" is vapor, and then they imagine the "proximate matter" to be drops of water, which are made from the freezing of the vapor. They even establish two efficient causes: cold and heat. For, they say, it is the job of the cold to condense and coagulate the rising vapor into the consistency of water, and it is the job of both heat and cold together to make the water mobile and able to flow. Therefore, wise readers, let me respond to these Peripatetic philosophers with their own axiom, and consequently defeat them with their own weapons. "In vain," they say, "is that done by many steps which can be done by fewer." <note>original: "Frustra fit per plura, quod fieri potest per pauciora"—a version of the principle of parsimony known as Occam’s Razor</note> Now indeed, if this fundamental and original work in the generation of springs can be conveniently performed by nature through one and the same substance of water, without any resolution into vapor and then a second condensation back into water, then I do not doubt you will conclude with me that this part of their definition is inconsistent, vain, and imaginary. I shall make this apparent and manifest in the following sections by visual demonstration. Namely, that in the course of nature, it is possible for water—without any alteration of its consistency—to be raised through the secret veins and passages of the earth to the heights, even to the peaks of tall mountains, from the depths of the earth and sea. This occurs after the water has, in its hidden passage through the sandy and porous substance of the earth, laid aside its salty nature. <note>Fludd is suggesting that seawater is naturally filtered and desalininated as it rises through the earth's crust to become fresh spring water.</note> Once this appears clearly enough, the vanity of Aristotle's invention will be suddenly revealed to any wise person. Besides this, the sterility of his invention—or of his reasoning itself—will be rendered palpable and manifest. He imagines that vapors clinging to the sides of earth's caverns must be converted into water, and then later become springs and rivers;

<column-break/>

but if we consider that drops made in this way would be more ready, because of their weight, to tend and return downward into the bowels of the earth through the same passages from which they rose in the form of smoke, rather than moving sideways. Therefore, it is likely that water made in this way, or at least the greater portion of it, would fall back into the place from which it came in the form of vapor. But leaving aside those arguments for a little while, I will examine and compare this part of his description with the authority and truth of the Holy Bible, so that we may better discern whether they agree in this matter or not.

We find in the first place that it is not some accidental or imaginary thing—neither cold nor heat in the bowels of the earth—that effects the generation of this "Meteor" <note>in the 17th century, "meteor" referred to any natural phenomenon in the atmosphere or earth, including springs</note>, but God, who works either through the angelic spirits of the winds or from his solar palace for the completion of this business. And even though in his action, both privative and positive, coldness and heat express themselves in the place of servants (For the text has: <margin>Psalms</margin> *Who can stand before his cold?*), nevertheless, His universal positive act is in the sun and the warm winds, which He extends from His solar Tabernacle and from His warm winds; and His privative or contractive power is that which He manifests through the distance or absence of His bright Tabernacle from an assigned region, and also the proximity of the polar seat and the presence of cold winds, which annually alter and transform the created Element into various forms. And therefore, it is God Himself who, by means of His spiritual organs—both in the heaven above and in the earth and water below—works all things, and among others produces and generates the springs from which rivers are later made. Consequently, it is an act of that Spirit <margin>Wisdom 1</margin> which, as Solomon testifies, fills the whole world and works all the wonderful effects within it. The Psalmist also confirms this in these words: <margin>Psalm 104:10</margin>
> **You who send forth the springs through the valleys, so that they walk between the mountains, and provide drink to all the living things of the field, so that the wild asses may break their thirst.**
Therefore, we see that the only universal agent, and thus the creator of springs, is that divine spirit. Here again is the "final cause": for the sake of the multiplication of fruits, herbs, and grass, and to provide drink for the animals of the field. Truly, our Peripatetics will reply that they have heard nothing new yet from the Scriptures to refute the Aristotelian opinion regarding the "matter" of springs assigned by him. But, so that I may take away the marrow of this objection, I will indeed make it so that they may clearly behold the truth of the matter without eyeglasses: if they look into this assertion of Solomon with accurate in—

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s critique of Aristotelian physics regarding the origin of water. While the previous page examined the "Remote Matter" and "Proximate Matter" of springs according to the Peripatetics, Fludd now turns to the authority of the Bible and other philosophers to prove that springs originate from the sea, not from condensed vapor.</meta>

### OF THE FIRST SECTION, BOOK V.

<margin>Ecclesiastes 1.</margin>
...they incline their minds with great intention. *All the rivers,* he says, *run into the sea, yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again, that they may flow once more.* <note>original: "Omnia flumina, inquit, intrant in mare, & mare non redundat, ad locum, unde exeunt, revertuntur, ut iterum fluant"</note> By this speech, the wise man <note>Solomon</note> explains to us that the real material of springs, or their material cause, is water, and not vapor. For he says in express words that it is nothing other than one and the same water which performs its perpetual circulation from the sea through the bowels of the earth, and by means of springs and rivers, back into the sea. This palpable error in Aristotle was the reason why not only many of the most learned men, both ancient and modern, but even some of his own faithful disciples, are seen to disagree with him on this matter.

<margin>
Albertus Magnus, book 2 on Meteorology.
Agricola, On the Origin of Subterraneans.
Seneca, Book 3 of Natural Questions.
</margin>
Among the older philosophers, some argue that the entire supply of water, from which perennial springs gush so abundantly, is collected from celestial waters or rain. But Seneca seems to overturn this opinion with these reasons: First, because he observed from the digging of vineyards that no rain penetrates and moistens the earth beyond ten feet. Second, because mountains full of bare rocks, which therefore do not admit rain, sometimes produce large and perennial springs. Third, because in the driest places, wells are found driven three hundred feet deep into the heights: by which it is right to understand that this water is not made from collected moisture, but from "living water." <note>term: "viva aqua" (living water) refers to naturally flowing spring water as opposed to stagnant or collected rainwater.</note>

Others think that springs are generated from a massive supply of water in the bowels of the earth; among these, Seneca believes that springs are produced from earth transmuted into water, insofar as all Elements are mutually transmutable. But that opinion is condemned by its own improbability without needing further refutation.

<margin>
Aristotle's Meteorology, Book 1, Ch. 13.
Cardano, Book 2 on Subtlety.
</margin>
Aristotle’s opinion is that they come from the vapors of the air enclosed in the passages of the earth and condensed by the cold, as has been said. Against him, Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano, a 16th-century polymath</note> primarily argues that it is incredible that such a vast and perennial quantity of water could be produced from air. Therefore, Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a scholar who often critiqued Cardano</note> rightly joins Cardano in refuting that opinion which thinks rivers are generated from air, especially since a tenfold or even greater proportion of air must coincide for the generation of one part of water. Thus, there is not enough concave space found in the earth for such an immense quantity of air that could produce such a great abundance of water. Furthermore, if so much air were consumed, it would be necessary for a vacuum to be found inside. These are the words of Scaliger.

<margin>Bodin, Book 2 of the Theater of Nature.</margin>
Bodin <note>Jean Bodin, a French jurist and philosopher</note> insists even more sharply against that opinion, saying that Aristotle’s view on the origin of springs lies discarded and mocked. For it cannot happen or even be thought that air could be corrupted <note>term: "corrupted" here means transformed from one element to another</note> with such speed as the waters flow; nor could all the elemental air do this in a moment, since it is very thin in its substance. Therefore, it would not suffice to produce that abundance of water which flows in a single day. But in this matter,

<column-break/>

Bodin is mistaken, for air is that most ancient idea among the Greek philosophers—namely Plato, and indeed Thales himself, who was the very first philosopher in Greece—ideas which long before had been recorded by the most learned and holy writings of the Hebrews: namely, that springs take their origin from the sea, according to the doctrine of Ecclesiastes. They confirm this by two reasons: first, because no other body besides the vast sea would suffice for such a great supply of water as gushes from springs; second, because despite such a great supply of water flowing daily into the sea, the sea itself does not increase.

Even among the most obedient disciples of Aristotle himself, such as Johannes Velcurius <note>a 16th-century commentator on Aristotle’s physics</note> (a man most well-versed in worldly philosophy, who spent much time unshelling the mysteries of Aristotelian philosophy and composed a commentary on his teacher’s *Physics*), when he comes to the treatise on the generation of springs, he seems to explain his teacher's ignorance or lack of skill in this matter with these words:

<margin>
Book 3 of the Commentary on Physics, ch. 6.
</margin>
> The Holy Scriptures, he says, do not agree with the Physicists <note>natural philosophers</note> regarding the birth of rivers and springs; for the Scriptures teach that rivers flow from the sea through various channels and passages, and flow back to their sources. Ecclesiastes 1 testifies to this, saying: *All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again.* However, the Physicists say that the "matter" is vapor resolved into water and liquefied by cold and heat together within the earth.

Thus he spoke. From this we gather that either this disciple is right to rebuke his teacher for this false doctrine, or he must consider the judgment of Solomon to be erroneous. For if the teaching of one is contradictory to the other, the more excellent must be chosen, and the inferior must be rejected by Christians. Who among the wise, by rejecting the opinion of Solomon, would embrace that of Aristotle? Or who, for the sake of saving and preserving the honor or dignity of Aristotle—a heathen and unfaithful man—would estimate Solomon, a man taught by God, to be a liar or a deceiver? But if our Christian Peripatetics, led by I know not what obstinacy, refuse to believe Solomon's assertion, I shall bring it about by means of the **Visual Experiment** explained in the following chapter, so that they might follow Solomon of their own accord and willingly, leaving behind that mind of Aristotle.

I conclude, therefore, by the authority of the Holy Bible, that a definition or description of springs of this sort must be made:

> Springs are continuous flows of water which, beginning from the sea and passing through the veins, fissures, and passages of the earth (closed on all sides), reach all the way to the surface of the valleys and the summits of the mountains by divine act...
