# CHAPTER IX.

### *In which Solomon's assertion concerning the origin of springs and rivers is approved and supported, partly by ocular demonstration and partly by reasons produced from the true source of Philosophy.*

I informed you, learned Reader, in my preceding discourse, that the Spirit of God acts annually within the universal <note>original: "Catholico"</note> Element of the lower world with a dual power. One of these is expanding or rarefying, which is perfected in its positive, manifest, bright, active, and hot disposition—the Treasury box whose chief palace or Tabernacle is the Sun, full of Divinity. The other is contracting, which in its privative and secret disposition is dark, cold, and fixed, whose seat and chief Treasury is around the poles of the world. Since this is, in effect, contrary to the former or active power, it claims its place in the quarters of the world furthest from the Sun; thus, the life-giving Spirit, which has its seat in the Solar Tabernacle, works in the common Element solely by expanding and banishing the Northern <note>original: "Borealia"</note> colds by its presence, and destroys the Northern actions by way of Rarefaction. So also, by way of Condensation, the cold Spirit of the Polar property shall have dominion in that portion of the universal Element, and by way of Condensation will reduce to nothing all those subtle effects which the heat of Light and Solar power produced. For example: all that which is produced in the universal Element during the Winter time in the Southern regions—that is, beyond the Equinoctial line—by the Arctic cold (while the Sun at that time remains in the Northern Hemisphere and creates summer with us), namely the condensation of air, the elevation of springs, the multiplication of waters, the production of snow, ice, and hail, and the...

<column-break/>

...killing of herbs, fruits, and plants, etc. The Sun, in its next visitation of those regions—which will be while the Northern Winter reigns with us—will, by the rarefying, expanding, and life-giving property of its Spirit, destroy and alter these things, converting thick air into subtle air, depressing the springs downward toward the bowels of the earth (which were sublimated on high in winter), dissolving the snow, frost, ice, and hail; and from fixed and opaque bodies, it will make mobile and transparent ones, namely waters. It will revive the spirits of trees, plants, and herbs, which were half-dead by reason of freezing; it will clothe their mournful and, as it were, grieving bodies with green garments, adorn them with flowers, and finally produce health-giving fruits. Briefly, there is nothing over which that Polar Coldness dominates in one Hemisphere during the absence of the Sun, in which the opposite summer of the Solar region does not act in the same proportion in a contrary manner. Were this not so, it would be necessary for the world to suffer either an increase or a decrease of its substance every year—that is, it would exist as sometimes larger in quantity and sometimes smaller. But, as Solomon affirms, just as the sea does not overflow despite the constant flow of rivers into it: so, even if springs rise up in one hemisphere of the world, it is necessary that in the opposite Hemisphere they descend into the earth and be diminished in equal proportion. Similarly, although the air, by means of that thinning which happens through the Spirit of the Lord in the sublunary universal Element, is accustomed to fly away from the Summer Hemisphere into the Winter one: yet it is necessary that the air so rarefied in a hot...

Whence it becomes evident that the contractive or attractive virtue of the Northern Spirit <note>original: "Spiritus Borealis"; Fludd associates the North with the divine power of cold and contraction</note> or of divine power, which is manifested in cold, first contracts and condenses the dilated air, and thus that contracted air attracts the waters to itself and raises them on high; and that without any alteration of the water which was below in the deep instrument, so that in the conclusion there is but one and the same water. Behold, therefore, from this you have it demonstrated and proved that it is possible in nature for that water to be raised on high from the caverns of the earth even to the peaks of mountains—water which is nourished by the sea—and that by a natural path and reason, without the mutation of water into vapor, as Aristotle vainly imagines, contrary to the sense of that Axiom: *It is done in vain through many things which can be done through fewer.* <note>original: "Frustra fit per plura quod fieri potest per pauciora" – a philosophical principle of parsimony, suggesting the simplest explanation is best</note> On the other hand, we see in the glass of the Instrument that if the rarefying or dilating virtue, either in the Sun or in warm winds, heats the top of the glass or renders the external air hot, then the air within the glass will dilate itself and precipitate <note>push down</note> the water which had been raised into the neck of the glass by the action of cold; and also the descent of the water denotes the rarefaction of the enclosed air.

## CHAPTER X.

### That the actions of Contraction and dilation, and consequently the Attraction and expulsion of air, enclosed within the glass of the Experimental instrument, can be fittingly applied to the Macrocosmic air and water, along with the effects of Elevation and depression of water which are derived from them.

Truly, various disputes have arisen among Philosophers, both ancient and modern, regarding the possibility and the reason for the ascent of water from the inner depths of the earth, through its veins to the peaks of mountains, among which one seems to disagree with another: And in the end, if we consider the matter seriously as it is, none of them reaches the desired end or the complete explanation of this Mystery. Plato in the *Phaedrus* <note>original: "Phædro"</note>, following the mind of Socrates, concludes and believes that there is a vast chasm in the belly of the earth, without foundation or firmament, full of immense water, perpetually agitated upward and downward: Thus he believes it is urged into various channels of the earth reaching into both Hemispheres and flows all the way to the springs: But truly, he himself in this assertion seems to allege no cause for this

<column-break/>

# ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

...rather that the earth is weighed down by the heaviness of water. Among the moderns, Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a famous Italian scholar</note> thinks that this squeezing out of water and its elevation to the heights is caused by the compression of the sea. Because experience shows that water is raised and stretched upward by the compression of the weight of a stone, he says that the sea is higher than the springs. This does not seem likely; for if the sea were as high as the mountains, it would submerge the whole earth. Others think that the waters are drawn upward and sublimated by the power of the stars. Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher</note> thinks that vapors, raised and reflected in the caverns of the earth, attract the water to themselves. Some claim that the earth is like a sponge and, for that reason, they have supposed it lifts the waters to the higher places. Finally, there are some who believe that the veins of the earth move the waters upward by a certain Spirit, no differently than we see blood in the veins of animals being driven upward and everywhere. In the end, we see that there are as many opinions about the upward motion of spring water as there are so-called Philosophers; none of these seem to carry the logic of truth, nor indeed even the face of probability, because they are unable to give a genuine and clear reason for those opinions of theirs.

But as for what my own opinion is in this matter, I will reveal it in a few words—which I do not blush to bring forward into public (even though I am the least of the Apostles and Philosophers <note>original: "Apostolorum Philosophorumque minimus"</note>)—because I shall endeavor to prove and demonstrate it not only by reasons drawn from the quiver of truth, but also by ocular <note>visual</note> experience.

We ought therefore to consider, as was said before, that the Universal <note>original: "Catholicus," meaning all-encompassing or universal</note> air and water of the world fill the vast cavity of the world, no differently than the air enclosed in a glass Instrument <note>the weather glass or thermoscope</note> fills its hollow guts. Thus, the spring water of this world, gushing from a single sea, is seen to penetrate into the guts of the earth and fill its veins, or general passages. Through these, it is attracted and raised all the way to the summits of the mountains by the same means and the same virtue by which the water enclosed in the glass Instrument is sublimated to the very top of the matrass <term>matratij|a long-necked glass flask used in chemistry</term> or glass. By these things it is also established that there is a very close relationship between the springs of the Northern Hemisphere and those of the Southern; for it was indicated in the preceding pages that the Southern air—namely, that which exists beyond the Equinoctial line <note>the Equator</note>—is continued in its own uniform consistency with that air which is in our Northern

---

### Visual demonstration of this matter via the Instrument.

<column-break/>

Hemisphere: so that the volatile and expanded air passing from the South is condensed into clouds by the Northern cold. For this reason, it is evident that the water nourishing the springs in the North is continuous with that of the South; no differently than the water raised to the top of the glass Instrument is continuous and plainly the same as that in the bottom of the vessel, which has its origin from the large vessel at the base of the instrument, which we compare to the sea. We conclude, therefore, in this manner: When the fiery spirit of the Sun in the depth of summer thins the air in a more intense way in the Northern Hemisphere, then that air, thus thinned and seeking a wider space everywhere for its expanded spirit (as we see in the extraction of the Spirit or Oil of Vitriol <note>Sulfuric acid; Fludd is comparing atmospheric pressure to the pressure in a chemical still</note>, where the receiver sometimes breaks unless a larger space is opened to receive the expanded spirit), it depresses and drives down the water of the Northern springs. This is exactly how the air enclosed in the glass, once expanded, is observed to push down and drive out the water that had been raised into the neck of the glass. On the other side, the cold—which at the same time predominates in the Southern Hemisphere by reason of the Sun’s absence—attracts and lifts the waters of the springs in those regions upward, and does so through the condensation and contraction of the Universal air into a narrower place. This is no different than what we see in our Experimental Instrument: external cold contracts the air enclosed in the glass, and in that contraction or central attraction, the water in the vessel at the bottom is raised upward. From this it is clear that two means offer themselves both for depressing the springs and for raising them up. For just as the warm summer spirit in one Hemisphere drives the waters of the springs lower through the thinning of the air, so the cold Winter Spirit of the opposite Hemisphere raises them and attracts them to the heights. Thus, on the summer side, the spring waters are repelled downward by the thinned air and are forced to make their way through the guts of the earth toward the winter side; and also, to perform that work more easily and quickly, the cold of the Winter part draws the spring waters upward to itself—those same waters which the expanded air depressed in the opposite summer part or Hemisphere. Finally, the Winter cold assists in the elevation of the springs through the contraction of the air, and from the opposite region, the summer heat assists in their depression and their driving back into the guts of the earth.

The right side is labeled "South Wind / Antarctic Pole / South." A central circular area is labeled "K" and is surrounded by a stippled or dotted ring. Various points on and within the spheres are labeled with letters: N at the top; A, B, C, D marking a subterranean channel; E, F, G, H, I, L, M marking points on the concentric circles. A horizontal line connects points E and G, passing through the center.</image-desc>

In this figure, **E**, **F**, and **G** represent the **Northern Hemisphere**, in which the Sun is most remote and, as it were, absent—being in the sign of Capricorn <note>The Sun's position during the Northern winter solstice</note>. This results in **Winter** dwelling there, and in the air (or its **Universal Element** <note>original: *Catholico ejusdem elemento*—Fludd refers to the all-pervading atmospheric spirit</note>), the **Northern cold** holds dominion. **E**, **H**, and **G** are the **Southern Hemisphere**, where the Sun is present and which is, consequently, the seat of **Summer**, as heat holds dominion in its air. **E-G** is the **Equinoctial line** <note>The Equator</note>, which distinguishes the Northern Hemisphere from the Southern. **A** and **B** are the openings of the **vein** <term>vena: Fludd uses the biological term for a vein to describe subterranean water channels, viewing the Earth as a living organism</term> or **General passage** in the earth, indicating two springs. This vein appears to communicate with both Hemispheres: for there is a continuous path from the opening or spring of the Northern region, **A**, passing through the "bowels of the earth" at **D** (which is full of seawater purged of its saltiness), and making its way to the Southern region or spring, **B**. Therefore, **D** represents the seawater which, through the porous substance of the earth, is as if **sifted** <note>original: *quasi cribrata*</note> into the concave center of the earth and cleansed of its salt, and which communicates with both the Northern spring **A** and the Southern spring **B**.

I conclude, therefore, that since the **Universal Element** or air of the Northern Hemisphere (**E, F, G**) is cold, it is immediately **contracted** by that cold. Through this contraction, it draws toward itself and lifts the water contained in the vein or passage of the earth (**A, B, D**), whose source is nonetheless the seawater at **D**. This (as I have said) is demonstrated in the **experimental instrument** <note>Fludd’s weather glass or thermoscope, a device where water rises and falls in a tube based on the temperature of the air trapped inside</note> by the rising of water in the glass due to the presence of cold. For when the cold external air contracts the air enclosed in the head and neck of the glass through chilling (which head and neck I compare to the vein, passage, or channel in the earth, which must be closed so that nothing escapes), then the water is lifted high from the large pot full of water contained at the bottom of the instrument, which I compare to the purged and sifted seawater.

<column-break/>

On the other side, during the summer time—or in the Southern and Eastern regions—in the hemisphere **E, H, G**, where the sun is present, the **Universal air** is **rarefied** <note>thinned or expanded</note>. This expansion of the air around those springs gradually thrusts the waters down into the water duct or its Southern vein toward the "bowels of the earth" at point **B** or **C**. From this, it often happens that in the summer time, springs are found to be very parched and dry, or either completely dry or significantly lowered. Finally, **I, K**, and **L, M** designate the return of the rivers formed by the springs back into the sea, so that they may flow again.

Now, I say that by reason of the lowering of the waters in the Southern summer (due to the excessive thinning of the air pushing the waters downward from that side) and their elevation in the cold region (due to the strong attraction of the thick and condensed air), the water is more or less inclined to abound in the **Winter region**, and conversely to be diminished in the **Summer region**, according to the greater or lesser dominion of cold and heat in them. This whole process is clearly enough demonstrated by observation of the **Experimental glass**: namely, that by the greater or lesser expansion of the air, the water is pushed more or less downward toward the bottom of the instrument. Conversely, according to the proportion of cold dominating in the external air, the water is lifted more or less into the heights. 

But I will show you another visible example confirming this same thing: namely, the principle of the rising of water on one side through attraction and its depression on the other through compression. Imagine some kind of **double syringe**, joined to one another at their openings; at the junction of these openings, there is a small globe perforated on all sides, common to both openings, and this globe is in the middle of a cavity entirely full of water and exactly closed on every side.

**A. R.** is the **Winter** or **Northern syringe**, **B. K.** is the **summer syringe**; the orifices of both meet and are securely fitted into the openings of the perforated small globe **K**, which sits in the middle of the cavity **D. D.**, which is full of water and sealed exactly on all sides. We say, therefore, that if the compressor or "tongue" <note>the plunger of the pump mechanism</note> of the **Southern Syringe I. M.** is pushed downward from **B**, and the tongue of the **Northern syringe L. N.** is drawn upward toward **A** in the same proportion, then it is necessary that the water be raised into the spring **A** of the **Winter Hemisphere** by a double power: namely, by the suction at **A** pulling upward and by the pressure at **B** pushing downward. And then **D. D.** acts as a kind of common cistern <note>original: *cisterna communis*</note> full of water, which is the origin of both springs, insofar as it perpetually supplies them with watery food. For (as we said above) in the same proportion that cold reigns and operates in the Element of the Winter hemisphere, so also heat reigns and operates in the air of the summer hemisphere. And consequently, it follows that in whatever proportion water is pushed down in the South, it is also raised in the North, and as a result, it is depressed in the south. And so it happens in reverse, when winter is present in the south and summer in the North. From these things, therefore, we see clearly that the opinion of **Solomon** is true and beyond doubt: Namely, that all rivers—and consequently all springs—enter into the sea, yet the sea does not overflow; to the place from whence they come, they return, that they may flow again <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:7</note>, and this happens without any change in the form of the waters. There are indeed many other visible experiments by which it is proven that water can be raised from the bottom of vessels to a height without any alteration of its existence. You will find two of these mechanical devices proving the same thing depicted in chapter 12, section 1, portion 4, part 2, book 3, member 2 of my *History of Meteors* <note>original: *Historiæ meæ Meteorologicæ*</note>, where I discuss watery meteors springing from the earth in liquid form or residing within the earth.

<column-break/>

But, let us examine that opinion of **Aristotle** a little more precisely, the better to expose its absurdities more clearly. If the matter of a spring were vapor exhaled from the bowels of the earth, then it would be necessary for such a conversion of central water into vapor to proceed from a great heat enclosed within the earth's bowels; without this, the **Abyss** <note>original: *Abysfus*</note> or such a vast mass of cold waters could not be resolved into vapor. But if it were admitted that a great fire is kindled in the earth's bowels, I pray you observe what a great absurdity would follow from that. For, first, he <note>Aristotle</note> admits that springs are colder in summer than in winter, because the extreme heat of summer encloses and, through **antiperistasis**, preserves and increases the cold property of the earth. Since this is so—as is apparent from the coldness of springs in winter time—then by this same reasoning, this increased or fortified cold in the earth ought also in summer time to retain, preserve, and strengthen that heat enclosed in the center of the earth, which is the immediate cause of that vapor procreating the spring. Observe, I beseech you, the conclusion: for if it happens that the central heat in the earth becomes greater in the summer period, then vapors would be more abundant at that time. For the greater the fire, the greater the vapor and smoke of the water will be. And again, by reason of the great cold contracted in the earth's caverns and fissures, those vapors would condense into drops more quickly and easily. From this it would follow that in summer time springs would become more prominent and fuller of water, and therefore rivers would more frequently exceed their limits and cause floods in summer than in winter. But experience testifies that all of this is contrary to the truth. But it will be objected (I know well) that ponds and lakes and similar damp places are observed to be dried up by summer heat, and how is it possible...

Hence it is that we observe mists and dew to be more frequent around lakes and rivers in summer time. Thus, as the sun recedes from one Hemisphere to the other, the waters are in motion through the bowels of the earth to the opposite place. ### CHAPTER XI. ###

->Lightning and Thunder are described in this chapter according to the opinion of Aristotle,<-

<margin>Book 2 of the *Meteorologica*</margin>
Having now made an inquiry in Aristotelian Philosophy concerning the nature of winds, clouds, snows, and springs, it is necessary in this place that I explain his mind's sentiment regarding the admirable origin and condition of Lightning and Thunder: indeed, these are meteors of such great wonder that they require the deepest speculation for their explanation. The opinion of the Peripatetics, therefore, is that the material cause of thunder and lightning is a hot and dry exhalation extracted from the earth and raised into the middle region of the air by the power of the sun and stars; where, partly by reason of the strong collision or clashing of clouds, and partly through that **Antiperistasis** <term>Antiperistasis: the Aristotelian theory that a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more concentrated when suddenly compressed by cold</term>, which exists between the hot disposition of the exhalation and the cold disposition of that region, that inflammable matter, thus narrowed in the belly of a cloud, is ignited, and violently breaking out from its prison, it tends downward by reason of its earthliness or compact consistency. And he concludes that by the violence of its eruption from the cloud, a sound is made—that horrendous voice which is called Thunder. This, I say, is the summary of the Aristotelian mind concerning lightning and thunder. And truly, Aristotle seems in some way worthy of excuse if he errs in a matter so abstruse, since there remains a doubt about the origin of lightning and thunder not easily resolved by philosophers. Hence it is that they do not seem to agree with themselves in the investigation of this thing’s nature. For **Empedocles** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 494–434 BC)</note> was of the opinion that lightning arises from the interception or obstruction of the descent of solar rays; but **Anaxagoras** <note>Another early Greek philosopher who focused on the physical causes of celestial events</note> maintains that they are a portion of ethereal fire which descends into the cavity of a cloud, in which it is then later enclosed, and he says that this light shining from the hollow of the cloud is called lightning, and that the effect of its eruption is called thunder. Others believe that fiery flashes of this sort 

<column-break/>

->which then afterwards are refuted by the testimony of holy scripture.<-

happen from the collision of hot winds, which, when they are enclosed on all sides by a cloud and narrowed within it, are ignited by it, and from this arises that murmur and the disturbance of the clouds. Again, many others have determined otherwise concerning them, so that in this matter it may be said without injustice: there are as many opinions of this sort as there are philosophers. And now, as far as the opinion of Aristotle is concerned, it is indeed so contrary or contradictory to the rudiments of true wisdom that some of his more faithful Christian disciples have opposed him in every way regarding this opinion. <margin>The *Margarita Philosophica*, in the chapter on Lightning</margin> Whence we have these things written in the *Margarita Philosophica* <note>original: "Margarita Philosophorum"—The *Margarita Philosophica* (The Philosophical Pearl) was a famous 16th-century encyclopedia by Gregor Reisch</note>: "Certain philosophers, considering the wonderful operation of Lightning, judged it to be not a work of nature, but the immediate effect of the most high God."

But let us come to the particulars of the Aristotelian definition. He says that the material cause of lightning is drawn from the earth, but he makes the efficient causes many: for he affirms that the "Agent" in its elevation is the attractive power of the stars. Furthermore, the external agents in the ignition of the exhalation create "accidents," namely the collision and clashing of opposing clouds, and that **Antiperistasis** which occurs between the heat of the exhalation and the cold of the middle region of the air. For from these he concludes that the ignition of the exhalation happens, and finally he shows the reason why lightning tends downward—namely, because its matter is earthy or of a compact existence. It will be my task to refute each of these particulars in order, and that as much by reasons drawn from the chest of nature as by the authority of Holy Scripture.

...elevated by an attractive power. First, it seems to me that this is merely a fiction, because it was proven before that the heat of the stars is devoid of any attractive faculty. Second, if a windy exhalation—which is light and not very compact, and consequently not so disposed to ascend and penetrate into the middle region of the air by reason of its subtlety—is denied entry into that region, then an entry into such a cold place will be much more prohibited for an exhalation of a more terrestrial and compact substance, even if it is easily ignited. <margin>Psalm 17. 9-15. <note>In modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 18</note></margin>

At the brightness in his presence the clouds passed, hail and coals of fire. And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice: hail and coals of fire. And he sent out his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightnings and troubled them,* etc. What then? Shall we gather from these things that the substance of this flashing material was extracted from the earth by the methods devised by Aristotle—namely, by the power of the stars? Or has any literate person, living in the Christian world, dared to think that a thing so abject and of such vile importance as the "excrement of the earth" <note>Fludd’s derisive term for Aristotle’s terrestrial exhalations</note> should be ascribed by Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles with such audacity and without any reverence to the essential power of God, and derived and kindled from his presence and Throne; indeed, even from his very mouth and face? Nor shall it be judged as unheard-of impudence in them, regarding the Divinity of the matter, to assert that *God is a consuming fire*, as we find in both the New and Old Testament? Or would the Prophet affirm that he made *his Angels winds and his ministers burning fires*? How poorly could a diligent watcher of divine mysteries judge the origin of Angels and spiritual lights if their material substances were merely accidental exhalations! Again, we are taught that the heaven or air is a *Treasury*, from which the winds, clouds, snows, hails,

<column-break/>

lightnings, and Rainbows are drawn out, and that all these are proportioned by the Spirit of God to perform his pleasure.

<margin>Job 28. 25.</margin>
Hence, in the place cited before: *God by his wisdom fits the weight for the air, and weighs the clouds in measure; he makes a decree for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunders.* By which it appears that the matter of all <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, 'meteor' referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, snow, and lightning, not just falling rocks from space</note>, whether they be watery or fiery, is drawn from the aerial substance or the universal sublunary Element <note>The "Catholic" or universal element of the air below the moon</note> through the word or wisdom of God. Consequently, it is not from the earth, nor is there any need for stellar attraction or elevation in this business, since the pure substance of lightning is perpetually reserved in the divine power and in his Treasury chest, until he who created it calls it forth to perform his pleasure. Would it not be a thing worthy of wonder if such an immense supply of exhalations were elevated by astral power from the earth into the middle region of the air by accident at one and the same time—just as happened suddenly in the exuberant rain of sulfur over Sodom and Gomorrah? But our Aristotelians will reply, according to their custom, that this was not done naturally, but miraculously. I respond that I cannot deny that this <term>meteor</term> was material: for it was composed of sulfur and fire. Now, I would like to know from them from what sanctuary or Treasury it was produced, and whether the stars extracted it from the earth and elevated it into the middle region of the air or not—or whether rather God called it forth from his invisible *aerial Treasury*:

<margin>Hebrews 1.</margin>
For St. Paul says *that visible things were first made from invisible things.* <note>Though cited as Hebrews 1, this is the sentiment of Hebrews 11:3</note>

Secondly, as far as the active or efficient cause is concerned, Aristotle errs more in that than in the material cause, as is explained by the aforementioned speech of the Royal Psalmist <note>King David</note>. For first, Aristotle says that the agent which attracts and elevates that exhalation is the attractive power of the Sun and Stars; then he imagines the efficient cause for the kindling of the material to be partly the clashing of clouds, and partly that <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>An imbalance or disharmony</note> which exists between the heat and dryness of the exhalation and the coldness of the middle region of the air, which, fighting against each other, cause the kindling of that fire which is called lightning. Good God! How poorly these things fit together, and how confused is the Chaos of that chimerical invention, which feigns a multitude of external efficient causes! In truth, there is but one, and that a marvelous one in this business, which is entirely essential, internal, and central; it moves to where and when it wishes, and works all in all. Are all these superficial, accidental, and external agents the primary movers and animators of lightnings and Thunders? And yet it is said that God animates and vivifies them by his presence:

<margin>Psalm 17. 9.</margin>
For the aforementioned Text of David has: *Fire from his face burned, coals were kindled by him at the brightness; in his presence the clouds passed, he multiplied lightnings,* etc.

He uses numerous biblical citations from Job, Psalms, and Revelation to prove that lightning is a spiritual and material manifestation of God’s power rather than a mere accidental byproduct of nature.</summary>

<margin>Job 41:2, 9.</margin>
His sneezing is a splendor of fire, his eyes are like the ignited fire, and smoke comes forth from his nostrils. His breath makes coals burn, and a flame goes out of his mouth, etc. By these things it is made manifest that lightning is an act performed immediately by God; it is, as it were, a certain power essentially proceeding from Him, which puts on and illuminates the transparent <term>worldly spirit</term> <note>Fludd refers here to the "spiritus mundanus," a semi-material substance he believed filled the universe and transmitted divine light.</note>, just as on the fourth day of creation, He put on His <margin>Psalm 104:2.</margin> Solar Tabernacle. And in this sense David said: *He is clothed with light as with a garment*, not because He Himself is the lightning, but because He exists in the lightning and as the bright "soul" of the lightning. Whence some say: *Light within light, light within the divine power.* And <margin>Leviticus 10:2; Numbers 11:1.</margin> Moses says: *Fire went out from the Lord and devoured them.* And elsewhere: *The fire of the Lord was kindled against them and devoured the furthest part of the camp.* And elsewhere: *Fire went out from Jehovah <margin>Numbers 16:35; Deuteronomy 4:24.</margin> and consumed those two hundred and fifty men who had offered incense, etc.* So it is said elsewhere: *A consuming fire.* And elsewhere: *A fire is kindled in my fury, which shall burn even to the lowest depths of the Grave, and shall consume the earth with her increase, and set on fire the foundations of the mountains, etc.* So it is said that the fire of God descended from heaven <margin>Deuteronomy 32:22.</margin> by the power of Elijah. And elsewhere, at the presence of God, the mountains melt like wax. <margin>2 Kings 1:12; Psalm 97.</margin> 

Therefore, having considered these things, what have we Christians to do—regarding the mystical creation of lightning—with the superficial, accidental, and external agents of the <term>Peripatetics</term>? <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, who taught that weather was caused by physical "exhalations" from the Earth.</note> Or why do they imagine I-know-not-what "movers" or "animators" in lightning that is produced by the divine? What shall we Christians imagine of the Aristotelian doctrine, when it feigns that the immediate act of God in His angelic creatures is something as vile and frivolous as the accidental rising of smoke from stellar creatures, the collisions of clouds happening by chance, and conflicts between cold and heat? It was indeed no wonder if (since his own invention deceived him in the investigation of a mystery of such great weight) he was forced to propose things to us that seem scarcely probable to the eyes of the wise. For, if we consider the wonderful effects of lightning—how it penetrates a scabbard while leaving it unharmed yet melts the sword inside; how it passes through a purse; how it penetrates a barrel and absorbs the wine without any sensible damage to the vessel; how it dissolves bones into pulp without any apparent injury to the animal's body—truly, what is even more beyond understanding and reason (to the punishment of the disciples of Aristotle's false doctrine, who hold such wonderful and fearsome works of God in contempt and neglect), it must be stated: We cannot deny that Aristotle was versed only in worldly wisdom, and consequently was utterly ignorant of the decrees of True Wisdom, insofar as he quite thoughtlessly imagined that lightnings

<column-break/>

do not have their own internal principles or most essential agents which make them act and move according to their own desire, where and when they will. This is just as I proved above against his mind: that the wind blows where it wills. In exactly the same way, lightnings are driven and carried according to their pleasure and, by consequence, enjoy a "will," since their central agent is that Spirit of Wisdom which (as Solomon says) is more mobile than any thing, more excellent in clarity than the Sun and stars, and more penetrating than all: <margin>Wisdom 7; Job 28:25.</margin> Job seems to hint at this where he says, *Wisdom makes a decree for the rain and a path for the Lightning of the Thunders.* That is, She herself, through Her spirit, animates, governs, and causes the lightning to move by whatever path pleases Her. It is as if one were to say that a man is moved by the soul inspired into him by God, to where and when he wills. Therefore, Aristotle indiscreetly assigned an external and accidental cause to the composition and animation of lightning, rather than an internal and essential one. 

But, to confirm what I have said—namely, that there is reason and intellect in creatures of this kind, and that men who detract from God’s omnipotence and hold His Great Works in contempt (after the manner of pagan philosophy) pay the penalty—I have proposed to recite to you two very true stories that happened in my own time concerning this matter. By these, it will be clearly manifested that there is a divine will in the thunderbolt or lightning.

<margin>The First Story.</margin>
In Ireland, two country girls were returning home from the marketplace of a certain town. One of them had bought herself new shoes and was carrying them in her hands. These girls, I say, traveling through the fields, were caught on the road by a certain horrific thunder. One of them was struck with fear and, calling upon God, hurried toward a tree; the other, rebuking the faint-heartedness of the one fleeing, mocked her with a great laugh and behaved in an impious manner. For, holding the voices of the thunders in contempt and derision, she said, "Why do you fear the thunders?" And striking her backside <note>original: "anum seu podicem"</note> with her other hand and turning it toward the place from which the sounds were emitted, she said, "Let the thunder kiss my backside, as long as it leaves my shoes untouched, I don't care." Whereupon it happened that the first girl, moved by the fear of God and His voice, escaped safely; but the other’s backside and buttocks were immediately torn and mangled, and thus that blasphemous girl died miserably. 

But, to press on now to the reward earned by the foolish assertion of the Peripatetics, <margin>The Second Story.</margin> at one time certain merchants and several others were in the company of a certain Peripatetic, coming with others at that time from the <term>Oxford Act</term> <note>The "Act" was the formal ceremony at Oxford University where students publicly defended their theses to graduate.</note>. He was a young man of good character who lived in the city of Shrewsbury <note>original: "Salopiæ"</note>, where he had undertaken the business of a schoolmaster and was held in high esteem by many for his knowledge of Aristotelian philosophy. These people (I say) were traveling together across the broad Shrewsbury plain...

## SECTION ONE, BOOK V.

...while they were there, they noticed thick clouds approaching them with sounds and thunder, wherefore the greater part of them were struck with no small fear. But that young man, in order to show himself to be quite well-versed in Peripatetic Philosophy <note>The "Peripatetics" were followers of Aristotle; Fludd frequently targets their reliance on physical logic over spiritual revelation.</note>, boldly urged them not to fear in such a confusing situation. He claimed that this was a common occurrence in nature, happening by chance, and told them there was no real danger. He explained that it was generated merely from a hot and dry exhalation raised from the womb of the earth into the middle region of the air by the power of the Sun and stars, and ignited through <term>Antiperistasis</term> <note>original: "Antiperistan"; a philosophical concept where a quality intensifies when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more violent when compressed by cold air.</note> between the heat of the exhalation and the cold of that place.

But God, ignited by the impiety of such advice, showed the listeners that the matter was far different than what the man preached. For that unhappy man, who dared to publish the false doctrine of Aristotle in derogation of God's work, paid the penalty: he alone among the others was suddenly killed by lightning, while the rest remained merely stunned with astonishment. And so, by the just judgment of God, Aristotle’s opinion on this matter was condemned.

See and behold (my "Christian" Peripatetic!) these examples worthy of note: do you not see from these that an intellectual mover and a divine will reside within the lightning? Do you not see here a wretched and miserable mortal, destroyed because of his excessive confidence in the Philosophy of Aristotle? For if he had rejected that doctrine or philosophy which is founded upon earthly and demonic wisdom, and had devoted himself with reverence to the discipline of true Wisdom, he would undoubtedly have been struck by a true fear. He would have wished to revere Him who speaks in the Thunder and to pray with his companions, that God might turn the effects of His wrath away from them and preserve them under the shadow of His wings from His striking and wounding ministers. Then, without a doubt, both he and the others present would have escaped safely. Then (I say) by rejecting the fictions of Aristotle, he would have gathered from the Scriptures the divine power in the thunder and lightning, and seen that they are His ministers, most fit for perfecting His will.

<margin>Job 28:25 <note>Likely referring to Job 37:11-13.</note></margin>
The clouds, says Job, scatter their light, which illuminates all things round about; wherever the Will of the Creator moves them, they act, performing everything He commanded them over the face of the earth, whether for a scourge or for mercy. And elsewhere: Do you send forth lightnings, and will they return to say to you, "Here we are"?

<margin>Job 36; Wisdom 5:22.</margin>
And Solomon says: The shafts of lightning will go directly, and as if from a well-curved bow to the target. That is, the lightnings themselves, animated by God, go forth and are sent by Him, in whom their will resides and who works all things. This is also clearly established from this Text: There went up, it says, a smoke out of the nostrils of Jehovah, and fire out of His mouth devoured; coals were kindled by Him. He bowed the heavens also, and came down; and darkness was under His feet. And He rode

<column-break/>

<margin>2 Samuel 22:8 <note>Fludd cites this as "2 Reg.", following the older naming convention where 1 & 2 Samuel were called 1 & 2 Kings.</note></margin>
upon a Cherub, and did fly upon the wings of the wind. He made darkness pavilions round about Him, sifting the waters from the clouds of the heavens. At the brightness that was before Him, the clouds were kindled, and coals of fire flew. The Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High uttered His voice. He sent out arrows and scattered them; lightning, and He discomfited them.

By this discourse, it is argued that there is no "essential efficient cause" that is merely natural; rather, it is God alone, both within and outside of nature, who works all things. For in the preceding discourse, it is not said that either the clouds or the wind had sent out their own flashes, nor that the fire descended from the Sun or any other heavenly body, but that smoke went out from the nostrils of Jehovah and fire from His mouth. Nor is it said that vapors or exhalations were the material causes of the clouds; rather, Jehovah "bowed the heavens" (or the air) and gathered the clouds from the air according to His pleasure. 

Neither was the cold of the middle region of the air the "acting cause" in accumulating the air into a dense mass of clouds; rather, Jehovah collected them in His private and contractive property. For the Text says: He made darkness His secret place. Nor was there any Angelic efficient cause that did these things by itself; rather, Jehovah, ascending upon a Cherub (or an Angelic spirit), animated it and drove it to perform His pleasure. Nor was it the wind that was a mover by itself, but the Cherubic Spirit, animated and inspired by Jehovah, which made the wind move. 

Neither was that dark place for Jehovah's secret Tabernacle merely arranged by Angelic winds; rather, Jehovah, moving upon the Cherub, incited the Cherub to move and breathe the wind to collect the clouds in and from the air. Nor was it the resolving faculty of the Sun that melted the clouds into rain; rather, Jehovah "sifted the waters from the clouds." Nor was there any collision of opposing clouds or "Antiperistasis" of cold and heat that produced the lightning or the kindling of the clouds, but rather the lightning and inexplicable splendor of His presence. For the words of the Text are: *At the brightness in His presence the clouds were kindled.* Nor was there that "contentious struggle" between fire and water in the bursting of the cloud which produced such a stupendous voice; rather, it was the voice of Jehovah, who thundered from heaven by means of that instrument (His dense Tabernacle). It was, I say, the Most High who uttered His voice from the cloud and sent forth His lightnings to destroy the impious.

Since this is so, what business do we Christians have with fictitious "Natural causes," acting as efficient causes in their own right? For it is certain to us, and confirmed by Holy Writ, that God works all things in all. As for that distinction of the Peripatetics—that an acting cause is either "principal" or "secondary and subordinate"—you see from the preceding Text that it should be considered a worthless and mere fiction.

For the sole efficient cause in the first, second, third, and fourth organ or instrument was Jehovah: For it was He himself who inspired the Cherubim; it was He himself who ascended the Cherubim; it was He himself who, being upon the Cherubim, animated the wind, sifted the water from the clouds, and ignited those very clouds through His own lightning sent forth from Himself. Finally, although He may use many organs, nevertheless the essential act which operates in and through them emanates from a single, pure, and simple truth or identity. This identity encompasses all things within itself, no differently than **Unity** in Arithmetic encompasses any number whatsoever. For **Unity** is always found in the first, the middle, and the last; indeed, in every place where numbers exist. There are various other wonderful histories regarding this subject, all of which I have clearly expressed in my *Meteorological History* <note>original: "Historiæ meæ Meteorologicæ"; Fludd refers to his own massive work on weather and cosmic cycles, where he treats weather as a spiritual science.</note> in Chapter 20, Section 1, Portion 4, Part 2, Book 4, Member 1; for this reason, I shall omit them in this place.

But the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who sought physical rather than divine causes for natural events.</note> (I know well) will rise up against this opinion of mine, replying that it was said *metaphorically* in the Scriptures that Jehovah speaks and emits His voice in Thunder; and consequently, that it should not be understood literally as it presents itself to the eyes. But if this were true, it would follow that the words for "cloud," "snow," "hail," and so on, must also be understood in a metaphorical manner. From this it is clear that the speech would be either real or not real: if not real, men would be led into error rather than toward the truth. But Scripture is full of this kind of speech, wherefore it is certain that the whole Harmony of the Bible interprets it exactly as it truly is. Again, some of them acknowledge that those speeches are genuine and real; however, they say that where <margin>Job 37:11</margin> God speaks in Thunder, that act is miraculous and not natural. To these I respond with the mouth of Job: *For irrigation God tires out the thick cloud and scatters the light of his cloud, etc.* By this it is made manifest that God is the Actor in the **usual** gathering of clouds, and He makes them His common instruments or organs to produce His voice and sounds for the world—both for the growth and increase of the fruits of animals <note>likely referring to the sustenance of all living creatures</note>, and for the punishment of creatures. Whence it is said elsewhere: *If a man should consider the extensions of the thick clouds, the crashes in His Tabernacle, He extends His light upon it; with these things He shall judge the people and <margin>Job 36</margin> give food in abundance.* And elsewhere even more clearly: *Look upon the rainbow and bless Him who made it; it is very beautiful in its brightness, it has encircled the heaven in the circuit of His Glory, the hands of the Most High have fitted it; by His command He hastens the snow, and sends forth the lightnings of His judgment.* <margin>Ecclesiasticus 43:14</margin> <note>Fludd cites "Eccles." which commonly referred to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) in this period, rather than the book of Ecclesiastes.</note> Because of this the

<column-break/>

Treasuries were opened and the mists flew out like birds; in His greatness He placed the clouds, and the hailstones were broken; at His sight the mountains were moved, and by His will the South Wind <note>original: "Notus"</note> blew; the Voice of His thunder rebuked the earth, the storm of the North Wind <note>original: "Aquilonis"</note> and the gathering of the spirit sprinkles the snow, etc. This Syriac discourse seems to argue and prove that the **sole essential efficient cause** in the generation of "Meteors"—namely rain, snow, lightning, cloud, hail, thunder, wind, storm, etc.—is the act of the divine Spirit itself. It also denotes that their material existence is air <note>original: "aër"</note>. Wherefore it says in conclusion: *The gathering of the Spirit scatters the snow.* This means that from gathered air a cloud is made, and from the dissolution of the cloud, snow is scattered everywhere. Finally, it makes us certain that the hand or Spirit of God is not idle in the production of such works which Aristotle calls **Natural**; and consequently, He operates not only primarily and secondarily, but universally and entirely—that is, "all in all," as the Apostle says—both in the generation and preservation of things as well as in their corruption and destruction. In doing so, He does not wander in His action from the limits of His own Identity, or the division of His Unity. Therefore, against the opinion of Aristotle, I acknowledge no other nature besides the one and only God in His Creatures, or, if you prefer, a single infinite nature in every created thing, which is the sole actor of all things. I acknowledge, I say, with the Apostle <margin>1 Corinthians</margin>—excluding all the Gods of the Heathens whether in the heavens or on the earth, to whom they falsely attribute primary, secondary, or tertiary action—one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and besides these I understand no essential efficient cause in the worldly machine.

Regarding the last clause of the Aristotelian definition, in which he asserts that lightnings move downward because the matter from which they are made is more compact and earthly: I respond that this reasoning is too weak and insufficient for such a "giant" author. For by the same logic we could infer that **Gunpowder** <note>original: "pulvis Bombardalis"</note>, the substance of which is much coarser and more compact than that of lightning, must necessarily descend downward. And yet we see (by the experience of those places where this powder is applied, and also in artificial fire) that the power of that powder is to tend upward. Now indeed I come to the true descriptions of Lightning and Thunder, assigned to us even by the writing of the whole truth,

...is described: For Jehovah was the sole <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary agent that brings a thing into being or produces an effect.</note> in the first, second, third, and fourth organ or instrument: For it was He himself who inspired the Cherubim, He who ascended the Cherubim, and He who, within them and above the Cherubim, gave life to the wind, sifted the water from the clouds, and ignited them through His own lightning bolts sent forth from Himself. But if this were true, it would follow that the words "cloud," "snow," "hail," and so on, must also be understood in a metaphorical manner. From this it is clear that the speech would be either real or not real: if it is not real, men would be led into error rather than toward the truth. But Scripture is full of this kind of speech, wherefore it is certain that the whole Harmony of the Bible interprets it exactly as it truly is. Again, some of them acknowledge that those speeches are genuine and real, but they say that when God speaks in Thunder, that act is <margin>Job 37:11.</margin> miraculous and not natural. To them I respond with the mouth of Job: *For the sake of watering, God fatigues the dense cloud and scatters the light of his cloud,* etc. by which it is made manifest that God is the Actor in the usual gathering of clouds, and He makes them His common instruments or organs to emit His voice and sounds to the world; as much for the growth and increase of animal fruits as for the punishment of creatures. Whence it is said elsewhere: *If man would consider the extensions of the dense clouds, the crashes in His pavilion, He extends His light over it; with these He shall judge the people and <margin>Job 36.</margin> give food in abundance.* And elsewhere even more clearly: *See the rainbow and bless him who made it; it is very beautiful in its brightness, it has circled the heaven in the circuit of His Glory, the hands of the Most High have fitted it, by His command He hastens the snow, and sends forth the lightnings <margin>Eccles. 43. 14.</margin> of His judgment.* Because of this, the treasuries are opened...

<column-break/>

...and the mists fly out like birds; in His greatness He has placed the clouds, and the hailstones are broken; in His sight the mountains were moved, and by His will the South wind blew, the Voice of His thunder reverberated through the earth, along with the storm of the North wind and the gathering of the spirit scatters the snow, etc. This speech of the <term>Syriac</term> <note>original: "Syriaci"; Fludd refers to the Wisdom of Sirach, also known as Ecclesiasticus, which was part of the biblical canon he studied.</note> seems to argue and prove that the sole essential efficient cause in the generation of <term>Meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena: rain, snow, wind, and lightning.</note>—namely rain, snow, lightning, cloud, hail, thunder, wind, storm, etc.—is the act of the Divine Spirit itself. It also denotes that their material existence is made of air. Wherefore it says in the conclusion: *The gathering of the Spirit scatters the snow:* That is, from the gathered air a cloud is made, and from the dissolution of the cloud, snow is scattered everywhere. Finally, it makes us more certain that the hand or Spirit of God is not idle in the production of such works, which Aristotle calls "Natural," and consequently He works not only primarily and secondarily, but <term>catholically</term> <note>In the sense of "universally" or "wholly."</note> and entirely—that is, "all in all," as the Apostle says—both in the generation and preservation of things, as well as in their corruption and destruction. And in doing so, He does not wander in His action from the limits of His own Identity or the division of His Unity.

Therefore, against the opinion of Aristotle, I acknowledge no other nature except the one and only God in His creatures, or, if you prefer, a single infinite nature in every created thing, which is the sole actor of all. I acknowledge, I say, with the Apostle <margin>1 Cor. 8.</margin>—excluding all the gods of the Heathens whether in the heavens or on the earth, to whom they falsely attribute primary, secondary, or tertiary action—one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things: and besides these, I recognize no essential efficient cause in the machinery of the world.

To the final clause of the Aristotelian definition, in which he asserts that lightning moves downward because the matter from which it is made is more compact and earthy, I respond that this reasoning of his is too weak and insufficient for such a "giant" author. For by the same respect, we could infer that gunpowder <note>original: "pulvis Bombardalis".</note>, whose substance is much grosser and more compact than that of lightning, must necessarily descend downward: and yet we have seen (by the experience of those places where this powder is used, and even in artificial fire) that the power of this powder is to tend upward. Now indeed I come to the true descriptions of Lightning and Thunder, assigned to us even by the writing of all truth.

BOOK V of the FIRST SECTION.

# CHAPTER XII.

## ->How lightning is to be correctly described by a true Philosopher and according to the principles of the Holy Scripture.<-

Since it appears from the discourse of the preceding chapter that Aristotle erred greatly and monstrously in his opinion and conception regarding both the <term>material</term> and <term>formal cause</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, the "material cause" is what something is made of, and the "formal cause" is its essence or pattern.</note> of lightning and thunder, let me be permitted in this place, according to the strength of my slender capacity, to fish out their true and genuine definition from the deep sea of the sacred scriptures, so that by this reasoning I may show you their sincere nature and essential origin.

Lightning is a certain fiery air, which is drawn out from the heavenly or aerial Treasury of God and is animated by His glowing presence, and is sent forth onto the earth and the sea to execute His will, whether it be for the good or the detriment of His creatures.

<margin>Or thus.</margin>
Lightning is a certain flashing brightness proceeding from a cloud, as if from the cavity of a divine Hut <note>original: "Tugurij"; likely referring to the "tabernacle" or "pavilion" of clouds mentioned in the Psalms.</note>, which is sent forth from the Throne of Jehovah onto the earth and the seas to perform His pleasure.

If we wish to describe lightning with all its <term>accidents</term> <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are the non-essential properties of a thing, such as its color or timing.</note> and consequently describe the whole essence of Thunder (which is of a mixed nature), we can perform it in this way from the Holy Testimony:

Lightning is a consuming fire, which is ignited from the face or presence of Jehovah, at the sight and contact of whose brightness the clouds pass away, and the Most High thunders or utters His voice from heaven, and is accustomed to hurl arrows for the destruction of the wicked.

<margin>Or thus.</margin>
Lightning is a fire flying forth from the mouth of Jehovah, sent from above from His Tent, in whose sight the waters or clouds (as if fearing, and the Depths, as it were, troubled) pass away, and the voice of the thunder of Jehovah moves in a wheel <note>A reference to Psalm 77:18, where "the voice of thy thunder was in the heaven [or wheel]."</note>, and fiery coals or His arrows are hurled to execute His will in the heavens and on the earth.

<margin>Or thus.</margin>
Lightning and also the Flashing is a certain pure and bright light made in the upper clouds, which the passing wind has cleansed.

In the first description of lightning, you have it manifested that its material cause is air; the fiery place from which it is brought forth is the Treasury-chest of God, or heaven. The formal cause is explained therein when it is called Spirit or fiery air. We make its <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The agent that brings the thing into being.</note> to be the immediate act or divine will. Finally, we detect the <term>final cause</term> <note>The purpose or end goal of the thing.</note> in it by the fact that it is sent forth at the will of Jehovah, either as a scourge and punishment for mortals, or 

<column-break/>

to offer them mercy and kindness: all of which is clearly confirmed by the holy testimonies expressed in the preceding chapter.

<margin>Revelation 4. Psalm 17:9. Job 41:10. Psalm 76:17. Job 36.</margin>
The second description is confirmed by the Sacred Page: Lightning, says the Text, proceeds from the Throne. And elsewhere: *At the brightness in His presence the clouds passed away.* And elsewhere: *fire flew out from His mouth.* And: *from His mouth, as if torches preceded and as if His breath ignited coals, and a flame came forth from His mouth.* And elsewhere: *Your flashes lit up the world.* Furthermore: *Jehovah spreads out the clouds, like His Tent, and lightens with His light from above, and covers the hinges of the sea.* <note>The "hinges of the sea" (cardines maris) refers to the foundations or depths of the ocean.</note>

Moreover, we confirm the parts of the third description (by which the entire nature of Thunder is explained) by the sacred testimonies partly mentioned before and partly following. And primarily, the material cause of Thunder is expressed by these, namely: that it is a burning fire or fiery air, and through the description of its matter we elicit its form. Furthermore, we have said that its efficient cause is the spirit of an angry Jehovah. We have also asserted that the effect of that agent is the agitation of the clouds and the voice of Thunder; and finally, we indicated the end goal is the fulfillment of the divine will in the destruction of the wicked.

<margin>Psalm 17:9.</margin>
The confirmation of these parts of the description is as follows. The Psalmist says: *smoke ascended in His anger and fire burned from His face: Coals were kindled by Him: He bowed the heavens and came down with darkness under His feet, etc: and He placed darkness as His hiding place around Him, His Tabernacle dark water in the clouds of the air. At the brightness in His presence the clouds pass away, as do coals of fire: the Lord thundered from heaven and the Most High gave His voice, hail and coals of fire, and He sent His arrows and scattered them, He multiplied lightnings and troubled them, etc.* In the thread of which words, indeed, all parts of the preceding description are revealed and confirmed.

The small portions of the fourth description are also established by the authority of the preceding text.

As for what pertains to the confirmation of the fifth, it is confirmed from the preceding; furthermore, we have more fully grounded the third and fourth by these:

<margin>Psalm 76:17, 18.</margin>
*The waters saw You, O God, the waters saw You and they feared, and the depths were troubled: The multitude of the sound of waters, the clouds gave a voice: For indeed Your arrows pass through: The voice of Your thunder in a wheel, Your flashes lit up the world.* <note>Fludd uses the Vulgate numbering; these verses correspond to Psalm 77 in modern English Bibles.</note>

The clouds poured out a multitude of water, the clouds sent out a sound; the voice of your thunder was in the whirlwind.* <note>original: "Viderunt te aquæ, Deus... vox Tonitrui tui in rota." — Psalm 77:16-18.</note> The **formal cause** <term>formal cause</term> <note>The "formal cause" refers to the essential nature or "pattern" of a thing—here, Fludd defines thunder's essence by its sound and light.</note> is also described therein, in that it occurs with a crash and with flashes of lightning. The **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being.</note> is seen to be the lightnings, or rather the fiery gaze of God, animating the lightnings themselves and directing them toward the goal ordained by God. For this reason, lightnings are like the instruments of God in His wrath, just as a sword is the instrument of a man who strikes—where we say that he struck with such a sword, and do not credit the sword itself. Therefore, we say that God alone is the actor in worldly affairs, the Father of the thunders themselves, who sends forth lightnings like his arrows from his Throne. We have placed the **final cause** <note>The "final cause" is the purpose for which a thing exists.</note> as being for the fulfillment of the divine will.

Or finally, in this manner:

->Thunder is the voice or speech, or the utterance or sound proceeding from the mouth of Jehovah, which is directed under the whole heaven, with light, over the ends or borders of the earth; after which a sound roars, or God thunders with the voice of his majesty, and it cannot be tracked; after his voice has been heard, he who thunders performs wonders with his voice.<-

<margin>Job 37.</margin>
We have this confirmed thus: *Hear with trembling,* says Job, *the voice or speech or* (as another interprets it) *the utterance proceeding from the mouth of Jehovah; he directs it under the whole heaven and his light over the ends or borders of the earth; after it a sound roars, he thunders with the voice of his majesty and it is not tracked when his voice is heard: God, thundering with his voice, does wondrously.* <note>original: "Hanc sic confirmatam habemus... Tonans Deus voce sua facit mirabiliter." — Job 37:2-5.</note>

From these things, therefore, it clearly appears—contrary to the insane opinions of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum" — Fludd frequently uses this term for non-Christian philosophers like Aristotle.</note>—that these are neither exhalations nor vapors combined with them, nor the sun with the stars, nor earth or water, nor the Elements, nor created nature; but God alone, who is the operator of all wonders, who is the immediate efficient cause of these miracles. This, as you see, you have confirmed by the sacred scripture, lest you attribute this work—as the Pagans do—either to an imaginary nature, or to the Elements, or to things composed of elements; for these works must be attributed to the Creator first and before all things. Therefore, conclude that there is the greatest imprudence in those Philosophers distinguished by the Christian name—indeed, even a madness beyond recovery—to place such great faith in the vain and lying opinions of the Pagans regarding lightning and thunder. By these opinions, men are easily persuaded that thunders and lightnings are merely incidental things, arising from a natural imbalance of the air or sky, and not at all sent by divine power. And so, looking only at the effect, they falsely estimate it as the efficient cause, as if it were just and religious to ascribe works produced by God the Creator to his creatures. Therefore, I would have you know that I

For it seems that other Philosophers, far deeper than I in the more hidden mystery of Jehovah, agree with me: Namely, those who, considering the admirable nature of Lightning and noticing the hidden method by which other Meteors are generated, judge them to be not the works of some secondary nature (whose fame the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle was said to teach while walking.</note> seem to celebrate with so much praise), but rather, according to the Scriptures, the immediate acts of the most high God. We conclude, therefore, that it is evident that the opinion of the Peripatetics, both Christian and Pagan, is wandering and distant from the truth; for it says that lightnings are nothing other than hot and dry exhalations, drawn out from the earth and elevated into the middle region of the air by the attractive power of the sun and stars, which, being enclosed in a dense cloud, are ignited partly by the collision of clouds and partly by **Antiperistasis** <term>Antiperistasis</term> <note>A scientific theory of the time suggesting that a quality (like heat) intensifies when surrounded by its opposite (like cold).</note>, which exists between the cold of that place and their own heat; then, by the eruption of the flame from the cloud, thunders are forced out. I wish that any wise Christian would diligently observe, from what has been said before, whether the mystery of the Tempest, the Whirlwind, and the Thunders depends upon a matter of such little weight and value as Aristotle has handed down to us, or on the contrary, whether it does not emerge from the inscrutable abyss of divine depth—since lightnings are handed down by the source of truth to be the fiery torches and lights of Jehovah, which emanate from his Throne: and since Thunders are called the voices, words, and utterances of the Most High, etc.

And for that reason, Jehovah—rebuking the audacity of such worldly Philosophers, who presume so greatly to judge his secret actions in advance, and who precipitously plunge themselves into the depth of the essential causes of Meteorological Mysteries without the assistance and guidance of the divine spirit, and who intend to seduce the world with scarcely probable arguments, persuading it to believe that such secret Great Works of God proceed from things so foolish and vain, and produced according to the imagination of their own fantasy—seems to address them from the Whirlwind in these words:

<margin>Job 38.</margin>
> Give ear and consider the wonders of our strong God, when God disposes of them, when the Light of the cloud shines? Or: Do you know the balancing of the thick cloud, more wonderful than the knowledge of the perfect God? Which is the way by which the Light is scattered? From whose womb did the ice come forth? Or who begot the frost of heaven? By what way does one go where the Light dwells, and where is the place of darkness? Who gave a course for the most violent rain, and a way for the sounding thunder? Who is the Father of the rain? Or who begot the drops of dew? Will you lift up your voice in the mist, and will the rush of waters cover you? etc.

For thus the paths of those who are on earth were corrected, and so they were saved by wisdom, etc. <note>original: "Quis hominum cognoscit consilium Dei?..." — Quoted from the Book of Wisdom, a deuterocanonical book often attributed to Solomon.</note>

<column-break/>

This is testified by Solomon, who confessed that he possessed knowledge—by means of that very spirit—of the forces of the Elements and the natures of the winds, etc. Secondly, we gather that the discipline of true wisdom and the subject of holy Philosophy is not to be found in the Philosophy of Aristotle, but in the book of all truth, that is, the Holy Bible, which is indeed the living model of the revealed word. Thirdly, that it is the greatest madness in Christians to seek truth where it is not to be found: I mean in the works of the Gentiles or Heathens. This is made manifest because their works fundamentally contradict the truth of the scriptures; for this reason, their wisdom is pronounced by the Apostle James to be *earthly, sensual, and devilish*.

Allow me now, in the conclusion of this section (O you Europeans, who wear out your lives in the Christian Religion with such seriousness and zeal), to turn the sharpness of my pen and the thread of my speech toward you. You, seduced by the false doctrine of Aristotle, think that Meteors—and especially lightnings and thunders—are things happening by natural chance, and consequently of little or no importance or value, as if produced either by a hot or cold imbalance in the air. I earnestly beseech you to consider in a Christian manner and observe this warning, which I commend to you as a final "Farewell" to this section. I would wish you to know frankly, therefore, that the wise men of this Christian age—namely, the followers of the Heathen philosophers—are to this day so blinded by the wisdom of this world and deceived by their own imaginations, that they know not how to have faith that God, by means of His word, works all things immediately in heaven and on earth. OF THE FIRST SECTION, BOOK 5.

### E P I L O G U E.

<margin>Deuteronomy 30:19</margin>
<margin>Colossians 2:3</margin>
From these things which have been put forward in this first section (O Christian reader, endowed with judgment and learning), you may be able to discern with open eyes, unless I am mistaken, that immense difference which exists between worldly wisdom (which the Apostle considers mere foolishness before God) and that which descends from heaven from the Father of Lights (which is the essential spirit of wisdom). Consequently, it may be seen that the Peripatetic Philosophy <term>Peripatetic Philosophy</term> <note>The school of philosophy following the teachings of Aristotle, so named because he often walked while teaching.</note>—which is founded upon the wisdom of this world, insofar as it relies on the traditions of men and the elements of the world, and not upon Christ or the true Cornerstone—is an empty fallacy or a deceptive fiction. In contrast, that philosophy of the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles, which is founded upon Christ, or the Universal <note>original: "Catholicum." Here used in the sense of universal or all-pervading rather than referring to the Roman Catholic Church.</note> Spirit of God—in whom the fullness of the Divinity dwells bodily—is uniquely true, real, and essential, descending immediately from God.

Therefore, by way of conclusion, let me address you Christian Peripatetics in these words of Moses himself (of whose philosophy this work of ours is an exact model <term>type</term> <note>original: "typus." In Fludd's Hermetic context, this suggests that his writing is a formal representation or mirror of Moses's original divine insights.</note>): I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that I have set before you life and death, good and evil, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life, so that you and your seed may live and may become rich in the knowledge and understanding of the true God. For in true wisdom consists a sincere, pure, and holy Philosophy, in which the infallible science and discipline of all things is situated and rooted; as the Apostle testifies, saying that in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and consequently they are not found in that Pagan <term>Ethnic</term> <note>original: "Ethnica." Fludd uses this to denote non-Christian, specifically Greek and Roman, classical sources.</note> philosophy.

## *A certain appendix annexed to this first section of Mosaic Philosophy, extracted from a certain German volume printed in Frankfurt not many years ago, the title of which is "The Table of the Revelation of Divine Majesty contained in the first chapter of Genesis," which sharply attacks the Doctrine of the Pagans and their Christian disciples.*

->The Author’s Preface.<-

Since it can be hidden from no one endowed with a sound mind how many—and indeed almost infinite—adversaries of the truth are active everywhere in the world (for no enemy is to be found more base or dangerous than one ignorant of true science and wisdom, a breed of men of which a vast multitude is scattered throughout all lands), I must believe that for this honest and proper effort of mine, undertaken for the sake of truth, I shall receive nothing but laughter, cackling, reproaches, curses, satirical attacks, and every kind of insult from wordly men—partly blinded by ignorance, and partly contaminated at the root by Peripatetic Philosophy <term>Peripatetic Philosophy</term> <note>The traditional university curriculum based on Aristotle; Fludd viewed it as a "pagan" corruption of true, divinely-inspired knowledge.</note>—instead of a reward or prize. Indeed, I would not understand what to do or where to turn, were it not that I have Truth itself fighting for me; for it is the nature of Truth to conquer all things, even the Devil himself and his followers. 

But since it is no small comfort to a man surrounded by calamity to have a faithful and God-taught <term>Theodidactus</term> <note>From the Greek 'theodidaktos,' meaning one taught directly by God rather than by human systems.</note> companion in his distress—one who can endure a portion of the arrows drawn from the quiver of envy and malice and wickedly shot at him, and who can alleviate his labors and the blows inflicted upon him—I have therefore chosen one such man in this conflict of mine. I speak of a man quite vigorous in knowledge and a thousand times more deeply immersed than I am in the Mysteries of God and the secret operations of His word. For what I have learned by theory and contemplation alone, and by the diligent reading of the Holy Scriptures, he has understood not only through speculation and reading, but also as one instructed by ocular practice <note>original: "oculari praxi." This implies experimental or visual proof, likely referring to alchemical or mystical observation.</note> and a real inspection of the "Table of the Wise." 

Thus, he has not only clearly and vividly depicted the errors and vanities of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum." Referring to the non-Christian Greek philosophers like Aristotle and Plato.</note> in his book, but he also sharply rails against them. It is for this reason that I have extracted several members from the works of that most learned man, which accurately and clearly uncover the emptiness of the Pagans' books, the vanity of their philosophy, and the foolishness of their Christian disciples. I have bound these together into a single bundle, as it were, and made them an appendix to this first section of my Mosaic Philosophy. I have done this primarily to indicate to the malicious people of this age that I was not the first mover or author of such a pious reformation, and secondly because the master of that volume seems to agree with me in all things and to support my opinions exactly. 

For he acknowledges that all things were originally made from water; he confesses that the universe was created by the Word of God <note>original: "Verbo Dei."</note> and is even now, to this very day, continued, preserved, increased, and multiplied in it. He says that God works all in all through the Word without the assistance of [other] creatures, and consequently he admits neither the "Nature" of the Pagans, nor their secondary or tertiary causes. He relates that the air, or the entire heaven, is water (whence I regard it as the Universal Element <term>Elementum Catholicum</term> <note>The "Catholic" or "Universal" element refers to the primordial substance from which Fludd believed all things were composed, often identified with a celestial or spiritual water.</note>) and that it is led by the Word of God through the mediation of Angelic instruments. Furthermore, he says that the Angels, moved by the Word, produce every kind of meteor and storm in and from the air, as if from the treasury-chest of God. And he concludes that the Word moves the Angels, the Angels move the wind, and the wind moves the air, as is stated in the Appendix.

as will appear more clearly in what follows.
