—known, before they were created. And **Esdras**: By the power of God, the end and the beginning of all things were finished before they were created. 
<margin>4 Esdras 6.</margin>
And **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus.</note>: All things depend upon one principle, and the principle is from one alone; and the principle moves so that it may again stand as a principle, yet it remains one, nor does it recede from unity. 
<margin>Pimander 10.</margin>
These words of the Savior also seem to intimate this same thing: *I and the Father are one*, and *the Father is in me and I in the Father*, and *the Father remaining in me, he does all things*. 
<margin>John 10:30.</margin>
In this sense also, Hermes seems to speak of the Archetypal structure of the world, after whose image this typical world was formed. Therefore, he calls it elsewhere the "visible son of God": The Monad (he says) generates the Monad, and reflected the heat into itself. 
<margin>Pimander 4.</margin>
By which words he seems to argue that the Typical world was described "enfolded" within the Archetypal world (God so willing), which he then afterwards depicted "unfolded." From these things, it is clear that this world was made in the image of the Archetypal world. 

But lest some captious people, attacking this opinion of mine, should take exception against it by alleging that it altogether contradicts the consensus of the ancient Fathers of the Church, I will explain the sentiments of several of them on this matter in this place. **St. Augustine** says: 
<margin>Book of 83 Questions, q. 46; Book 1, dist. 3.</margin>
**Ideas** are eternal and immutable forms in the divine mind. **Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus, a major medieval Scholastic philosopher.</note> says that they are objective things, known by the divine intellect: since the Deity is nothing but one and the same spirit. From this it follows that the Ideas in God—although they are many according to the various pleasures of the divinity (for man was made in one way, and a horse in another, etc.)—nevertheless, all are but one in God, as St. Augustine seems to confirm more clearly elsewhere in these words: 
<margin>On the Trinity, Book 6, last chapter.</margin>
The first and highest intellect is a certain art of the Omnipotent and Wise God, full of all living, immutable reasons; and all are one in it, just as it is one from the One with whom it is one. And elsewhere he says: You are my God and the Lord of all things which you have created, and with you are the causes of all stable things, and the immutable origins of all changeable things remain with you; and the reasons of all rational, irrational, and temporal things live forever with you. 
<margin>Soliloquies, ch. 31.</margin>
And **Boethius** has these lines:
<margin>Book 3, On Consolation.</margin>

->Drawing from a celestial example, you, most skilled craftsman,<-
->Bearing the beautiful world in your mind, shape it in a similar image.<-

In which sense Hermes also says in the place cited before: The Monad generates the Monad and reflected the heat into itself; because unity, in the construction of the Ideal or Archetypal world, sent forth the **Word**, as an essence generated from itself, yet in no way distinct from it in unity; and finally reflected that spirit of wisdom, proceeding from both, back into itself. 
<margin>Pimander 12.</margin>
Hence the **Son of Sirach**: 
<margin>Ecclus. 1:5.</margin>
The source of Wisdom is the Word of God on high, and its going forth is eternal commands. In this manner, therefore, was the Archetypal world...

# BOOK I, OF THE SECOND SECTION

...the type <note>The "type" or "typical world" refers to the physical universe as a reflected pattern of a higher reality.</note> was created before all things in and from one and the same Unity, but in a threefold manner: namely, through the progression of a certain eternal **square** from the **one** (acting as an eternal root), and through the return of that emanation back into a **Cubic** form. This completes the Ideal Archetype of all things, by which the three divine properties in a single infinite essence can easily be discerned. This also explains the logic by which all things of the typical world were "infolded" <note>original: "complicitè." A philosophical term meaning everything is contained within the cause before it is "unfolded" into creation.</note> within the Archetype as ideas before any actual creation occurred. 

We conclude, therefore, that according to this ideal image, this Typical world was afterwards formed in a threefold variety and proportionally adapted to the pattern of the divine likeness. For, from the unity in its divine and hidden existence—which was originally concealed from us in darkness or a potential **chaos**—there emanated a most brilliant flame of formal, universal essence. Then, the spirit of wisdom proceeding from both joined that formal emanation with the potential matter of the waters. Through the union of these three—divine light, the substantial matter of darkness, and the "waters"—the heavens were first made, then the Earth, and consequently the entire 

<margin>2 Peter 3. Psalms.</margin>
world, as St. Peter testifies. But the Royal Psalmist <note>King David, traditional author of the Psalms.</note> confirms this best in these few words: *By the Word of the Lord,* he says, *the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their power.* In this speech he reveals everything: for by "the Lord" he understands the Father, from whom are all things; by "the Word," the Son, through whom are all things; and by "the breath" or Spirit mediating from the mouth of both, he shows that every essence, power, or act in this world is derived. 

We can conclude, then, that if the unities of the Ideal world are extracted from a single radical unity (like sons from one Father) and are included within that same unity (which is infinite in itself), it must necessarily follow that the triple members of this created world must exist in and from that same unity. This is because the Typical world and its parts were made in the image and representation of the Archetype—that eternal **monad** <note>The "Monad" is the ultimate, indivisible One.</note> in which all things exist. Thus, it is said by the Apostle, not without cause, that God is *all in all.*

<margin>Colossians 3:11. Colossians 1:16. Romans 11:36.</margin>
And again: *All things are created through him and in him, and he was before all things, and all things consist in him.* And elsewhere: *From him, through him, and in him are all things.* Because of this, he is frequently called both the circumference and the center: the center of all things, whose circumference is nowhere. And, by the Apostle, he is called the Father of all, who is over all and in all.

<margin>Rabbi Zoar. Plato.</margin>
Hence Rabbi Zoar <note>Refers to the Zohar, the foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah.</note> says: "All things are one in respect to God, though they seem varied in respect to us." And Plato says that not only are all things in God, but even all things that already exist are—insofar as they are in God and proceed from him—nothing but a single Entity.

<margin>Hermes. Proclus in Theological Problems.</margin>
And Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of Hermetic philosophy.</note> in his *Emerald Tablet* says: "As all things were by the mediation of one, so also all things 

<column-break/>

proceed from this unique adaptation." And Proclus adds: "As all things are derived from the one, so they hasten to return again to that unity in a continuous course; the greater the harmony through which they meet each other, the more they participate in that unity."

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Again, Plato says elsewhere: "All things proceed from God Most High and strive with their utmost power to return to him, because in him consists their greatest comfort, sustenance, and final rest." For this very reason,

<margin>Leucippus.</margin>
the philosopher Leucippus made this unity his "Supreme Good." By these examples, one may see that the Ancient Philosophers do not differ at all from the Harmony of the Holy Bible. Finally, Job reveals all this even more clearly: *God,* he says, *reveals foundations out of darkness and brings the deadly shadow into light.* By "foundations" he understands the waters that were contained in the dark abyss, from whose later existence the heavens, the earth, and consequently the whole world were fabricated, mediated by the aforementioned Word according to the pattern or image of the Archetype. 

Therefore, we can justly conclude that principles of opposite conditions proceed from one and the same unity or Identity: namely, from "nothing" (as far as we are concerned), or privative darkness and a deadly shadow, through a change in the form of that same identity from a potential state into a positive act, by the emanation of light out of darkness.

<margin>Wisdom 11:18. Job 26:7.</margin>
Hence Solomon says: *The hand of the Almighty made the world out of formless matter.* And Job: *God stretches the North over the empty space and the void, and hangs the earth upon nothing*—that is, upon a thing empty and void of form. For by "the empty," "the void," and "the Nothing," he understands those formless darknesses and that deadly shadow he mentioned before, or the **formless matter** of Solomon cited above. As long as this matter remained in divine potential, it was, to the weak senses of mortals, merely "Nothing," because it had not yet been given form. 

By these things, it is clearly established that all things are essentially comprehended in that radical, eternal unity. Since that unity is one, it is also infinite; and because it is infinite in its dimensions, essence, and power, it must contain all finite things within itself. Whence the Scriptures say: *He is all in all;* he fills all things and yet is outside and beyond all things; and in comprehending and concluding all things, he is only in himself. Yet he is never absent from his creatures, which he formed by his word: first, by his will, his word proceeded—*Fiat* <note>Latin: "Let it be."</note>—and it was made.

Now that we have extracted the privative principle—the deadly darkness—from the infinite center of all things (whose circumference is nowhere), let us immerse ourselves deeply into the nature of the formal and life-giving light, the active principle, which drew its origin from that same primordial root.

ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY

...so that by this reasoning I may most skillfully depict for the more excellent intellects, using my colors, that most excellent essential form which redeemed the moist or watery nature of the world from the deep captivity of darkness and, as it were, a lethal shadow.

### CHAPTER III.

->How the lovely and splendid light of Universal and life-giving Love<-
->shone forth from the source of all goodness, and removed the<-
->contentious and hateful darkness from the throne of the<-
->dark Chaos or the shapeless Abyss, so that from<-
->then on the most beautiful world might be<-
->created out of actual Nothingness by its<-
->very presence and be adorned with<-
->its divine beauty.<-

**I**t is wonderful and beyond human grasp that from a single Unity in essence, two branches—differing in properties and in a manner so opposite to each other—should grow out: namely, darkness, which is the origin of weakness, error, deformity, contention, deprivation, and death; and light, which is the vehicle and sole cause of information <note>In this context, "information" means the act of giving form or shape to matter.</note>, truth, beauty, love, affirmation, and life. It was not for nothing that the Manichæans <note>A dualistic religious movement that taught a fundamental struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note> held with such confidence that there were two co-eternal principles, one of which they made God, whom they acknowledged as the prince of light and the author of life, holiness, and all goodness; and they fashioned the other as the devil, whom they called the prince of darkness and the origin or beginning of contention, death, sickness, and all evil. And they believed the devil was co-eternal with God in his very essence because they thought no goodness can exist which does not have a relation to its contrary, namely, malice. By this reasoning, I say, they wish for the God of malice and wickedness to be co-eternal in existence with the God of goodness. With these imaginings, they not only attempt to exclude the devil from the limbo of created things, but even to expel unity from the limits of nature, and to erect and crown a "Dyad" <note>A pair or duality.</note> or duality (which in truth is nothing other than a confusion of unities) in its place. And truly, this point or doubt seemed to be of such difficult discussion and resolution that some of the wiser Poets and Philosophers seemed to agree with them in this matter in some way, as appears through certain of their mystical and allegorical expressions, which they wrapped in fabulous discourses in an enigmatic manner. Among these, a Poet named Pronapis, in his *Protocosmos*, asserts that Demogorgon (by whom he means the highest of the Gods) was surrounded on all sides by Eternity and rude Chaos before all things. He imagines that at a certain time, while Eternity remained in its majesty, he suddenly noticed a great tumult and commotion arising in the bowels of Chaos. Whereupon, so that he might offer help in this difficult birth, he reached out his hand to the one in labor and, performing the office of a midwife, suddenly caused it to give birth to a certain monster,

<column-break/>

deformed and tempestuous, to whom the name *Litigium* <note>Strife or Contention.</note> was given because of its contentious condition. After this monster had stirred up great disturbances and commotions in the air, and attempted to fly upward with ambition and fight against Demogorgon its Creator, it was immediately cast down by Demogorgon into the deep abyss. But observing that Chaos labored again with a new birth, and that in its labors it emitted fervent sighs with heavy sweats, he did not wish to remove his hand from it until it had brought forth a second birth, in which Pan was born along with his three sisters, who were called the Fates <note>original: "parcæ." The three deities who spun, measured, and cut the thread of life.</note>. When Demogorgon was captured by the extraordinary beauty and form of Pan, he made him the presiding officer and governor of all worldly affairs, and commanded his three sisters to obey the orders of their brother in the manner of handmaidens and servants. It followed thereafter that Chaos, now relieved of its burden or that great heap or mass with which it labored, placed its Pan (at the persuasion of Demogorgon) upon its Throne. This is that parabolic fable concerning Demogorgon and Chaos commonly recited by the Poets. Their allegory implies that the generation and procreation of all things proceeded from the Most High and supreme God the Creator, whom they signify by Demogorgon, to whom Eternity is joined by an indissoluble bond in a single essential society: since he alone is to be called eternal who is and always was the principle, or first cause of all things. And they also imagine that Chaos claims a third place in that eternal society, because it is (according to the account of Ovid) that confused and undigested matter or subject from which all things of this world are fashioned. And for this reason, the Ancients handed down the tradition that it was co-eternal with God, as it was that rude heap from which Demogorgon, the Father of Universals, created or formed all things according to his will. And consequently, they believed this subject or matter of all things to be the general Mother of all things, from whom and upon whom the Universal Father of all begot and fashioned all things. Wherefore...

### OF THE SECOND SECTION, BOOK I.
<meta>catchword: or</meta>

...concluded that there were two parents of all things from all time, one of whom was the Father and the other the Mother. And yet, they seem to agree in this: namely, that God was the primary cause, and they wish for Chaos itself to serve in the place of a passive companion to the Demogorgon <note>A primordial deity often associated with the origin of the universe in Renaissance mythology.</note>, so that from her, as if from a universal mother, he might generate all things. And although the wise and divine Plato seems to suggest that Chaos was the companion of God from all antiquity, nevertheless, he and others of similar depth intimate to us that it proceeded from God by a certain eternal generation or production, and that he afterwards fashioned all things out of it.

Wherefore they conclude that Chaos proceeded from God and is by no means to be divided from Him, and also that it serves Him in the place of a feminine partner for generation and procreation: not otherwise than Eve, extracted from Adam, was called his companion and a helpmate to him in the production of the human race.

This is the opinion of both the Pagan philosophers and the mystical Cabalists <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism that influenced many Renaissance thinkers.</note>.

But I shall proceed to the explanation of the aforementioned allegory: The hand of the Demogorgon signifies divine power; the first-born and deformed Chaos—namely, Strife—signifies the prince of darkness, who is the Father of opposition and discord. Wherefore, on account of his ambitious rebellion against the Lord of light and life, he was cast headlong into the abyss of the dark whirlpool. By the second birth, which was Pan <note>In this context, Pan represents the "All" or the totality of Nature.</note>, they indicate the universal nature of the world and the harmonious arrangement of the Elements. From this they argue that after that great discord or commotion and perturbation which offered itself in the first expansion of the womb of Chaos, a peaceful concord followed in the second birth; this was as beautiful and acceptable to God in this final birth as the deformed discord was foul, hateful, and unwelcome to Him in the first.

By these things, therefore, you may see how all the Elements in the beginning struggled and contended in the confused belly of Chaos. The three Parcae (or fatal sisters) called Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, who were with Pan, denote the three orders of time: namely, present, past, and future. The present time is committed to the care of Clotho, and her duty is to spin the thread of life. Lachesis presides over the future time, looking toward that material—whether of hemp or flax—which Clotho begins to spin. And Atropos signifies the past time, which is irreparable and irrevocable, finishing the work by cutting the thread.

<margin>Isaiah 45:7</margin>
Upon this parabolic relation I insert my own view: that although Chaos or the dark Abyss was with God and in God before the creation of the world, nevertheless the infinite and sole eternal unity and radical essence created and produced it from itself. For that Essence speaks these words in its own person: *I am the Lord, and there is no other, forming the light and creating the darkness, making peace and creating evil.* <note>original Latin: "Ego Dominus, & non alter est, formans lucem & creans tenebras, faciens pacem & creans malum."</note> As if it had

<column-break/>

said: I am the Father of light or the Spirit of shining wisdom, and I created the Dark Chaos, out of which I then afterwards introduced the existence of the world and even both the discord and the concord of the Elements—that is, strife and peace—into this world. Thus, it is evident that there is only one eternal unity, which in itself is both male and female, and is everything that can be imagined; it produced all things from itself and within itself, not otherwise than Adam contained within himself Eve, who was then afterwards the mother of the microcosm <note>The "small world," referring to humanity as a reflection of the "macrocosm" or the universe.</note>.

<margin>Pimander 1.</margin>
Hence Hermes Trismegistus says: *The Mind, which is God, being most full of the fruitfulness of both sexes, being life and light, brought forth by his word another Mind.* <note>original Latin: "Mens autem Deus utriusque sexus fœcunditate plenissimus, vita & lux cum verbo suo alteram mentem peperit."</note>

And the scriptures seem to testify to this same thing, saying: *Shall I, who grant generation to others, be myself sterile?*

Therefore it is manifest that from one and the same radically existing eternal unity, both the matter and the forms of all things proceed. Regarding their existence and progressions, they appear only "aevial"—that is, having a beginning but being without end <note>The "Aevum" was considered a middle state between Time (beginning and end) and Eternity (no beginning or end).</note>. Yet in their essential root—namely, in God, the most hidden unity of unities from which they proceed—they are eternal. Thus, just as the dark Abyss (or obscure Chaos) and the bright informing spirit are two opposite principles, contrary to each other in condition and property—for from the dark principle proceed discord, evil, cold, freezing, rest, death, deprivation, and negation (or the "not-will")—so from the bright principle, which is the type of beauty and grace, are derived light, concord, goodness, heat, rarefaction, motion, life, and affirmation (or the "will"). Yet both of these are nothing but general branches rising from one and the same essential unity. Since they cannot exceed the limits of their infinite source, they are light and darkness within it, and consequently differ in no way in their essence from the root from which they spring, which is "all in all."

<margin>Psalm 138:12</margin>
Hence the Psalmist says: *The darkness is to him even as the light.* <note>original Latin: "Tenebræ sunt ei sicut lux ipse." This is Psalm 139 in modern English Bibles.</note> For all things are one in Him, who is solely one and the same in Himself; from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things.

<margin>Romans 11:36</margin>
For His "will" and His "not-will" are only one in Him, who is one simple Identity; and that which is His will is both His affirmation and His negation, which are nothing but a unique good in Him, who is total goodness.

And yet, in respect to the creature, when His negation dominates, He hides the light of His kind countenance, and everything is, as it were, darkness; then He works "privatively" <note>Acting through absence or withdrawal rather than through an active force.</note> toward us. For where He hides His face, everything appears deformed, empty, and destitute of essence and goodness.

Behold here the negative or privative will, which can rightly be named His "not-will" in respect to us, because in His willing in respect to Himself, He seems to "not-will" in respect to men from whom He withholds His presence. Conversely, if His affirmation or...

<meta>This page continues Fludd's argument that all dualities—light and darkness, life and death—originate from a single Divine Unity. He bridges the gap between the "Demogorgon" and "Chaos" mentioned on the previous page by explaining that God's will possesses both an affirmative (giving) and a privative (taking) aspect, both of which are essentially good within God.</meta>

# ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY. Folio 72.

<margin>Job 9</margin>
...or if the positive property holds dominion, then it emits to us the luminous benevolence of its beauty, and thus the spirit of the creature is refreshed by its presence and, consequently, is filled with its goodness. Behold, even here is His affirmative or positive will, which, in respect to both God and ourselves, is called "will" <note>Latin: *voluntas*</note>. But, lest this should seem strange to anyone, I would have him diligently observe the nature of that mental ray in man. For God imparted a mind to him to inform him and clothe him with reason and intelligence. "The spirit," says Job, "is in man, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives him understanding." <note>original: "Spiritus est in homine, at inspiratio Omnipotentis facit eum intelligere" — Job 32:8.</note> And yet this unity of essence, which is the image of God, operates through two contrary properties in general: one of which is to affirm, to give, and to grant the petition of the requester through a certain lovely emanation. Behold here the positive act depicted in the unity of the human spirit.

The other is to deny and take away, or to oppose the petition and desire of the seeker, through a certain privative removal or refusal of the desired reward. Behold, here is the effect of negation or "not-willing" <note>Latin: *noluntas* — Fludd uses this term to describe the divine refusal or the negative aspect of the will.</note> described on this side; for the mental ray does not shine forth or emanate to the petitioner, but is contracted or reserved within itself.

In these two contrary actions, we observe nothing but a single praiseworthy effect in this unity alone. For although the mind grants a request because of the friendly and merciful emanation of the mind's ray—so that it smiles upon the seeker's expectation—or if, on the contrary, the requester's petition is denied to his great loss or misfortune, nevertheless, to the mind of both the one who wills and the one who wills not, both the affirmation and the negation seem good, as they are founded upon good reason. Whence it is clear that both of these are but one and the same in effect, however much they appear to the petitioner to differ.

By the same reasoning, in the eternal and archetypal Unity (which is also called the Divine Mind, whose type and image is the human intellect or mind), the act of both willing and not-willing is one and the same; and there is nothing but goodness in it, which is total and absolute goodness, admitting no contrariety in itself. This is true even though to the creature—who is subjected to the effects of both His privative and positive will—the privative or negative action seems evil. Conversely, His positive or affirmative emanation, being full of kindness and love, is held by the creature to be good and is consequently received with joy.

<margin>Ecclus. 11:14. Psalm 104. Psalm 4:7. Psalm 18:29. Psalm 42. Job 1. John 1. Nahum 1. Deut. 31:17.</margin>
Are we not taught by holy authority that good and evil, life and death, poverty and riches are from God? <note>Ecclesiasticus 11:14</note> And elsewhere: that when God hides His face from creatures, they are troubled; when He takes back their spirit, they expire; and when He sends forth His spirit, they are recreated with good. <note>Psalm 104:29-30</note> And elsewhere: "Your visitation preserves my spirit." <note>Job 10:12</note> And again: "Lift up Your face and send light upon us," and He shall cause us to see light and shall make our darkness shine. <note>Psalm 4:6 and 18:28</note> And the Prophe-

<column-break/>

t: "I will make darkness light for them." <note>Isaiah 42:16</note> And Job: "The crafty shall run into darkness in the daytime and grope in the noonday as in the night." <note>Job 5:14</note> And the Apostle: "He who hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness." <note>1 John 2:11</note> And the Prophet: "Darkness pursues the enemies of God." <note>Nahum 1:8</note> And Moses: "God hides His face from them, so that many evils and distresses befall them." <note>Deuteronomy 31:17</note> And yet, there is neither of these two properties that is not absolutely good in its essential and radical unity, however much the latter might be privative, passive, hateful, deformed, contentious, and deadly to the creature who feels and suffers their effects.

<margin>Wisd. 16:13.</margin>
Is it not written that He Himself has the power of life and death, and that He leads down to the gates of death and brings back again? <note>Wisdom of Solomon 16:13</note> And yet, the whole is accomplished according to His dual property—namely, not-willing and willing—within the unity of essence, in which nothing is evil.

<margin>Hermes Trismegistus, Pymander 14.</margin>
Wherefore the wise Philosopher, not dissenting from the sense of the Scriptures in this, said: "In the divine Monad there is nothing but the One and the Good, for in the Maker Himself nothing is evil, nothing base." <note>original: "Non est in monade divina, nisi unum & bonum..." — from the *Pymander*, a foundational text of Hermeticism.</note> And for this reason, when Job felt himself struck by God—and that without cause and beyond the laws of justice (as it seemed to him)—insofar as he was esteemed a just man and (as the Text says) was after God's own heart: nevertheless, he himself (notwithstanding his pains), prompted by a certain pious zeal toward his Creator (however much he acknowledged that all his evil came to him from the turning away of the face of Jehovah), <margin>Job 34</margin> says: "Far be it from God to do wickedness, and from the Almighty to do iniquity," etc.

Furthermore, it is clear to anyone even moderately skilled in Philosophy that God is concerned with both the corruption and privation of the creature, as much as with its generation and positioning. And yet no Christian can be ignorant that both of these properties in the unique, pure essence are absolutely good, insofar as that essence is complete in goodness—even though, from the other perspective, nothing is more terrible, fearful, abominable, and destructive to the creature than its own death or corruption.

<margin>Ecclus. 11.</margin>

For they testify with the wise man that good and evil, life and death, honor and poverty are from God. ...recognizes the visible: For he himself and the aforementioned mystic Poets call that unity **Apollo** during the day: For they claim that in his positive and benign nature—which is manifested through his life-giving virtue in the Sun—he composes the creature out of seven parts. For by the number four <note>the quaternary</note>, the **Pythagoreans** signified the Elementary matter of things, insofar as it is a square, with the root of two, which is an imperfect number and therefore designates matter; and through the number three <note>the ternary</note>, which is the number of perfection, they hieroglyphically depict the forms of things. Thus, from the conjunction of these numbers arises the number seven <note>the septenary</note>, which includes the perfect complement of the creature, perfected in the composition or union of the soul (or form) and the body (or matter). 

Again, they call this same unity **Dionysus** during the night, namely in his dark or privative property. They assert that under this title, he is accustomed to tear apart into seven pieces the creature created or composed during the reign of **Apollo** (or the daytime): so that they seem to argue that one and the same unity is, in essence, the author of both destruction and corruption, as well as generation and life-giving. Therefore, they assign double names to him, not in respect to his essence, which is unique, but by reason of his properties; namely, so they may distinguish one property of the same essence from another by a variation of the name. 

Hence, he is called by the Cabalists <note>Jewish mystics</note> in one of his properties—namely the privative and dark one—**Dark Aleph** <note>original: *Aleph Tenebrosum*</note>, specifically when he contracts his rays into himself or turns his face away from the creature. In his other property, however—namely the positive and bright one—they call him **Bright Aleph** <note>original: *Aleph lucidum*</note>; specifically when he emits the rays of benevolence, beauty, and life. From these things, therefore, it appears to us Christians that the **Ethnics** (or **Gentiles**) recognized alongside the Holy Scriptures, and recorded in parables, that it is in the power of one and the same radical unity to save and to destroy—that is, to give life or to take it away, or to either will or not-will—and (to put it in a word) to work all in all according to his pleasure. 

And so you have it confirmed that two members of opposite natures spring from a single eternal root, and that these members or essential and principal properties act in the world in a contrary manner, and consequently produce effects differing from each other. From this it is clear that since the waters—from which and through which (as St. Peter testifies) the heavens and the earth formerly came forth from the dark abyss—were as it were the fertile offspring of **Chaos** itself, which the Poets imagine to be **Pan** or the universal moist nature; it will be very easy for the wise Philosopher to consider that the passive portion of this world inclines by a certain natural instinct toward the property and conditions of darkness, such that if it were not

Having well considered this, it will not be difficult, from the detection of these two principles—namely light and darkness—to reach a radical knowledge of true **Sympathy** and **Antipathy**. The latter <note>Antipathy</note> is derived from that discordant, privative, and contentious affection which darkness and deformity bring forth against the children of light and life.

...and darkness was light, and consequently none of these could be discerned by human grasp; nothing was really to be distinguished, but all things were one in the primary matter of all things, <margin>Colossians 1:16, 17</margin> which consisted in eternal unity: In Christ, says the Apostle, all things are founded; through Christ and in him all things were created; he is before all things and all things consist in him, etc. Thus, in that respect, there was neither light nor darkness, nor day nor night, nor heaven nor earth, nor Spirit nor body, nor good nor evil, nor pure nor impure, nor that which can be generated nor that which can be corrupted, nor this nor that. And yet, nonetheless, all these things—whether they be spiritual or corporeal—proceeded from that potential subject which remained folded within that infinite unity, which was, is, and shall be all in all and above all. 

O admirable wisdom of God in his works! All things (I say) come from one single matter, which nonetheless is none of those things that were made. All things were hidden and concealed, but according to the saying of our Savior: *Nothing is so secret and hidden that it should not be made manifest or revealed.* And this happened through the mediation of the penetrating operation of that admirable word <note>original: "Fiat"</note> "Let there be," by the alchemical <term>spagyric<gloss>Refers to the process of separating and recombining elements, a core concept in Renaissance alchemy used by Fludd to explain creation.</gloss></term> action and virtue of the eternal spirit, dividing that unique thing into two principles of contrary condition, to which names fitting their natures were assigned. For one, as was said, was called Light, and the other Darkness. They also called the first Day and the second Night, and thus the pure was separated from the impure. 

From this, therefore, it followed that the world was originally divided into two contrary kingdoms corresponding to the two aforementioned branches rising out of unity. By relating these, it will be very easy to unravel what light and darkness truly are, what day and night are, what good and evil, what heaven and what hell, what truth and what falsehood, what humility and what pride, what justice and what injustice, what joy and what sadness and sorrow, what sweet and what bitter, what peace and concord, and what strife and discord, what action and passion, what life and what death, what generation and corruption, what pure and impure, what health and what disease, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what is medicine and what is poison; and finally, what is lovable and what is hateful, and consequently, what is that Sympathy and what is that Antipathy which dominates among the infinite creatures of this world.

Indeed, the highest good itself, namely the Divine Majesty, does not exist without its opposite.

This spirit is also within us and breathes where and when it wills, and is called by many names in the scriptures: namely, it is called the spirit of truth, the spirit of sanctification, the spirit of illumination, the spirit of revelation, who was the first interpreter of the divine secrets contained in the sacred page. Nor indeed does it befit us to inquire from ourselves why God did this or that, or how or why he formed it thus or so: but it is fitting for a zealous Christian to refer all these things to that time in which this secret shall be revealed; which indeed will happen when the **seventh seal** is opened. ### CHAPTER IV.

At the start of this discourse on the World Soul, my purpose is to review the opinions of the ancient Cabalists and mystical Rabbis, as well as those of the wise philosophers, regarding this subject. This topic is condemned by some who are unskilled and ignorant of such profound mysteries, yet it is established and celebrated with great constancy by others who, with the lynx-like eyes of their intellect, penetrate into the secret inner parts of nature and have contemplated its central and eternal agent with due reverence. Afterward, I intend to explain the harmony that exists between their opinions and the sense or mind of the Holy Scriptures. 

I begin: It is the opinion of the Cabalists <note>The "Cabalists" refers to practitioners of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism that influenced many Renaissance thinkers like Fludd.</note> that the great Angel whom they call by the name Metatron (which they interpret as "The Gift of God") is that universal spirit <margin>Johann Reuchlin, *On the Art of the Kabbalah*, Book 3.</margin> which gives life to the entire universe. For this reason, Rabbi Moses <note>Referring to Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a foundational Jewish philosopher.</note> takes him to be the general "Active Intellect" from which all particular forms descend. They hold that from this universal spirit proceed all powers—animal, vital, and natural—which they also call "Angels," the number of which is infinite in our eyes. 

Among the philosophers, Democritus, Orpheus, and various Pythagoreans did not differ much from these opinions of the Rabbis and Cabalists, except in the variety of names. They claimed that all things were full of "Gods," to whom they attributed divine honors within creatures. They worshiped them with various cults and different ceremonies—offering prayers and sacrifices—yet they did so with this careful consideration: they referred all these Gods back to the One, whether they called him Jove or, more rightly, Jehovah, the eternal Unity and Father of all things. Nevertheless, this intention of theirs, being poorly understood by the ignorant, was a chief cause of idolatry

<column-break/>

among the Gentiles; specifically, under this pretext, they came to venerate the creatures in place of the Creator, or the divinity within the creatures. For this reason Solomon said: *Vain are all men by nature in whom there is ignorance of God, and who, from those good things which are seen, could not understand Him who is, nor by considering the works did they acknowledge the Craftsman, but took the creature for the Creator.* <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 13:1</margin> 

By clearly similar reasoning, the Platonists called that universal power, by whose mediation all things are generated and preserved, the "World Soul" <note>original: "Animam mundi"</note>. The Arabic astrologers also seem to agree with these intentions, for it is their view to assign to every specific thing in this world a particular soul derived from that general universal spirit. Hermes Trismegistus, Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus.</note>, Avicenna, Algazel, and others—both Stoics and Peripatetics—likewise seem to adhere to this opinion. 

Furthermore, Zoroaster and Heraclitus of Ephesus conclude that this World Soul is an immense, invisible fire, from which and through whose action all things are generated and brought from potentiality into actual being. Virgil, that distinguished poet, calls it the "Mind" which is poured through the limbs and joints of the world, by which its entire mass is moved in a certain hidden way. For he says:
> *A spirit nourishes from within, and Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass,* etc. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 726-727.</note>

Marcus Manilius, Boethius, and Augurellus seem to fall in with Virgil’s opinion. Manilius writes:
> *A divine power of the soul rules this work constructed of the vast body of the world,* etc.

Boethius also writes these words:
<margin>Book 3, *Consolation of Philosophy*</margin>
> *You connect the soul of a triple nature, moving all things, placed in the middle.*

But this is clearly indicated by the discourse of **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical, alchemical, and philosophical texts were attributed.</note>: *From the voice of light,* he says, *the Word comes forth as a deed; yet standing by the moist nature, it cherished it. From the bowels of the moist nature, a pure and light fire immediately flew out and sought the heights; the air, being a light offspring of the spirit, took its place in the middle region between water and fire; but the earth and water lay so mixed together that the face of the earth, being overwhelmed, appeared nowhere, etc.* 

By these things it is evidently proved that this thin spiritual water, or "moist nature," is no more deprived of a soul than the human spirit is destitute of the life-giving act of life. For, just as in the soul of any living creature two things are chiefly required—namely, the active and the passive—so, where one of these is missing, no created soul can exist. Indeed, if the world's soul were only the inspiration of God without the vehicle of the created moist Spirit (which is the matter of heaven), then that life of the world would be a simple **Identity** <note>In Fludd's philosophy, "Identity" refers to the absolute, unchanging oneness of God, while "Otherness" refers to the diversity of creation.</note> and of one and the same property. Consequently, there would be no variety of action in the world, nor any contraction and dilation of things in **systole and diastole** <term>systole and diastole</term><note>The rhythmic contraction and expansion of the heart, here used as a metaphor for the pulse of the living universe.</note>, and it would then follow that neither action nor passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or to receive an impression.</note> would be in the soul. For without a passive nature, active power cannot stand, just as, conversely, without active motion, the passive cannot exist. 

Chaos (as has been said) stood in the place of the feminine

<column-break/>

or passive principle toward the act of **Demogorgon** <term>Demogorgon</term><note>A mysterious primordial deity mentioned in late Roman and Renaissance literature, often identified by Fludd as a symbol for the creative power of God acting on the world.</note> or God. Likewise, the act or form which proceeds from the emanation or outflow of divine light is the masculine source and fountainhead of action, just as the waters, which are obtained from the womb of Chaos, are the subject of passion. 

From this, therefore, one may easily gather first what the **soul of the world** is, and consequently of how many and what parts it consists. For we must consider that, just as every creature has its internal and external, so it is necessary that we first inquire into the internal and external of the worldly soul, insofar as it is a creature. Furthermore, that it *is* a creature is declared by the fact that it is not Identity, but **Otherness** <term>Otherness</term><note>Original Latin: "alteritas." This signifies the state of being distinct or "other" than God's pure unity, a prerequisite for being a created thing.</note>, such as is the existence of Angels. For if it were Identity, there would be no difference between it and the divine unity, and consequently, it would not admit the act of creation, as it would be eternal. 

Now, however, that this soul is "Otherness," and consequently created, is clear from the fact that it is composed of two things, according to the consistency of an Angel. Its internal part is that life-giving light or flame which proceeds immediately from the bright and splendid emission of the eternal spirit; its external part is the created aeviternal spirit <note>A spirit that has a beginning but no end, existing in "aevum" or everlasting time.</note>, or the purer and clearer substance of the upper waters, which is created and animated by the act or power of the Divine Spirit.

Again, it is assimilated to every thing, insofar as it is "One in all."

But all those things are nothing but one essence, though diverse in property etc.: where that mind and spirit are treated not according to essence, but in respect to their properties of operating. Therefore, the union of the worldly spirit with the divine mind constitutes the **soul**, so that the soul includes both the mind and the spirit; of which the former is uncreated, and the latter created, acting as the internal and external of a single "otherness" or Angelic composition.

### ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY. Fol. 76.

...they take for the universal intellectual agent, which is nothing other than that whole spirit of wisdom <note>Latin: *sapientiæ spiritus*</note> which God sent forth from his Throne, or, as it is held elsewhere, from his mouth, as the greatest proof and gift of his love and kindness toward both worlds. By its presence, the substance of the waters comes forth from nothing, and those waters are led back from deformity and non-existence into action and living beauty. Life and existence are explicitly attributed to those things which were previously enclosed implicitly in the dark shadow of death, as it were. I mean that from the deformed Chaos, or the Dark Abyss, they are led forth into a pleasing form, out of a lethal sleep and a dark quiet into a living action and motion, and from obscurity into light. And that benefactor to both worlds is deservedly called Metatron <note>A significant figure in Jewish mysticism, often viewed as the celestial scribe or a mediator between the divine and the human</note>, or the Universal Gift of God, since by his mediation the universal, deformed nothingness is rendered into something universally beautiful.

But, so that I may better indicate to you by philosophical demonstration the Angelic nature of that supreme intelligence called Metatron, and consequently the soul of the world <term>Anima Mundi: the "world soul," a concept suggesting that the universe itself is a living being with an underlying spiritual structure</term>, I would like you to understand in the first place the manner by which the ancient philosophers, and especially the Platonists, demonstrate the harmony of the world and its spirit. The Heptachord <note>original: *Heptachordum*; a seven-stringed musical scale</note> which Plato discovered and adapted to prove the soul of the world, consisted of seven strings or properties, partly even and partly odd: namely **1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 27.** Although Proclus and Porphyry <note>Neoplatonic philosophers who commented extensively on Plato's works</note> described these proportions in a single line, it nevertheless seems to me that Adrastus and Calcidius adapted them more properly to the sides of a Pyramid or Triangle in this manner:

<image-desc>A triangular diagram representing the Platonic Lambda. At the peak is the number 1. The left side is labeled "Material proportion in the Dark Kingdom," with the numbers 2, 4, and 8 descending. The right side is labeled "Formal proportion in the Bright Kingdom," with the numbers 3, 9, and 27 descending. Horizontal lines connect the numbers across the middle.</image-desc>

->In creation.<-

In the cone or summit of this Pyramid, **1** is expressed, which is unity. Insofar as it participates on one side with material existence—namely with **2, 4, & 8**—and on the other side has commerce with formal emanation, it is evident that this point or **1**, this unity from which both these different lines proceed, is the fountain and origin of both

<column-break/>

matter and form. Hence it is the opinion of Synesius <margin>Synesius</margin> as well as other Theosophers <note>Philosophers who seek direct knowledge of the divine</note>, in no way departing from the sense of the Scriptures, that God is all that is; for from him, through him, and in him are all things. He is both male and female, or (as Hermes Trismegistus <margin>Synesius</margin> holds) most fruitful in both sexes; he is power and act, form and matter. Indeed, he says, there is nothing that He himself does not exist as. But all of this (as we have said) agrees with the harmony of the sacred letters, which recognize that God is all in all and above all, and that in him all things consist, and that from him, through him, and in him are all things. <margin>Romans 11</margin>

The six other figures correspond directly to each other, looking from the material side to the formal side: namely, the even numbers in the material kingdom look upon the odd numbers of the formal kingdom, which agree with them proportionally. That is, **2** looks toward **3**, and **4** looks toward **9**, and **8** toward **27**. By these correspondences, the species of all creatures are vividly expressed with their Harmonies. In the first series, it designates in a hieroglyphic fashion that Harmonic grade of the world soul which was in the beginning and still remains in that same state.

For first, according to the pattern of the Archetype, from (1) one are produced (2) two, which is called by the Pythagoreans the "confusion of units" <note>Pythagoras and his followers viewed the number two as the beginning of division and therefore less perfect than the unity of one</note>. For this reason, it is the radical and beginning number of imperfection. In respect to its confusion and imperfection, it is in the same relation to the unity from which it has its origin as the bright eternal unity is to the dark Abyss or the unformed Chaos, which is called by the Poet a "rude and undigested mass" <note>A reference to Ovid's *Metamorphoses* describing the state of the universe before order was imposed</note>. And it is most rightly called an imperfect number, since the efflux of the light of eternity, which is all perfection, had not yet made it perfect by its presence, as it were, like waters in potential.

For this reason, the watery matter which is extracted from Chaos is confused and imperfect in itself, just as the number two (**2**) is judged imperfect in respect to the Ternary (**3**), and nothing but a confusion of units. This is because all perfection consists in three terms: namely, a beginning, a middle, and an end. Thus, if you choose one unit from the 2 for a beginning and another for a middle, nothing is left for an end, and consequently perfection is lacking. If you place one unit for a beginning and another for an end, then two extremes are present, but the unit for the middle is missing. If you assign one unit for the middle and another for the end, then the beginning will be missing. Therefore, it follows that this number is imperfect in itself, and consequently the waters are imperfect by themselves, as the nature of the dark abyss (the mother and the moist nature) is present in their constitution, but that formal unity is missing, which still contains itself in the cone of the Pyramid or Isosceles Triangle. ### OF THE SECOND SECTION, BOOK I.

...his own outflow, so that if he had not sent forth that very beautiful and splendid unity of life, the number 2—or the deformed waters—would have remained in its obtuse, confused, or imperfect state within the belly of Chaos. That is to say, it would have remained without the form of any perfect thing: namely, as nothing, or as something existing only in potential. Thus, the Catholic <note>original: *catholica*; here meaning "universal" rather than referring to the Church</note> matter or water, before it was informed by the luminous unity (which constitutes the third unity), was plainly empty and void. It lacked the presence of the Informing Unity, by whose mediation it puts aside the indisposition of emptiness and vanity and puts on the beauty of fullness. Thus, its emptiness is changed into fullness, its potential into act, its darkness into light, and its deformity into a clear, spacious, and life-giving beauty; and finally, its imperfection is changed into perfection. And hence it is said that "God saw that this creature was good," which is to say, it was filled with the life-giving essence of divinity, which is absolutely and solely good. By this reasoning, namely by the addition of formal unity, the number of confusion and imperfection—which was in the material duality symbolizing Chaos (which is the mother of matter)—is brought forth into the light of the world and the perfection of the Ternary number <note>The number 3</note> is produced. For that formal unity, by animating and clothing the higher waters, creates the primary, most perfect, and most worthy species of mixture: namely, by uniting the unity of mental light and the heavenly spirit into the Angelic essence, which is then afterward handed over to animate and inform all worldly things. And this formal union is symbolized by 3, or the Ternary number, which for this reason is called the number of perfection, and the number of the soul, or the radical number of form in the course of nature. Hence it is that the Platonists and Pythagoreans express matter—which is imperfect in itself—by even or imperfect numbers. Just as in the Archetypal world, designated by 1, 2, and 3 in the form of the Holy Trinity, there appear only three Ideal dimensions in a single divine or eternal nature and essence. These, in their manner of progression, designate in the Cossic art <term>Cossic art: an early form of algebra (from the Italian 'cosa', meaning 'the thing') used here to describe the mathematical relationships of the universe</term> the root, the square, and the cube, which signify the supreme soul, the spirit, and the body of the world as depicted ideally in the Archetype. And it is clear that these three seem to arise from a single 1 or unity: for by multiplying 1 by 1, 1 and itself are produced, which are two, as if a simple ideal square; and again, by multiplying that square unity into itself, 2 and one arise, which make 3, or the cube of simple unities, which proves the perfection of the Ideal world that is in God. So, if we take the radical and simple number of two unities as the root, we shall produce, according to the aforementioned Archetypal model, the created Typical world—namely, if we seek the three dimensions of matter: its length, breadth,

<column-break/>

and depth, through the progression from the root into the square, and from the square into the cube of matter. The root of matter, therefore, was 2: for although the supreme unity multiplies and dilates itself into 2, thereby proving its firstborn; nevertheless, because the Holy Spirit of illumination was not yet emanating, all things were dark as far as we are concerned. Wherefore we must imagine that the multiplication of matter in this world is nothing other than the penetration of formal light into the watery abyss or material multitude. For the denser the matter exists, the more closely it approaches its root 2, or the dark Chaos. Conversely, as it is made thinner through the richness and abundant presence of the luminous formal emanation, it approaches more closely to the root of formal unity. This mystery being rightly understood, I say, all science—even in the most abstruse Philosophy—can be very easily discerned. Therefore, the root of matter, which is 2, signifies the dark Chaos; but the root of form, which is 3, seems to prove that root 2 (which designates the dark waters) is animated through the formal and splendid emanation or extension of unity (or 1). And thus the first (2) or binary number was completed and the soul of the world was created or revealed: namely, through the Angelic emission or efflux. And in this way the Kabbalists' Metatron <note>original: *Mitattron*</note>, or the Gift of God, or the Soul of the World, was first produced, who according to their traditions is called the first creature or the first of all things created. This indeed <margin>Ecclesiasticus 1</margin> agrees perfectly with this Syriac saying: "Wisdom," it says, "was created before all things: God created her in the Holy Spirit." And in and through that Angelic creation, all the other Angels were also made. Whence it is said: "Christ is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, in whom all things were produced, visible and invisible in heaven and on earth, whether they be Thrones, or Dominions, <margin>Colossians 1:13</margin> or Powers; all things are through him and in him, and he is before all things and all things consist in him," etc. Behold, here you have described the true Catholic <note>universal</note> Spirit, who not only made all things, but also *is* all things, inasmuch as he gives them life (since all things are in him), but he also performs the will of the Father in every creature he has formed. Hence he is called by the Rabbis "Metatron," or the Gift of God, and by the Prophet, "the Angel of Great Counsel": and <margin>Isaiah 9</margin> "his name shall be called" (says the Prophet) "the Angel of Great Counsel." Therefore, by multiplying 3 in him, we shall have the created formal square, which signifies the 9 orders of Angels, who are specifically called "varied" according to the disposition and property of that holy efflux, which is sent forth from the infinite fountain of light to operate in many forms in this world. And the formal square of 9, multiplied by its root 3, produces the corporeal cube: so that all things...

## ON THE MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

...all bodies are forged from thin substances, by multiplying any square into its root, and there will come forth 27 for the formal Cube <note>3 cubed (3x3x3=27), representing the spiritual form.</note> and 8 for the material one <note>2 cubed (2x2x2=8), representing physical matter.</note>: which represent any Elementated body or composed matter. Just as matter, the more it is multiplied into itself, the lighter, thinner, more spiritual, and clearer the creature it informs will be—so that the formal root, square, and cube signify the essences and souls of creatures, whether super-celestial (everlasting), celestial, or Elementary, which are rendered more or less worthy according to the greater or lesser proportion of form. For according to these multiplications in form, creatures shall be exalted more or less in value and glory.

You see now how far, and by what proportions—both spiritual and material—the Platonic harmony of the world extends. From these you may also observe that where this Harmonic proportion is not present between matter and form, there must necessarily be both a bodily and spiritual dissonance or discord, and consequently, an **Antipathy**. <note>original: *Antipathia*; in Fludd's time, this meant a natural repulsion or lack of resonance between two things.</note>

We see, moreover, that the root of life is fixed in the Angelic composition or "otherness": namely, in the mixing of the simple, eternal, and uncreated light with pure spiritual matter. Thus, eternal wisdom is the first act and essential soul of the Angels, and the everlasting or Angelic Spirit is the act and essential life of the Stars (or celestial bodies) and their influences. The Stellar influence is the life and soul of the winds or Elements (for the power of life is rained down by the **Olympic Intelligences** <note>original: *Intelligentijs Olympicis*; celestial spirits or angels that govern the planetary spheres.</note> into those elementary ones); or rather, the governors of the winds and spiritual emanations or outpourings from the four winds inform the Sublunary **Catholic** <note>original: *Catholicum*; meaning "universal" or "general," not the religious denomination.</note> Element (or the lower waters) in a fourfold way.

And then afterwards, the Element—according to the property assigned to it by the prevailing wind—informs **meteors** <note>original: *meteora*; in the 17th century, this included all atmospheric phenomena like rain, snow, and clouds, not just shooting stars.</note> or Meteorological impressions in many ways. From these, composed Elementated things are then made, which by this reasoning draw their entire essence and way of living in many forms from the divine source; and this occurs by reason of the difference of the organs through and in which [the divine source] acts indifferently in this world.

From this it appears that God, in the beginning, first animated the higher heaven—the **Empyrean** <note>The highest, most spiritual part of heaven, associated with pure light and fire.</note>—and the intellectual spirit (which heaven is the seat of the Angels). We compare this to the root, where 2 is animated by 3 through the addition of 1 (or formal light) to the matter 2. And the Empyrean heaven (I mean the Angelic Spirit) animates the stars and the ethereal region, infusing its influences into the Olympic intelligences, which we relate to the square. And the starry heaven is like a male and

<column-break/>

multiplier in the Elementary heaven and its creatures, which we compare to the Cube. Truly, not only the hidden Cabalists, but also the most profound of the Philosophers have left an eternal memory of that most perfect and most formed root (or the **ternary number** <note>The number 3.</note> with its three dimensions). I do not mean that mercantile or common number known in Arithmetic, but that purely spiritual and essential **Character** in formal numeration, which proceeds from a certain circular revolution and a squared and cubic multiplication. And for this reason, those more skilled in the secrets of nature founded their formal and Mystical Arithmetic and Geometry upon that subject. These do not deal with common or vulgar subjects, but are entirely occupied in the profound meditations of true **Cabala** <note>A Jewish mystical tradition involving the study of divine names and numbers, which Fludd integrated into his Christian philosophy.</note>, natural Magic, and essential Alchemy. These sciences—which the ignorant masses rashly and without legitimate cause condemn under those titles—are called by the more secret artists "Elementary, Celestial, and Super-mundane science." This is partly because they treat the natures of "separate intelligences" (as they say) and substances, and partly because they are the most worthy of all, insofar as they are concerned with the knowledge of the Creator.

For the greatest perfection in which a man can most glory is that he reaches a certain knowledge of God. Whence says the Prophet: 
<margin>*Jeremiah 9:23*</margin>
> Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth God. 

And certainly these are those three mystic sciences that are appropriated to the knowledge of the three worlds (I mean the Intellectual, Celestial, and Elementary). According to the sayings of the Cabalists, these worlds are represented by these three letters of the name **אדם** <note>The Hebrew letters Aleph, Daleth, and Mem, spelling "Adam."</note>

They also relate to the three parts of man (the **Microcosm** <note>The idea of man as a "miniature world" that mirrors the structure of the entire universe.</note>), namely the intellect, the soul, and the body, which is subject to alteration and corruption. **Rabbi Zour** <note>Fludd likely refers here to the *Zohar*, the central text of Jewish Kabbalah.</note>, founded upon these bases, says that there are three things which correspond to each other in this ternary dimension, as they are formed after the example of the Archetype or radical Idea: namely, the Tabernacle of God which Moses erected, the Temple of Solomon, and the human body. This is according to the species of those three numbers applied to them: namely, the vocal or operative (which is the extract of the measure for the formal Elementary world), that which is the extract from the vocal for the celestial, and the rational or divine (which is the extract from the formal for the intellectual). All of this is made apparent through the description of the Tabernacle. This Tabernacle symbolized the three aforementioned worlds in its parts or regions. For its outer part was uncovered and [exposed] to the air, winds, snow, rain, and all other impressions...

...exposed to meteorological impressions, and was subject to almost perpetual alterations of the air. Therefore, that region representing a material cube is most correctly compared to the Elementary world, which is composed of matter or thicker water, like a fluid and inconstant substance: and for this reason, it is properly called the world of darkness. Hence the Apostle calls the Devil the Prince of Darkness, and elsewhere calls him the prince of this world. This region is also referred to the human body. The second portion of the Tabernacle, which was gilded on all sides and decorated and illuminated by the lampstands of seven lights, is a Symbol of the starry heaven with its seven remarkable lights, namely the planets. And as this heaven is between two extremes—namely, the Empyrean and the Elementary—so it participates in both extremes: water and fire. Hence the Hebrews call heaven **Shamaym** <note>original: שמים (*Shamaym*)</note>, as if from **Esh** <note>original: אש (*Esh*), meaning "fire"</note>, and **Maym** <note>original: מים (*Maym*), meaning "water"</note>; and the Greeks call it *Ether*, as if it were "fiery air." But its watery existence is therefore incorruptible, because its desire is so intoxicated by the formal nectar sent down from above that it has become forgetful of all alteration; it receives its motion or activity from the same eternal efflux, which <margin>Wisdom 7.</margin> according to Solomon’s saying is more mobile than all things. And in truth, it is the first Universal Mover <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere that sets all other spheres in motion.</note>, who is said to preside over the "first moveable," by whose act all inferior Intelligences are moved, and sweep their glowing fires with them in a circuit—no differently than we see that all outer wheels, being as if dead in themselves, are observed to be moved by the motion of one central wheel, which wheel is their life. From these things, we can gather why that region of the world is called Heaven, and the Sphere of Equality: namely, by reason of its mixture from an equal portion of form and matter. Also, why it is called the Sphere of the Soul: specifically, because it is forged from the pure and incorruptible spirit of the waters, which is feminine and passive, and from the bright fire or eternal act. For the Divine mind acts by means of this moist nature, which is its Vehicle or organ, and expresses and exercises its vivifying property in this world. Hence even the Heathens recognize that all life consists of innate heat and radical moisture, of which the former is active and from God; the latter is passive and from the purer spirit of the waters, which some call the quintessence. This region, therefore, refers to the human life or soul...

<column-break/>

...and has a close relation to the square, both formal and material, which is a certain middle between the root and the cube. The third portion of the Tabernacle was the Holy of Holies, which represents the super-celestial, intellectual, or Empyrean spirit, which is almost nothing else but pure and sincere fire, and is handed down by the Fathers of Theology to be the seat of Angels and souls, who are the immediate ministers of their great Lord and Prince of Light. This is witnessed by the presence of the two Cherubim, who cover the propitiatory <note>The Mercy Seat or lid of the Ark of the Covenant, where God's presence was said to dwell.</note> with their wings. This heaven is referred to the human intellect, which is called *Nesshamah* <note>original: נשמה (*Neshamah*), often referring to the highest part of the soul.</note> by the Hebrews, *Nous* <note>original: Νούς</note> by the Greeks, and *Mens* by the Latins, which has dominion over the human soul. Thus, it may be seen that in the great world, the Angelic Heaven—which is most formal, fiery, and full of divine light—is like the soul of the ethereal heaven. For through it and from it, that region receives its life, motion, and existence; and by a similar proportion, the ethereal or celestial heaven is the life or soul and agent in the Elements of heaven itself. For by the mediation of the Sun, Moon, and other Stars, which rain down their influences and roots upon the earth, the earth and water and all creatures in them act, live, generate, and multiply—so that heaven is estimated by all Philosophers to be the male, and the sublunary Element the female, whose womb is the earth and water. For earth and water receive influences like male seeds, and thus all generations in earth and water are made. For the earthly body cannot work without the aerial impression or contact; indeed, man himself requires (as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on natural philosophy.</note> maintain) celestial assistance for his generation. Whence Aristotle says: *The Sun and man generate man.* <note>original: "Sol & homo generant hominem."</note> Furthermore, all Philosophers seem to agree in this: namely, that higher things act upon lower things like a male upon a female. <margin>Reuchlin, book 3 of The Art of the Kabbalah.</margin> And it is a common Axiom among the more skilled Kabbalists <term>Kabbalists<gloss>Scholars of Jewish mysticism who believe the physical world is a reflection of divine attributes.</gloss></term> that all lower things are representative of higher things. And indeed, a very learned man well-versed in such abstruse science affirms that the age-abiding or Angelic heaven was created according to the pattern of that eternal or Ideal one; and likewise, that the temporal Elemental world was an image of the celestial, and that it was also formed according to the pattern of the age-abiding: so that the images and actions of the darker world have their Ideal similarities in and from the brighter celestial heaven; and the images and actions of the Stellar world were first depicted or outlined in the intellectual and Angelic heaven; and its images likewise received their origin from the radical pattern, or principle existing in the Archetype. I conclude, therefore, that both the Theologians and the mystical Philosophers agree in this: namely

...namely, that God delights in the **ternary** <note>The number three.</note> number, which is the first odd number in Arithmetical progression. For we Christians worship the **Trinity** of persons in unity. And **Aristotle** says that, by a certain natural instinct, we are instructed to revere God himself according to the ternary number. Nor is this said without consideration, since in the **Ideal world** <note>The world of divine patterns or ideas in the mind of God.</note> there were three properties extracted from unity (as we proved above), according to whose exemplar the real world was then later fabricated, so that the Trinity in the Divinity was the root of the entire formal arrangement of the world. For by the **root 3**, the intellectual and Angelic world was designated; by the **square 9**, the celestial world; and by the **cube 27**, the Elemental world, just as we can elicit from the aforementioned doctrine of **Plato**. 

But as for the opinions of the **Rabbis** and **Cabalists**, they considered the quantitative proportions of that ternary in another way. For the Cube of the root 3 consists of three 9s or **novenary** <note>Groups of nine.</note> numbers: thus they indeed take these three 9s and join them in Arithmetical order thus: 9. 9. 9., which constitute **999** (nine hundred ninety-nine), so that according to the Arithmetical rule, the first nine toward the right is a simple digit or digital number, which, by reason of its simplicity, formality, and essentiality, is attributed to the nine orders of Angels who belong to the intellectual world. But the (9) nine standing in the middle seems, on one side, to participate more in form or simplicity, and on the other, in matter; and for that reason, they attribute it to the nine orbits or spheres of the starry heaven. The third (9) novenary, which is placed in the position of the hundreds, signifies a deeper and more material composition, which pertains to the Elemental world. All these numbers and even the regions of the world finally terminate in **man**, who is, as it were, a passage according to the image of unity, from the elements themselves to celestial things, and from those to intellectual things. 

Finally, if **unity**—in which the philosopher **Leucippus** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who, along with Democritus, is credited with founding atomism.</note> placed the highest good—is added to the aforementioned three nines, it will constitute the complete **millenary** number <note>The number 1,000.</note>, which is the cube of 10, and the end of all numbers according to the calculation of the Hebrews. Also, the square of the root 3, which is 9, by the addition of **Aleph** <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, signifying 1 and Unity.</note> (which is 1), produces the **denary** number <note>The number 10.</note>, beyond which (as Aristotle says) no one has ever found a number. 

<column-break/>

According to the exemplar of the aforementioned type, therefore, the ancient or **Mosaic light** caused the partitioning of fruits and goods arising from the earth to be divided into three parts: of which it assigned the **hundredth** number <note>The bulk of the harvest.</note>, as being more material and gross, to the Laity and the profane; the **tithes** <note>The tenth part.</note> to the Church and the Priests; and finally, **unity** (or a tenth part of the tithe) for God, who, as He is all things, so indeed He is nothing but one. 

But to the purpose: the Cabalists adopted the name of their **Angel**—whom they, along with the Platonists, refer to the **Soul of the World**—to this triple ternary or formal proportion, namely **999**. From this they argue for the radical, square, and cubic extension (or the emanation of the divine form) into the depth of matter. Consequently, it is demonstrated that this Soul is the **Alpha and Omega**, the life-giver of all, who is present to all and penetrates through all things. For the letters or elements of the name **Mitattron Sarhapanim** <note>original: מטטרון שר הפנים (*Metatron Sar Ha-Panim*), meaning "Metatron, Prince of the Presence/Faces."</note>, which signifies the "Prince of Faces" (who is taken for the Soul of the World), according to the calculation of the Hebrews, add up to **999**. And therefore this name, with its letters, signifies this number, but nevertheless with this consideration: that the etymology of the word, through interpretation, signifies the **GIFT OF GOD**. 

For what greater gift, I ask, could God bestow upon his potential creatures and generally upon the whole universe than the eternal spirit of his **Wisdom**, or his **firstborn**? So that through the mediation of his essential presence, something might be made, as it were, out of nothing; and so that by setting aside the deformity and emptiness of the waters, and by leading their potential into act, and by dividing them into heaven and earth, they might be rendered beautiful and fair, and be preserved in existence, essence, and vital faculty. This was therefore the true and **Universal** <note>original: *Catholicum*. In this context, it means "universal" or "all-encompassing" rather than specifically the Roman Catholic Church.</note> **Gift of God**, 

<margin>Wisdom 12:1.</margin>
whose incorruptible nature is in every thing, that it may preserve it; 

<margin>Wisdom 1.</margin>
and it fills all things, so that it is never lacking to creatures. And just as this 

<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>
spirit is more mobile than any thing, so it works all in all, according to the will of 그 Unity that sent it forth. For this cause and in respect of its office, and insofar as it was a spirit sent forth, this name of the **Universal Angel** was, not without good reason and consideration, imposed upon it according to the testimony of Scripture. We can also demonstrate in another way that the world itself and its soul were created according to the image of the **Archetype** <note>The original divine model of the universe.</note> in this manner:
